19:39:00 KST

Breadcrumb
Designer Zahra Al-Najjar brings the Iraq of vintage magazines, beauty queens and family memories to the runway
Every fashion designer has somewhere they return to for inspiration, whether it is an era, a place, a person or a particular image. For Iraqi-Canadian designer Zahra Al-Najjar, it has always been magazines.
From a young age, Zahra would leaf through her mother’s Arabic magazines, studying the clothes, beauty looks and photography across the pages. They offered glimpses of a side of the MENA region, particularly Iraq, that felt familiar through her family but distant from her own life.
Now 27, she collects vintage magazines from across the region, particularly from Egypt and Lebanon, sourcing old issues on eBay, some dating back to the 1950s.
For her, they are more than fashion references; they are records of how people dressed, lived and saw themselves.
"I've always gravitated towards magazines," Zahra tells The New Arab. "They were how I discovered visual references, both from the Arab world and from fashion, through my mum's Arabic magazines."
Her interest in these publications eventually led her to the Iraqi Print Archive, which holds Iraqi magazines, books and other printed material documenting the country’s cultural life, particularly before 2003.
Much of the archive is available online, with publications also translated into English.
She turned to the archive while developing her Central Saint Martins graduate collection, asking to see publications from the 1960s through to the 1990s and early 2000s, with a particular focus on Iraqi women and their contribution to society.
The archive sent her a wide selection, which she narrowed down to stories about Iraqi women working in factories, contributing to the workforce and the arts, as well as other glimpses of Iraqi life before the 2003 US-led invasion.
One publication focused on vinyl and the music industry, with some of its images later appearing as prints across her collection.
For Zahra, the focus on women was personal.
Born in Montreal and raised in Milton Keynes, she has only visited Iraq once and grew up hearing about the country from her parents and grandparents. She also grew up around women who were engineers and doctors, while her grandmother raised seven children in Iraq and ran a large factory.
"Everything I know about Iraq comes from my parents and grandparents, and the stories they have told me about growing up there. They're also very proud of it and have always spoken about it with so much love," she says.
This was part of what drew Zahra towards stories that showed Iraq before 2003, rather than the country as it is often represented through the 2003 invasion and the wars that followed.
“We're often known for the invasion, but a lot of people don't know about the heritage and everything we achieved as a society before then," she adds.
She saw how much these images could mean when she showed her mother the publications she had selected. Her mother had not seen them in more than 30 years.
"She actually started crying," Zahra recalls. "She said she had reached a point where she almost believed it had never happened because it had been so long ago."
Zahra says her mother's reaction captures what sits at the heart of the collection: these are not simply old magazine pages being repurposed as fashion prints, but fragments of a visual history that her generation can look back on and her parents' generation can recognise, giving the images another life while bringing a part of Iraq that once felt distant much closer to home.
A collection rooted in memory
Reflecting on her participation in the Central Saint Martins graduate runway, Zahra says it was a really special experience.
Of the around 140 final-year students who presented their work, only 40 were selected for the press show, making her inclusion an important opportunity to represent an identity she says is still underrepresented at Central Saint Martins and in the wider fashion industry.
“There aren't many Arab students at Central Saint Martins either," she says. "There might be one or two in each year, and we all kind of know each other. So it was really meaningful to have that platform and bring this part of my identity into the space."
That sense of identity also influenced the collection, which brought together prints from the Iraqi Print Archive with references to her family and the clothes she grew up around.
Two of the six looks feature archival imagery, printed using sublimation so that the small text and photographs from the original magazines remained clear. She also worked with wool, cotton, silk chiffon and vintage fabrics, using layering throughout the collection.
The idea of layering came directly from photographs of Zahra’s family after they moved to Canada in the early 1990s.
Used to a much warmer climate, they would wear draped dresses underneath large coats, mixing lighter fabrics with heavier ones. Zahra brought that same combination into the collection, pairing chiffon and silk with wool.
That contrast between lighter and heavier fabrics can be seen in one of her three favourite looks, a pair of black-and-white trench coats. One is layered over the other, with both featuring text, imagery and faces from the Iraqi Print Archive, including an iconic photograph of a former Miss Iraq.
"I wanted it to feel like physical media right in front of you, where you can see the identities and the faces, and feel like you've been transported into that world," she explains.
Another favourite is the calligraphy dress, created with London-based artist Nayab Ahmed. Nayab travelled to Egypt during the collaboration to train with traditional calligraphy artists, before returning with the materials they used.
The pair then created a print that looks like Arabic calligraphy but says nothing.
For Zahra, the decision to create calligraphy without a specific meaning reflects her own relationship with Arabic. She speaks the language but is less confident reading and writing it, so she wanted to explore calligraphy through its appearance rather than its meaning.
"I wanted to stay true to myself, and I wanted it to reflect what Arabic calligraphy is to me," she says. "It's beautiful, but maybe because of my reading and writing, I'm not able to appreciate it as much. Just appreciate it visually."
The calligraphy print was then transferred onto silk chiffon, which was crystal-pleated and paired with two jackets finished with a fraying technique Zahra developed during her final year.
Her third favourite look takes a different approach, featuring a leather jacket covered in small vintage frames.
Each frame features an Arab female singer, including Fairuz and Umm Kulthum, alongside other singers who influenced Zahra as she grew up.
These references extend beyond the clothes and into the collection’s accessories. Zahra sourced vintage headpieces from sellers in Europe and the US, some of which were decorated with feathers that looked like hair from a distance.
She also built small mobile phones into headbands underneath the headwear, inspired by her mother and aunties putting their phones into their hijabs in the early 2000s.
"I thought that was quite a funny pop culture reference," she says.
The early 2000s references also carried through into the beauty looks.
Zahra looked to the vintage magazines she collected, particularly Egyptian publications, for the models’ thin eyebrows, dark lips and heavy eye makeup.
While the look may recall the late 1990s and early 2000s, Zahra found the same beauty style much further back in Egyptian magazines from the 1950s, particularly Al-Kawākib Magazine, where she found narrow eyebrows, dark red and almost-black lips and heavily lined eyes.
To complete the look, Zahra gave the models a serious expression that reflected the same early-2000s references, asking them not to look angry but "as if they're on the phone, focused and on their way somewhere."
What comes next
Upon reflection, Zahra says the references in her collection reflect a wider interest in archival fashion among young diaspora designers today, as a generation looks back at the places their parents came from and finds its own ways of engaging with that history.
"I think that it's growing because we are growing," she says. "We're kind of expressing our childhood, and we're expressing what we've been through here in the West."
For Zahra, that connection to heritage also gives her work a political edge, even when she does not set out to make political fashion.
“I wouldn’t necessarily say my work is political, but because of my background, it becomes political,” she says.
That is also where the archive plays a larger role in her work. The images allow Zahra to present a side of Iraq that she feels is often missing from the way the country is represented.
"We're trying to change the narrative and communicate a different perspective that isn’t often seen," she says. "That's why it's so important."
With her graduate collection now complete, Zahra is turning her attention to what comes next.
She has been accepted into a master's programme at Central Saint Martins and is awaiting news on her scholarship applications, while also considering returning to the fashion industry for a few years.
She has already gained experience at Viktor & Rolf in Amsterdam, working in the couture department, and at Louis Vuitton as an assistant designer for women's leather goods.
The two placements exposed her to very different sides of the industry.
At Viktor & Rolf, she learnt couture techniques and worked on showpieces, while Louis Vuitton gave her insight into the commercial side of design, from researching trends to developing products for a wider market.
Both experiences, she says, helped build her confidence when she returned to Central Saint Martins for her final year.
Ultimately, Zahra hopes to build a fashion house of her own, with "my own atelier and my own team."
For now, her work is already attracting attention, with a museum expressing interest in acquiring several looks from her graduate collection. Zahra cannot reveal more yet, but says she will share the details when she can.
Zainab Mehdi is a British Iraqi journalist and the Associate Features Editor at The New Arab. She holds a BSc in Modern History and International Relations from the University of Essex and an MA in Near and Middle Eastern Studies from SOAS

EDF: Russian mobilization would put pressure on Ukraine and change wider security situation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:39:00 UTC
19:39:00 KST

EDF: Russian mobilization would put pressure on Ukraine and change wider security situation
If Russia announces a mobilization following September State Duma elections, it would increase pressure on Ukraine and also change the security situation in this region, said Col. Janno Märk, chief of staff of the EDF Division.
International media have recently reported extensively on the possibility of mobilization in the Russian Federation, which, according to speculation, could take place after the country's State Duma elections in mid-September.
"If Russia decides in favor of mobilization, pressure on Ukrainian forces will certainly increase in the fall, particularly during a period when weather conditions also reduce the effectiveness of drones," Märk said.
He added that mobilization would also change the situation among units stationed in border areas, affecting security in this region as well.
According to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, a strong position on the battlefield would allow Ukraine to enter negotiations from a fairly strong position.
"Ukraine wants to do everything possible to end the war with Russia before winter arrives, although based on current assessments, that is very unlikely," Märk said.
Over the past week, Russia continued carrying out long-range strikes against Ukraine's logistics, agricultural, industrial, energy and transportation infrastructure. The strikes hit targets in at least 12 Ukrainian regions.
As a result of these attacks, shipping remains suspended at ports in Odesa region, while Ukrainian Railways has been forced to reorganize its operations and transit services.
The share of jet-powered drones used in Russian attacks has also increased in an effort to exploit Ukraine's shortage of interceptor missiles, including those used against ballistic missiles. Russia is using munitions produced both domestically and in North Korea.
According to Ukrainian military intelligence, Russia is producing these missiles at a faster rate than planned and is prioritizing the production of weapons that have a better chance of penetrating Ukrainian air defenses, Märk explained.
Ukraine has also continued its own long-range strikes, targeting six oil refineries over the past week, as well as a petrochemical plant in Russia. Märk particularly highlighted a Ukrainian attack on the naval base in Novorossiysk.
"The attack involved a combination of different weapons and, according to preliminary information, succeeded in damaging two frigates and one Buyan-M-class small missile ship," the colonel said.
The extent of the damage to the vessels still needs to be determined, but the attack itself continues Ukraine's campaign that forced Russia's Black Sea Fleet to leave Crimea.
Maj. Robert Brovdi, commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces and also known by his call sign Magyar, said Ukrainian forces have succeeded in expanding the engagement zone along the front line, which is also slowing the advance of Russian units.
"Ukraine has been intensifying this type of medium-range deep battle since the end of last year and its effectiveness increased significantly in the first half of this year. Targets immediately behind the front line, within a zone roughly 100 kilometers deep, include concentrations of enemy personnel, supplies, fuel, ammunition and various types of military equipment before they can reach the battlefield," Märk said, explaining that this has also allowed Ukraine to offset its shortages of conventional systems and personnel.

News
Sofia among Europe’s most affordable capitals and cites for weekend getaway
Friday 14 August 2026 11:53
Friday, 14 August 2026, 11:53
PHOTO BGNES
Font size
Sofia ranks sixth among the most affordable cities in Europe for a short break, with the cost for two people remaining significantly below the European average. The Bulgarian capital is the only destination outside Poland in the top six, according to a new study comparing accommodation, food, and transportation costs in 100 European cities, BGNES reports.
The study was conducted by virtual card provider Getsby, using data from the travel website Budget Your Trip.
The analysis compares typical daily expenses for accommodation, food, and local transportation for two travelers on a mid-range budget. Airfare was excluded because ticket prices vary considerably.
Sofia ranks sixth, behind six Polish cities, while the Bulgarian capital comes ahead of Zagreb, Malmö, Budapest, and Warsaw. The average daily cost for a traveler in Sofia is approximately €77.25.
Wrocław ranks first, with an average daily cost of around €41 per person.

Balkan developments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:38:01 UTC
19:38:01 KST

Friday 14 August 2026 12:39
Friday, 14 August 2026, 12:39
PHOTO nuclearelectrica.ro
Font size
Bucharest declares energy crisis, seeks EU extension for coal-fired power plant
Romania has asked the European Commission and the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Electricity (ENTSO-E) to conduct a new regional assessment to support the country amid the worsening energy situation. The request comes against the backdrop of the shutdown of Unit 2 of the Cernavodă Nuclear Power Plant due to the continuing low water levels of the Danube.
State Secretary for Energy Cristian Bușoi said Bucharest wants to know how much electricity neighboring countries could provide if Romania’s domestic generation were restricted. Speaking to the European Commission’s Electricity Coordination Group, Bușoi also asked Romania to be allowed to retain its coal-fired generation capacity at the Oltenia Energy Complex. Under Romania’s commitments to the EU, Unit 5 of the Turceni Power Plant is due to be shut down by August 31, Digi24.ro reports.
PHOTO Reuters
Law grants amnesty to PKK militants who give up their weapons
The Turkish parliament has passed legislation aimed at the reintegration into society of Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) militants as part of a peace process that began two years ago, Anadolu Agency reports.
The law provides for the return to civilian life of PKK members who surrender their weapons, but does not establish a blanket amnesty after more than 40 years of armed conflict. Those wishing to benefit from the law will have six months to do so.
The legislation does not address broader Kurdish demands for expanded political and cultural rights or changes to Turkey’s counterterrorism laws. The PKK-linked ANF news agency described the law as a “beginning,” but said it contains “serious shortcomings and gaps.”
The PKK is designated as a terrorist organization by Turkey, the United States, and the European Union.
PHOTO Reuters
After three snap elections, Kosovo still has no functioning regular parliament
Kosovo risks losing millions of euros in EU funding allocated under the Western Balkans Growth Plan because of the political crisis and institutional deadlock, Radio Free Europe reports.
Two months after the June 7 snap parliamentary elections, Kosovo’s 11th parliament in Pristina remains caught in a procedural crisis. The Self-Determination Movement has 53 of the 120 seats, while the Democratic Party of Kosovo holds 22, the Democratic League of Kosovo 18, and the Alliance for the Future of Kosovo 7. Representatives of ethnic minorities hold 10 seats.
Before proceeding with the election of a parliamentary speaker and the country’s president, Self-Determination is demanding the signing of a governing agreement. The opposition has rejected the demand and has boycotted parliamentary sessions, with verbal and physical confrontations breaking out in the chamber.
PHOTO BGNES
Serbian president Aleksandar Vučić threatens to alter the flow of the Ibar River
“Because of the harassment of Serbs in Kosovo, we are considering changing the course of the Ibar River in Serbia,” Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić said.
He added that engineers and specialists had already been brought in to examine the possibility of restricting the flow of water to Kosovo, BTA reports. Kosovo’s acting president, Vjosa Osmani, described the idea as “absurd” and “chauvinistic.”
The Ibar feeds the Gazivoda Reservoir, and seven municipalities receive water from the river. In addition to irrigation, its waters are used to cool the Obilić power plant, which produces most of Kosovo’s electricity.
The European Commission, the United States, and Albania have criticized the threat. Brussels said that such actions would not contribute to the normalization of relations between Belgrade and Pristina.
PHOTO greekherald.com
Greeks abroad urged to register as voters
Greeks living abroad can now register to vote in the next parliamentary elections through a new online portal, The Greek Herald reports.
Under recently adopted legislation, voters abroad will be able to cast their ballots by mail or in person at designated polling stations outside Greece. Previous registrations for the 2023 elections are no longer valid, while registrations for the 2024 European Parliament elections remain valid only for voting within the EU.
Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis has urged Greeks living abroad to exercise their right to vote in the upcoming elections, expected in spring 2027, BGNES reports.

State Prosecutors Seek 12-Year Prison Sentence for Lev Shlosberg
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:37:56 UTC
19:37:56 KST

State prosecutors in the northwestern city of Pskov have asked a judge to sentence veteran opposition politician Lev Shlosberg to 12 years and one month in prison for “discrediting” and spreading “fake news” about the Russian military, the liberal Yabloko party said Friday.
The requested sentence combines maximum penalties under wartime censorship laws with a previous November 2025 conviction in which Shlosberg was sentenced to 420 hours of community service for violating Russia's “foreign agent” law, the exiled news outlet Mediazona reported.
Shlosberg, a senior member of Yabloko, pleaded not guilty, instead accusing prosecutors of “discrediting” Russian law.
The military “fakes” charge stems from a Feb. 25, 2022, Telegram post in which Shlosberg reshared content from the now-defunct Ekho Moskvy radio station. The post featured a British tabloid cover depicting President Vladimir Putin alongside a bloodied woman.
Shlosberg argued in court that he made the post before Russia passed its wartime censorship laws.
The separate “discrediting” charge, meanwhile, is linked to a January 2025 public debate in which Shlosberg was accused of calling for a ceasefire in Ukraine. Shlosberg denied publishing a video of the debate on social media and noted that the specific statements cited by prosecutors were actually made by his debate opponent.
The legal proceedings have been marked by procedural irregularities, according to independent news outlets. Novaya Gazeta reported that the Pskov City Court judge refused to question Shlosberg directly, reading transcripts from earlier sessions instead.
In addition, after Shlosberg’s three defense attorneys missed hearings due to illness and scheduling conflicts, the judge appointed a state lawyer and rejected motions to decline the representation.
The sentencing request comes days after Russia’s Supreme Court barred Yabloko’s federal candidate list from upcoming State Duma elections. An appeal of that ruling is scheduled for Monday.
A date for Shlosberg’s verdict has not yet been announced.

Tusk orders closer monitoring as anti-Ukrainian violence rises in Poland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:36:37 UTC
19:36:37 KST

Jo Harper
14 August 2026•Update: 14 August 2026
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk on Friday instructed the Interior Ministry and security services to closely monitor a rise in anti-Ukrainian violence and hostility, as government officials warned that growing tensions threaten Poland’s security interests and relations with Kyiv.
Polish media reported Friday that the government was increasingly concerned that anti-Ukrainian sentiment was moving beyond political rhetoric and online hostility into real-world aggression.
The concern follows a series of attacks and incidents involving Ukrainians in recent weeks. Police received 180 reports of hate crimes against Ukrainian citizens in the first half of 2026, around 30% more than in the same period last year.
Speaking after several recent attacks, Tusk said those responsible for xenophobic violence were acting “against Poland’s interests” and helping both Russian and nationalist agendas.
He said Russian information operations are specifically designed to blur that distinction and undermine cooperation between the two countries, which remain strategically linked by the war in Ukraine.
Polish security services have identified operations aimed at manipulating Ukrainian communities in Poland and inflaming bilateral tensions. Special services coordinator Tomasz Siemoniak said in July that Russia’s information war against Poland had intensified significantly and that Moscow wanted to create “as much tension as possible between Poland and Ukraine.”
In another case announced in July, Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) said an 18-year-old Ukrainian had been charged with carrying out 47 acts on behalf of Russian intelligence, including attacks on memorial sites aimed at provoking conflict between Poles and Ukrainians.
Tensions between Warsaw and Kyiv have risen sharply this summer, particularly over historical disputes surrounding the World War II-era Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA).
The group is regarded by many Ukrainians as part of the country’s struggle against Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union, but in Poland it is held responsible for massacres of Polish civilians in Volhynia and eastern Galicia.

Ukraine has begun forcibly filling a reservoir due to the shallowing of the Danube
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
13:35:49 EEST
19:35:49 KST

Ukraine has begun forcibly filling a reservoir due to the shallowing of the Danube
Kyiv • UNN
On August 10, the forced filling of the Katlabukh Reservoir in Odesa Oblast began due to a critical drop in the water level of the Danube. This is necessary to stabilize the water level, reduce environmental risks, and meet the needs of the population and the agricultural sector.
Due to the critical drop in the water level of the Danube, the forced filling of the Katlabukh Reservoir in Odesa region has begun, the Ministry of Economy reported on Friday, UNN writes.
On August 10, the State Agency of Ukraine for the Development of Melioration, Fisheries and Food Programs began the forced filling of the Katlabukh Reservoir in the Izmail district of Odesa region. To this end, the main pumping station of the Suvorivka Irrigation System of the Izmail Water Management Department was launched
The need for such measures arose due to the critical decline in the water level in the reservoir and the Danube River. "The situation created risks for the water ecosystem of the Danube region, the water supply of the population, and the needs of the agricultural sector," the statement said.
Katlabukh, as noted, is a critically important water body for the Danube region. Its forced filling was called "a necessary step to stabilize the water level, reduce environmental risks, and meet the needs of the population and the agricultural sector."
As stated, to ensure the stable filling of the reservoir in the long term, the first stage will involve reconstructing the power supply system of the main pumping station of the Suvorivka Irrigation System. The project is expected to be launched this year, with the energy-independent pumping station scheduled to begin operating in April 2027.
In summer, virtually all of Europe faced unprecedented low water levels on the Danube. In some areas, the water level fell to record lows.
"While chairing the International Commission for the Protection of the Danube River, Ukraine initiated the preparation of a joint overview of the low-water situation in the Danube Basin countries. We seek to show that climate change recognizes no state borders, and therefore the response to these challenges must also be developed jointly," said Iryna Ovcharenko, Deputy Minister of Economy and Environment of Ukraine.

Minister outlines education priorities for new academic year in Belarus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:33:00 UTC
19:33:00 KST

MINSK, 14 August (BelTA) – Belarusian Education Minister Andrei Ivanets outlined the priorities for the new academic year at the plenary session of a seminar-meeting on preparations for the 2026/27 academic year at the Education Ministry on 14 August, BelTA has learned.
 
Andrei Ivanets stressed the importance of creating flexible working arrangements for kindergartens to accommodate parents raising young children. “The focus should be on establishing short-stay groups of two to four hours, 12-hour groups, and continuing to expand nursery groups for children under two. This should become a key priority in the coming school year so that every young mother can pursue her professional goals while raising her child,” he said.
 
The central figure in general secondary education remains the teacher. “Starting this academic year, we are launching a teacher training school at the Academy of Education for subject teachers. It will be based on a thorough analysis of admission campaign results, including centralized exams, national education quality assessments, and new approaches we will implement as part of a pilot project for eighth-graders with in-depth study of mathematics, physics, chemistry, and biology,” Andrei Ivanets added.
 
Regarding children with special needs, the minister noted that inclusive education must provide a flexible educational path for each child. Working with such children requires an individual approach. This includes not only a network of special kindergartens and schools but also the development of integrated groups and classes in pre-school and general secondary institutions. These should become more flexible and responsive to each child’s needs. “We see the need to expand the functions of correctional and developmental centers. This is a crucial element that gives parents and children access not only to education but also to socialization,” he emphasized.

Oxy fire in Brussels: cause remains unknown a month after tragedy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:32:46 UTC
19:32:46 KST

A month after the fatal fire at the Oxy building in central Brussels, the cause of the disaster remains unknown. Construction on the former Muntcentrum remains at a standstill.
Around 250 workers were on the building site at the time of the fire. Hours after the evacuation, the bodies of six workers were recovered from a lift shaft. They included five Belgians and one Romanian.
A further two people were taken to the military hospital in Neder-over-Heembeek with severe burns and were in a critical condition for some time. Brussels mayor Philippe Close described the disaster as “a tragedy that affects us all deeply”.
The Labour Inspectorate has launched a criminal investigation into persons unknown. This includes examining whether health and safety legislation was complied with. An inspection by forensic experts immediately after the fire revealed that one of the lift cables had been damaged.
“It is a very large building; there are many pieces of the puzzle to put together,” said auditor Brecht Speybroeck at the time.
A month later, the exact circumstances of the fire remain unclear, the Labour Inspectorate confirmed in a statement to VRT NWS. Although most of the findings have been established, the investigation is still under way. The construction site remains cordoned off in the meantime and the Labour Inspectorate is unable to say when work can resume.
Four of those who died in the fire – one of the worst workplace accidents in recent history – worked for contractor On Time Metalworks from Alken in Limburg. Relatives of all six victims visited the scene last month.

Bosnian Serb Police Questioning Of Srebrenica Staff Triggers Bipartisan Warning From US Congress
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:31:35 UTC
19:31:35 KST

A bipartisan group of US lawmakers is seeking action, including possible sanctions, against Bosnian Serb officials after police began questioning staff at Bosnia's Srebrenica Memorial Center following the publication of a new report showing a marked jump in cases of genocide denial.
Police from Republika Srpska, the Serb entity in Bosnia, questioned 26 current and former employees and associates of the Memorial Center on July 31, a day after the center published its latest report on genocide denial, which documented an increase of more than 50 percent in recorded cases compared with the previous reporting period.
Senators and House representatives from both sides of the aisle issued a statement saying they were "deeply concerned" by the questioning and urged authorities to ensure that the Memorial Center could operate free from intimidation.
"The scale and timing of these actions are troubling, particularly because the work of the Memorial Center is central to preserving the truth, honoring the victims, and defending human rights," the bipartisan group said, calling on US President Donald Trump's administration to restore sanctions on Republika Srpska officials.
International and Bosnian courts have ruled that the killing of more than 8,300 Bosniak men and boys from Srebrenica and the surrounding area by Bosnian Serb forces after they captured the UN-protected enclave in July 1995 constituted genocide.
Genocide denial and the glorification of convicted war criminals have persisted in Republika Srpska for decades, including among the entity's highest political officials.
Edin Ikanovic, one of the authors of the Memorial Center's report on genocide denial, said seven people had been questioned so far, while others, including himself, were still waiting to receive summonses.
"It is becoming clearer that this is a political game, probably initiated by senior political officials," Ikanovic told RFE/RL.
"We have seen attacks on the report and its authors for years. We know our work makes some people uncomfortable, especially because it documents patterns of genocide denial. These reports will remain an important archive for future researchers," he added.
The District Prosecutor's Office in Bijeljina told RFE/RL that the questioning is part of a case examining allegations concerning the Memorial Center's financial operations in 2022.
It said no formal investigation had been opened and that current and former employees were being questioned as witnesses while prosecutors gathered documents and other evidence before deciding whether to take further action.
The Memorial Center has repeatedly said the institution has faced political and institutional pressure from Republika Srpska authorities because of its work documenting the genocide and tracking genocide denial.
The entity's political leadership has for years rejected court findings that the Srebrenica killings constituted genocide.
"The House and Senate have been unequivocal: the Srebrenica massacre was genocide. More than 30 years later, we have a solemn responsibility to remember the victims, stand with their families, and ensure that this tragic history is neither denied nor erased," the group of lawmakers said in their statement.
They called on the Trump administration to reinstate sanctions on Republika Srpska officials that had been imposed by the United States and lifted in October 2025.
They also urged the administration to enforce provisions of the Fiscal Year 2026 National Defense Authorization Act, which provides for sanctions against people found to be undermining security, stability, or democratic institutions in the Western Balkans.
US sanctions on former Republika Srpska leader Milorad Dodik, members of his family, several close associates and related companies had originally been imposed over actions Washington said undermined the Dayton peace accord, constitutional order, and the Bosnia's territorial integrity.
They were lifted in October 2025, two months after he was removed from office following a criminal conviction by Bosnia's state court for defying the decisions of the Office of the High Representative, the international body overseeing civilian implementation of the 1995 Dayton agreement that ended the Bosnian War.
The Memorial Center was opened in 2003 at the site of the former UN base in Potočari to commemorate the victims of the Srebrenica genocide, the only genocide officially recognized in Europe since World War II.
More than 50 people have been convicted of genocide and other war crimes committed in and around Srebrenica, including former Republika Srpska President Radovan Karadzic and former Bosnian Serb military commander Ratko Mladic, both of whom were sentenced to life imprisonment.
In May 2024, the UN General Assembly adopted a resolution declaring July 11 the International Day of Reflection and Commemoration of the 1995 Genocide in Srebrenica. The resolution also condemns genocide denial and the glorification of people convicted of genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes.
Genocide denial and the glorification of convicted war criminals became criminal offenses in Bosnia-Herzegovina in July 2021.

Panama Canal retains key role in global economy on 112th anniversary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:31:04 UTC
19:31:04 KST

Irmak Akcan
14 August 2026•Update: 14 August 2026
The Panama Canal continues to play an increasingly important role in the global economy as it marks the 112th anniversary of its opening.
One of the most critical links in global supply chains and maritime transportation, the canal remains at the center of international commerce because of its treaty-based legal framework, sophisticated lock system and growing trade performance.
Anadolu compiled the latest data on the canal, along with details of its structure and operation.
Located in Panama, between Costa Rica and Colombia, the approximately 77-kilometer (48-mile) waterway supports the local economy while shortening intercontinental shipping routes by thousands of kilometers.
Data show that the canal connects 180 maritime routes and 1,920 ports, serves 170 countries and handled 13,404 vessel transits in 2025.
Total vessel tonnage passing through the canal during the 2025 fiscal year reached approximately 489.2 million Panama Canal Universal Measurement System (PC/UMS) tons.
An average of 34 vessels passed through the canal each day in January, rising to 37 in March. On the busiest days, the number of transits exceeded 40.
The canal handles around 5% of global maritime trade, while more than 70% of the cargo passing through it either originates in or is destined for the US.
Its operations are supported by 9,014 employees, while revenue generated by the canal reached approximately $5.7 billion in 2025.
Its contribution extends beyond international trade to Panama’s domestic economy. The canal contributed around $4.2 billion to the country’s economy in 2025, with its direct contribution to gross domestic product estimated at 3.4%.
A 26-meter water staircase
The defining geographical and technical feature of the Panama Canal is its stepped lock system, which raises vessels 26 meters (85 feet) above sea level.
Because of the varying elevations along the canal, a full passage generally takes between eight and 10 hours.
After entering the canal, a vessel moves into enclosed lock chambers, where rising water gradually lifts it 26 meters above sea level. It then crosses Gatun Lake, a freshwater reservoir, before gravity-powered locks lower it back to sea level and it continues its ocean voyage.
The canal shortens a voyage between the eastern and western coasts of the US by approximately 15,000 kilometers. For vessels traveling between Europe and East Asia, it reduces the journey by around 3,700 kilometers.
The route is operated by the Panama Canal Authority, an autonomous public institution that applies dynamic pricing based on global shipping demand and seasonal water levels.
Under Article 3 of the 1977 Neutrality Treaty governing the canal, warships belonging to all nations may pass through without being subjected to inspection, search, or surveillance as a condition of transit, regardless of their internal operations, means of propulsion, origin, destination, or armament.

Congress Is Headed for a Massive Turnover
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:30:06 UTC
19:30:06 KST

The 120th Congress is set to feature an unusually large number of new faces.
Ahead of the November elections, at least 83 incumbents across the U.S. House and the Senate won’t be returning to their seats.
Even now, the 119th Congress already looks different from when it began in January 2025, after a handful of resignations as well as deaths.
But the expected turnover at the end of the term will be even higher. The reasons vary: some members announced their retirement after decades of service, others have sought different offices. More than usual have lost primaries.
According to Ballotpedia, as of July, the number of lawmakers not seeking reelection is the highest since 2000.
According to a TIME analysis, as of Aug. 13, at least 70 sitting House representatives—30 Democrats and 40 Republicans—are not returning for another term. In the Senate, 13 incumbents also don’t plan to return next year, including one appointed this March, Sen. Alan Armstrong, to replace the seat vacated by now-Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin. These counts do not include the 16 lawmakers who have resigned from or died during the 119th Congress.
With some primaries still underway, not to mention the November general elections in which every House seat and 35 Senate seats are up for a vote, the number of new faces expected in the upcoming Congress will only increase.
Here’s an overview of the lawmakers so far who won’t be returning in the next Congress.
Retirements
In the upper chamber, 10 Senators have announced their retirement. These include Republican stalwarts Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, whose recent health issues have raised questions of fitness for office, and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, an intraparty critic of President Donald Trump. Sen. Armstrong, who took over the seat vacated by Mullin, has said he will serve only until the end of Mullin’s term, which ends in January. Joining them are Sen. Steve Daines of Montana, Sen. Joni Ernst of Iowa, and Sen. Cynthia Lummis of Wyoming. On the Democratic side, Sen. Dick Durbin of Illinois, Sen. Gary Peters of Michigan, Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, and Sen. Tina Smith of Minnesota have also said they will retire.
In the lower chamber, 32 sitting representatives—or almost half of those not seeking reelection—are retiring. Among them is Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi (D, Calif.).
Others who have announced their retirement are Reps. Mark Amodei (R, Nev.), Jodey Arrington (R, Texas), Don Bacon (R, Neb.), Julia Brownley (D, Calif.), Vern Buchanan (R, Fla.), Steve Cohen (D, Tenn.), Danny Davis (D, Ill.), Lloyd Doggett (D, Texas), Neal Dunn (R, Fla.), Chuck Edwards (R, N.C.), Dwight Evans (D, Pa.), Darrell Issa (R, Calif.), Chuy García (D, Ill.), Jared Golden (D, Maine), Sam Graves (R, Mo.), Steny Hoyer (D, Md.), Barry Loudermilk (R, Ga.), Michael McCaul (R, Texas), Morgan Luttrell (R, Texas), Jerry Nadler (D, N.Y.), Troy Nehls (R, Texas), Dan Newhouse (R, Wash.), Burgess Owens (R, Utah), Jan Schakowsky (D, Illinois), Elise Stefanik (R, N.Y.), Marc Veasey (D, Texas), Nydia Velázquez (D, N.Y.), Bonnie Watson Coleman (D, N.J.), Daniel Webster (R, Fla.), Frederica Wilson (D, Fla.), and Ryan Zinke (R, Mont.).
Delegate Eleanor Holmes Norton (D, D.C.), a non-voting member of the House, is also set to retire.
Resignations
The 119th Congress also saw several resignations.
Mike Waltz was reelected for a fourth term as representative of Florida’s 6th district in 2024 but resigned from the 119th Congress days after it opened to join the Trump Administration, first as national security adviser, then as U.S. ambassador to the U.N.
Mikie Sherrill, who represented New Jersey in the House since 2019, resigned from the chamber in November 2025 after winning the state’s gubernatorial election.
Marjorie Taylor Greene, a MAGA stalwart who represented Georgia, left office earlier this year amid a dramatic fallout with President Trump, and Mark Green, a Republican who represented Tennessee, left in 2025 in what he said was a “business decision.”
Other resignations were mired in ethics-related scandals: former Reps. Eric Swalwell (D, Calif.) and Tony Gonzales (R, Texas) abruptly left office amid threats of expulsion due to sexual misconduct allegations, while Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick (D, Fla.) also quit amid questions about her campaign finances.
Deaths
Five House representatives died during the 119th Congress: Rep. Gerry Connolly (D, Va.) at age 75, Rep. Raúl Grijalva (D, Ariz.) at 77, Rep. Doug LaMalfa (R, Calif.) at 65, Rep. David Scott (D, Ga.) at 80, and Rep. Sylvester Turner (D, Texas) at 70.
The lone Senator to have died in office this Congress was Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina, a Republican fixture in the Capitol since 1995 and a Trump critic-turned-ally until his death in July at age 71.
Seeking other office
Twenty-eight members of Congress—27 representatives and Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R, Ala.)—announced that they were giving up their current seats to pursue another office. So far, 13, including five Democrats and eight Republicans, have lost those campaigns for new offices in primaries.
Six Republican House members have secured the Republican nomination for seats in the upper chamber: Andy Barr in Kentucky, Ashley Hinson in Iowa, Barry Moore in Alabama, Mike Collins in Georgia, Julia Letlow in Louisiana, and Kevin Hern in Oklahoma. Other Senate aspirants fell short: Rep. Buddy Carter lost to Collins in the Georgia primary, while Rep. Wesley Hunt (R, Texas) lost the Texas primary to state attorney general Ken Paxton.
Three other GOP representatives—Arizona’s Andy Biggs, Michigan’s John James, Wisconsin’s Tom Tiffany—as well as Tuberville have secured their party’s nominations in their respective gubernatorial races. Reps. David Schweikert (R, Ariz.), Dusty Johnson (R, S.D.), John Rose (R, Tenn.), Nancy Mace (R, S.C.), and Randy Feenstra (R, Iowa) lost their gubernatorial primaries. Rep. Chip Roy (R, Texas) also lost the Republican primary runoff for state attorney general.
On the Democratic side, several House members have lost Senate bids to progressives. In Minnesota’s Democratic Senate primary, moderate Rep. Angie Craig was defeated by Peggy Flanagan. And in Michigan’s expensive Senate primary, Rep. Haley Stevens narrowly lost to Abdul El-Sayed. In Illinois, Democratic Reps. Raja Krishnamoorthi and Robin Kelly lost the Senate primary to Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton, who had the backing of Gov. J.B. Pritzker. In Texas, Rep. Jasmine Crockett, who announced her run for Senate after a Republican-led redistricting push placed her residence out of her existing district, ultimately lost in the Democratic primary to state representative James Talarico.
No Democratic lawmakers seeking other office have won their primaries so far, though some departing congressmembers on both sides are still awaiting primaries. On Aug. 18, Trump-endorsed Rep. Byron Donalds (R, Fla.) will compete for Florida’s Republican gubernatorial nomination, and Trump-endorsed Rep. Harriet Hageman (R, Wyo.) will seek the Republican nomination for Lummis’s seat. On Aug. 25, Rep. Ralph Norman (R, S.C.), who entered the special election for Graham’s seat after losing the state’s gubernatorial primary, will face Graham’s sister interim-Sen. Darline Graham, who has received Trump’s endorsement. On Sept. 1, moderate Rep. Seth Moulton (D, Mass.) will challenge 80-year-old progressive Sen. Ed Markey in a competitive primary. The final primary contest comes on Sept. 8 in New Hampshire, where Rep. Chris Pappas is favored to win the Democratic nomination for retiring Sen. Shaheen’s seat, potentially setting up a key battleground in the general election.
Reelection primary losses
Twelve incumbents lost their party’s nomination while seeking reelection, an unusually high count with several primaries still to go. House incumbents historically win more than 98% of the time when they seek another term. The 10 House losses so far already exceed the average of 6.5 per cycle since World War II. Seven Democratic incumbents have lost their primaries so far, already tying with 2012 for the most Democratic House incumbent defeats this century.
Democratic primaries have been shaped by a progressive revolt against the party establishment. Brad Lander and Darializa Avila Chevalier, both endorsed by New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, respectively defeated incumbent Reps. Dan Goldman and Adriano Espaillat. In Michigan, state representative Donavan McKinney, backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, unseated Rep. Shri Thanedar. In Colorado, 29-year-old democratic socialist Melat Kiros toppled 15-term Rep. Diana DeGette for the party nomination. Democrats are favored to win all four races, according to Cook Political Report.
In a campaign centered more on generational change than ideological difference, 47-year-old former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin beat 78-year-old, 14-term Rep. John Larson to secure the nomination in Connecticut’s 1st Congressional District earlier this week.
Other Democratic races took place amid a broader redistricting push. In Texas, new Republican-drawn maps pitted 78-year-old Rep. Al Green against 38-year-old freshman Rep. Christian Menefee, the latter of whom ended up winning their primary runoff for a Houston-area district. Also in Texas, Rep. Julie Johnson, whose 32nd district was redrawn to favor Republicans, ran instead in the 33rd district, where she lost in the primary runoff to former Rep. Colin Allred.
Republican primaries, meanwhile, have appeared largely to be tests of loyalty to Trump. In Texas, Trump-endorsed Paxton beat four-term Sen. John Cornyn in the most expensive Senate primary in history. Sen. Bill Cassidy (R, La.), whose vote to convict Trump over the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol attack became a defining issue in his race, also lost renomination after he failed to advance to the runoff, which was ultimately won by Trump-endorsed Rep. Letlow.
Reps. Thomas Massie (R, Ky.) and Dan Crenshaw (R, Texas) also lost their reelection bids. Massie lost to Trump-backed challenger Ed Gallrein after repeatedly criticizing the President over his foreign policy moves, federal spending, and the Epstein files. Crenshaw, who criticized Trump over the Capitol attack and supported aid to Ukraine, lost to conservative Texas state representative Steve Toth.
In a rare defeat for a Trump-endorsed incumbent, Rep. Andy Ogles (R, Tenn.) lost the Republican primary to Charlie Hatcher, who benefited from a redrawn, more rural district and heavy outside spending from a clean-energy super political action committee.

I Wore an Electrical Muscle Stimulation Body Suit to Zap Myself Into Fitness
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

The use of electrical muscle stimulation as a shortcut to improving physical fitness was first commercialized sometime in the early 19th century, and while EMS has waxed and waned in popularity over the years, it’s never gone away. Today it is widely used across rehabilitative medical applications but also to boost strength and stamina.
The promise is simple: Stimulate the muscles with pulses of electricity while you’re working out and you can create thousands of muscle contractions in a short amount of time, far more than you can achieve through standard reps. You still have to activate the muscles through flexing and the like—you can’t just lay on the ground and zap your way into shape—but you can accomplish more with a lot less if you’re using EMS as part of your workout.
Studios like Body20 and Manduu now outfit clients with electrodes and pair them with trainers to guide them through EMS sessions. Both companies promise complete body workouts in 20 minutes or less.
The latest spin on EMS is even more appealing: Rather than requiring a studio visit, why not give consumers an EMS suit they can wear at home and use on their own schedule? To that end, German EMS suit maker Pepper offered to let me try out one of its fancy electro-suits to gauge its long-term impact. The company claims that working out while wearing the suit for 20 minutes gives you the equivalent caloric burn and muscle activation of an hour-long traditional workout, all with less strain on the joints.
At least five companies occupy this space at present, ranging from Apeborn’s $4,000 offering to Pepper’s $1,400 suit, which is the cheapest one I’ve found. And even though the idea of getting ripped with minimal effort tickled my lazy bone, it took me a while to come around to the idea of zapping myself on purpose. Could this possibly do any good?
It turns out EMS has been exhaustively studied—dozens of research papers have been published in the past 20 years—and while results vary, researchers seem optimistic on the whole. One 2021 meta-study determined there is “significant evidence for significant, large-sized effects of [whole body]-EMS on muscle mass and strength parameters, but not on body fat mass.” A 2012 study on trained athletes measured the benefits of using EMS for three to six weeks directly: Vertical jump height increased by up to 25 percent, and sprint times got faster by as much as 4.8 percent.
Another meta-analytical study from 2023 offered perhaps the most compelling commentary, concluding that “eight weeks of continuous resistance training combined with daily upper body, lower body, and abdominal EMS training can significantly improve muscle mass and upper body muscle strength performance, as well as significantly reduce body fat percentage in healthy subjects.”
It all sounds promising, yet despite the extensive research into EMS, there’s no general medical consensus about the tech.
I spoke to a half-dozen physicians about EMS for this story, and opinions varied along quite a wide spectrum. At one end, Andrew Mock, a primary care physician in Newport Beach and five-time winner of the California’s Strongest Man competition, lightweight division, said that EMS had proven beneficial for rehab or critical care situations in patients with severe mobility restrictions, but healthy patients were unlikely to see much value. “If you go outside and start shivering, those are muscle contractions,” he says. “But shivering doesn’t make you stronger.”
At the other end, I heard from Ethan Kellum, the team doctor for the NFL’s Tennessee Titans, who said he uses a form of EMS not just for rehab but to supplement his own workouts. “It’s really a function of the nervous system,” he says, noting that in older patients, muscles can become unresponsive and “go to sleep,” requiring significant effort to reawaken them. “When used appropriately, EMS can help improve the efficiency of communication between the nervous system and the body. Add it to what you’re doing. It can be really helpful.”
Across the board, everyone I spoke to hedged by saying that EMS could, at least for some users, provide some benefit. Perhaps the most representative comments came from Joseph R. Hribick, a professor of physical therapy at Lebanon Valley College. “Current research does not suggest that EMS alone is superior to strength training for developing strength,” he says, “Instead, it should be looked at as a tool to complement strength training and not replace it.”
Suiting Up
After speaking to Pepper founder Emilia von Keyserlingk at length, I relented. To mimic the aforementioned 2023 study, I would work out with the Pepper suit regularly for two months, three times a week—in addition to maintaining my regular cardio and strength-training workouts and keeping my diet and daily routines the same—and see what transpired.
The suit is a lot like a spring-weather wetsuit that stops at the knees and the elbows. Like with a wetsuit, putting it on can require some effort. Twenty electrodes cover the abs, pecs, glutes, thighs, pecs, biceps, and multiple parts of the back. These are dry electrodes, so you don’t have to wet Pepper’s suit down before you put it on (a common requirement for older gear), but your sweat will improve the conduction of electricity. Of course, if you’re pregnant or need a pacemaker, you shouldn’t use an EMS suit.
Pepper’s suit, available in sizes from XXXS to XXXL, is designed to be very tight so that the electrodes won’t slip into places you don’t want them. Since the suit is intended to be worn with nothing underneath it, that’s a particularly important consideration. And based on the way certain body parts are situated beneath the fabric, it is definitively not something I felt I could wear in public without a cover-up layer.
The only removable part of the suit is a small box that connects at your hip. This is the brains of the operation and its power source. Charge it with a USB-C cable and it’s good for at least 10 training sessions.
Pepper’s app divides workouts into three categories: strength, cardio, and relax, each with a different electrode firing pattern. (Oddly, I discovered that a few workouts were available only in German.) I tried workouts across all of the categories but spent nearly all of my time in strength, as my goal was to build muscle. Strength sessions all involve electricity pulsing through the suit for four seconds, then pausing for four seconds, then repeating for up to 24 minutes.
The workouts—there are dozens, I rarely repeated any—are tuned to the pulses so that you’re activating muscles across your body while the pulse is on, then usually resting while it’s off. Again, Pepper’s approach is that EMS only works if you are using your muscles while they are being energized, so many of the workouts involve entire body flexes, stretches, and crunches, four seconds at a time.
Plugging In
I’ve experienced isolated EMS for a back injury once before, so I had an inkling of what Pepper might feel like, but the full-body experience is on another level entirely. Fortunately, Pepper eases you in, starting off with soft pulses you can’t even feel. Each of Pepper’s 10 workout zones can be individually controlled, with the power level ranging from 1 to 100. My first video-based trainer said she starts to feel the pulses at level 25, so I slowly ratcheted my way up, bit by bit, until I had all regions hitting around 20.
The shocks on the lower settings don’t really hurt, but you can definitely feel them; powerful, rapid vibrations that shake your insides and sometimes burn a little on the skin. No pain, no gain, right? As I continued to push the levels up, I discovered there was a fine line—really 1 or 2 points on Pepper’s 100-point scale—between tolerable and painful. Those vibrations turned into racy shocks that could be almost paralytic at times, and I spent the rest of my initial 12-minute session dialing the power level back down.
One key discovery is that sweat really matters. When you start your workout, presumably with dry skin, the shocks aren’t as powerful because conductivity is minimal. Start sweating and the shocks increase, even without adjusting the power level in the app. One pulse could be manageable, the next debilitating, just based on how much I was sweating.
My abdominal muscles were the most sensitive to the shocks. Bent over in a crunch position, the contractions could be so powerful in the stomach that I sometimes got a bit nauseous. I was constantly adjusting the levels and ended up with most of my levels around the 30s. To be sure, many of the workouts would be tough even if I weren’t getting zapped.
I asked von Keyserlingk for guidance on the appropriate power level. “The intensity should be high but not too high that you cannot do the exercises in the correct form,” she says. “Being able to breathe normally is key.” Von Keyserlingk says that her levels range from 40s in the lower body to 20s in the back and abdominals—pretty close to my own settings. She notes however that Pepper’s internal EMS expert regularly works out with levels in the 90s. Masochist.
After my first workout, I felt good but was happy to peel off the suit, which was sweaty and unpleasant to linger in. (The suit can be machine washed.) If Pepper’s app was to be believed, my short workout burned a whopping 306 calories and earned me 182 “Pepper points,” which are used as the currency for gamified leaderboards across the Pepper user base. By the end of my testing, I could regularly accrue over 1,000 Pepper points per session and have even earned a few top-10 positions on those leaderboards, which are specific for each workout.
After three sessions, I found myself getting more comfortable with the EMS pulses. I also felt soreness visiting different body parts almost at random. On one day my left hamstring was achy. On another, my right biceps was in so much pain I could barely use it. I figured these were all signs that Pepper was doing something—though, again, I alternated standard workouts with Pepper workouts, taking only Mondays off from disciplined exercise.
Considering Gains
Two months went by. The only workouts I missed were during a weeklong vacation, and I made up the extra time afterward.
The experience was marked by a few problems. After an update, Pepper’s app began glitching and failed to record several of my workouts, costing me thousands of hard-earned Pepper points. Midway through the experience, Pepper released a new, thinner version of its suit with the zipper in front, which the company sent to me. I was excited to give it a try until a piece of the electrical connector snapped off, leaving me unable to connect the battery. The battery pack of suit number three disconnected from the app on two occasions, aborting the workout but at least recording my progress, and it came with an unexpected power boost that left my entire body aching the next day.
Regardless, I muddled through. When the experiment was finished, I’d accumulated 24,000 Pepper points and, purportedly, burned a total of more than 11,000 calories across more than 9 hours of EMS workouts.
To measure my progress, I captured physical data with a tape measure before and after the experience, and I used three different smart scales to further evaluate my stats. All of the scales agreed that the trend line was good: muscle up by 2.7 pounds, fat down by 1.6 pounds—and that’s with smoothed data, since all of these numbers can vary considerably day to day. I added a half-inch or more to my measurements of biceps, thigh, and chest circumference, and my strength was slightly improved, as I’ve been able to add a plate or a few reps to most of my resistance exercises at the gym. Qualitatively, I would say that my physique looks slightly more toned, and I did receive one unsolicited opinion that my arms had better definition. Gains, folks.
What didn’t change? My waistline, which I had hoped to improve, didn’t budge at all. While my abdominal muscles feel noticeably stronger, they remain covered by a layer of blubber that is apparently impervious to electricity. That said, the research predicted as much.
Is EMS responsible for my gains, however modest? While there’s no way to say whether my stats improved due to EMS training, my regular workouts, or dietary changes, I think it’s reasonable to conclude that shock tech did have some impact on my fitness level, since my results are in line with what the 2023 study found. I can’t say whether EMS is responsible for 80 percent or 10 percent of those gains, but I think it’s fair to deduce that some good has been happening.
Going forward, I plan to keep using the suit, though perhaps dropping down from three sessions a week to two. If for no other reason than, while it’s great that my level of fitness is improving, the suit has become quite the topic of conversation at social gatherings. I may be able to slack on my personal fitness, but I can’t let down my people.

So Nigel Farage has beaten a man in a bin. But he's in deep trouble, and he knows it | Owen Jones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:29:27 UTC
19:29:27 KST

Nigel Farage is a rattled, embattled politician. Perhaps he feels buoyed up by securing slightly more votes in a byelection boycotted by all the main parties than he did in the general election two years ago. That was despite 10,000 fewer people turning out to vote. But there was never any question that he was going to win a byelection he called purely to deflect scrutiny of his undeclared £5m personal gift from a Thai-based crypto-billionaire and donations from a convicted fraudster.
Farage chose Clacton as his parliamentary launchpad for a reason. It was here that his previous outfit, Ukip, secured its breakthrough in the byelection of 2014. It is one of the most pro-leave seats in Britain, while Electoral Calculus estimates that almost no other constituency is this rightwing.
When I visited, I found no shortage of voters who were defiant about Farage’s scandals. They saw no problem with a politician being showered with dosh by a foreign-based billionaire, arguing that Farage deserved it because he was a “nice man” and even suggesting he might invest it locally. They bought the narrative that the establishment was out to get their man, as if a millionaire ex-City broker who is a sometime friend of the US president is some plucky outsider.
They are representative of about a fifth of the country who laud Farage as the mainstream politician most hostile to immigration, and who are contemptuous of a Conservative party that failed even on its own terms in office. What should concern Farage, however, is that most Britons are more opposed to him than ever, and are determined to block him from power. That majority delivered victory to the Greens in February’s Gorton and Denton byelection, and to Andy Burnham in June’s Makerfield byelection.
That the parody candidate Count Binface won more than a quarter of the vote in this ultra-rightwing heartland is a warning in itself. Yes, this “independent space warrior” secured plenty of media attention, but he had precious little ground game – that is, an army of volunteers to get out the vote. Many voters I spoke to hadn’t even heard of him. It seems plausible that some of those who made Count Binface the most successful joke candidate in history had previously voted not just Labour, Lib Dem or Green, but Conservative too.
Farage refused to attend the official declaration of this election he chose to call. That suggests not just petulance and contempt for his own voters, but the insecurities of a jittery man. He claims Essex police had told him about an “organised campaign to disrupt and degrade the result”, but the local force said there had been no “incidents or issues” related to the byelection and that attendance was up to candidates. And did Farage not claim that his £5m personal gift was needed to pay for his security?
The explanation is probably more mundane. Being mocked on stage by a man in a bin does not exactly provide the optics of a heroic struggle against the establishment.
What next for the Farage show? If he thought the byelection was an effective ruse to deflect from his money issues, reality caught up with him quickly. The parliamentary watchdog has now reopened its investigation into Farage’s gift and donations, and another byelection may be forced if there is an adverse ruling.
But it is not just finances that have plunged Reform UK into crisis. Farage’s proud association with Donald Trump – toxic even to most Reform voters – has become an ever greater drag. Absorbing so many former Conservatives was surely another big error. The last government was bitterly rejected for a reason, not least by Farage’s own supporters, and filling Reform’s ranks with its former leading lights hardly helped the party’s anti-establishment pretences.
And then there is the pivot to ever more toxic rightwing politics, perhaps partly driven by pressure from the even further right Restore Britain, founded by the former Reform MP Rupert Lowe. Farage now talks of “anti-white discrimination” – rhetoric once confined to the ugliest reaches of the far right. His talk of “pure cold rage” after the conviction of Henry Nowak’s murder – just hours before riots over it – rightly disturbed many.
Then there’s Zia Yusuf, his home affairs spokesperson, whose increasingly aggressive social media posts speak to Reform’s authoritarian underbelly. Yusuf repeatedly describes his opponents as “traitors” – his latest target was the Tory former defence secretary Ben Wallace – and threatens that an unspecific “reckoning is coming”.
All of this alarms most Britons, who have concluded that Reform must be kept from power and will vote tactically if needs be. Yet this is of scant comfort to the absurdly underscrutinised Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, because Reform’s hardened core shows no interest in returning to her camp. Rightwing Britain, then, is divided.
It would be a mistake to write Farage off, however. We are in the midst of the Andy Burnham bounce. Voters are relieved to be rid of Keir Starmer, and for now Labour is tempting back some progressive voters who defected to the Greens. But Burnham has yet to be forced into many big decisions. Britain’s economic plight, its crisis-stricken public services and Burnham’s slowness to hike taxes on the booming rich could all come to a head in October’s budget. Disillusionment could swell, and Reform could benefit – unless, of course, Burnham calls a snap election first.
But you have to ask whether Farage’s heart is really in this. Reports that he received his £5m gift after saying he would need “a million a year” to serve as an MP are telling. Here is a man who appears to enjoy the high life and feel parliamentary politics damages his earning potential. He seems increasingly riled by the sort of scrutiny he has long managed to avoid. Perhaps, after a pointless triumph over a bin, he may simply decide he has had enough.
- 
  Owen Jones is a Guardian columnist

Over the past five decades, Nepal has established itself as a model for wildlife conservation. Nearly 20 percent of the country’s territory has been designated as protected areas. Seven killed in tunnel accident at Indian hydropower project
Water and debris burst into a state-run hydropower tunnel in Uttarakhand following a landslide, trapping the construction workers inside.
At least seven workers have been killed and 13 others injured after a tunnel accident at a construction site in northern India, according to local officials.
Water and debris burst into the tunnel, part of a state-run hydropower project in India’s northern hill state of Uttarakhand, late on Thursday following a landslide, trapping the construction workers.

Experts say climate change, coupled with poorly planned development, is increasing the frequency, severity and impact of such disasters.

German auto industry employment falls to lowest level since 2005
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:27:23 UTC
19:27:23 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
14 August 2026•Update: 14 August 2026
Employment in Germany’s automotive industry fell to its lowest level in more than two decades in the first half of 2026, the country’s statistical office Destatis said Friday.
The sector employed 691,500 people at the end of the first half, down 42,300, or 5.8%, from a year earlier.
The contraction was the largest recorded among Germany’s major industrial sectors with more than 200,000 employees and brought automotive employment to its lowest level since 2005.
Despite the decline, the automotive industry remained Germany’s second-largest industrial employer, behind mechanical engineering, which had 905,900 workers.
Employment among manufacturers of motor vehicles and engines fell 6.1% year-on-year to 429,200, while the workforce at parts and accessories suppliers decreased 7.6% to 219,500.
In contrast, employment among producers of vehicle bodies, superstructures and trailers rose 10% to 42,800.
Germany’s manufacturing sector as a whole employed 5.29 million people at the end of the first half, a decline of 144,100, or 2.7%, from the same period last year.
Employment also fell 3.8% in fabricated metal products, 3.7% in basic metals, 3.6% in the chemical industry and 3.4% in electrical equipment manufacturing.
Mechanical engineering employment declined 2.7%, while smaller decreases were recorded in plastics, food, and computer, electronic and optical products manufacturing.
