CM Yogi Adityanath said the Congress had failed the country by prioritising political power.
NEW DELHI: Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath has accused the Congress of being responsible for India's Partition and the violence that followed, arguing that the country's history could have been different under leaders such as Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel or Prime Minister Narendra Modi.Speaking at an event in Lucknow marking Partition Horrors Remembrance Day, CM Yogi said the Congress had failed the country by prioritising political power and alleged that the consequences of Partition continue to affect India.“Had Narendra Modi been the Prime Minister of India at the time of Independence, nobody would have been able to damage India in the slightest,” he was quoted as saying by news agency PTI.He also invoked Patel, saying that a leader of his stature would not have allowed India to be divided.“If a person like Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel were the Prime Minister at that time, nobody would have been able to disintegrate India ... The country had to pay a heavy price for the cowardice of these Congress members -- a character you all witnessed during the CAA protests,” he added.Adityanath alleged that areas including Sindh, Punjab and Bengal were handed over to Pakistan despite what he described as their Hindu and regional demographic character.
“Bengal was Bengali-dominated. All Hindu villages were forcibly given to Bangladesh. This shameful act was committed by the Congress, which was extra-restless for power, and on whom the country had reposed its trust. It repaid that trust with betrayal,” he said.The chief minister also criticised the Congress over its response to attacks on Hindus in Bangladesh. He alleged that the party remained silent because it was concerned about losing electoral support.“They feared that reacting to the events in Bangladesh might cause their vote bank here to drift away. To them, the murder of Dalit Hindus holds no significance; what matters is their own vote bank,” he said.Adityanath further argued that internal divisions based on caste, region and language had historically weakened India and created opportunities for outside forces.“When such infighting exists, then conspiracy easily creeps in,” he said.He said the consequences of Partition could still be seen in the form of terrorism, Naxalism, Maoism and extremism. He also questioned the Congress's claims about its role in India's freedom struggle and accused the party of presenting itself as indispensable to the creation of modern India.“This also draws our attention to the silence we have all maintained regarding that pre-1947 conspiracy. Yet, even today, these people move before society, acting as if they were the ones who created India, and that without them, India would not have come into existence. It is a truly strange situation,” he said, describing Partition as the “darkest chapter of humanity.”Turning to what he described as the Congress's political legacy, Adityanath said institutions across the country had been named after one political family.“Every institution in the country came to bear the name of that very clan. Every single institution was named after that clan, and we all stood by silently, merely watching. What are they doing even today? What are their actions like now?” he said.The UP chief minister also defended the Citizenship Amendment Act and attacked the Congress's opposition to it.“There was no justification for opposing the act. The act contained a provision regarding Afghanistan, Pakistan, and Bangladesh -- territories that were once part of undivided India and share a heritage spanning thousands of years. It stipulated that if a Hindu, Sikh, Jain, Buddhist, Parsi, or Christian from these countries had been forced to leave and had sought refuge in India for five years, they would be granted Indian citizenship,” he said.He argued that the legislation did not provide for taking away land or property from Muslims or political parties, and accused opponents of using the issue to provoke protests.“Nowhere did it say that we would seize land belonging to Muslims, the Congress, or the Samajwadi Party. There was no such provision in the Act. Yet, attempts were made to incite agitation across the country,” he said.
Adityanath also targeted the Samajwadi Party, claiming that Uttar Pradesh would have witnessed widespread unrest had it been in power during the CAA protests.“What kind of unbridled mayhem would have taken place? The rioters knew the price they would have to pay, which is why they could not act as they pleased; yet, their audacity was evident,” he said.“If you wish to see their true character, you would have witnessed it during the CAA protests, and their silence regarding the recent events in Bangladesh once again puts them in the dock,” Adityanath said.The event also featured a silent march led by Adityanath and other party leaders from the statue of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel to Lok Bhavan, according to the Uttar Pradesh government.

A mudslide in Zhejiang province on Friday killed one person and three others remained missing, while eastern and southern provinces were bracing for more downpours and floods, the nation's state media reported.
The mudslide occurred around 6.30am in Changxing County and caused a house to collapse, Xinhua News Agency said.
A preliminary investigation showed that the mudslide was triggered by a flash flood after a sudden burst of heavy rain. 
Rescue work was underway, Xinhua reported.
The nation is increasingly battling destructive weather that scientists link to climate change, especially this year, as an emerging El Niño pattern boosts temperatures and fuels more frequent and intense typhoons. 
Natural disasters on the mainland in July, when the country was affected by typhoons Maysak, Bavi and Noul, left 318 people dead or missing and caused direct economic losses of 57.15 billion yuan, according to data released by the Ministry of Emergency Management.
Both numbers were higher compared with a year ago. 
Typhoon Dolphin, which made landfall on Sunday, unleashed extreme rain across eastern, central and northern regions this week, breaking single-day rainfall records at 13 weather stations across the country.
In central Henan province, authorities were organising the evacuation of 781 people after a riverbank was breached late on Thursday in the city of Zhoukou, state broadcaster CCTV reported on Friday.
Remnants of Typhoon Dolphin, combined with cold air and a monsoon trough, are expected to bring more heavy rain in eastern and southeastern parts of the country from Friday to Sunday, CCTV said in a separate report.
A basin-wide major flood is expected in Lake Tai in the east, the country's third-largest freshwater lake and the origin of a number of rivers, according to CCTV. (Reuters)

Brad Pitt is drinking again. As a fellow alcoholic, I think he’s making a mistake
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:11:28 UTC
19:11:28 KST

Brad Pitt is drinking again. As a fellow alcoholic, I think he’s making a mistake
Brad Pitt has started drinking again and this really is cause for celebration among millions of ordinary people around the world, because after all, what brings us closer to the great and famous, but our vices?
I have often heard people who enjoy a glass of cognac in the morning point out that Winston Churchill used to do much the same, but when asked in what other respects they resemble the First Lord of the Admiralty, twice British prime minister, and Nobel Prize winner, they usually have less to say. And now, if Brad Pitt has started drinking again, perhaps he has become a little closer to us ordinary people, or perhaps we have become closer to him.
But if Pitt has started drinking again, there must have been a reason he stopped, given in 2019, Pitt spoke openly about giving up alcohol. “I’d taken it as far as I could take it, so I removed my drinking privileges,” he said, and by then, he had been sober for about three years.
The decision followed the notorious 2016 confrontation aboard a private jet carrying Pitt, Angelina Jolie, and their children from Europe to the United States. Just look at the problems stars have – even the family rows take place aboard private jets. According to Jolie’s account, Pitt spilled beer on her, grabbed and shook her, and behaved aggressively towards their children. The FBI investigated the incident, although Pitt was not charged and Jolie filed for divorce shortly afterwards, while Pitt stopped drinking.
Of course, it wasn’t as though he had accidentally got drunk for the first time in his life that day, and the point isn’t how much someone consumes on one particular occasion, it’s the cumulative effect. Alcohol can erode a person’s character slowly and gradually, so gradually that the person himself may barely notice, with good physical health, professional success, wealth, and modern medicine allowing someone with a serious drinking problem to remain highly functional for an extraordinarily long time.
Brad Pitt was never found unconscious under a fence and that particular image is worth mentioning because, in our society, lying under a fence is traditionally regarded as the definitive proof that someone has finally become an alcoholic. But alcoholism rarely looks like that, and many people with serious alcohol problems remain successful, go to work, raise families, and are seldom seen visibly drunk. However, money and status don’t change what ethanol does to the human body.
Pitt himself has been remarkably candid about his past, such as when in a 2017 interview, he said that after leaving college he could not remember a period when he was not drinking or using something. He has described alcohol as a means of escaping his feelings and problems, and once joked that he could drink a Russian under the table with his own vodka and a Frenchman with his own wine. It’s not much to boast about, but we Russians certainly understand the cultural context in which such things become a source of pride.
Then came sobriety, but now, according to a recent interview, Pitt has begun allowing himself an occasional drink again. Bottles were noticed at his home, and when asked about them he reportedly described what he was doing as “moderate drinking.”
Here’s what I would tell you, dear Brad Pitt, should you ever care to listen: those morning cognac drinkers are no more Churchill than I am Brad Pitt. I’ve never appeared in a film, I’ve never seen Angelina Jolie or Jennifer Aniston up close, I’ve won neither an Oscar nor a Golden Globe, millions of female admirers have never written to me, and advertisers have somehow resisted offering me multimillion-dollar contracts.But there’s one respect in which you and I are not merely similar but indistinguishable, because illness is wonderfully democratic and dear Brad, I too am an alcoholic.
You are 62 years old and by my standards, you possess an almost unlimited amount of money and access to the finest medical care in the world, but you know something as well as I do, for an alcoholic, the idea of “moderate drinking” is a dangerous one. A person who returns to alcohol after years of sobriety doesn’t necessarily return as the person he was before he began drinking, but decades of habits and associations are still there.
That’s the insidious thing about alcoholism as gradually, every important event becomes connected with alcohol. Celebration means alcohol, disappointment means alcohol, meeting friends means alcohol, being alone means alcohol, and success, failure, boredom, anxiety, holidays, funerals, Friday evenings all mean alcohol. Eventually the brain finds a reason to drink in almost everything.
And Hollywood, I imagine, provides more reasons than most places because they certainly know how to drink there, with beautiful houses, beautiful glasses, expensive bottles, and hard-earned dollars. It all looks considerably more elegant than the man under the Russian fence, but the chemical inside the bottle remains much the same.
The way out begins with understanding that life is richer, more interesting, and ultimately more fulfilling than the experiences alcohol promises us. Pitt already knows this and he’s spoken about Alcoholics Anonymous and about the men he met there with considerable affection and respect.
Seven years of sobriety is no small achievement, but neither are three decades of drinking habits easily erased, so think again, Brad. Remember that flight from Europe. Remember the row with your family and the beer spilled over your wife, remember the moment when you decided that enough was enough and, in your own excellent phrase, revoked your own drinking privileges.
Perhaps there was wisdom in that decision that shouldn’t now be discarded simply because enough time has passed to make the past seem less dangerous. There’s an English expression about “falling off the wagon.” Don’t fall off the wagon, Brad, because it’s much harder to climb back on.

The siege has drawn US criticism, and White House officials are pressing for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to publicly condemn the siege, according to a US official and an Israeli official with knowledge of the discussions.

Men in uniform prayed with settlers

Assad-era officer convicted in Austria returns to Syria a free man, sources say
DAMASCUS/FRANKFURT, Aug 14 - A former Syrian security officer sentenced to prison in Austria for abusing detainees during Bashar al-Assad’s rule left the country while appealing against his sentence and returned to Syria earlier this month, according to four sources and messages reviewed by Reuters.
Lieutenant Colonel Musab Abu Rukba was handed an eight-year prison sentence last month by a Vienna court that found him guilty of bodily harm, aggravated coercion and sexual assault against detained opponents of Assad while he headed the police's criminal investigations department in the city of Raqqa more than a decade ago.
The Syria Justice and Accountability Centre, a Syrian human rights organisation, said the case exposed shortcomings in the Austrian judicial system after authorities allowed Abu Rukba to remain at liberty throughout proceedings and while challenging his prison sentence on appeal.
Abu Rukba had pleaded not guilty. In early August, he arrived in his hometown of Nawa in southern Daraa province, where his family held a reception to celebrate his return, the four sources familiar with the case said.
The invitation said he had been granted "release from prison," according to a message sent to local dignitaries and seen by Reuters.
Syria's ministries of Interior and Justice did not immediately respond to a Reuters comment request.
A spokesperson for the Austrian court that convicted him told Reuters on Friday that ahead of the trial, he was found not to pose a flight risk because he had been living in Austria since 2014 and was seeking asylum there along with his family.
He was not remanded in custody during the trial and was also not subject to other restrictions. Until the appeals process is included, his departure from Austria does not constitute a breach of any Austrian laws or rulings, the spokesperson said.
“The escape of a lieutenant colonel accused of torture, sexual coercion and serious bodily harm demonstrates a failure by the Austrian authorities to assess the danger posed by this defendant and their failure to place him in pre-trial detention,” Mohammad al-Abdallah, executive director of the Syria Justice and Accountability Centre.
He said Abu Rukba’s return and his celebratory reception also raised questions over accountability in post-Assad Syria, adding that trials now taking place there had little to do with justice.
Syria’s new authorities have pledged to hold former Assad officials accountable for abuses committed during his rule. A Syrian court on Tuesday sentenced Assad to death in absentia for killings, torture, arbitrary arrest and crimes against humanity. The ousted leader fled to Russia in December 2024. REUTERS

Adel Abdelrheem and Rania Abushamala

Heavy rainfall and flooding displaced 975 families and completely or partially damaged 1,348 homes in North Darfur state in western Sudan, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said Thursday.
The flooding struck Tawila town and the villages of Masal, Marar, Katur and Tabsa in Tawila locality on Wednesday, the UN migration agency said in a statement.
IOM field teams reported that 975 homes were completely destroyed and another 373 were partially damaged.
The displaced families sought temporary shelter in open areas within the same locality, the agency added.

Sudan typically experiences heavy rainfall during the June-October rainy season, with flooding affecting large parts of the country each year.
The flooding comes as Sudanese civilians continue to face the consequences of a war between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces that began in April 2023.
The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced or forced about 15 million others to flee, according to UN and local estimates.

====================================================================================================

from casa malaparte to the sheats-goldstein residence, these homes became movie stars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:05:50 UTC
19:05:50 KST

Some houses become famous because of the architects who designed them. Others are remembered because a film gave them a second life. Over the years, a surprising number of architect-designed homes have crossed into popular culture, becoming inseparable from the stories they helped tell. They may begin as private residences, but once they appear on screen, they often take on another identity altogether. Audiences return to them long after the credits roll, not simply because they are beautiful, but because they hold a particular mood, memory, or emotion.
Few architects have left a bigger mark on cinema than John Lautner. His houses seem almost made for the camera. Expansive glass walls, dramatic concrete roofs, and interiors that flow into the landscape create spaces that feel slightly unreal. The Sheats–Goldstein Residence in Los Angeles became instantly recognizable as Jackie Treehorn’s home in The Big Lebowski (1998), where its geometric skylights and sunken living room create an atmosphere that is equal parts glamorous and surreal. A few decades earlier, Lautner’s Elrod House in Palm Springs was chosen for Diamonds Are Forever (1971). Production designer Ken Adam reportedly looked around the house and said, ‘I don’t have to do anything.’ The architecture already embodied the futuristic world he wanted to build.
Stahl House (Case Study House #22) | image by Julius Shulman
residences that became cinematic icons
Lautner’s work keeps returning to film because it always seems to offer something beyond aesthetics. The Chemosphere, balanced on its single concrete column above Hollywood, became the mysterious home in Brian De Palma’s Body Double (1984), while the Garcia House made a brief appearance in Lethal Weapon 2 (1989). His buildings sit somewhere between fantasy and reality, making them easy to imagine as the homes of billionaires, recluses, or characters hiding something beneath the surface.
Richard Neutra’s houses tell a different story. Where Lautner’s architecture feels theatrical, Neutra’s restrained compositions often communicate calm, precision, and emotional distance. The Lovell Health House appears in both L.A. Confidential (1997) and Beginners (2010), while the Kaufmann Desert House has become one of modernism’s most photographed homes on and off screen. After inspiring countless productions for decades, the house itself finally appeared in Don’t Worry Darling (2022), where its clean lines and expansive desert setting help create an image of perfect domestic life that gradually begins to crack.
In Milan, Villa Necchi Campiglio became the backdrop to Luca Guadagnino’s I Am Love (2009), where its quiet rationalist interiors reflect the emotional restraint of the family who inhabits them. He later chose Villa Albergoni for Call Me By Your Name (2017), allowing the house to become part of the rhythm of a long Italian summer. Every corridor, staircase, and shaded garden feels lived in. Decades earlier, Jean-Luc Godard transformed Casa Malaparte on Capri into one of cinema’s most unforgettable settings in Le Mépris (1963). Suspended between sea and sky, the house expresses as much about the film’s emotional tension as any dialogue ever could.
Some houses become so familiar on screen that they almost stop belonging to architecture alone. Pierre Koenig’s Stahl House is one of them. Originally built as Case Study House No. 22, it has appeared in films including Playing by Heart, Nurse Betty, and Galaxy Quest, while its image has become shorthand for Los Angeles itself. Likewise, the A. James Speyer House outside Chicago entered popular culture after Ferris Bueller’s Day Off sent a Ferrari through its glass pavilion, turning a refined modernist residence into one of the most memorable scenes in American cinema.
Modernist houses rarely serve as neutral backgrounds. Their openness, transparency, and carefully composed geometry often become visual cues for wealth, ambition, isolation, or control. What was once imagined as an optimistic vision for modern living has frequently been reinterpreted by filmmakers as the ideal setting for villains, tech billionaires, lonely geniuses, or people living behind carefully constructed facades.
That association continues in more recent films. Alex Garland’s Ex Machina (2014) turns Norway’s Juvet Landscape Hotel into the secluded home of an AI entrepreneur. Surrounded by forests and rock formations, the architecture feels both deeply connected to nature and completely removed from everyday life. Production designer Mark Digby later explained that the team deliberately tried to move away from the familiar image of the wealthy villain’s modernist retreat, even if audiences inevitably brought those associations with them.
Glass Onion (2022) plays with similar ideas. Edward Tuttle’s Amanzoe resort in Greece becomes the extravagant island compound of a technology billionaire, where monumental colonnades, endless pools, and carefully framed views mirror the excess and performance of its owner.
Production designers often speak about searching for buildings that already contain the emotional qualities a script requires. For Don’t Worry Darling, Katie Byron described looking for spaces that conveyed idealized wealth before allowing subtle feelings of unease to emerge. The location team behind The Big Lebowski reportedly kept returning to Lautner’s Sheats–Goldstein Residence because no other house created quite the same atmosphere. Architecture already carries its own narrative, and filmmakers recognize it.
Edward Tuttle’s Amanzoe resort in Greece | image by Pygmalion Karatzas
When a film changes a building’s legacy
Cinema, in return, reshapes the lives of these buildings. Some are now known as much for their film appearances as for their architectural significance. Casa Malaparte has become inseparable from Le Mépris. The Stahl House owes part of its international recognition to decades of appearances on screen. The Ben Rose House found renewed public attention after Ferris Bueller’s Day Off, helping fuel preservation efforts years later. Film gives these houses another history, one that often reaches audiences far beyond architecture.
Perhaps that is why these buildings continue to fascinate us. A house can shape the way a story feels without demanding attention for itself. Sometimes it reflects the inner life of a character. Sometimes it creates tension before anything has happened. Sometimes it simply stays with us long after the film ends.
The most memorable movie houses become memorable because they become part of the storytelling. Like the best supporting actors, they never steal the scene, yet somehow the film would not feel the same without them.
Casa Malaparte, Capri, Italy, 2019 | image by Sebastiano Pellion di Persano
Edgar Kaufmann House | image Shulman Photo Archive Getty Research Institute
Villa Necchi Campiglio | image via FAI
This article is part of designboom’s MODES OF HABITATION chapter, exploring how the spaces we inhabit can reshape the ways we live together. Discover more stories rethinking domesticity, shared living, and the many forms a home can take here.
happening now! lumion pro’s render capabilities eliminate the friction when traditional technical drawings fail to communicate an ambitious design concept.
since 1989, children’s play is understood as a fundamental right alongside education, shelter, and care – explore what that means for our built environment.
a series of rounded rock-like forms rise as a vertical landscape of planted terraces, public routes, and immersive spaces designed to make climate action tangible.

Amid the Ceuta crisis, how do EU citizens view refugees?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:05:41 UTC
19:05:41 KST

Migration is a hot topic in the EU: the issue of refugees in particular has become even more pressing following the surge of migrants into the Spanish territory of Ceuta, but how do citizens feel across the bloc?
Migration is a hot-button issue, especially when displacements peak, such as the recent episode in the Spanish territory of Ceuta, which saw around 80,000 people cross the border from Morocco in just 48 hours at the end of July.
Despite the global number of refugees falling by 3% in 2025 compared to the end of 2024, according to the UN Refugee Agency, UNHCR, the issue remains firmly on people's minds: Google searches on the topic have increased by 150% in the past five years.
While overall public support for offering refuge remains strong, there are still widespread doubts about whether the people claiming to be refugees are in actual need of protection, according to Ipsos Global Attitudes Towards Refugees 2026.
In general, among EU countries, support for refugees is strongest in Sweden, the Netherlands, and Spain, with almost eight in 10 people agreeing that people should be able to seek refuge to escape from war or persecution.
In contrast, those in Hungary and Poland tend to show the least support among EU countries, at 54% each.
Opinions on how countries should deal with refugees vary significantly. For instance, more than half of the Hungarian, Belgian, and German respondents claim that their country should close the borders to refugees entirely and not accept any refugees at this time.
Some countries' positions have shifted over time, however: support for accepting refugees in France has climbed to 68%, up from 43% in 2019.
Do Europeans see most refugees as genuine?
Around 54% of German respondents believe many people claiming to be refugees are not genuine, as they say that these individuals appear to have adequate financial resources already, such as being able to pay smugglers or owning smartphones.
Meanwhile, 46% of Dutch respondents state that genuine refugees would seek asylum in the first safe country they reach, rather than travelling further to other countries.
In addition, more than six in 10 respondents in Germany and Ireland believe that most refugees just want to come to their countries for economic reasons or to take advantage of the country's welfare services, while respondents in Sweden and Italy tend to agree the least with that idea.
Who do EU citizens think should assist refugees?
Three in 10 German respondents believe the governments of other wealthier nations should contribute more to assist refugees globally.
Meanwhile, the rest of the countries say that international organisations, such as the United Nations and the World Bank, should be the ones contributing more to assist refugees globally.
While not as prevalent, some respondents also support the idea that foundations and non-governmental organisations that fund charitable causes should do more to support refugee funding.

UAE says Iran attacked two vessels in Strait of Hormuz
The United Arab Emirates on Friday blamed Iran for attacks on two vessels linked to its state-owned oil company as they passed through the Strait of Hormuz a day earlier.
Iran has imposed an effective blockade of the strait, frequently attacking commercial ships, and wants to charge users for passage, which the U.S. fiercely opposes.
The UAE foreign ministry denounced what it called "the hostile Iranian attack" targeting two vessels affiliated with the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) "with no injuries reported."
ADNOC confirmed "two of its vessels were attacked while transiting" the waterway on Thursday evening, adding the situation was "brought under control," the official WAM news agency reported.
On Friday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported two identical incidents of drone strikes on tankers in Hormuz a day earlier, causing minor damage but no casualties.
It was not clear whether they were referring to the ADNOC-affiliated ships.
"UKMTO has received reports from military authorities that a tanker was struck by a Uncrewed Aerial Vehicle (UAV) whilst conducting an outbound transit of the Strait of Hormuz. The vessel was subject to minor damage, crew are reported as safe and accounted for and no environmental impact has been reported," it said in both statements.
Last week, ADNOC had said three of its tankers had been attacked in the strait, with the UAE foreign ministry reporting an attack on an ADNOC tanker a day later.
U.S. threatens Iran with "economic isolation like the world has never seen"
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is threatening to subject Iran to economic isolation "like the world has never seen before," adding that new measures are expected next week.
"It will be a combination of economic isolation, like the world has never seen before," Bessent told conservative television network Newsmax Thursday, adding that "the continued blockade in the Strait of Hormuz ... will keep anything from going in or out of the Iranian ports."
"Watch this space for more announcements coming next week," he said.
Bessent described a two-pronged approach featuring financial pressure and a physical blockade of Islamic republic's ports.
Vice President JD Vance said earlier that the top U.S. priority in the Iran war was bringing oil and gasoline prices down for Americans, with preventing Tehran from acquiring a nuclear weapon now ranking second.
The tougher stance contrasts with remarks by Bessent on August 4, when he told CNBC an agreement with Tehran to reopen the strait could be reached within days.
CENTCOM defends conditions on USS Abraham Lincoln amid monthslong deployment
The U.S. military's Central Command called a spate of news reports about dire conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier "false."
The ship has been deployed for almost nine months, and is currently in the Middle East region. Lawmakers and family members have raised concerns about supply shortages, inadequate food, broken plumbing and mental health issues — and earlier this month, a sailor went overboard and was recovered, the Navy told CBS News.
In a post on X, CENTCOM said service members "remain resilient and resolved after more than 260 days at sea, 10,000 aircraft flights, and 1.5 million pounds of ordnance expended."
"No service members aboard the aircraft carrier have died, and the one Sailor who fell overboard Aug. 3 was quickly and safely recovered," CENTCOM added. "The rampant misreporting on Abraham Lincoln's historic deployment is a disservice to our men and women in uniform and their loved ones."
Kushner planning to travel to Jerusalem and Cairo next week amid Gaza peace push
President Trump's envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner is planning to travel to Jerusalem and Cairo next week, according to an official with the Board of Peace, the Trump-backed body that is pushing for a resolution to the Israel-Hamas conflict — as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pushes back on the board's plan.
Former U.K. Prime Minister Tony Blair and Board of Peace Director-General Nickolay Mladenov will accompany Kushner, the official said.
The official says they will continue the "constructive" conversations they've been having on how to advance Mr. Trump's 20-point Gaza peace plan, which calls for the militant group Hamas to disarm and give up any role in governing Gaza while Israeli forces withdraw from the enclave.
Late last month, Mr. Trump announced Hamas and the Board of Peace had agreed on the next steps in his peace plan, with Hamas giving up its arms in stages and Israeli forces withdrawing from parts of Gaza as "disarmament is completed." The Board of Peace laid out a 15-point roadmap covering the withdrawal and disarmament.
But last weekend, Netanyahu said Israel "rejects the 15-point document," saying the military "will not make any withdrawal until Hamas is truly disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and citizens."
During their visit to the region, the three Board of Peace representatives plan to hear the concerns that have been raised, and talk about next steps, the Board of Peace official said.
In Cairo, there are meetings planned with Egyptian officials and other mediators.
Vance says Trump administration's core Iran goals are "keeping oil and gas cheap," blocking nuclear weapons
Asked about the Iran war, Vice President JD Vance told Fox News' Will Cain that "goal number one" for the Trump administration is to "keep oil and gas cheap for Americans all over our country," followed by ensuring "Iran never gets a nuclear weapon."
"I feel confident we're accomplishing both of those goals, but it's inherently an unpredictable thing because the Iranians themselves are unpredictable, and they sometimes don't honor the commitments they've made to us," Vance said.
As oil shipments remain largely blocked in the Strait of Hormuz, global oil prices are currently above pre-war levels but below their heights during the war's early weeks. The Trump administration has pressed Iran to allow ships to pass through the strait, but Iran has said it plans to hold onto some control of the vital waterway.
The benchmark for U.S. crude oil, West Texas Intermediate, stood at around $81 per barrel for next month's deliveries as of 5 p.m. Thursday, compared to less than $70 in February and over $110 in April.
The price of gasoline is also elevated, averaging $4.07 per gallon nationwide, compared to $3.16 a year ago, according to AAA. In May, the price surpassed $4.50 per gallon.

Civilian deaths in Ukraine jumped in July as Russia hit cities, UN says

Civilian deaths in Ukraine jumped in July as Russia hit cities, UN says
Aug 14 - Civilian casualties from the war in Ukraine rose by nearly a third month-on-month in July, to the highest level since May 2022, as Russia struck towns and cities far from the battlefield with missiles and drones, the U.N. said on Friday.
The United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine said in a report that it had confirmed at least 437 civilians killed and 2,610 injured in July, a 30% rise from June and a 70% jump from the same month last year.
Long-range weapons, such as missiles and drones, remained the leading cause of civilian deaths last month, accounting for 38% of the total.
"Most casualties from these weapons occurred far from the frontline in urban centres," the U.N. report said.
BALLISTIC MISSILE ATTACKS
In recent months, Russia has stepped up its attacks on Ukraine with ballistic missiles, which due to their speed and steep trajectory are much harder to intercept than drones or cruise missiles.
Ukraine has a chronic lack of U.S.-made Patriot interceptors needed to defend against these attacks. President Volodymyr Zelenskiy urgently appealed to Washington this week for more supplies.
Russian glide bombs – an air-launched guided munition – became the second-largest cause of death. Civilian casualties from aerial bombardments increased by 143% month-on-month in July to 105 killed and 753 wounded.
The U.N. also noted a rise in the number of deaths from short-range drones near the frontline, which killed 111 people and wounded 710 in July, the highest monthly level since the war began in February 2022.
Residents in cities close to the battlefield – such as Kherson – have coined the term "safari" to refer to Russian drones "hunting down" civilians and vehicles in the streets.
Overall, Kyiv was the hardest-hit city, with a total of 54 civilians killed in July, followed by Kherson and Zaporizhzhia, the U.N. said.
"The number of child casualties (17 killed; 166 injured) was the highest since April 2022," the report stated.
The figures also included 25 civilians killed and 50 wounded in parts of Ukraine occupied by Russia, the U.N. said. Due to increasingly limited publicly available information – the actual figure was probably significantly higher, it noted.
Both Russia and Ukraine deny deliberately targeting civilians.
More than 16,000 civilians have been killed in nearly four-and-a-half years of fighting, according to the United Nations, the overwhelming majority of them Ukrainian.
Ukraine is also increasingly attacking Russia with drones and long-range missiles, some of which have caused civilian casualties, Russian authorities say.
On Monday, authorities said that a Ukrainian drone strike in the Russian city of Nizhnekamsk killed at least 13 people.
The Conflict Intelligence Team, an independent group that tracks the war, estimated that a total of 634 civilians were killed in July on both sides of the frontline. Reuters was not able to verify that figure independently. REUTERS

Trump to tout drop in US crime rates with an eye on midterms
WASHINGTON, Aug 14 - U.S. President Donald Trump is set to showcase falling violent crime rates on Friday as evidence that his law-and-order agenda is working, seeking to shift attention away from economic concerns that have dented his approval ratings ahead of November's midterm elections.
Trump will visit the Nassau County Police Academy in New York to unveil 2025 data from the Federal Bureau of Investigation that a White House official says will show the largest year-to-year decline in violent crime on record.
FBI Director Kash Patel and newly sworn-in Attorney General Todd Blanche are expected to join the president at the event with police.
The appearance comes as Republicans look for issues that resonate with swing voters amid concerns about inflation and the economic fallout from the war with Iran, while casting Democrats as out of step on public safety.
"President Trump promised to make America safe again and the data proves he has done just that," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said.
According to excerpts from the FBI report shared by the White House before its publication, murder and non-negligent manslaughter decreased an estimated 18.1% in 2025 while robberies fell an estimated 18.5%.
Some violent crimes, including homicides, surged at the end of the first Trump administration during the COVID pandemic to the highest levels in decades. But the data shows that the subsequent fall predates Trump's return to office, with homicide rates plummeting in 2023 and 2024 to pre-pandemic lows.
The decline has occurred in cities big and small, in places with officials touting both aggressive policing and progressive police reform and with both a high density and low density of police officers, suggesting no single policy explains the nationwide trend.
Trump has long complained of a "crime epidemic," particularly in Democratic-run cities, and used that message to justify aggressive federal intervention, including last year's deployment of federal agents and National Guard troops to Washington.
Trump's touting of the crime decline comes as he has also sought in recent months to make socialism and communism a defining theme in the midterms. He has recently intensified attacks on self-described democratic socialist New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and other progressive candidates.
Democrats say Republicans are overstating the role of federal policy in a crime decline that began before Trump returned to office, and progressives have largely backed away from supporting the "defund the police" movement that emerged after George Floyd's murder in 2020.
They now say policing should be reformed while arguing that immigration officers, who have killed two U.S. citizens, have made communities less safe. REUTERS

Turkey's AKP pushes for new 'civilian constitution'

Breadcrumb
Time for a new 'civilian constitution'? Turkey's ruling AKP says so
Efkan Ala, deputy chairman of Turkey's ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP), told The New Arab that the party, which marks 25 years since its founding on 14 August, is preparing for the next elections, with President Recep Tayyip Erdogan as its candidate.
To mark the 25th anniversary of the Justice and Development Party, The New Arab interviewed the second-in-command of Turkey's ruling party, discussing the party's trajectory, the challenges it has faced, its future and its position on the most important events that have taken place and are taking place.
Efkan Ala stressed that the Justice and Development Party had worked to resolve the country's problems through democracy, including electing the president by the people, for which constitutional amendments were introduced and the issue was resolved.
In the next phase, the party has set the goal of making Turkey one of the world's 10 most developed and advanced countries.
He revealed that preparations are still underway to amend the constitution, while explaining that Turkey's "terrorism-free" process is continuing and that the issue of non-Turkish elements will be resolved through diplomacy with neighbouring countries, particularly Syria and Iraq.
He explained that Turkey supports the two-state solution in Palestine, warning that the policies of Benjamin Netanyahu's government leave it without a future.
The following is an edited version of that interview:
The Justice and Development Party marks 25 years since its founding. What challenges did it face, and how did it overcome them?
The Justice and Development Party was founded 25 years ago, when the atmosphere in Turkey at the time was affected by the events of 28 February 1997. The Turkish National Security Council held a meeting that led to decisions resulting in the removal of former Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, leader of the Welfare Party, and the end of his coalition government.
The economy was facing major difficulties, a severe economic crisis and political instability, and the party was founded amid all these challenges.
There is no doubt that the events of 28 February 1997, dealt a severe blow to freedom of belief. The atmosphere was suffocating, and freedoms were restricted, particularly freedom of belief.
Amid these circumstances, the Justice and Development Party was founded. The party founder, Recep Tayyip Erdogan, said on 14 August, 2001: "From now on, everything will not be as it was in Turkey."
Since then, as a party in power for 24 years, we have achieved a great deal across various fields and brought about real revolutions. We did all this for our people.
The Justice and Development Party put every problem it faced on the political arena before the people and resolved it through the ballot box.
We are a movement that has held 19 elections and referendums during our 24 years in power.
For example, presidential elections had always been a problem in Turkey before the Justice and Development Party. There were always difficulties that led to political crises.
We also witnessed the 360 crisis during our period in power, referring to the 2007 presidential election in Parliament, when problems emerged, but we resolved them.
We did not stop there. We amended the constitution and put the change before our people and said: Since presidential elections have always been a problem, let us give them to their rightful owner.
Who is their rightful owner? The people.
We said: Let the people elect the president directly.
Have the goals for the second quarter-century of the party's life or its vision been determined?
In the second century of the Turkish Republic, we set our main goal as becoming one of the 10 most developed and advanced countries in the world.
To achieve this, we shared the vision of the Turkish Century with our people, and from now on we will begin the second wave of reforms that are necessary.
With the first wave of reforms that we implemented over 25 years, we in fact demonstrated achievements and hard work spanning an entire century in Turkey.
With the reforms we will undertake in the future, we are laying the foundations and core principles for Turkey in the coming century.
Therefore, as our president said, a more just world is possible, and we believe that the world is bigger than five because the world needs these policies.
During our 25 years in power, while confronting many problems, we also succeeded in unifying Turkey and giving it all the opportunities available.
We implemented highly important infrastructure projects.
In foreign policy, Turkey previously adopted a more passive approach, but during our period in power and under the effective leadership of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Turkey became a regional power and a global actor.
Nevertheless, without ever overlooking the principles I mentioned at the beginning, we opposed all forms of injustice and declared this to the world through our foreign policy.
We have always been a country that denounces the genocide in Gaza and crimes against humanity elsewhere in the world, even from the platform of the United Nations.
If there is anything positive that needs to be built, we have worked hard to take the initiative in doing so.
That is why we pursue an active foreign policy that is just, fair and virtuous.
We continue our path by supporting this foreign policy through developing our defence industry, as well as other economic, social and political fields, and providing the necessary opportunities and means.
When talking about the future, there are upcoming presidential and general elections. In this context, what preparations is the Justice and Development Party making?
We have a distinctive approach, and this is a political method that our president taught us.
Elections are held, and the people choose us to come to power, but the very next day we begin working as if no election had taken place, as if there were another election the following day.
We begin preparing for the next election from the day after the election, which concerns the entire people.
We turn to them, go into the field, meet our people, and have representatives in every neighbourhood, village, city and province.
We hold monthly programmes to meet our people, explain our vision and listen to their demands.
We discuss their demands in our relevant institutions.
In our party and government committees, we conduct research and public opinion polls, and we do this every month.
We assess matters. The people's priority is our priority, the people's wishes are our wishes, and the will of our people is our will.
Everything our people oppose, we oppose, and everything our people support, we support.
What are the current public opinion trends regarding the party? What do the polls show?
Public opinion is very positive.
In the public opinion polls we are currently conducting, our president is clearly in the lead.
This is because our people are closely following what is happening in the world and our region.
Here, our president's initiatives, which are just, humanitarian and accepted by people's consciences, have broad public support, and our people continue to maintain their strong support for our president.
When problems emerge elsewhere, such as the Russian-Ukrainian war, our president demonstrates a high level of leadership experience and is able to take the most effective initiatives to save the world from problems arising from the grain crisis.
Within the party itself, there is cohesion, and the country is witnessing cohesion and progress.
Of course, there are problems, but there is a government that resolves problems through democracy.
There is a president who does not surrender his will or the will of the nation in the face of any threat.
Therefore, the situation of the opposition in Turkey is also difficult, as it suffers from serious internal problems.
Accordingly, what will lead the Justice and Development Party to achieve its goals is its ability to renew itself internally and maintain its unity, a leader who has demonstrated his position and will, and a people who trust him.
We are continuing on our path and hope that the research will show this clearly.
Do you have any statistics? Can you give some figures?
Well, first and foremost, we are 10 points ahead even of our closest competitors, so I can say that today, of course, we will continue with the People's Alliance.
Looking at it this way, our president can easily exceed 50% in the presidential elections.
Likewise, when looking at the Justice and Development Party within the alliance, the percentage is much higher, because our people see that the other parties are incapable of solving their internal problems.
A party that cannot solve its internal problems cannot in any way solve Turkey's problems.
It cannot connect Turkey's opportunities with the people.
Therefore, the Justice and Development Party and our president enjoy very strong popular support.
Justice and Development Party spokesman Omer Celik previously announced that the party's presidential candidate in the next elections is Erdogan. But how will the constitutional obstacles be overcome?
When our parliament decides to hold elections, this is clear and explicit in the constitution.
There are no obstacles.
The matter depends on a decision by parliament, and when parliament decides, Erdogan is the candidate of the alliance and the Justice and Development Party, and, God willing, the people will support him.
No one can oppose what the people want.
Therefore, through a decision by our parliament and the nomination of our president, he will have the opportunity to serve Turkey in the best possible way during the next term.
After the 2023 elections, there was a focus on a new constitution, but this issue is no longer on the agenda as it was previously. Is a new constitution or constitutional amendments on the agenda?
Turkey has witnessed constitutional debates since the constitution was adopted in 1982.
Because it is a constitution dating back to the coup era, many amendments have been introduced since then.
However, every amendment requires further amendments.
We have therefore also made many changes.
But the constitution should be viewed as a whole, in terms of its spirit, its drafting methodology and its understanding of the principle of consensus.
We have a committee formed by our president dealing with the constitution, and I am a member of it.
We have completed our work and are currently conducting several assessments.
We will then conduct studies to assess them with the relevant parties.
We will meet civil society organisations and non-governmental organisations to assess them.
Our desire to unite Turkey through a new constitution has remained alive from the beginning, and we still believe in it.
We believe that the time has come for Turkey to adopt a civilian constitution.
For this reason, we have completed our work from our perspective.
We have concluded, but discussions and assessments with other parties and non-governmental organisations will certainly reveal the issues on which we agree and those on which we disagree.
The aim is to draft a constitution through consensus and with the participation of all segments of society, and, if possible, with the participation of all political parties, which would ensure political consensus.
If this is achieved, the constitution will have a longer lifespan.
Then, with the support of the people, Turkey will have achieved the constitutional amendments it aspires to.
Therefore, we want a more robust constitution that guarantees rights and freedoms, including freedom of work, thought and belief; a constitution that builds an effective state, strengthens predictability, prioritises transparency and enables the participation of all segments of society.
Most importantly, the constitution must be drafted through civilian consensus, and the importance of following the same civilian procedures in this process is clear.
Therefore, our programme for drafting a new constitution is continuing.
Will the constitution be amended before the elections, or will it remain unchanged until after them?
Of course, we will continue this process, but because it concerns many parties, parliamentarians and civil society organisations, we want to complete it as soon as possible.
Nevertheless, the timing, timeframe and duration will be determined based on consensus and negotiations.
What is the timetable for the next stage of Turkey's terrorism-free process, and what mechanism will you follow?
Turkey has been fighting terrorism since the 1980s.
Terrorism is a major problem for all humanity. We want to completely eliminate terrorism in our region.
We say a terrorism-free Turkey and a terrorism-free region.
In other words, there should be no terrorism in the Middle East or anywhere else, because its costs are enormous, it has a huge capacity to cause harm, and there is no hope of victory.
Therefore, Turkey has brought the situation to this stage.
With broad participation and support from all sides, we submitted the bill to parliament and established specific mechanisms in it to eliminate the terrorist organisation and hand over weapons.
We are assigning tasks to state institutions under the law, and we will work with society to manage the dialogue transparently.
We have established these mechanisms, selected them and defined them in the law, and we will complete them soon, freeing Turkey from these constraints and implementing policies that will enable Turkey to move forward confidently towards its long-term goals.
We are working hard to do everything we can through an active foreign policy to end the suffering in our region, in Syria, Iraq and the Middle East, and to establish terrorism-free areas in those regions.
Are you concerned about external interference or the possibility of international actors intervening and sabotaging this process?
The possibility of provocation always exists, and this is what happens in the Middle East.
Even coincidences are orchestrated.
Therefore, we have to act with great caution while being aware of this.
That is why we pursue a firm foreign policy to resolve these issues peacefully and decisively and implement these policies by taking measures to thwart the plans and schemes of these powers.
Within the legal framework, details have been set out regarding the fate of Turkish citizens belonging to banned organisations. Is any work underway regarding non-Turkish nationals?
Some of our foreign policy issues can be resolved within the Turkish legal system, while others are resolved through international negotiations.
Turkey has sufficient experience in these matters, has an active foreign policy, maintains good relations with its neighbours, and pursues a high-quality and effective foreign policy.
I believe these issues will be resolved through cooperation with the Syrian and Iraqi governments, as well as regional and central governments, in a way that benefits the countries and peoples of the region.
I am certain of this as long as we maintain our active position.
The Israeli government recently issued statements against Turkey, and Erdogan was also targeted. What is Israel's aim with these provocations?
Israel issues these statements, but it receives a strong response from Turkey.
Since its establishment, it has pursued a policy based first on destabilising areas outside its borders, then occupying those areas and then attempting to annex them.
This is happening before the eyes and ears of the entire world.
It has committed a crime against humanity in Gaza, a horrific genocide.
Once again, our president was the one who strongly protested against this, and we have always stood on the side of justice and stood with Gaza.
Our policy is completely clear regarding the two-state solution.
We know that without recognising a Palestinian state with East Jerusalem as its capital, it is impossible to build lasting peace in the region with Israel.
We have always supported this solution and will continue to support it.
The policy pursued by Netanyahu's government today has no future and benefits no one.
While they bury the people of Gaza, they are also burying their own future.
It has never been known for a state to prosper through an unjust foreign policy, an unjust system or repression.
Therefore, we believe that the two-state solution is the only solution, the just solution in the region and the region, and we are working hard to achieve it.

“At first I thought they were €1 coins,” says Kobe, the 18-year-old student who found a gold hoard while working on a building site in Dendermonde. The haul is thought to be worth around €9 million. It’s not yet clear who is entitled to keep the money.
What began as a normal working day turned out to be something completely different for Kobe and his colleagues. They were set to demolish a building on Van Langenhovestraat in Sint-Gillis-Dendermonde on Tuesday when they discovered a trove of gold coins and ingots bricked into a wall in the cellar.
“Our first reaction was actually disbelief, amazement. We certainly hadn’t expected to find gold,” Kobe said. “We stumbled across it while carrying out groundworks to lay a pipe for the sewerage system.”
Then we saw a gold nugget lying there. That’s when we realised it was something bigger
When they removed a section of the foundations, they saw something unexpected. “At first, I thought they were €1 coins. But then we also saw a gold nugget lying there. That’s when we realised it was something bigger.”
Site manager Mario couldn’t believe his eyes. “They shouted: ‘We’ve found gold!’ I went to have a look and picked up the gold,” he says. “We kept digging up more coins and bars. Only then did it really sink in what we’d found. It was a strange feeling.”
Mario rang his manager, who told him to notify the building owner and the police. Did the workers consider keeping the gold for themselves? “There are so many coins and bars; it would be almost impossible,” he says. “Besides, that would be theft.”
“That’s what I thought too,” says Kobe. “Of course, we did briefly consider keeping it. But it’s simply too much money. If it were a few thousand euros, it might be feasible. But €9 million – you simply can’t keep that hidden.”
After 33 years in the construction industry, this is the first time I’ve experienced anything like this
He hopes there might be a finder’s fee for him and his colleagues. Any fee, and the question of who the money belongs to, are still to be determined. The gold is with the police at a secure location and the East Flanders public prosecutor is conducting an investigation to determine how it ended up at the site. “For all we know, this discovery is the result of some kind of fraudulent activity and the gold has been hidden there,” a spokesperson for the building owner said.
“After 33 years in the construction industry, this is the first time I’ve experienced anything like this,” says site manager Mario. “I don’t think it will ever happen again.”

Surrendered women naxals walk on the ramp during a participation in a Tribal fashion show programme.
NEW DELHI: For nine women from Chhattisgarh's Naxal-affected Bastar region, the stage in Raipur offered a strikingly different kind of experience. Once part of an armed insurgency, they recently walked the ramp in handloom outfits at a National Handloom Day event, as part of efforts to help surrendered Naxalites rebuild their lives.The women, all from Sukma, took part in a Swadeshi fashion show organised as part of rehabilitation efforts for former Naxalites.Sukma SP Mayank Gurjar said the event also gave them an opportunity to promote Swadeshi products.For some of the women, the experience was unlike anything they had done before. One former Naxalite, who had worked with the Pamed Area Committee, said she surrendered in 2026 and travelled to Raipur for six days of training before taking part in the programme."I used to work in the Pamed Area Committee. I surrendered in 2026. We went to Raipur recently. There, we were trained by people who had come from Bombay...prominent ministers also came. The training was of six days...it was the first time we did something like that...we enjoyed it," the former Naxalite told news agency ANI.Another participant, Poonam Devi, said her journey with the Naxalite movement had begun in November 2007.
She surrendered on July 12, 2025, bringing that chapter of her life to an end."I surrendered on July 12, 2025. I liked the program...we were trained for it...I joined the Naxals in November 2007 and left in 2025," she said.According to Gurjar, the women's participation reflects the opportunities being offered under the rehabilitation policies of the Central and Chhattisgarh governments to those who surrender and choose to return to mainstream society."As you all know, through the rehabilitation policy of the Government of India and the Chhattisgarh Government, various benefits and advantages are being provided to surrendered Naxalites. In that context, on National Handloom Day, nine surrendered women who had surrendered in Sukma participated in a Swadeshi fashion show," he said.The nine women had held different positions within the Naxalite organisation. Some were associated with the Pamed Area Committee, while others had served as gunners for senior Naxalite commanders in Battalion Number 1. One had worked as a school teacher within the organisation, according to the SP."Among the nine surrendered women, some were working in the Pamed Area Committee. Some worked as gunners for major Naxalite commanders in Battalion Number 1. One of the surrendered women Naxalites was working as a teacher in a school," Gurjar said.Their past also included handling weapons. Gurjar said one of the women had carried an INSAS rifle and that the participants had surrendered around six months earlier.Now, instead of carrying weapons, the women are being encouraged to explore skills and opportunities that can help them build a different future.
Gurjar said their participation in the fashion show showed a change in their outlook and suggested that their confidence in the rehabilitation process was growing."They are now actively promoting Swadeshi products and refining their artistic skills," he said.For women who once lived amid the forests and violence of the Naxal movement, walking a ramp in handloom clothing may appear like a small moment. But within the larger rehabilitation effort, it represents something much more significant, a visible step away from an armed past and towards an ordinary life.

Where to go in Kyiv on the weekend of August 15–16
Kyiv • UNN
A number of cultural events will take place in Kyiv on August 15–16: a workshop for children, a play, chamber music concerts, and a Rammstein tribute. You can also attend a full-dome film about space and an Italian music concert.
This weekend, Kyiv will host numerous cultural and entertainment events for adults and children. UNN will tell you where you can go on August 15 and 16.
A workshop for children on drawing pets
When: August 15 at 11:30.
Where: Kyiv Cultural Cluster "Krakow", 12 Rusanivska Embankment.
How much: UAH 400.
About the event:
In Kyiv, children will take part in an Art Island creative workshop dedicated to drawing pets. Participants aged 5 to 10 will work with soft chalk pastel and create their own picture depicting a cat or a dog.
The class will be led by artist, painter, and teacher Viktor Veres, who will help the children complete all stages of the work. The organizers will provide all the necessary materials on site. After the workshop, each child will be able to take their work home.
Performance "Andriivskyi Descent. Lantern. Pierrot"
When: August 15 at 14:00.
Where: "Koleso" Theater, 8 Andriivskyi Descent.
How much: UAH 270.
About the event:
The "Koleso" Theater will present a joint production with the M. Kulish Kherson Theater, "Andriivskyi Descent. Lantern. Pierrot," based on a play by Serhii Pavliuk. It is the story of an actress who left the stage and went to another country for the man she loved. The lead role is performed by Honored Artist of Ukraine Oleksandra Tarnovska.
"Music of August": Bach, Vivaldi, Dvořák, Rolla
When: August 15 at 15:00.
Where: St. Catherine's Church, 22 Lutheran Street.
How much: UAH 350–450.
About the event:
An evening of chamber music featuring the National Chamber Ensemble "Kyiv Soloists" will take place in the historic St. Catherine's Church. The program includes works by Vivaldi, Bach, Rolla, and Dvořák. Antonii Kedrovskyi will conduct, and the soloist will be violist Yaroslav Venher.
Voyager: Journey into Infinity + Earth from the ISS
When: August 15 at 17:00.
Where: Kyiv Planetarium, 57/3 Velyka Vasylkivska Street.
How much: UAH 300–500.
About the event:
The Kyiv Planetarium will screen a fulldome film about the Voyager space mission. Viewers will travel to Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune and learn more about the two spacecraft launched in 1977. The film also tells the story of their exploration of interstellar space and the Golden Record containing messages for extraterrestrial civilizations.
RAMMSTEIN TRIBUTE
When: August 15 at 18:00.
Where: "Solomianska Brewery," 2B Solomianska Square.
How much: UAH 250–350.
About the event:
A Rammstein tribute concert will take place at the "Solomianska Brewery." The band Rammstahl will perform well-known songs by the German band, including "Du Hast," "Sonne," "Ich Will," "Deutschland," "Engel," and "America."
D.I.S.C.O. dance project
When: August 5 at 19:00.
Where: Docker Pub, 25 Bohatyrska Street.
How much: UAH 250–300.
About the event:
The D.I.S.C.O. project is an event for those who want to spend the evening with music and dancing. Guests can look forward to a dynamic program in the atmosphere of a club night.
Organ and Vocals Under the Stars: Bella Italia
When: August 15 at 19:30.
Where: Kyiv Planetarium, 57/3 Velyka Vasylkivska Street.
How much: UAH 800–1,200.
About the event:
The Kyiv Planetarium will host the fulldome concert "Organ and Vocals Under the Stars: Bella Italia." The program features Italian music, from works by Vivaldi to Neapolitan songs, accompanied by video projections on the dome of the Star Hall. People's Artist of Ukraine Valeriia Balakhovska will perform on the organ, while the vocal part will be performed by Honored Artist of Ukraine, tenor Serhii Androshchuk. The program will include works by Vivaldi, Rossini, Petrali, Bixio, Capua, and Puccini.

Turkish Super Lig club Fenerbahce terminated the contract of Brazilian midfielder Fred on Thursday.
The Istanbul side notified the Turkish football federation that the 33-year-old's contract had been terminated.
Fred is reportedly set to join Brazilian side Atletico Mineiro on a three-and-a-half-year contract.
Brazilian media reported that Atletico Mineiro would pay around €2 million ($2.3 million) for his release, plus up to €500,000 in performance-related bonuses.
Fred joined Fenerbahce from Manchester United in 2023 and spent three seasons with the club.
He scored 12 goals in 129 appearances across all competitions for Fenerbahce.

Marcos says Philippines will not attack China if it invades Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
10:01:53 UTC
19:01:53 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The Philippines will not allow offensive operations from its territory if China invades Taiwan, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said Friday.
He was responding to questions during a luncheon with the Foreign Correspondents Association of the Philippines, the Manila Bulletin reported. He was asked whether he would allow the US military to launch offensive operations from bases in the Philippines.
The country would not be a belligerent nation in the region, but would only promote peace and stability, Marcos said. He added that allowing an attack from the Philippines against anyone contradicted its policy of defending regional peace and stability.
Marcos described decisions by the US and other countries as their own internal matters and part of their foreign policy, the Manila Bulletin reported. The Philippines is only interested in defending its own sovereign rights and territorial independence, he said.
The president also said that cooperation with Taiwan would continue as the two are close neighbors, per Liberty Times. The “one China policy” will remain an important principle governing relations with China and with Taiwan, he said.
As to talks with Japan about maritime borders east of Taiwan, Marcos described them as a bilateral process, but they would welcome hearing the views of other interested parties. He said there was no timetable for the talks, but he hoped Japan and the Philippines could reach an agreement before the end of the year, per Liberty Times.

RG Kar victim's 'hurried' cremation: Mob attacks arrested ex-TMC MLA with footwear, eggs, muck; video
TOI News Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 14, 2026, 15:53 IST
Comments

Text Size

Former TMC MLA Nirmal Ghosh was attacked outside a West Bengal police station. He was arrested in RG Kar victim's 'hurried' cremation case.
NEW DELHI: Former TMC MLA Nirmal Ghosh, arrested in connection with the alleged “hurried cremation” of the RG Kar rape-murder victim, was attacked by a mob outside Khardah Police Station in West Bengal’s North 24 Parganas district on Friday.Ghosh, who was arrested in Odisha a day earlier, was being escorted to a prison van to be produced before the Barrackpore sub-divisional court when the crowd broke through the security cordon and attacked him with blows and kicks. Protesters also threw footwear, eggs and muck at the former MLA.
Police and RAF personnel formed a tight cordon around Ghosh and placed a helmet over his head to shield him from the assault. By the time he was taken to the court lock-up, stains of egg and muck were visible on his white kurta.The former TMC MLA also faced protests at Barrackpore court, where a group of people waiting outside shouted “chor, chor” as police rushed him inside.Another accused in the case, former Panihati municipality councillor Sanjib Mukherjee, was also confronted by protesters while being escorted to the vehicle. Mukherjee, reportedly a close aide of Ghosh, was allegedly present at the Panihati crematorium when the doctor’s body was brought there after the autopsy.
The police have also named former Panihati municipality chairman Somnath Dey as an accused, but he remains absconding.The arrests followed a fresh complaint filed by the victim’s father on Monday, which was subsequently converted into an FIR. The complaint alleges that Ghosh, who was then the sitting MLA from Panihati, used his influence along with Mukherjee and Dey to ensure that his daughter’s body was cremated in haste against the family’s wishes.
