US debt burden to rise to 123% of GDP by 2028: Fitch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
06:57:01 UTC
15:57:01 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
14 August 2026•Update: 14 August 2026
The US government debt burden is expected to continue rising and reach 123% of gross domestic product (GDP) by the end of 2028, Fitch Ratings said.
The ratio stood at 117% at the end of 2025 and is already more than twice the median for countries in the “AA” rating category, according to the agency.
Fitch said the US government has not taken meaningful action to address its large fiscal deficits, while spending pressures are expected to intensify over the next decade due to an aging population.
The general government deficit is projected to widen to 7.4% of GDP in 2026 and remain at that level in 2027, the highest among “AA”-rated sovereigns.
Rising military and interest costs, alongside increased Medicare and Social Security spending, are expected to limit efforts to reduce the deficit.
Fitch also estimated that the US will reach its statutory debt ceiling of $41.1 trillion around the middle of 2027.
The agency also affirmed the US long-term foreign-currency issuer default rating at “AA+,” with a stable outlook.
It said the rating is supported by the country’s large economy, high per capita income, dynamic business environment and exceptional financing flexibility stemming from the dollar’s position as the world’s leading reserve currency.
However, high fiscal deficits, a substantial interest burden and rising government debt continue to constrain the rating.
Fitch forecasts the US economy to grow by an average of 1.9% in 2026 and 2027, despite higher tariffs, government spending cuts, tighter border controls and increased policy uncertainty.
The agency said economic resilience in the face of tariff changes and sudden increases in oil prices demonstrated the country’s ability to absorb shocks.
It noted, however, that labor demand has weakened and job creation has slowed significantly in 2026.
Annual inflation is forecast to average 3.4% this year, remaining above the Federal Reserve’s 2% target, before approaching the target toward the end of 2028.
Tariffs have contributed to higher core goods inflation, although their pass-through to consumer prices has been more limited than initially expected, Fitch added.

Swimmers spot hand grenade in Zurich river
A live hand grenade that was spotted by swimmers in Zurich's river Limmat has been removed by army specialists.
The small bomb from the former Yugoslavia was revealed when the water level dropped at the Unterer Letten outdoor river pool in the Swiss city. No-one has been injured.
According to Zurich police, swimmers reported the presence of the grenade at the bottom of the river on Thursday morning. Divers from the river police then carried out a reconnaissance mission at the scene and confirmed that it was indeed a hand grenade.
+ Swiss army vigilant about lake-dumped munitions
The object was lying about one metre from the bank. It had come to the surface due to the current low water level of the Limmat. As is standard procedure in such cases, specialists from the Swiss army’s explosive ordnance disposal unit were called in, working in collaboration with police.
The live hand grenade, which originated in the former Yugoslavia, was recovered shortly after 3.30pm, according to the police statement. The Zurich Institute of Forensic Medicine, called to the scene, then transported it in a specialised vehicle to detonate it safely.
During the recovery operation, the relevant section of the river Limmat was cordoned off as a safety precaution.

France evacuates hundreds as new wildfire threatens southwestern Landes region
Authorities evacuated 525 people from the village of Luglon Friday as a new wildfire tore through southwestern France, burning 1,100 hectares and advancing to within a few kilometres of the village centre amid an unprecedented wildfire season.
French authorities evacuated 525 villagers after a wildfire broke out in the pine woods of the southwestern Landes region, near an area already devastated by major blazes this summer.
The fire, which razed 1,100 hectares (2,700 acres) after it began on Thursday, spread to within 2 kilometres (1.2 miles) of the centre of the village of Luglon, regional official Gilles Clavreul told reporters on Friday.
Roads to the north and south of the village have been closed.
Read moreWestern Europe lived through hottest June and July ever recorded
“The situation is unfavourable,” he said, adding that 500 firefighters were tackling the flames, with the help of six aircraft sent to assist.
"The next fifteen hours will be decisive," Clavreul told reporters.
Clavreul did not comment on the possible origin of the fire.
Fire chief Arnaud Fabre said the fire was slowing down but he added he was concerned about potential flare-ups as the heat returns.
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
Police took 525 in the village to safety, with road links to the north and south closed.
No homes have been destroyed.
Luglon is about 100 kilometres (62 miles) southeast of the tourist area of Arcachon Bay, where two major wildfires devastated more than 50,000 hectares (124,000 acres), spurring the evacuation of as many as 220,000 people in late July.
The area has broiled in heatwaves this summer and temperatures are expected to soar to 36 degrees Celsius (97 Fahrenheit) on Friday afternoon, as France’s unprecedented wildfire season continues.
Read moreNearly 70 percent of France under water restrictions amid record heat
The area burned so far exceeds that of the previous record year of 2022. The Landes area is swathed in pine forests that become highly flammable when dry.
French officials are still taking stock of the damage caused by a series of fires, mainly in the southwest of France, including the largest wildfire since 1949 in the department of Gironde.
French media reported on Friday that a 15-year-old has been arrested in connection with a July fire near Bordeaux airport, in the same region, that killed two firefighters.
The youth, who has been placed under judicial investigation, allegedly threw away a cigarette butt that sparked the fire, local newspaper Sud Ouest reported. The Bordeaux prosecutor's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The French interior ministry said 474 people have been arrested on suspicion of starting a fire, whether that be intentional or not. Of that total, 183 are younger than 18. About 70 percent of the people detained are suspected of arson, the ministry has previously said.

A prolific hacking group known for exploiting software vulnerabilities to attack multiple targets simultaneously claimed it had stolen large volumes of data from nearly 50 companies worldwide, including Philips, Shell, Fiserv, and GE, according to a posting on the group's website.

"We are working with our security teams and relevant experts to investigate the situation," a Shell spokesperson said.
"Philips has identified and contained an attempted cybersecurity compromise of a specific enterprise server related to internal data," Philips said in a statement, adding that the incident does not impact customer environments.
A spokesperson for Fiserv said the company is aware of the threat actor's claims, but "based on our comprehensive review to date," it had found no evidence that customer, banking, transaction, or personal data had been compromised, or that its operating environment had been affected.
A GE spokesperson said the company is aware of the claim, and had "initiated our cyber response protocols and are working to assess the potential issue."
Reuters could not independently verify the hacking group’s claims regarding the kind of data it stole and how much. The hackers did not respond to a request for comment.
Hackers exploiting vulnerabilities in engineering, manufacturing software
While it’s not clear how the hackers allegedly accessed the companies, Ransom-ISAC, an industry information sharing group, issued a notice July 22 warning that the hacking group was exploiting vulnerabilities in PTC Windchill and FlexPLM, software used to aid in engineering and manufacturing processes.
Boston-based PTC did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The company has issued multiple security notices to its website, dating to June 18, urging customers to apply a patch for a vulnerability and sharing details about an unnamed attacker attacking its products.
Brandon Parsons, threat intelligence manager with Ascent Solutions and the author of the Ransom-ISAC advisory, said some companies began receiving notices from Cl0p on July 19 or July 20. The group focuses on vulnerabilities in key software packages rather than specific companies, he said, calling them “professional data extortionists.”
“They don’t really target a specific company, they target a specific zero day vulnerability and go after it,” Parsons said, referring to previously unknown bugs that software vendors haven’t yet issued patches for.

American defense startup launches new Anthem cruise missile in Morocco military test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
06:53:33 UTC
15:53:33 KST

American start-up Covenant Industries successfully conducted a live launch of its innovative new Anthem cruise missile last week in the Tan Tan area of southern Morocco, as part of a joint military exercise involving the US military and the Moroccan Armed Forces.
The test marked the operational launch of the new Africa Multidomain Training and Experimentation Center (AMTEC). The new facility, established amid close cooperation between Washington and Rabat, is intended to become a permanent "military laboratory" for advanced warfare technologies.
During the test, US and Moroccan forces, together with company engineers, set up a temporary launch site in the dunes of the Sahara Desert and tested the missile's communications systems, launch mechanisms, and the collection of communications and climate data in real time.
Covenant was founded in 2024 by Michael Kaufman, an American investor and entrepreneur operating out of Israel. The company, which has subsidiaries in Israel and Germany, has so far maintained an exceptionally low public profile and has no official website. That has not prevented it from raising hundreds of millions of dollars from major Silicon Valley funds, including Founders Fund and Andreessen Horowitz.
As part of the wave of defense tech companies, Covenant focuses on developing advanced warfare technologies at relatively low cost. Anthem is intended to be its flagship product, offering a cheaper alternative that is easier to mass produce than heavy and expensive cruise missiles such as the US Tomahawk, while maintaining long range capabilities and precision strike capacity.
New initiative enables access to US military testing grounds
The launch in Morocco was made possible through an initiative by the office of the US Secretary of the Army, which allows private technology companies to gain rapid access, within 30 days, to military testing grounds belonging to the US and its allies.
Covenant was the first company to make use of the initiative. The test represents a critical milestone toward serial production as early as the beginning of 2027.

====================================================================================================

China's export of electric trucks across Asia spikes, as Iran war fuels higher oil costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
06:52:58 UTC
15:52:58 KST

China's exports of electric trucks to other Asian countries have spiked, adding to a surge in domestic sales as higher fuel costs as a result of the Iran war accelerate regional electrification.
China’s rapid adoption of e-trucks - from lighter vehicles to tractor-trailers - has partially shielded the world's biggest auto market from the impact of the conflict. Now other countries are scrambling to follow.
In the four months after the US and Israel launched the war on February 28, China's exports of heavy e-trucks more than doubled from the same period last year to 16,823 vehicles. Half went to South and Southeast Asia, with shipments to South Asia up more than fivefold and to Southeast Asia nearly tripling.
South and Southeast Asia are particularly dependent on the Middle East for oil, and Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz has triggered some of the biggest jumps in diesel prices, according to GlobalPetrolPrices.com, creating an opening for China, the world's largest e-truck maker.
Diesel prices are up 48% in Sri Lanka since the start of the war and 57% in the Philippines, according to GlobalPetrolPrices.com, while the fuel is 15% higher in China, government data shows.
“The war has opened the door to these new markets,” said Zhaoting Yue, vice president of international marketing at Sany, the world's biggest maker of electric heavy trucks.
Sustained growth of e-trucks could put dent in carbon emissions
Exports remain relatively small, dwarfed by China's exports of cars and bikes, while regional truck fleets number in the millions. But if growth is sustained and follows a similar arc to e-truck adoption in China, it could make a notable dent in diesel consumption and carbon emissions.
E-trucks in China have gone from almost zero in 2021 to 30% of truck sales last year, with 140,000 e-trucks sold in the first half of this year. Diesel use in China began falling last year.
Sany previously focused on Europe but is pivoting to Southeast Asia and developing cheaper models, Yue told Reuters. In June, the company shipped its largest single order, 880 heavy trucks, he said, declining to say where because the contract was private.
“Before oil prices rose, buyers in these countries might have needed 28 months to recoup their investment in an electric heavy truck," Yue said. "Now, it takes only 18 months.”
Sany expects the war to sustain rapid growth for at least the next year, particularly in Asia, Africa, and Latin America, he added.
In the United States and Europe, electric delivery vans are increasingly mainstream, but the rollout of larger e-trucks has been far slower. Tesla, for example, which promised to revolutionize the economics of trucking with its electric Semi almost a decade ago, has dropped its goal of “volume production” of the truck by this year.
By not burning diesel, China's e-truck fleet will save the equivalent of 141 million barrels of oil this year, more than 3% of China's total and equal to all its imports from Kuwait, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.
By comparison, China's e-truck exports in the first half replaced fuel at an annual rate of 1.6 million barrels, the Helsinki-based center estimates.
E-trucks double the price of diesel before fuel savings
Hurdles to e-truck adoption include higher purchase prices for the vehicles and gaps in charging infrastructure.
In Australia, an e-truck costs about A$500,000 ($350,000), twice the diesel equivalent, although that is quickly recouped by fuel savings that even before the war cut operating costs by as much as 70% compared to diesel, said Daniel Bleakley, co-founder of Australian electric trucking firm New Energy Transport.
To boost charging infrastructure, Sany is selling customers systems to generate and store power, as well as charge its trucks, said Yue.
The rapid adoption of Chinese electric passenger cars in many markets will also help expand charging networks and provide a boost to truck adoption, said CREA co-founder Lauri Myllyvirta.
"High fuel prices are going to focus minds and get businesses to move fast," he said.

Imagining Ukraine's Political System After the War
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
09:50:00 EEST
15:50:00 KST

Imagining Ukraine's Political System After the War
Even if the terms of a ceasefire or peace settlement are satisfactory to most Ukrainians, the country's democracy will face its fair share of challenges.
Any projections about Ukraine's postwar politics should start with the recognition that Russia's ongoing war has taken the country into unknown territory.[1] It is possible to say that the war's scope and scale have had a social impact in Ukraine that can be compared only to that of a revolution. The war has dismantled the old social contract between the ruling elites and the people. Moreover, it has reshaped, if not redefined, the fundamentals of Ukrainian statehood. The war revealed the central role of civil society (including volunteer movements, grassroots mobilization, independent media, and influencers), exposed the strengths and weaknesses of state institutions and the legal system, and forced the Armed Forces and security services to adapt rapidly. However, to borrow Alexis de Tocqueville's phrase, no matter how profound the revolution, the new order inherits important traits and patterns of the old one.
The Long Shadow of Corruption
Populism and corruption have been formidable impediments to the economic and political development of independent Ukraine. In November 2020, the editorial board of the Financial Times opined on the constitutional and legal challenges facing President Volodymyr Zelensky in achieving his stated goal of dismantling the oligarchic state capture that had characterized Ukraine's political and economic system since independence in 1991. It expressed concerns that Zelensky, whom it called "a textbook populist," wanted to avoid an uphill struggle in tackling the roots of the problem, instead preferring quick solutions that enjoyed broad public approval.
After Zelensky was elected in 2019, he succeeded in converting his wide popular support into unprecedented control of the legislative and executive branches of government. During the first eighteen months of his presidency, terms such as "turbo regime" and "deoligarchization" reflected his almost unlimited power and the steamroller-like process he used to push new laws through parliament. He and his allies argued this was necessary to "reset" the political system and rid the country of entrenched oligarchic influence and high-level corruption.
However, it soon became apparent that members of Zelensky's entourage had taken over the existing schemes of illegal personal enrichment, even after the start of the full-scale Russian invasion in 2022. Since then, key figures of the executive have been investigated for corruption, including: the head of the Office of the President Andriy Yermak; three of his deputies (Oleg Tatarov, Rostyslav Shurma, and Kyrylo Tymoshenko); deputy prime minister Oleksii Chernyshov; former minister of defense and Secretary of the National Security and Defense Council Rustem Umerov; minister of justice and of energy Herman Halushchenko; and head of the State Property Fund of Ukraine, Dmytro Sennychenko. Some of the figures who faced charges—including Shurma, Sennychenko, and Timur Mindich, a businessman and the president's close friend—left the country days or hours before arrest warrants were issued, which infuriated the public because it showed that powerful figures could violate strict wartime border controls and had access to privileged information about investigations.
In addition, as of December 2025, fifteen members of parliament from Zelensky's Servant of the People party were being investigated for corruption, with some facing accusations of buying the votes of their colleagues. In January 2026, former prime minister Yuliya Tymoshenko, who leads a parliamentary faction that has aligned itself with Servant of the People, was caught red-handed by the National Anticorruption Bureau as she offered bribes to secure the votes of fellow members of parliament.
Already in 2023, one of the authors warned that Ukraine was backsliding in its fight against corruption and that the public would blame Zelensky and the government if the issue was not addressed. In a public opinion poll that year, 78 percent of respondents said that Zelensky was directly responsible for fighting corruption in the government and the military. Even though Ukrainians saw him as a national symbol of resistance against Russia, the implications of high-level corruption scandals were clear at the time: Unless the president took action against accused top members of his administration, perceptions of impunity risked undermining trust in him and damaging society's cohesion and will to resist the invasion.
The situation has grown worse since then. In a September 2025 poll, 71 percent of respondents—including 62 percent of those who said they trusted Zelensky—said that corruption had increased during the full-scale invasion. In an April 2026 poll, 54 percent of respondents said that corruption was a greater threat than military aggression, compared to only 39 percent who said the opposite.
These figures suggest that most Ukrainians see high-level corruption as a form of state treason and a threat to statehood. There is strong evidence that Zelensky, earlier in his presidency, was sensitive to such public attitudes; in 2023, for example, he publicly expressed a positive opinion about amending legislation to make the punishment for high-level corruption equivalent to that of state treason, which is a life sentence in most cases.
However, by 2025 popular outrage over corruption had turned against Zelensky. The clearest evidence of public anger about high-level corruption was the "cardboard Maidan" in July 2025—the wave of peaceful student protests against Zelensky's moves to curtail the powers and reduce the independence of anticorruption institutions in order to shield his allies from criminal investigation, including his longtime friend Mindich. It was a powerful reminder of the mass protests in 2004 and 2014 and showed that Ukrainians were willing to defy martial law,[2] which limits the constitutional right of peaceful assembly, in order to pressure the president on corruption.
Decentralized Resilience
Amid the invasion and malfunctioning state institutions, powerful civic activism, modern entrepreneurship, and the experience of decades of those who studied in the West went a long way toward enabling the national struggle for survival. Ukrainians' long tradition of solving problems in a decentralized manner when the central government was unwilling or unable proved critical to the country's resilience. Mayors and volunteers independently built ties with military units and used their resources to procure necessary lethal and nonlethal equipment needed on the front. Nongovernmental charity foundations like the Serhiy Prytula Foundation, the Come Back Alive Foundation, and the Sternenko Community led the way in providing millions of strike and reconnaissance drones, interceptor drones, electronic warfare systems, and access to commercial satellite imagery. These grassroots initiatives more than supplemented the state's resource-constrained and bureaucratically burdened efforts.
Moreover, the agility and adaptability of the defense forces were key factors that allowed Ukraine to survive in the initial phases of the full-scale war. This was the result of decentralized and self-organized networks of cooperation across broader sections of society. Just like community leaders and civic volunteers, the Army and National Guard brigades that turned out to be the most effective did not wait for plans to be introduced from the top. Rather, they independently established their own unmanned systems units, supply chains, research and development laboratories, medical infrastructure, training programs, and public-relations infrastructure.
These innovative practices reflect profound long-term shifts in the attitudes of Ukrainians, who have developed new expectations toward private initiative and state intervention, and have grown even more skeptical of relying on welfare provided by the government. This portends major shifts in postwar politics. Ukrainians will almost certainly continue to trust decentralized but well-connected networks of professionals at the national and regional levels more than they trust central government institutions or legacy political parties. Officers, volunteers, and entrepreneurs who made a difference during the war will have strong credentials for postwar leadership roles. Intense clashes are likely to emerge between wartime leaders and political figures viewed as products of the corrupt "old system." The victors in this competition will be those capable of mass mobilization through appeals to national security and justice, and who can build efficient nationwide political machines.
Zelensky's decision in mid-July to fire Mykhailo Fedorov, the tech-savvy minister of defense who is well-connected with top Western defense companies, illustrates this "clash of generations" in Ukrainian politics and governance. In his farewell statement, Fedorov outlined what he sees as major deficiencies in the "old way" of running the army and country during wartime. If Zelensky does not find a way to mend fences, Fedorov's dismissal might prove to be a watershed moment for old and new elites to consolidate and prepare for a postwar power struggle.
Moderates Versus Radicals
After the war, Ukraine will face the dual challenge of rebuilding while deterring new threats from Russia. The role of the state in recovery and development will grow significantly. This will require strengthening independent oversight and institutional checks and balances. It may also raise the issue of guaranteeing the welfare of all those working in the security and defense sector.
The public will expect the state to assist and support veterans, the relatives of fallen servicemen and civilians, former prisoners of war and deportees returning from Russia, and citizens who lost their homes and property because of hostilities. Debates over the extent to which the Ukrainian state should seek to hold Russian officials accountable for war crimes (if the international community fails to do so) and punish collaborators for their misdeeds are also likely to dominate the political landscape. Inevitably, there will be a national debate about the responsibility of Zelensky and the government for decisions made—or not made—before and during the war. Ukrainians will also demand close scrutiny of the activities of those who controlled politics and the economy before the invasion. These debates are likely to divide political actors and citizens into camps of "moderates" and "radicals," depending on whether they demand symbolic or uncompromising justice on key issues, and whether they favor selective or equal approaches to different actors and social groups.
The moderates camp will probably try to shift the focus away from immediate justice toward building a stronger state that is capable of protecting Ukraine and preventing a new attack. Figures such as Fedorov and Head of the Office of the President Kyrylo Budanov, who have consistently called for national unity and looked to the future rather than focusing on the past, might emerge as leaders of this camp. Moderates will try to direct public anger against Russia while seeking to defuse internal feuds. They will call for an acceleration of reforms necessary for joining the EU—which they will argue is the ultimate prize for postwar Ukraine and future generations. This camp will support special and "black" operations inside Russia and other countries to bring war criminals and traitors to justice.
Mobilization will be another issue that will divide Ukrainians after the war. Many thousands of men paid bribes to leave the country during the war or escaped mobilization by securing, through any means, exemptions from military service. At the same time, military commissions drafted thousands of unfit men, including with physical and mental disabilities, into service. These men cannot fight, but they also cannot be released from service until the end of the war, burdening the military and inflating the number of troops.
To address Ukraine's human-resources challenges, the moderate camp will probably call for the return of Ukrainians from abroad or argue in favor of migration from Africa, Asia, or Latin America to fill labor shortages. Moreover, to decrease public tensions over mobilization, moderates will argue in favor of increasing immigration and enrolling more foreigners in the ranks of the Armed Forces. (For instance, before his dismissal Fedorov was preparing a plan to substitute up to 50 percent of assault troops with contracted foreigners.) The idea is that such measures would encourage young Ukrainians not to leave the country because of the risk of being drafted to the frontline. In addition, Budanov has spoken out against mobilizing young Ukrainians, which in his view would threaten to eliminate an "entire generation."
However, the moderates will face a serious political dilemma. It will be hard to convince millions of refugees to return without strong security guarantees and economic stability, but it will be impossible to maintain a capable army and economic development in a situation of severe deficits of human resources.
The radicals will claim that any dilution of justice will lay the groundwork for another national disaster and a new Russian invasion. Their arguments may resemble those made in the early 1990s and in 2014, when certain political actors argued that all remnants of the old regime—whether former communists or collaborators of president Viktor Yanukovych and his Party of Regions—needed to be purged.
Several public figures with significant political and social influence—in the form of large followership in social media, the permanent attention of traditional media to what they say or do, and evident political ambitions—have the potential to become leaders of the radical camp. They are Serhiy Sternenko, a prominent volunteer and vocal opponent of Zelensky since 2021; Bohdan "Tavr" Krotevych, ex–chief of staff of the Azov Brigade; and Yuriy Butusov, former editor-in-chief of the Censor.net news portal and a drone company commander in the Khartiia Brigade. All three have attacked Zelensky for what they argue were poorly conceived and implemented decisions before and after the full-scale invasion.
Moreover, the radicals will call for the prosecution of political, administrative, and military leaders whose decisions contributed to Ukraine's devastation and huge human losses. Figures in this camp have already begun to criticize what they see as reckless, politically driven decisions that have cost the lives of thousands of the country's defenders with no operational or even tactical benefit on the battlefield. They have stressed the need for independent investigations of pointless offensive operations led by the assault regiments commanded by protégés of General Oleksandr Syrskyi, whom Zelensky removed as commander-in-chief of the Armed Forces in late July in response to public protests. They have also pointed out the absence of relevant basic military training for the majority of recruits in the Army. The public reaction to a recent independent investigation that uncovered the suspicious deaths of twenty-five recruits in the 425th Assault Regiment "Skelya" shows how sensitive and explosive this issue will become after the war.
Several whistleblowers, including decorated officers like ex-battalion commander of 46th Airborne Assault Brigade Colonel Anatoliy Kozel (Kupol), Major Oleksandr Shyrshyn from the elite 47th Mechanized Brigade, and ex-commander of 58th Mechanized Brigade Colonel Dmytro Kashchenko, have at different times warned about these and other critical shortcomings among senior political and military commanders. In April 2026, Colonel Roman Chervinskyi of the Security Service publicly accused Budanov of abusing power during the war.
These developments are alarming signs that after the war radicalized veterans and civic activists are going to shape the national agenda by saying that Zelensky and the executive failed to provide justice and security during the war. They will have a strong case to make if they can draw on the vivid memories of hardship felt by ordinary soldiers and their families.
Moreover, Zelensky himself has played a part in creating moderate and radical contenders. His dismissals of General Valeriy Zaluzhny from the position of commander-in-chief of the Ukrainian Armed Forces in 2024 and Fedorov in July were reminiscent of politics under former president Leonid Kuchma (1994–2004). Kuchma prosecuted moderate deputy prime minister Yulia Tymoshenko in 2000 and fired moderate prime minister Viktor Yushchenko in 2001. Both later came together to unite opposition forces and challenge Kuchma's regime during the election cycles of 2002–2004, culminating in the Orange Revolution and end of Kuchma's rule.
New Nationalism and Grassroots Structures
Two factors will determine whether the moderates or radicals win the support of the public and the postwar competition for power.
First, to be successful, political leaders and organizations will have to show that they embrace and practice a modern, sophisticated version of Ukrainian nationalism. The war proved to most Ukrainians that the nationalist political parties and groups who consistently warned about Russian threats and subversion in the fields of popular culture, education, and the economy had a point. The mainstream political establishment is already increasingly adopting elements of nationalistic ideology in its rhetoric. For instance, Zelensky in January 2026 issued an order to establish a "national pantheon" to commemorate the heroes of the fight for independence in the twentieth century, including leaders of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN) and the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA). In May, he announced the reburial of one of the OUN's leaders, Andriy Melnyk, and issued a decree renaming a unit of the special operations forces after the "heroes of the UPA." These decisions sparked a diplomatic crisis with Poland, which blames the OUN and UPA for Second World War atrocities against ethnic Poles. Many Ukrainians, however, see these organizations as having fought for Ukraine's independence against the Soviet Union, as well as against Nazi Germany.
At the same time, as one of the authors argued in 2022, Ukrainian nationalism has been transforming into a nonpartisan, inclusive civic ideology that is embraced by the majority. In a poll in March 2023, 65 and 47 percent of respondents, respectively, said they thought that new public figures such as Zelensky and Zaluzhny had played key roles in defending the country, demonstrating that Ukrainians see these two men as nation-building figures amid the horrors of war. In another 2023 poll, 42 percent named Zaluzhny as a symbol of Ukraine, second only to the poet Taras Shevchenko (56 percent). With 31 percent, Zelensky was ahead of the Second World War radical leader Stepan Bandera (27 percent), seventeenth-century Cossack hetman Bohdan Khmelnytsky (26 percent), and Vyacheslav Chornovil, one of the leaders of the independence movement in the late Soviet period (26 percent).
The second factor is the importance of grassroots structures. Ukrainians have come to recognize the role of local communities, civic activists, and decentralized structures—especially military units—in building national identity. Popular units and leaders within them such as the Azov Brigade (Denys Prokopenko), the 3rd Assault Brigade (Andriy Biletsky), and the Khartiia Brigade (Oleh Kozhemyako) may become umbrella organizations for political movements. (Although its early roots were in far-right ideologies, Azov has the reputation of one of the most capable fighting units and one that cares about the lives of ordinary soldiers. It attracts volunteers from different age groups and gender, ethnic, and language backgrounds. Its commanders rarely take sides in political clashes.)
In sum, individuals who demonstrated leadership during the war and achieved military, technological, administrative, diplomatic, or humanitarian success will find themselves at the forefront of political competition after the war. The most successful postwar political forces will have strong national leaders with solid wartime credentials while relying on horizontal structures that emerged during the war, including volunteer networks, veterans groups, and informal associations of local community leaders.
In Search of a Unifying Figure
Amid public concerns over corruption and lingering questions about his wartime decisions, Zelensky's window of opportunity to be a national unifying figure has probably closed. But his political networks will give him a considerable opportunity to retain influence if he leaves office. Prior to his arrest in May 2026, Yermak—until then his closest aide—had launched a project to forge a coalition of military commanders, veterans, and volunteers with the goal of creating a new political force that could contest postwar elections under Zelensky's leadership. Since Yermak's arrest, Zelensky has continued this project on his own.
Zelensky has paid more attention to his standing and reputation among the military since he sacked Yermak in November 2025. Since the beginning of this year, he has participated in eight meetings with service members from various branches of the Armed Forces, suggesting that he is investing time and effort to rebuild support among veterans as a way to maintain political influence, whether he decides to run for another term or not.
On the other hand, former commander-in-chief Zaluzhny, now the ambassador to the United Kingdom, has emerged in the public consciousness as a strong contender for the presidency even though he has not yet declared his ambitions to run for office. He is a unique figure and is trusted both by moderates, who laud him for leading and modernizing the Armed Forces, and by radicals, who believe he is too strong to be subdued or corrupted by shadowy politics. At the same time, Zaluzhny is a political novice, and his knowledge of English and understanding of the economy, in particular, are significant shortcomings. He will have to prove to Ukrainians that he has the qualities to lead the country on the international stage through a turbulent postwar future.
Someone else may still yet emerge as a unifying figure. Ukraine needs its next leader not only to focus on healing a wounded nation, defending against Russian threats, and modernizing the economy, but also to unite political forces: If the first postwar president is accepted by moderates but not trusted by radicals, there is a high risk of dangerous civil division that will undermine medium- to long-term stability.
The Tough Task Ahead
On many occasions throughout its contemporary history, Ukraine has witnessed the emergence of new faces and new political forces. However, few of them survived the test of parliamentary democracy, especially when it came to coalition-building. Many leaders focused on their personal ambitions and created weak party structures that rose and fell in parallel with their own fate. Stronger political actors have tended to concentrate, if not monopolize, power in their hands at the expense of junior partners, and in some cases they went so far as to prosecute the opposition. Moreover, external influence, especially from Russia, has repeatedly turned heated domestic political competition into an existential fight. These factors remain and will frame postwar politics. Even if the terms of a ceasefire or peace settlement are satisfactory to most Ukrainians, the country's democracy will face its fair share of challenges.
Considering how bitter internal feuds undermined Ukrainian statehood in the past, Ukraine's key power brokers—including Zelensky, Zaluzhny, Budanov, Biletsky, and Prokopenko—should reach an agreement so that free and fair elections can be held across the country and then negotiate some form of power-sharing. Since all of them have armed men and women behind them, maintaining calm and ensuring that the next electoral cycle can proceed without voter intimidation will be critical. Ukraine has already seen in 1918–1921 a period of otamanshchyna, when anarchy and bitter power struggles between rebel warlords contributed to Ukraine being subjugated by Russia under Bolshevik rule. This time, Ukrainians must find a way to avoid bringing violence into the political process. It is vital that postwar election results be accepted and that power be peacefully transferred to the winners.
Ukraine's postwar leaders will have to decide how to reconcile national priorities—especially spending on defense and social welfare—with the demands of major donors like the International Monetary Fund and the EU, including those regarding democratic rights and the rule of law. They will also need to adapt domestic policies to the permanent threat from Russia without returning to martial law and without concentrating power under the executive.
So long as Ukraine is not a member of NATO or the EU, its leaders will have to build an agile and innovative national security architecture based on defense alliances and arrangements with other democracies, not only in Europe but also in the Middle East (Israel) and the Asia-Pacific (Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and the Philippines). Postwar Ukraine might also embark on trying to reshape its neighborhood. Ukrainians will have a hard time feeling secure with neighboring Belarus under the puppet regime of Aleksander Lukashenko and with Moldova's Transnistria region still a Russian-controlled enclave. Once the war ends, or even pauses, Ukraine's leaders are likely to address these threats, ideally in collaboration with the West but potentially unilaterally. They will need a more expansive and sophisticated view of engaging with countries in Africa, Latin America, and elsewhere. Its new leaders will need to maintain an equal focus on national defense and on securing the economic resources and trade relationships necessary to mitigate domestic demographic decline and fuel reconstruction.
These challenges will require the emerging crop of leaders to display a high degree of statesmanship. They must understand that personality-driven politics, polarization, legislative gridlock, and failure to respect the rule of law were profound mistakes that almost cost Ukraine its independence and statehood. If the country is to win the peace, it will need leaders who can break from the past once and for all.
Petro Burkovskyi, executive director of the Ilko Kucheriv Democratic Initiatives Foundation.
Olexiy Haran, is a professor at the Kyiv-Mohyla Academy.

'Total Eclipse Of The Heart' - Data reveals most popular songs played during this week's solar eclipse

06:47:07 UTC
15:47:07 KST

As millions turned their eyes to the skies for Wednesday's solar eclipse, fresh data shows they also listened to the much-missed Bonnie Tyler and her 80s power ballad 'Total Eclipse Of The Heart'...
This week, more than 90 per cent of the Sun was obscured by the Moon, and in some cases in mainland Europe, was completely obscured in the first total eclipse since 1999.
According to new listening data from Spotify, streams of eclipse and space-themed songs surged during the solar eclipse, with Bonnie Tyler leading the way.
The data comparing streams on eclipse day against the 1-11 August daily average shows that the Welsh singer's hit song 'Total Eclipse Of The Heart' experienced a 14 per cent boost worldwide, including a whopping 94 per cent rise in the UK on 12 August.
The 80s power ballad had already seen a rise in streams following 8 July, the day Bonnie Tyler died "unexpectedly" aged 75 at a Portugal hospital.
Other "celestial" tracks to gain global momentum during the eclipse were:
- Evolfo - Moon Eclipsed the Sun (+1,251%)
- Chris Staples - Dark Side of the Moon (+405%)
- Pink Floyd - Eclipse (+144%)
- Delta Goodrem - Eclipse (+40%)
- Bill Withers - Ain't No Sunshine (+3%)
Not to brag or anything, but three out of those six spiking songs were in Euronews Culture's curated eclipse playlist. Just sayin'...
Shannon Carragher, senior editor at Spotify, said: “Cultural phenomena like the solar eclipse naturally bring people together, and we instinctively look for the perfect soundtrack to share that moment."
She added: “Whether it’s collectively returning to iconic anthems like Total Eclipse of the Heart or seeking out more hidden celestial gems, these massive spikes in streaming show just how deeply we rely on music to elevate and connect us in the real world during shared human experiences.”
Tyler's 'Total Eclipse Of The Heart' was released on 11 February 1983 and featured on her fifth studio album, 'Faster Than The Speed Of Night'. The song topped the UK Singles Chart and became the fifth-best-selling single in 1983.
The iconic love song sold more than 13 million copied worldwide. Its music video has surpassed 1.3 billion views on YouTube and has had over a billion streams on Spotify.
Following Tyler's death, it re-entered the UK Singles Chart, peaking at number 29.
Tyler's funeral service will take place on 17 August at St Mary's Church in Swansea, Wales.

The Cabinet of Ministers has introduced a clear procedure for temporarily suspending the acceptance of new applications from participants in the eBook program.
The relevant decision was adopted at a government meeting on Thursday, Cabinet of Ministers representative to the Verkhovna Rada Taras Melnychuk said on Telegram.
Under the procedure, the state institution Ukrainian Book Institute will determine the maximum possible number of recipients who can receive assistance based on the amount of funds in the institute’s non-budgetary account, and will report that number to the technical administrator of the Diia portal.
Once the maximum number of recipients is reached, Diia’s technical administrator will suspend acceptance of new applications, and recipients will be notified accordingly.
As has been reported, the eBook service launched in Ukraine on Dec. 16, 2024, under which 18-year-old Ukrainians can receive UAH 908 from the state for books via the Diia app.
In 2025, 18-year-old Ukrainians purchased 434,808 books under the eBook program, or about three books each.
In April, Deputy Prime Minister for Humanitarian Policy and Culture Minister Tetiana Berezhna projected the launch of the eBook program for parents of newborns from July 1, 2026.
In late June, Deputy Culture Minister Bohdana Laiuk said the eBook program for parents of newborns was unlikely to launch by July 1 but should be operational in 2026.
Acting Ukrainian Book Institute Director Oleksandra Koval said the eBook program would work significantly more effectively if extended to school-age children.

Interview: S. Korean historian warns Japan against repeating its wartime past
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
14:46:54 CST
15:46:54 KST

SEOUL, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- Japan's growing military ambitions and its increasingly equivocal approach to its wartime past are raising fresh concerns about the direction of the country, according to a South Korean historian.
"Even in 2026, Japan has yet to truly break away from the imperialist era, which is deeply unsettling," Kim Joo-Yong, director of the Institute of Korea-China History and Culture at Wonkwang University, told Xinhua in an interview in Iksan, South Korea.
With the 81st anniversary of the Korean Peninsula's liberation from Japanese colonial rule approaching, Kim said Japan's recent moves, from expanding its military capabilities and strengthening military alliances to showing greater ambiguity over its long-standing Three Non-Nuclear Principles, should be viewed against the backdrop of its unresolved wartime history.
He warned that attempts to dilute Japan's responsibility for its past aggression could create new risks for peace and stability in Northeast Asia.
Kim was particularly critical of what he described as efforts by some Japanese political forces, including Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, to reinterpret the country's wartime history.
The issue, he argued, goes beyond the familiar debate over "historical revisionism."
"What we are seeing is closer to historical denialism," he said.
Both South Korea and China endured Japanese imperial rule and military aggression, leaving behind historical wounds that continue to shape public memory.
Kim pointed to the suppression of the March 1 Independence Movement on the Korean Peninsula in 1919 and the Nanjing Massacre in China in 1937 as two of the most devastating episodes of Japan's wartime history. He also cited the Japanese military's system of sexual slavery, commonly known as the "comfort women" issue, as a grave violation of women's rights.
Such episodes, he said, cannot be erased through changes in textbook wording or by reducing the degree of official responsibility attached to them. "Those are historical facts," Kim said. "But historical denialists are still passing distorted accounts of the past on to younger generations."
Against this backdrop, Kim welcomed the recent donation of 12 materials related to the anti-Japanese resistance to the Independence Hall of Korea by a Chinese collector.
The significance of the materials, he said, lies not only in the historical details they add, but also in what they reveal about the shared experience of the two peoples. "People in China and South Korea once stood side by side in resisting aggression and fighting for independence," Kim said, stressing that the sacrifices made during that period should neither be forgotten nor distorted.
He noted that academic research as well as exchanges between historians and public education from both countries should continue over the long term.
Kim, however, pointed out that the target of criticism is militarism and imperialism, not ordinary Japanese people.
Many ordinary Japanese, he noted, were themselves victims of the war. The central issue is the state violence that launched wars of aggression and the continuing reluctance to confront the history.
"Peace is one of the most universal values in human history," Kim said, adding that a return to militarism would bring new instability and suffering to Japan itself and to the broader Northeast Asian region.
"For Japan, the right path is to reflect deeply on its history, cherish peace and remain committed to a peaceful future," he added. ■

Death toll rises to 8 after record rain batters Japan's Chiba Prefecture

TOKYO, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- Eight people died in Chiba Prefecture after record amounts of rainfall pounded eastern Japan through early Friday, local authorities said.
Eight people have been confirmed dead in the cities of Chiba, Kashiwa, Ichikawa, Sakura and Yachiyo, while four people sustained minor injuries, according to the Chiba Prefectural Government.
According to the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA), Chiba City received 348 mm of rain in the 12 hours through 1:40 a.m. local time Friday, a record-breaking amount. It is roughly three times the city's average rainfall for the entire month of August, all falling in just half a day.
The JMA had earlier issued a Level 5 Emergency Warning for heavy rain and landslides in parts of Chiba Prefecture, its highest alert level. All of the warnings were downgraded on Friday morning to Level 4 or lower.
Weather officials warned that further downpours are possible, urging people to remain on their guard.
According to the Fire and Disaster Management Agency, as of 11 a.m. local time Friday, the evacuation orders remained in effect for around 102,600 people in Chiba Prefecture.
Approximately 7,000 passengers were stranded overnight at Narita Airport in the prefecture as the downpour paralyzed train and bus operations, the airport operator said. ■

ZAGREB, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- At least 1,000 residents and tourists have been evacuated after a massive wildfire spread into the coastal town of Omis in southern Croatia, local media reported early Friday.
More people are expected to evacuate across the affected areas, Omis Mayor Zvonko Mocic said.
The fire, which erupted at around 8:21 p.m. local time (1821 GMT) on Thursday in nearby Lokva Rogoznica, advanced overnight into the upper parts of Omis, directly threatening numerous houses and vehicles, Croatia's Hina news agency reported, quoting Viseslav Pesic, commander of the Omis Voluntary Fire Department.
A total of 157 firefighters and 44 fire engines fought the blaze overnight, with emergency reinforcements dispatched from other parts of the country.
The destructive blaze comes amid a prolonged summer heatwave and severe drought across Croatia. Weeks of extreme temperatures have left vegetation tinder-dry, sharply increasing the risk of wildfires along the vulnerable Adriatic coast. ■

Tokyo prepares a response to Putin’s visit to an island Japan considers its own
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
09:46:40 EEST
15:46:40 KST

Tokyo prepares a response to Putin’s visit to an island Japan considers its own
Kyiv • UNN
Japan plans to strengthen sanctions against Russia over Putin’s visit to Iturup, which Tokyo considers its territory. The prime minister called the visit unacceptable, and the Foreign Ministry summoned Russia’s ambassador to protest.
The Japanese government plans to consider countermeasures in connection with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to one of the four islands controlled by the Russian Federation but claimed by Japan. NHK reports, according to UNN.
Details
One possible measure is to strengthen the existing sanctions that Tokyo has already imposed on Moscow together with the international community over Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
In Japan, these islands are called the Northern Territories. The Japanese government insists that the islands are an integral part of Japan’s territory. According to the government, the islands were illegally occupied after World War II.
On Thursday, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi commented on Putin’s trip to Iturup, one of these islands. She emphasized that the islands "are an integral part of Japan’s territory in light of historical facts and in accordance with international law."
Takaichi noted that the visit by the incumbent president of Russia "is incompatible with the consistent position of the Japanese government" regarding these islands. She also stated that the visit "hurts the feelings of the Japanese people and is completely unacceptable."
The prime minister added that the visit "has further complicated the restoration of Japanese-Russian relations in the medium and long term."
Japan’s Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi summoned Russia’s ambassador to Japan, Nikolai Nozdrev, to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Tokyo.
During the meeting, Motegi strongly protested Putin’s visit. The minister stated that the very fact that the visit was carried out unilaterally has an extremely negative impact on bilateral relations. Motegi asked Nozdrev to promptly convey these positions to the Russian government.
In 2022, Russia announced its intention to suspend negotiations with Japan on a peace treaty after Tokyo imposed sanctions on Moscow over its invasion of Ukraine. The negotiations concern the territorial dispute over the islands.
The Japanese government continues to pursue a policy of maintaining contacts with Russia, despite the protracted conflict in Ukraine. Last month, Motegi briefly exchanged views with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in the Philippines.
Analysts note that the already-cool bilateral relations are likely to face even greater strain.
We remind you
Putin visited the Kuril island of Iturup for the first time; the island is the subject of a territorial dispute with Japan. He inspected a fish-processing plant, demonstrating Moscow’s position regarding control over the islands.

====================================================================================================

Study offers clues to nearly 100-year-old mystery of Strep A immunity
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
14:46:13 CST
15:46:13 KST

SYDNEY, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- Exposure to a mild or symptom-free strain of Streptococcus pyogenes (Strep A) can trigger the body's immune response and build natural protection, potentially solving a nearly 100-year-old mystery of immunity, new research reveals.
The study by Australia's Griffith University, in collaboration with the Murdoch Children's Research Institute, investigated how immunity developed over time as infection rates declined with age, suggesting progressive immune protection, according to a university statement released on Thursday.
The findings, published in Nature Communications, may help explain why most people develop immunity to Strep A by adulthood despite having had only a few bouts of tonsillitis.
Strep A can cause tonsillitis and school sores and, if untreated, can lead to rheumatic fever, rheumatic heart disease and kidney disease, which disproportionately affect Australia's First Nations peoples.
Researchers found that both symptomatic and asymptomatic participants developed robust immune responses after exposure to a Strep A strain. Antibodies from the asymptomatic participants were able to bind strongly to the exposed strain and kill the Strep A germ in a mouse model of tonsillitis.
"While a person may not feel sick, their body can still learn how to fight the bacteria and remember it from childhood into adulthood," said Ailin Lepletier, the study's lead author from Griffith University.
Up to 30 percent of people are known to carry Strep A in their throats without getting sick, suggesting such "silent infections" may help people gradually build immunity to most strains, Lepletier said. ■

KUALA LUMPUR, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- The East Coast Rail Link (ECRL), a mega rail project in Malaysia being built by the China Communications Construction Company (CCCC), is expected to begin commercial operations by January 2027, Transport Minister Anthony Loke Siew Fook said on Friday.
In the meantime, the railway has reached 95.08 percent overall progress and has entered its testing and commissioning phase, keeping with its project schedule, Loke said in his speech at the launch ceremony of the ECRL Comprehensive Inspection Train (CIT).
"This commendable development is in line with the schedule for the completion of the first phase of the ECRL from Kota Bharu to Gombak in December 2026, and commercial operations starting in January 2027. The second phase of the ECRL from Gombak to Port Klang is expected to be completed by December 2027 to enable full operations in January 2028," he said.
Meanwhile, Loke explained that the CIT, manufactured by CRRC Dalian, is a sophisticated and high-tech train that will be used for inspecting and maintaining the ECRL network. It is capable of recording track geometry parameters, checking train signaling systems, and examining the Overhead Catenary System electrical flow system of the railway.
Loke also said that electricity activation had been completed at all 10 feeder stations along the Kota Bharu-Gombak alignment three days ago, and the project has now shifted its focus towards integrating various railway systems and conducting testing and commissioning to ensure safe and reliable operations.
The ECRL extends from Malaysia's largest transport hub, Port Klang, and runs across the peninsula to the northeastern state of Kelantan. The railway is expected to greatly enhance connectivity and bring more balanced growth to the country by linking its less-developed region on the east coast to the economic heartland on the west coast. ■

S. Korea's money supply rises for 8th month in June
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
14:46:08 CST
15:46:08 KST

SEOUL, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's money supply rose for an eighth straight month amid lingering inflationary pressure, central bank data showed Friday.
The seasonally adjusted M2, called broad money, grew 0.7 percent from a month earlier to 4,213.0 trillion won (2.98 trillion U.S. dollars) in June, keeping an upward trend since November 2025, according to the Bank of Korea (BOK).
Driven by remaining inflationary pressure, the BOK raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 2.75 percent in July, turning toward monetary tightening in about three and a half years since January 2023.
The M1, or narrow money, added 0.4 percent in June on a monthly basis, slower than an increase of 1.8 percent in the previous month.
The M1 refers to currency in circulation, demand deposits and transferable savings deposits equivalent to cash. The M2 adds money market funds, time deposits and financial products that mature in less than two years.
The liquidity of financial institutions, called Lf, swelled 1.0 percent in the cited month, while the liquidity aggregate, the broadest measure of money supply, climbed 0.8 percent.
The Lf includes financial products with a maturity of over two years and liquidity at insurers and brokerages along with M2. The liquidity aggregate adds state and corporate bonds to the Lf. ■

S. Korean banks' household lending growth slows in July
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
14:45:58 CST
15:45:58 KST

SEOUL, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- South Korean banks' household lending growth slowed last month, affected by a cooling stock market and a fall in apartment transactions, central bank data showed Friday.
Debt owed by households to deposit-taking banks totaled 1,194.8 trillion won (about 844.2 billion U.S. dollars) at the end of July, up 5.4 trillion won from a month earlier, according to the Bank of Korea (BOK).
The July growth was slower than an expansion of 7.6 trillion won in the previous month, keeping an upward trend for a fifth straight month.
Banks' mortgage loan rose 3.4 trillion won in July after gaining 4.3 trillion won in the previous month.
The number of apartment transactions across the country slipped to 45,000 in June after staying at 49,000 between March and May.
Other loans, including credit loan, credit line and commercial real estate-backed loan, mounted 2 trillion won in July, lower than an increase of 3.3 trillion won in June.
The slower increase was attributed to the cooling of retail investor participation in the local stock market.
Net stock purchases by retail investors plummeted from 52 trillion won in June to 3.4 trillion won in July.
Banks' corporate loan came to 1,421.1 trillion won at the end of July, up 7.7 trillion won from a month earlier.
Lending to big companies swelled 3.8 trillion won, while loan to small firms climbed 3.9 trillion won. ■

====================================================================================================

New malaria approach turns mosquito bites into immune boosters: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
14:45:58 CST
15:45:58 KST

MELBOURNE, Aug. 14 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in Australia have discovered a new way to help prevent malaria that could turn mosquito bites from a source of deadly infection into ongoing immune boosters against the disease.
The team demonstrated a new vaccination approach that can prime the immune system to fight malaria parasites before they cause disease, with subsequent mosquito bites acting as boosters to strengthen immunity over time, according to a statement released Friday by Australia's Walter and Eliza Hall Institute of Medical Research (WEHI).
According to research published in Science, the approach protected mice from malaria for up to two years, a period covering two malaria seasons in real-world settings.
Researchers developed a novel immunization strategy that paired mosquito-delivered malaria parasites with investigational antimalarial drug compounds, developed by WEHI and biopharmaceutical company MSD.
The compounds were able to trap malaria parasites at the late liver stage, just before they entered the bloodstream and caused disease, triggering a robust immune response that provided durable protection against malaria, the study showed.
Researchers said subsequent mosquito bites could reinforce the immunity, potentially enabling a "vaccinate and boost naturally" approach in malaria-endemic areas.
A long-acting injectable based on the compounds is currently in preclinical development, the team said.
Malaria caused an estimated 610,000 deaths worldwide in 2024, according to the World Health Organization. ■

An Air India Airbus A320 that suddenly lost altitude on August 4 recorded losses in all three hydraulic systems, briefly losing crucial flight controls, media reports on Friday cited an initial Airbus analysis as saying.

Twenty passengers and four crew members were injured during the incident which was classified as "serious" by Indian aviation authorities.
India’s Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau is probing the incident with technical assistance from Airbus and France's BEA.
What do the Airbus findings say?
Airbus shared the technical evaluation after decoding the flight data recorder in a communication to Air India in response to the Indian flag carrier’s request for an assessment .
The plane’s elevators and ailerons, which control its pitch and roll, were unavailable for about four seconds, during which the aircraft pitched upward, Reuters cited Airbus as saying in its preliminary findings.
The first officer applied a full nose-down input during the timeframe but there was "no direct response" from the flight-control surfaces, Reuters cited the assessment as saying, adding that the hydraulic systems recovered within seconds.
The initial analysis has not established a root cause and Airbus has asked Air India to conduct checks on the aircraft’s systems and sensors and to provide more information about the incident.
Airbus has also asked Air India to share the recent maintenance history of hydraulic systems along with more detailed accounts from the pilots.
There was no statement from the planemaker and Air India on the assessment.
Earlier this week, Indian media reports said that the primary captain of the flight tested positive for marijuana in a confirmatory drug test.
On Thursday, an internal communication from Air India showed that the carrier would now conduct a mandatory dope test for all its pilots, expanding checks beyond regulatory requirements.
Under the current rules, airlines in India randomly test at least 10 percent of their flight crew for psychoactive substances each year.
Seven killed in Uttarakhand tunnel mishap, three missing
At least seven workers have died in a tunnel collapse in the northern Indian hill state of Uttarakhand, officials said on Friday, adding that a search was underway for three missing people.
The incident occurred overnight when a landslide sent water and debris streaming into an under-construction tunnel belonging to Tehri Hydro Development Corporation Limited (THDC) in Pipalkoti, in Chamoli district.
According to officials, 22 workers were inside the tunnel at the time of the disaster.
The injured are undergoing treatment.
A multi-agency effort is underway to reach the three workers still trapped inside the tunnel, with teams from the National and State Disaster Response Forces, the Indo-Tibetan Border Police and fire services at the site.
Rescuers are battling rising water and debris during the search, as the state has seen heavy rainfall in recent days.
Visuals circulated by local authorities show rescue teams wearing head-mounted torches and using makeshift rafts to reach the flooded section of the tunnel.
Uttarakhand Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami visited the collapse site on Friday morning and reviewed the rescue operations.
"Evacuating every worker safely is our topmost priority," Dhami said in a statement.
In 2023, a tunnel collapse in Uttarakhand left 41 workers trapped for 17 days before they were rescued.

Industrialized Steel Construction: Lessons From a Naval Foundry in Thailand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
06:45:00 UTC
15:45:00 KST

Industrial buildings are often expected to prioritize efficiency, production, and technical performance above all else. As a result, architectural quality is frequently treated as secondary to functional requirements. Advances in material systems, however, allow industrial facilities to balance both, creating buildings that respond to climate, improve working conditions, and establish a distinctive architectural identity.
Between design and construction, fabrication methods, logistics, and assembly are reshaping construction processes and workflows, particularly when steel systems are involved. Industrialized construction emphasizes the integration of design and production, recognizing the value of coordinated systems that deliver a high degree of predictability and precision—from material delivery to labor coordination. But it also depends on planning material and equipment transport and storage, and scheduling the people and equipment needed, operating simultaneously to make construction more efficient and precise.
Lightweight coated steel, for example, has become an important architectural resource. Reducing structural loads and simplifying construction, it enables larger spans, greater design flexibility, and durable envelopes suited to demanding industrial environments. Its versatility allows architects to integrate daylight, natural ventilation, and expressive façade compositions while meeting the technical requirements expected of industrial buildings.
Opened in 2023, the Foundry of the Royal Thai Naval Dockyard is dedicated to the production of bronze propellers for naval vessels and encompasses approximately 2,300 square meters. Originally located at the Thonburi Naval Dockyard in Bangkok, the new facility was relocated to the Phra Chulachomklao Naval Dockyard in Samut Prakan Province, minimizing its impact on the local community, the environment, and neighboring structures.
As a manufacturing facility requiring large, wide-span spaces, the range of suitable material solutions was limited and BlueScope's metal sheets were used for both the roof and facade cladding, providing a lightweight construction system that was easy to install. Inspired by the simplified wave patterns generated by rotating propellers, the design successfully harmonizes with the project's context.
 "To withstand the coastal environment, this project prioritizes the selection of corrosion-resistant materials by utilizing highly durable, specially coated steel alongside lightweight materials. These properties facilitate the design of architectural details that optimize ventilation efficiency, while also streamlining the construction process for faster and more convenient assembly."—Naksit Wisetmora
Designed by Naksit Wisetmora, the Industrial Foundry for Marine Vessels demonstrates how architectural design can be aligned with the capabilities of selected materials and their potential applications. While the project's design prioritizes daylighting and natural ventilation strategies, its material palette—composed of steel structures and pre-painted steel systems—supports this approach by offering significant advantages in terms of construction speed, cost efficiency, and design flexibility. These qualities make the system particularly effective for addressing complex architectural challenges.
 "The construction of this building was carried out entirely through on-site assembly and installation. This approach capitalized on the ample surrounding space, which served as an ideal staging and preparation area for materials prior to installation, thereby ensuring a seamless construction workflow." —Naksit Wisetmora
Just as the building's angled wall geometry is carefully calculated, the installation of louvers not only facilitates natural ventilation and controls the amount of daylight entering the interior but also enhances the building's visual appeal. Complementing the metal cladding of the architectural structure and reinforcing a cohesive aesthetic, these elements help prevent glare and reduce heat gain from the afternoon sun coming from the west. In addition, skylights reduce the need for artificial lighting during daylight hours.
As Naksit Wisetmora explained, the design team applied lessons learned from the previous facility, where natural light created uncomfortable glare for workers. The new structure continued to prioritize the integration of daylight to provide adequate illumination for operational tasks while supporting energy-efficiency goals. The openings allow just the right amount of natural light to enter the building. Triangular openings were strategically incorporated instead of placing them along the sides of the structure, minimizing direct sunlight exposure within the interior workspaces and for building occupants. In this way, technology and aesthetics come together to maximize not only the functionality of the spaces but also the performance of the materials.
Regarding ventilation, the factory's production process relies on brass-melting furnaces that generate substantial amounts of accumulated heat. The building was designed to maximize passive cooling and natural ventilation, reducing dependence on mechanical air-conditioning systems while promoting long-term energy savings.
By prioritizing optimal daylighting and ventilation as key design drivers, the factory's rectangular architectural form enables efficient space planning for machinery placement while also accommodating potential future expansion. Recipient of both the winner of 2024 BlueScope Steel Architectural Awards – Thailand – Industrial and winner of 2024 BlueScope Steel Architectural Awards – ASEAN – Industrial, The Industrial Foundry for Marine Vessels demonstrates how contemporary industrial architecture can meet demanding technical requirements while creating spaces that are efficient and thoughtfully designed.

Nigel Farage wins landslide, defeats comedian dressed as trash and returns to Parliament
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage won his self-triggered by-election in Clacton on Friday but saw his strategy to silence critics backfire when his main rival Count Binface, a comedian dressed as a trash can, took more than a quarter of the vote. Farage, one of Britain's leading Brexit campaigners, in a highly unusual move, did not turn up at the vote count in the southern English seaside resort of Clacton because he said the police had advised him there was a campaign to disrupt the result. He also cancelled a victory speech planned for later on Friday.
"I am damned if I am going to stand on a stage, having won a resounding victory ... and be demeaned and humiliated by nobodies," Farage told supporters at a party before the result was announced. The election was triggered after Farage resigned from parliament last month to seek a fresh mandate from voters in what he described as a war against an establishment bent on discrediting him over taking undeclared gifts from donors.
The result, while a victory, underscored the political risks of Farage's gamble. With a parliamentary investigation into his finances set to resume, the vote may have done little to remove a threat he wanted to sideline.
Reform's momentum shows signs of slowing
After Britain's main parties pulled out of the race, calling it a self-serving stunt, Farage's main challenger ended up being Count Binface, a figure created by comedian Jonathan Harvey, who has become a fixture of fun at British elections.
While Farage took 62.8% of the vote, Count Binface, whose policies included capping the price of ice cream cones and conscripting anyone using a speakerphone on public transport, secured 26.7%. The turnout was 44%. After enjoying a lengthy lead in national opinion polls, Reform has seen its popularity wane. That has been driven partly by the funding accusations made against Farage, who is under investigation in parliament over whether he should have declared a £5 million ($6.75 million) gift from a cryptocurrency billionaire investor.
Laura Richards-Gray, a politics lecturer at Birkbeck University in London, said the absence of major-party opponents undermined Farage's attempt to turn it into what he called a "people versus the establishment" contest.
"This has backfired, particularly nationally, as Farage lost control of the narrative," she said.
A rise in support for the governing Labour Party has also weakened Farage's position. Since Andy Burnham became prime minister last month, Labour has been enjoying a bounce in ratings, with the party leading Reform 28% to 25%. Burnham has dominated the airwaves and social media in his first few weeks in office, and while the next national election is expected in three years' time, he appears to be consolidating a left-leaning bloc around Labour.
Reform, on the other hand, is competing for a divided right-wing vote with the Conservative Party and the anti-immigration party Restore Britain gaining in support.
Gift from billionaire crypto investor
While Farage was always expected to win the election, his share of the vote was lower than forecast by a Survation poll conducted last month, which predicted he would secure 73% of the vote, with Count Binface on 20%.
The parliamentary watchdog is expected to continue its investigation into his financial declarations once he returns to parliament.
At the heart of the investigation is whether he should have declared the gift from a Thailand-based billionaire before the 2024 national election. Under parliamentary rules, members of parliament must declare any donations received in the year preceding an election within one month of taking office.
Farage has admitted receiving the money, but not declaring it, saying he has done nothing wrong because it was a personal gift.
If the parliamentary authorities conclude that Farage breached declaration rules, he could face suspension from parliament, and another vote to retain his seat, when the main parties would most probably field candidates.

From world leaders paying their respects to his economic legacy, here is some of the SCMP’s reporting on Zhu Rongji’s death

1. Zhu Rongji, China’s chief engineer of economic reform, dies aged 97

“Regardless of what lies ahead – be it a minefield or a deep abyss – I will forge ahead unswervingly, dedicating my entire life and energy to the country until my dying day.” Those words, spoken at the dawn of his premiership, came to define Zhu Rongji, China’s towering economic reformer who died in Beijing at the age of 97.

Turn-of-the-century images of Zhu Rongji alongside former US president Bill Clinton have largely accompanied coverage following the former Chinese premier’s death. The moment in April 1999 was more than a diplomatic milestone.

5. The 11 key achievements of China’s ‘iron premier’ Zhu Rongji – in his own words
Known for his sharp intellect, no-nonsense demeanour and relentless drive for reform, China’s former premier Zhu Rongji was the primary architect of the country’s transition from an isolated, rigidly planned economy to a market-driven titan connected to the rest of the world.
6. China’s Zhu Rongji remembered as chief engineer of economic transformation
Born in 1928, Zhu Rongji graduated with an electrical engineering degree before entering the civil service, working on economic policy at both regional and national levels. He became mayor in 1988 and the chief of China’s Communist Party in Shanghai in 1989, and then rose to become vice-premier, before serving as premier from 1998 to 2003.

Tributes have been flooding in for former Chinese premier Zhu Rongji, the reformist statesman who played a leading role in integrating China’s economy into the global system and charmed neighbouring countries with his candid diplomacy.

US CENTCOM chief pushing for renewed strikes on Iran, claims Israeli media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
06:36:44 UTC
