Tougher crops and beaver dams: how UK farmers are tackling drought
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
06:00:20 UTC
15:00:20 KST

Ponds and collection tanks, drought-resistant crops and a certain rodent. As the climate crisis brings more extreme weather to Britain, farmers are experimenting with new tactics to tackle drought – and flooding.
The string of heatwaves and drought conditions experienced across vast swathes of Britain this summer has brought a series of challenges for food producers, particularly those growing crops more suited to the UK’s traditional climate.
Hot and dry weather has resulted in the earliest UK cereals harvest in at least 20 years, according to the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board. The lack of rainfall has led to cauliflowers looking “suntanned” – with a yellow colouring instead of white, while cucumber plants have produced misshapen fruit and broccoli is undersized, forcing the UK to import more vegetables than usual this summer.
While many farmers have installed reservoirs to store water for periods of drought, these can be costly, require planning permission and are sometimes not sufficient to cope with long dry spells. But some farmers are turning to more novel solutions as they struggle to nurture crops and cattle in the heat.
Improving soils and digging ponds
In south Cambridgeshire, Martin Lines has already finished his harvest, a month earlier than usual, after navigating the second hot, dry and windy summer in a row.
“There’s like a hot hairdryer on everything, and it just saps the moisture out,” says Lines, an arable farmer who also leads the Nature Friendly Farming Network.
On his own farm and across the network he leads, farmers are improving the health of their soils, to allow them to hold more water, as well as creating water storage to save rain.
“We’re focused on the soil, we’re focusing on having bigger, bushier hedges and more trees in the landscape to slow the flow of air down,” he says.
Lines believes farmers should assess their annual water needs and how much rainfall they can store, through rainwater harvesting, where large tanks are connected to gutters on farm buildings.
“What we need to do is connect up to local drainage and rivers. Most rivers have digital flow sensors now, so the moment there is excess flow that is going to go out to sea, farmers should be messaged to say ‘turn your pump on’,” he says. “We could manage this flow a lot smarter than we are now.”
Reviving marshes as reservoirs
Many areas of farmland sit on former marshes and have been drained using pumps and ditches for decades, or even centuries.
In some areas, farmers are experimenting with changing the system so water is stored on their land instead of being pumped into rivers and out to sea. This can help cope with flooding in the winter and during periods of drought while increasing resources for wildlife.
West Pikefish Farm, run by the Smith family, has historically grown apples near the River Teise near Maidstone in Kent.
It is using an old orchard, grubbed up because it regularly flooded, to create ponds, scrapes and other wetland features that fill with water in the winter and feed into a larger winter lagoon. The land can still be grazed and is poised to be a traditional orchard in future.
The lagoon will store 4m litres of water for summer irrigation that has been filtered of silt by the neighbouring wetlands.
“It’s about risk management,” says farmer James Smith from Pikefish Farm, who says he was concerned about access to water during times of drought as it is becoming more difficult to take water from the Teise. The set-up also helps manage flooding. “When it is winter and the river is in spate it has a bellows effect and the river can flow into these features and reduce risk downstream.”
“We are proposing these features could be rolled out all along the catchment, at landscape scale, making it more resilient, holding water in the landscape rather than sending it down as quick as we can to the nearest village.”
His only frustration is that the project, which is in partnership with several bodies including the South East Rivers Trust, the government waste reduction body Wrap and the Environment Agency is taking longer than expected to break ground amid the need for planning consents and various surveys. He had hoped to start work this summer but it is now likely to be next year.
“We are trying to create a roadmap so hopefully it can become more streamlined,” he says.
Growing different crops
The changing climate is also requiring farmers to diversify, changing the crops they grow on their farms.
Lines says he is “now looking at what Europe is growing like sunflowers and soya beans”.
Lines and others believe legumes – a large family of plants including beans, peas, chickpeas and lentils – could also provide an answer for the changing climate, as they require hot, dry conditions, and could boost the UK’s food security.
Despite this, the variability of the British climate means such experiments are not always a success. “We tried sunflowers a couple of years ago and that was the wettest winter and spring. It’s the unpredictability that is really challenging, we don’t actually know how the next season is going to be,” Lines says.
Researchers including Prof Pete Iannetta at the James Hutton Institute, which focuses on researching land, crops, water and the environment, believe the UK needs to grow more legumes to feed both humans and livestock.
He says legumes occupy just 5% of UK cropped land. “In northern Germany they are growing tropical legumes, things like cowpeas [such as black-eyed peas] and soya beans. These were not traditionally associated with northern Europe and would come from India and Myanmar. Crops such as chickpeas are becoming more viable, we have even got some in the south of England and the quality will improve over time.”
Beavers – natural environmental engineers
There has been almost no rain since the beginning of June on Chris Jones’s beef farm in Cornwall and the intense heat means soil is drying out.
But Jones has not had to bring in feed for his cattle, which are still grazing the field thanks to some simple measures and some helpful rodents.
Jones has planted more trees to help keep water in the land and to provide shelter for cattle. He also practices rotational grazing, which involves breaking fields into smaller paddocks and moving the herd frequently so it only comes back to the same spot every three to six months.
But Jones’s best asset is a family of beavers who, although kept within a relatively small enclosure since their introduction nine years ago, have built a reservoir that contains 3m litres of water.
The beavers’ actions not only help retain water in the land but slow the flow of potential flood waters in rainy periods. Their work preserves damp areas that can be grazed during drought while their dam can be pumped out if necessary. It came in handy in 2022, when many farms ran dry in drought conditions.
This year, Jones is eyeing the dam again: “We haven’t yet had to pump out but we may well have to.”
He says his tactics are intended to work “with minimal financial and environmental cost” and beavers are “the most useful and cheapest way to build reserves of water on our land”.
“Since last year we stopped being green and occasionally hot and dry Britain and joined the Mediterranean. The race is on now to adapt.”
From crop shading to drone ‘dusting’
Katie Cross, a water specialist at Wrap, says farmers need a “combination of tools” to become more resilient, from nature-based tactics to water collection.
In Cumbria, not known for being a dry area, the changing climate has prompted an experiment in which nine cattle farmers are adding extra guttering and huge water butts to store water from farm building roofs during the winter for use during dry spells.
In Norfolk, farmers are trialling strip tillage – leaving strips of unploughed land between crops of maize or sugar beet so that more water is kept in the soil and there is less need for irrigation. Planting cover crops between seasons is a more widely adopted method of retaining moisture and preventing run-off.
Providing more shade – using trees or other methods such as “dusting” the top of polytunnels with specialist shading substances using drones – can also preserve moisture so plants need less irrigation.
In some parts of the world, including France and the US, farmers are experimenting with using solar panels above their crops as a form of shading while generating energy.

====================================================================================================

‘It’s one huge adventure playground’: readers’ best summer trips in the lakes and mountains of Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
06:00:20 UTC
15:00:20 KST

Late summer hiking in the Austrian Alps
Haldensee is a clear, sparkling cold lake located at the bottom of the Tannheimer Tal valley in the Austrian Alps (about 90 miles south-west of Munich). We visited last year, just when summer was on its way out, and it was too cold to skinny-dip in the lake (unless you were very brave). Nonetheless, if you’re a hiker, a ski lift takes you up into the Allgäu Alps where you can walk through dense forest to Bad Kissinger Hütte serving refreshing apfelschorle, warming soups and seasonal bakes to refuel for the journey downhill. When going down, we were accompanied by tinkling cattle, ambling along the mountain-side springs, which made the experience so much more memorable.
Kovida
Mountain tracks of Lake Garda, Italy
Northern Lake Garda, where the mountains tower above the lake, is one huge adventure playground: walking, cycling, climbing, boat trips and all manner of watersports on the lake. There are castles, waterfalls and valley cycle trails. The old Ponale mountain road might be the pick for cycling (best on ebike) and walking. It winds through tunnels and clings to the rock with spectacular views over the lake. At Ponale Alto enjoy a hearty pasta dish washed down with a local beer or wine, before returning downhill all the way.
Dave Thomas
Swiss bliss near Mont Blanc
Skip the crowds of Chamonix and spend a week at La Fouly, in south-west Switzerland. Some walking routes are busy (it is a hub for the famous Tour du Mont Blanc walk) but there are plenty of walks to choose from, many of which are not on the main trail. Walk to the Lacs de Fenêtre, where you can hear the gurgling burps of rock ptarmigans at first light, and the shrieks of marmots as you descend back down into the valley. We camped by cool, fast-flowing rivers at Camping des Glaciers in La Fouly.
Daniel
Meadows and cowbells in Slovenia
The loudest sound in Slovenia’s Logar Valley is usually a cowbell. A narrow road runs through flower-filled meadows to the foot of the Kamnik-Savinja Alps, but it’s best explored on foot or by bike, stopping at the little farms that sell homemade cheese and apple juice. Follow the easy trail to the 90-metre Rinka waterfall, then linger over lunch at one of the mountain inns to enjoy the view. I stayed overnight in a family-run guesthouse, and by early evening the day visitors had gone, leaving the valley almost silent except for swallows and grazing cattle.
Susanna C
Dragonflies and lilies on Italy’s secret lake
The spring-fed Lago di Monate, between the much larger lakes of Maggiore and di Varese, has possibly the freshest swimming water in Italy, chiefly because of its longstanding ban on motorboats. You can hire paddleboards to cross the calm surface to vast lily beds, blooming in summer and alive with dragonflies. The grassy beach with sunbeds and umbrellas at Il Coppale is very reasonable with evening meal (fresh fish, naturally) on their terrace at about €25 with a view over the lake to the Alps.
Tim Leadbetter
Alpine ambience in Bavaria
Looking for a reasonable budget autumnal trip, a search on the usual sites led us to Bavaria, and the outdoorsy town of Ruhpolding. Alpine atmosphere was immediately delivered, with a charming unpretentious ambience. There is a really impressive waterpark and cool blue lakes, such as Lödensee and Weitsee. Hikes through classical Alpine scenery took us to an alm, a mountain refuge in high meadows where local milk and beer was served with platters of meat and cheese. A little further away the huge Chiemsee gave us a day at the beach. A stop in Munich on the way back allowed us to visit the excellent BMW museum, part of which is free.
Brian Lowry
Cycling the foothills of the French Pyrenees
Cycling the Velosud this summer was the perfect trip to the mountains without having to cycle up or down them. We spent two weeks leisurely following the signposted route in the foothills of the Pyrenees, often alongside rivers, with mountain views every day. It’s all either traffic-free or on very quiet roads, and passes by spa towns such as Salies-du-Salat, the beautiful Foix and Mirepoix, and lovely, low-key but well equipped campsites (always with swimming pool, aperitif and morning croissants).
Rowan
A cross-border trek on the Camino Francés
I’ve walked close to 2,000km of the Camino de Santiago, traversing Spain from the Pyrenees to the Galician coast and following the crashing waves of the Atlantic Portuguese coast in northern Portugal. One of the most stunning stretches of the Camino Francés (part of the Camino de Santiago) takes you from the French Pyrenean town of St-Jean-Pied-de-Port to the Spanish village of Roncesvalles. It’s a very tough climb, but it’s well worth the effort. In the early morning mist, as you approach the border with Spain, the panoramic views from above the cloud line will take your breath away. A truly spectacular experience.
Stephen Taylor
Tuscany’s wild side
It’s amazing that the Alpi Apuane are not better known. This raw, jagged cluster of marble peaks forms a dramatic backdrop to the bucket-and-spade beaches of northern Tuscany. These mountains are laced with challenging trails, including the multi-day Via Vandelli, linking Modena to the coast. The valleys shelter quiet, refreshing streams and half-forgotten villages. Above the treeline, the hiker is rewarded with expansive views of the mountains, the sea, and the surreal marble quarries hewn from the mountainsides. This is the wild side of Tuscany.
Robert
Winning tip: The Vosges mountains by train
The Vosges mountains in eastern France are made up of forest-covered rounded peaks called ballons, and are accessible by train. The line between Colmar and Metzeral provides easy access into the Wormsa valley, where forest paths climb past streams to the peaceful Lac du Fischboedle, surrounded by trees. From there you can climb the third highest mountain in the Vosges, Hohneck (1,363 metres), for sweeping views towards the Alps. The food in the region is delicious, especially tarte flambée (flammekueche), a traditional thin flatbread topped with creme fraiche, onions and bacon.
Hannah

Family’s bankruptcy drives US-graduated Chinese student to become acclaimed chef

A former wealthy Chinese student in the US transformed her life into that of a private chef after her family faced bankruptcy, establishing a business that now earns her up to US$118,600 annually.
The 31-year-old woman, known by the pseudonym Chengzi, attended the New York Film Academy before completing a master’s degree in Britain.
She once lived in downtown Manhattan, aspiring to break into Hollywood as a film director, as reported by Sanlian Lifeweek.
Her parents, who owned a business, financed her education and living expenses. However, upon her graduation, her father revealed that the family had gone bankrupt and urged her to return to China.
Chengzi refused, expressing her desire to test her limits independently. Her father warned her that if she stayed in the US, she would need to be self-sufficient.

====================================================================================================

"In our country, abandonment is normalised": pets still left behind
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
05:59:08 UTC
14:59:08 KST

One day they have a bed, a sofa, a place in the home, with someone to fill their bowls. Then, in an instant, many pets lose everything and end up dumped on roads or left at shelters.
Ziro and Mike spent their whole lives in happy homes. For both of them, water, food and having their owners nearby was all they needed. Each lived alone with their elderly owners as one another's only company.
They did not know each other, did not walk the same streets, but at the end of their lives they shared the same home: SOS Animal Portugal. In both cases, the owners left no document indicating what should happen to their pets; most likely they did not realise they could. Their future was therefore decided by a relative who chose to leave them on the street.
Ziro wandered the streets of Setúbal, was run over and beaten, and was left with serious injuries to his mouth.
Mike was a ticking time bomb: a heart disease dictated his daily life and, despite the best efforts of the neighbours, friends of his owner, they could not help him in the way he needed. He stayed at SOS Animal until he died. Ziro is still at the association, waiting to be adopted.
Is animal abandonment punishable in Portugal?
Abandoning an animal in Portugal is a crime and has been punishable by law since 2014 with a prison sentence of up to six months or an income-determined daily fine of up to 60 days, but it is not always possible to see justice done.
Sandra Duarte Cardoso, a veterinary surgeon and president of SOS Animal, has been fighting numerous battles in the name of animal protection and welfare.
"The microchip [for companion animals] is registered in the name of the person who has died, so the administrative offence is issued in the name of the deceased," she explains.
"To date, of all the complaints we have filed – because whoever inherits the estate should also inherit the animals – none has ever resulted in a conviction, so no one has suffered any consequences for dumping their mother's or father's dog or cat on the street," she tells Euronews in an interview.
This Saturday, 15 August, is International Abandoned Animals Day. In Portugal, summer is one of the worst times for the problem. "Nobody thinks about moving country, or house, and leaving their children behind or dropping them off at an organisation, but with animals they do," laments Sandra Duarte Cardoso, who deals with the situation every day.
In Portugal, microchipping dogs became compulsory in 2008 and cats in 2022, a measure introduced to combat animal abandonment. However, the rule is often ignored and, on its own, does not appear to have led to a fall in the number of abandoned pets.
The president of SOS Animal distinguishes between two types of situation: "There are surrenders, when people hand over their animals and look for a solution for an animal they no longer want or are able to keep; and there is abandonment, when they simply open the car door and leave the animal, or put it in a bag and dump it at the door of an association," she explains.
The National Republican Guard (GNR) warned in a statement at the end of July that, between 2024 and the first half of 2026, more than 2,400 animal abandonment crimes had been recorded and, in this context, 28 people had been arrested across the country.
According to the force, July and August see the highest number of incidents, with 142 cases (38.1 per cent of the annual total), linked to people travelling on holiday.
'People would throw animals over the fence'
SOS Animal, a non-governmental environmental organisation formally established in 2007, has a mission to protect and defend animals and their habitat. In addition to its veterinary clinic, it runs a sanctuary whose address is currently not made public.
For a time, animals were being dumped there on a daily basis. "At the beginning, people would throw animals over the fence. I remember a case of a four-week-old puppy that was thrown in with other dogs running loose here, a goat that broke its legs, and cats were 'our daily bread'," she recalls in horror.
For Sandra Duarte Cardoso, there is a serious problem of "civic education" when it comes to our relationship with animals, and she struggles to understand how people capable of creating life can "discard another life".
"In our country, abandonment has been normalised," she begins, describing the daily stream of emails the association receives from people threatening the NGO that they will abandon their animals if it does not take them in.
"They are so completely comfortable with this option that it becomes a form of blackmail. When no one in their right mind says: 'If you don't help me with my child, who has a problem, I'm going to abandon them, I'm going to leave them by the side of the road'," she says.
Sandra Duarte Cardoso traces these attitudes and behaviours back to the way people see animals. "Animals are still seen as a possession, as something a person owns, that is useful up to a point and, when it no longer is, they think they have the right to get rid of this 'thing' and that caring for it is not a non-negotiable responsibility," she says.
Why do people abandon animals?
In an article for the scientific Journal of Applied Animal Welfare Science (JAAWS), published in 2022, the veterinary surgeon set out to identify the factors associated with the abandonment of dogs and cats by their owners in Portugal.
The reasons most often cited were "lack of time to care for the animal", "illness of the animal", "lack of space" at home or aggressive behaviour towards other animals. The fact that animals destroyed things at home also came up frequently.
The post-pandemic period revealed just how many people lacked real commitment. "During Covid there was a boom in adoptions because many people suddenly had more time at home and adopted without knowing what their lives would look like later," she recalls. However, many had to return to their workplaces and, once they resumed their former routines, many of the animals adopted during the pandemic were returned to shelters.
The rising cost of having a pet
According to Eurostat data from 2025, the cost of veterinary care and related services has risen by more than 30 per cent in the eurozone and by almost 37 per cent across the EU over the last decade, which has also been a factor that may be driving up the number of abandoned pets.
"In fact, people often let animals reach an indescribable breaking point, and it is not because they want to, or because they are unaware of the animal's pain, but because they have no money," says the veterinary surgeon.
Putting animals down also ends up being a decision that is often taken not because the animal has no other chance, but because people cannot afford the treatment. "This is a dreadful situation," she says.
For Sandra Duarte Cardoso, the state's responsibility for this issue is glaring. The veterinary surgeon is highly critical of successive governments. "We are facing this structural, nationwide, agonising problem, and there needs to be an effective national strategy that also includes the islands," she argues.
According to the president of SOS Animal, methodologies and cooperation proposals from international organisations have already been submitted, but "governments do not treat this as a priority".
Should pet sterilisation be compulsory?
One of the measures put forward by Sandra Duarte Cardoso is the compulsory sterilisation of dogs and cats. The proposal envisages large dogs being neutered by nine months of age and small dogs by six months. As for cats, she argues that "all should be neutered by five months of age".
In proven cases of financial hardship, people would receive a voucher for the sterilisation, which could cover the full cost or part of it.
In Greece, the sterilisation of dogs and cats may be compulsory, unless owners send in a sample of their animals' genetic material as a precaution. This allows the authorities to identify the animal in the event of abandonment or if litters from these animals are found.
Countries such as Belgium, Spain, Austria and Germany all have mandatory cat sterilisation laws, albeit with different nuances.
SOS Animal promotes responsible animal adoption and has its own protocol that requires supporting documents. It also urges people to reflect seriously on their routines and living conditions before adopting an animal. "We do not make things easy; we are quite demanding, because we care much more about quality than quantity," she explains.
"We would rather have 80 or 100 adoptions a year, knowing that the return rate is zero, than 300 adoptions followed by a huge number of animals being brought back. That is extremely traumatic for the animals," she concludes.

Trump ordered the U.S. Navy to return steam catapults to aircraft carriers - WSJ
Kyiv • UNN
According to media reports, U.S. President Donald Trump instructed the Navy to dismantle the electromagnetic system for launching fighter jets on Gerald R. Ford-class aircraft carriers and return to steam catapults. The decision, signed in a memorandum, is likely to cost billions of dollars.
U.S. President Donald Trump ordered the U.S. Navy to restore outdated technologies on aircraft carriers, which will cost billions of dollars, The Wall Street Journal reports, citing sources, UNN writes.
Details
"President Trump instructed the Navy to dismantle the complex system for launching fighter jets from aircraft carriers and return to using steam catapults," the publication says.
The U.S. Navy, as noted, has been contesting this for many years, and such a move will likely cost billions of dollars.
American officials say that on Thursday Trump signed a national security memorandum regulating these changes, which include dismantling the electromagnetic catapult system used on Gerald R. Ford-class aircraft carriers.

Kyrgyz president Japarov to seek second term
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14

World Insights: Do recent powerful earthquakes signal heightened seismic activity in South America?
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
13:53:50 CST
14:53:50 KST

by Xinhua writers Tan Huiting and Tian Rui
MEXICO CITY/CARACAS, Aug. 13 (Xinhua) -- A series of powerful earthquakes in Venezuela and Colombia, along with recent seismic events in Peru and Chile, has raised concern over whether South America is entering a period of unusually intense seismic activity.
Experts, however, said there is no evidence of an abnormal increase in earthquakes across the region, and the perception that earthquakes are becoming more frequent may partly reflect faster access to seismic information and heightened public attention after recent devastating quakes caused heavy casualties.
DIFFERENT TECTONIC SETTINGS
A magnitude-7.4 earthquake struck Colombia on Monday, with its epicenter about 20 km from San Jose del Palmar in the western department of Choco and at a depth of 96 km, according to the Colombian Geological Service.
The death toll in Colombia has risen to 281, with 3,971 people injured, 379 missing and more than 100,000 affected, the country's National Unit for Disaster Risk Management said Thursday.
Less than two months earlier, neighboring Venezuela was hit by two powerful earthquakes measuring magnitude 7.2 and 7.5 on June 24. The two shallow quakes, both at a depth of about 10 km, occurred less than a minute apart. Venezuelan authorities have put the death toll at more than 6,300.
Despite their geographical proximity, the earthquakes in Venezuela and Colombia occurred in different tectonic settings.
Feliciano De Santis, president of the Geological Society of Venezuela, told Xinhua that both countries lie on the South American Plate, but the tectonic processes responsible for their earthquakes differ.
In Venezuela, seismic activity is largely associated with the boundary between the Caribbean and South American plates, where horizontal movement produces predominantly strike-slip faulting. Colombia, by contrast, is strongly affected by the subduction of the Nazca Plate beneath the South American Plate.
Those differences help explain the characteristics of the recent earthquakes.
In Venezuela, De Santis said, earthquakes are often shallow, allowing seismic energy to produce particularly intense shaking near the epicenter and fault zone.
The Colombian quake, however, occurred much deeper. Although seismic energy weakens as it travels toward the surface, deeper earthquakes can be felt across a much wider area and produce varying degrees of damage over a broader region.
Andres Folguera, a geologist with Argentina's National Scientific and Technical Research Council, also said the two earthquakes involved different geological processes, with shallow faulting involved in Venezuela and deeper plate deformation behind the Colombian event.
NO EVIDENCE OF ABNORMAL SEISMIC CYCLE
Wang Tun, deputy director of the Key Laboratory of Mountain Hazards and Engineering Safety under the Chinese Academy of Sciences and head of the Institute of Care-Life in Chengdu, said the two epicenters were about 1,200 km apart and that there was no direct stress-triggering relationship between the events.
"They should be regarded as independent earthquakes," he said.
The recent events, Wang added, do not indicate that the South American Plate has entered a period of heightened activity.
De Santis reached a similar conclusion, saying current data provide no sufficient basis for describing seismic activity in South America as abnormal.
According to the Venezuelan geologist, global earthquake catalogs show that strong earthquakes are not rare on a worldwide scale, with roughly 15 to 20 earthquakes of magnitude 7 to 8 occurring in a typical year.
A more systematic assessment of whether 2026 has been unusual would require comparing the full year's global seismic record with data from previous years, he said.
Wang said the growing perception among the public that earthquakes are occurring more frequently is partly related to improvements in seismic monitoring and information services.
People today receive data on earthquake magnitude, location and aftershocks almost immediately, while the severe casualties caused by the recent Venezuela and Colombia earthquakes have further increased public sensitivity to seismic events.
The successive strong earthquakes do not mean that other South American countries also face a higher probability of a major quake this year, Wang said.
Nor would the seismic activity spread along the Pacific "Ring of Fire" toward Asia as a chain reaction, he added, noting that the distance over which stress changes from a magnitude-7.5 earthquake could significantly trigger another event is far smaller than the distance across the Pacific.
Scientists also caution against trying to predict which country might be struck next.
"These things cannot be predicted," De Santis said, stressing that disaster prevention is far more important than attempts to forecast the precise time and location of future earthquakes.
PREVENTION MATTERS MORE THAN PREDICTION
Whether a powerful earthquake develops into a major disaster depends on far more than magnitude alone.
Earthquake depth, local geology, the way seismic waves travel, population density and, crucially, the quality of buildings can all determine the scale of casualties and destruction.
These factors explain why earthquakes of similar magnitudes can produce sharply different outcomes between countries, cities or even neighborhoods within the same city, De Santis said.
For countries along South America's active plate boundaries, experts said, earthquakes themselves cannot be prevented. However, the scale of the disasters they cause can be substantially reduced through safer buildings, effective warning systems and stronger public preparedness.
Wang said current technology still cannot reliably predict when and where the next major earthquake will strike.
"Prevention is more effective than prediction," he said.
Strengthening buildings, expanding the use of seismic isolation and energy-dissipation technologies, improving construction codes and ensuring that those standards are strictly enforced can significantly cut casualties and economic losses, Wang said.
Earthquake early-warning systems and stronger public preparedness are also essential, he added.
De Santis pointed to Chile, one of the world's most earthquake-prone countries, as an example of how strict construction standards can reduce losses from powerful earthquakes.
He said governments in seismic zones should continuously update building codes, strengthen oversight throughout the design, construction, inspection and maintenance process, and assess and reinforce vulnerable existing structures.
Public education is equally important, De Santis said. People should know evacuation routes in their homes, schools and workplaces and understand how to respond calmly and correctly when strong shaking begins, he added. ■

25 years of AK Party and Türkiye’s rise as a regional and global actor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
05:52:38 UTC
14:52:38 KST

As the AK Party celebrates its 25th anniversary on August 14, a grateful Türkiye will look back at the quarter century as the defining period of the country’s rise in the global pecking order.
Coming to power shortly after its founding, the party has brought about a major transformation in Türkiye, both domestically and in the global order.
The AK Party-led government took control by eliminating entrenched military and bureaucratic power centres, acknowledging cultural and social diversity, fixing the economy and strengthening ties between the people and the state.
With a firm grasp of the country’s internal affairs, the party could then turn its attention to formulating and implementing a robust and pragmatic foreign policy – one that led to Türkiye’s growing regional and global role.
In its early years, the AK Party government focused on improving the economy and international standing, with the goals of European Union membership and better relations with neighbours.
Over time, it pursued a multifaceted opening extending to the Middle East, the Balkans, Africa, the Caucasus, Central Asia, and more distant geographies, both to strengthen and expand its economy and to increase its regional power.
At the heart of this transformation lies the transfer of increased economic capacity, an expanding diplomatic network, and more independent security tools into foreign policy.
According to World Bank data, Turkish GDP rose from $236 billion to $1.6 trillion in 2025.
The AK Party government sought to diversify Türkiye’s relations without severing traditional Western ties.
The start of EU accession negotiations in 2005 marked the Western dimension, while Türkiye sought to reduce tensions with neighbours, open to Africa, pursue economic rapprochement with Gulf countries, and strengthen institutional ties with Central Asia.
With public support and the influence of the international conjuncture, President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his allies ended military tutelage by amending the Constitution and laws.
During the second decade of its governance, the AK Party had to contend with the Arab uprisings in the Middle East, the chaos in Syria, tensions in the Eastern Mediterranean, the July 15 coup attempt, the West’s dislike of Turkish autonomy, tensions between Russia and Ukraine, and the Qatar embargo.
After this process, Ankara leaned towards a more security-centric and independent decision-making process.
This strategic independence characterised Turkish foreign policy orientation over the last fifteen years. The constitutional amendment in 2011, which broke the military's tutelage, enabled it to conduct security and foreign policy more freely.
Türkiye's strategic rise
The civilian AK Party administration has strengthened NATO ties while developing flexible relationships with other centres, including Russia, Central Asia, the Gulf, Asia, and Africa.
With this autonomy, Türkiye has strengthened its defence capabilities.
While the rate of domestic production in the defence industry was two percent in 2002, today it exceeds 80 percent and is still increasing, a very impressive achievement.
Turkish UAV technologies, warships, armoured vehicles, missile systems, and electronic warfare capabilities helped the Turkish economy and became foreign policy tools that deepened relations with Pakistan, Ukraine, the Gulf countries, Africa, and Central Asia.
The Bayraktar UAV and the 5th-generation Kaan fighter jet have stood out globally. As a result of these successes, Türkiye’s defence and aerospace exports have risen from $248 million in 2002 to $10.05 billion in 2025.
Developments in the defence industry have enabled Türkiye to conduct its military operations more independently, but it is aggressively investing in research and development to address the deficit.
Türkiye’s military power has proven itself in Libya by preventing a military coup there in 2020. Turkish military support helped Azerbaijan liberate its occupied territories the same year.
Over the past two decades, Türkiye has increased its military presence and cooperation with many countries, including Somalia, Qatar, Libya, Pakistan, and Azerbaijan.
On August 7, it launched a trilateral defence alliance with Pakistan, the only nuclear power in the Muslim world, and Saudi Arabia, one of the world's largest oil producers.
Other Arab countries are expected to join the alliance, marking a new era of regional security cooperation and peacebuilding.
The AK Party governments expanded Turkish diplomatic activity and missions globally.
According to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Türkiye’s network of foreign representations has reached 262 missions, making it one of the largest diplomatic networks in the world.
For example, while there were only 12 embassies in Africa in 2002, the number increased to 44 in 2026.
In parallel, the trade volume between Türkiye and Africa has risen from approximately $3 billion to $36.6 billion during the same period, and Turkish Airlines now serves 64 African destinations.
Türkiye developed strong economic and diplomatic relations with the Balkans and Central Asia.
With the Balkan countries, Türkiye established itself in the Balkan Peace Platform in 2025 to prevent the resurgence of previous conflicts and to encourage cooperation on border security, energy and transportation.
In Central Asia, Türkiye led the evolution of the Organization of Turkic States in 2021 out of the Turkic Council, institutionalising Türkiye’s relations with the region.
Meanwhile, Türkiye improved its relations with major Arab countries such as Saudi Arabia and Egypt after a rocky period during the Arab Spring, with the revolution in Syria being a major geopolitical gain in the region.
Türkiye’s role in mediation and crisis diplomacy attracted global attention too.
In the past, Türkiye mediated between Bosnia and Serbia, Syria-Israel, Iran-US, Russia-Ukraine, Afghanistan-Pakistan, and Ethiopia-Somalia, and among Iraqi factions.
Most recently, it mediated the Black Sea Grain Initiative during the war between Russia and Ukraine in 2022. This prevented famine and hardship in some parts of the world, demonstrating Türkiye’s diplomatic capacity.
Soft power and humanitarian diplomacy are also important components of Turkish foreign policy.
Institutions such as TIKA, the Yunus Emre Institute, Turkish Scholarships, the Maarif Foundation, AFAD, the Turkish Red Crescent, and Turkish Airlines have expanded Türkiye's social ties through various channels.
According to the OECD, Türkiye provided approximately $7.3 billion in gross bilateral development assistance in 2024; $6.1 billion of this was humanitarian aid.
TIKA has coordination offices in 61 countries, 22 of them in Africa.
Turkish Maarif schools educate thousands of students abroad, and a significant number receive scholarships to study in Türkiye.
In addition, economy, energy and connectivity form the material basis of Turkish diplomatic influence
Türkiye’s exports increased from approximately $36 billion in 2002 to $273 billion in 2025, marking a major achievement.
Pipelines such as TANAP, TurkStream, Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan, Kerkük-Yumurtalik, and Baku-Tbilisi-Kars have strengthened Türkiye’s transit position between Europe, the Caucasus, the Middle East, and Central Asia.
Beyond the Strait of Hormuz
The closure of the Strait of Hormuz during the Iran-US War increased the Arab need for connectivity through Türkiye, as seen in road, railway, and pipeline projects.
Both the Gulf countries and Iraq want to access the West through Türkiye, which welcomes the new trend of cooperation.
The discovery of natural gas in the Black Sea has been a considerable gain for Türkiye since 2020.
Recently, Turkish foreign policy has become more active within international organisations to influence regional and global agendas.
Its active role in platforms such as the G20, NATO, the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, the D-8, and the Organization of Turkic States; the evolution of the Antalya Diplomacy Forum into an international forum; and mediation initiatives within the UN and the OSCE are examples of this trend.
However, the capacity to set the agenda does not guarantee a positive outcome, as Türkiye focuses on consensus-building by engaging simultaneously with diverse, sometimes conflicting actors.
In conclusion, Türkiye’s growing international influence during the AK Party's quarter-century of governance must be attributed to its ability to combine active diplomacy with a win-win approach, supported by a strong economy, defence industry, trade, humanitarian aid, energy, transport, and strategic partnerships.
It was able to take risks in Libya and Karabakh when the cause was right.
Valuing international institutions, law, and cooperation, Türkiye attaches great importance to regional and global peace.
From the Balkans to Africa, from the Black Sea to Central Asia and the Middle East, Türkiye is a key actor to be reckoned with in numerous areas.
The institutional experience, diplomatic network, and technological capacity accumulated over the last 25 years have prepared Türkiye for a larger global role.
Its sustainability will depend on strengthening economic resilience and reducing dependence on energy and advanced technologies in the future.

The major citizenship ruling affecting Australians like Ophelia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
05:50:32 UTC
14:50:32 KST

IN BRIEF
- An Italian court's ruling could revive claims rejected under the so-called 'minor issue' interpretation of citizenship law.
- But new citizenship restrictions mean some applicants still face additional hurdles under Italy's current rules.
When Ophelia Bryant first travelled to Italy in 1986, she says she felt something she could not quite explain.
"It just felt like I came home," she told SBS News.
Her parents had been born in Italy, as had all four of her grandparents. They immigrated to Australia in 1955, where Bryant was born three years later.
Italy has remained a constant in her life, with Bryant returning more than a dozen times to visit relatives and reconnect with her family roots.
But when she began looking into whether she could formally claim Italian citizenship, she discovered her family history came with a legal complication.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Her parents became Australian citizens in 1961, when Bryant was a child, and later formally renounced their Italian citizenship.
Under a restrictive interpretation of Italy's citizenship laws, known as the 'minor issue', that could break the line of citizenship transmission.
"I thought the door was closed because of that minor rule," Bryant said.
Now, a landmark decision by Italy's highest court has changed that legal interpretation — and Bryant is "optimistic because that door may finally be open".
A rule that divided Italian citizenship cases
The so-called minor issue arose from conflicting interpretations of Italy's 1912 citizenship law.
One provision established that children born overseas to an Italian citizen could acquire Italian citizenship from birth.
Another was interpreted as meaning that when an Italian parent became a citizen of another country, their minor children could lose their Italian citizenship along with them.
That interpretation gained ground through Italian court decisions from 2023 onwards, leading to the rejection of citizenship-by-descent applications.
But in July, Italy's Supreme Court's United Sections, the court's highest panel for resolving conflicting legal interpretations, ruled that citizenship acquired at birth was not automatically lost when an Italian parent subsequently naturalised in another country.
Brisbane-based Italian lawyer Fabrizio Fiorino, who advises clients on Italian citizenship applications, said the decision effectively restores the previous interpretation of the law.
"It was not a change in a provision, but it was a change in the interpretation of rules," he said.
He told SBS News the ruling means people who were Italian citizens from birth cannot simply be considered to have lost that citizenship because their parents later became foreign citizens while they were minors.
For thousands of people whose citizenship applications were rejected on that basis, the decision could provide a pathway back.
A second chance for those already rejected
Italy's interior ministry has since issued a letter instructing authorities to follow the Supreme Court's interpretation.
It also provides a mechanism for people whose applications were rejected because of the minor issue to request their original applications be reconsidered, rather than starting the process again.
Fiorino says he has already seen the consequences of this play out.
One of his clients was recently denied citizenship after the consulate rejected her application because of the minor issue while the Supreme Court case was still pending.
He is now preparing a request for her application to be reviewed under the new interpretation.
"I think in a few weeks they will know the outcome," he said.
But there is an important catch.
The new pathway does not mean everyone affected by the minor issue automatically becomes an Italian citizen.
What does it mean for Ophelia?
Bryant's situation is more complicated because she never actually lodged an application.
Having spent more than two years trying to secure an appointment with the Italian consulate in Melbourne, she told SBS News that she repeatedly found that no appointments were available.
She also said she came to believe she was ineligible under the minor issue and therefore never formally submitted a claim.
That means she cannot simply ask the consulate to reopen a rejected application.
Fiorino said people in her position will need to apply under the current rules and have their individual circumstances assessed.
"The minor issue aspects may not affect, in this situation, her position, because it's been sorted out from the [Italian] Supreme Court," he said.
But other criteria introduced under Italy's separate 2025 citizenship reforms may still apply.
For Bryant, that distinction is frustrating.
"I think the way the law is going, I think Italy would recognise the claim," she said.
"But it is a question of how you get the claim in."
Administrative barriers
The legal victory could also create a new administrative challenge.
Fiorino said consulates are likely to face a significant increase in requests for reviews, while demand for new citizenship applications is already high.
From 2027, Italy's new system will also change how citizenship applications are processed, with applications ultimately being handled through a central office in Italy, he said.
For Bryant, the prospect of another bureaucratic hurdle is daunting.
"If you can't get an appointment at the embassy, how can you even get the ball rolling?," she said.
She has already collected certified copies of Italian family birth records, travelled repeatedly to Italy and researched her family history.
She will return again in September and is considering seeking further legal advice while she is there.
'I'm actually joining the circle'
After years of uncertainty, the ruling has renewed Bryant's hope that she may still be recognised as an Italian citizen.
When she first heard the minor issue had been overturned, she said she was "blown away".
For Bryant, Italian citizenship is not about rejecting Australia, a country she said gave her family the opportunity for a fresh start.
Instead, she said formal recognition of her Italian citizenship would connect her with the history they left behind, and the heritage she has maintained throughout her life.
"It would sort of validate that I am in fact Italian," she said.
And after years of believing the legal door was closed, she is prepared to try again.

BCI chief clarifies ‘no inquiry’ into judicial internships
NEW DELHI: Bar Council of India (BCI) Chairman Manan Kumar Mishra on Friday clarified the Council has withdrawn its order concerning judicial internships following an emergency meeting, saying that no inquiry will be initiated.Mishra said the BCI’s primary objective was to ensure that law students face no obstacles or loss of opportunities while seeking internships in the judiciary."An order was issued yesterday, but the Council's meeting was held immediately. The Council discussed it and said, 'No, there is no need for this'. Actually, the intention is that no student should face any loss in getting an internship in the judiciary. Sometimes, we have seen in the past that due to certain reasons, the judiciary posed obstacles for students regarding internships," he said, as cited by news agency ANI.Mishra added that BCI's interests are aligned with the Cockroach Janta Party's (CJP) Abhijeet Dipke and Saurav Das."The Bar Council of India aims to protect the interests of the youth of India. I want to communicate to Abhijeet Dipke and Das (Sourav Das) that our interests are the same as theirs, to protect the rights of the students," he said."There will be no inquiry; there will be no inquiry whatsoever, nothing of the sort will happen.
We have wished the students well for their bright futures," he added.
Mishra also reaffirmed the BCI’s commitment to strengthening ties between the legal fraternity, the judiciary and aspiring lawyers, ensuring that students can pursue their training without obstacles or hardship."My belief is that students should not face any hardship during their internships. I will coordinate from everywhere so that the judiciary remains happy, the students remain happy, and no one suffers any loss. With this objective in mind, the order was completely withdrawn last night following the meeting. There will be no inquiry, and no blow will be dealt to the students' interests," he said.The latest order modifies an earlier BCI directive that had raised concerns over an alleged campaign at NALSAR linked to the proposed participation of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant at the university’s convocation.
The BCI had initially sought a factual inquiry into the circumstances surrounding the campaign and the individuals allegedly involved in initiating or organising it. The inquiry was intended to determine whether any individual or group had engaged in conduct warranting further statutory action.The Council has now clarified that the 2026 graduating batch should not be denied entry into the legal profession over allegations concerning the conduct of some individuals.Under the latest decision, NALSAR’s 2026 graduates can proceed with their enrolment before the State Bar Councils of their choice. The factual inquiry into the controversy surrounding the convocation-related campaign, however, will continue.

The weakened sex: Why testosterone levels are declining among men worldwide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
05:46:59 UTC
14:46:59 KST

Testosterone levels among men have declined significantly over the past half-century, an international group of researchers has determined after analyzing data on more than 100,000 men from seven countries. Testosterone has long been seen as a symbol of male health, physical strength, sexuality — in short, of “masculinity.” There are several reasons for the decline, but the main one is an obesity epidemic leading to related metabolic disorders. Among other factors, cientists cite changes in lifestyle, chronic stress, and environmental pollution. There is a hypothesis that the trend toward declining testosterone production could be reversed by the spread of drugs such as Ozempic, which promote weight loss. In fact, this theory is already gaining scientific support.
What the new study actually showed
The British newspaper The Guardian, which published widely circulated news about a 54% global decline in men’s testosterone levels, described the trend as one of the most alarming findings in modern reproductive medicine. However, it is important to understand that the article was based not on a full scientific publication but on a presentation given at the annual congress of the European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology (ESHRE). The researchers published only a brief description of the study — its main findings — without explaining the methodology, statistical analysis, or limitations of the research.
The authors examined data from studies on changes in men’s testosterone levels between 1972 and 2019. Of the more than 8,600 publications identified, only 12 studies met the selection criteria. These contained data on 102,334 men from seven countries — mostly, as the authors note, high-income ones. This means the findings may not fully reflect the situation in regions where comparable long-term data are still virtually nonexistent.
The researchers analyzed three measures: total testosterone, free testosterone, and sex hormone-binding globulin. According to the meta-analysis, all three measures have declined significantly over the past 50 years. The authors also noted that after the year 2000, the rate of decline in total testosterone nearly doubled. However, the 54% figure cited by The Guardian does not appear in the study materials. It may have been mentioned during the presentation itself or included in the slides accompanying the talk (but this cannot currently be verified, as the slides are not publicly available).
It is also important to understand that such a meta-analysis can identify a statistical trend but cannot establish its causes. It shows that the measures are changing over time but does not answer the question of why. Moreover, the authors themselves note that the results may have been influenced by changes in the characteristics of the populations studied (such as the growing prevalence of obesity). As a result, they stress the need for further research.
What you need to know about testosterone
In modern medicine, testosterone is regarded as one of the important markers of a man’s overall health. It plays a role in the development of the reproductive organs even before birth, and also plays a critical role in puberty, sperm production, libido, and erectile function. The hormone affects muscle mass, bone density, fat distribution, blood cell production, metabolism, and even brain function. Testosterone receptors have been found in virtually all tissues of the body.
Modern medicine regards testosterone as a marker of a man’s overall health
But testosterone levels are not constant — they decline with age, and also follow circadian rhythms. Testosterone concentrations are usually highest in the early morning and gradually decline throughout the day. Because of these variations, it is recommended that blood tests be taken in the morning, and if the result is borderline or unexpectedly low, that the test be repeated on another day.
In addition to natural daily fluctuations, testosterone levels are affected by body weight, sleep quality, physical activity, chronic diseases, certain medications, alcohol consumption, and stress. In other words, the level of testosterone reflects the overall state of the body.
However, even taking individual fluctuations in testosterone levels into account, a decline in the average level may indicate that real biological changes are occurring in the population. If such a trend does indeed exist, what exactly is driving it?
Why testosterone levels are declining
Today, most researchers view declining testosterone levels as the result of an interplay of aging, chronic diseases, lifestyle, and environmental factors. At the same time, the strength of the evidence for different causes varies considerably. Some factors are supported by large epidemiological studies, clinical observations, and mechanistic data, while others are backed only by isolated observations and experimental models.
Metabolism
Scientists are most confident about the negative role played by excess weight. Adipose tissue, particularly visceral fat (the kind that accumulates around the internal organs), literally converts testosterone into estradiol, the most active of the estrogens (female sex hormones). The more of this fat there is, the faster estrogen levels rise — and in turn, they suppress signals from the brain that trigger testosterone production in the testes. Low testosterone makes it easier to accumulate the same visceral fat, and so the cycle closes.
Excess weight is the main factor behind declining testosterone levels
This process is reversible, as numerous studies have confirmed. One of the first major meta-analyses, published in 2013 by a group of scientists from the University of Florence in Italy, showed that a low-calorie diet can increase testosterone levels (as can bariatric surgery to reduce the size of the stomach). Obesity is perhaps the only factor that can be effectively addressed: lose the excess weight, and hormone levels return to normal.
Type 2 diabetes also causes testosterone levels to decline and leads to hypogonadism — a condition in which the body does not produce enough of the hormone. Persistently high blood sugar and insulin resistance disrupt signaling in the brain and directly affect the cells that produce testosterone. At the same time, low testosterone levels, in turn, reduce the sensitivity of organ tissues to insulin, creating another vicious cycle.
Metabolic syndrome works in a similar way — a dangerous “cocktail” of high blood pressure, disrupted cholesterol levels, and abdominal obesity (when excess weight accumulates around the abdomen, surrounding the internal organs with metabolically active visceral fat).
The authors of a large population-based study, the Study of Health in Pomerania (SHIP), conducted in northeastern Germany, identified a pattern: the more components of the syndrome (a sagging belly, high blood pressure, and hormonal imbalances) a man has, the more rapidly his testosterone levels decline, with the effect particularly pronounced in younger patients.
The more factors that lower testosterone accumulate in a man, the faster his hormone levels decline
Almost all metabolic disorders are accompanied by so-called systemic chronic inflammation. In obesity and diabetes, fat cells and macrophages (cells of the immune system) continuously release “alarm signals” into the bloodstream — pro-inflammatory cytokines — which directly attack the body’s testosterone “factories.” Laboratory experiments using cultures of Leydig cells (which synthesize the hormone in the testes) have shown that the higher the concentration of cytokines, the more strongly testosterone synthesis is suppressed.
Chronic inflammation literally “switches off” key enzymes inside cells, blocking the production of the hormone. Many modern endocrinologists agree that inflammation is how the harmful effects of excess weight, impaired glucose metabolism, and even the natural aging are mediated (the latter is known in science as “inflammaging,” or inflammatory aging).
Lifestyle
Unlike obesity or diabetes, the effects of lifestyle on testosterone levels have not been studied as extensively. The concept itself is too broad to be measured as precisely as blood sugar levels. Taken together, the evidence suggests that chronic stress, insufficient sleep, alcohol abuse, certain medications, and excessive physical activity can indeed lower levels of male sex hormones.
Sleep is the most extensively studied factor in this group. Men produce the most testosterone at night, during the deeper stages of sleep, so it is logical to assume that sleep deprivation would directly affect the hormone. Evidence supporting this hypothesis was provided by a 2011 study by researchers at the University of Chicago: ten healthy young men slept for five hours a night for a week instead of their usual eight, and by the end of the experiment, their daytime testosterone levels had fallen noticeably, with the participants themselves beginning to complain of low energy and reduced libido.
Dozens of observational studies involving much larger groups subsequently confirmed the same pattern — an analysis by the U.S. National Center for Health Statistics involving thousands of participants, for one. However, when the effects of obesity and associated diseases are removed from the calculations, the link between sleep and testosterone levels weakens considerably, suggesting that insufficient sleep most likely reinforces the metabolic mechanisms described above.
The mechanism by which chronic stress affects testosterone has been well-studied at the experimental level: it triggers the production of cortisol, which suppresses the signal from the brain that is essential for initiating the entire chain of testosterone synthesis. The problem is that at the population level, it is extremely difficult to standardize the very concept of “stress” — after all, strenuous physical work, anxiety, depression, and chronic illnesses produce very different hormonal effects. As large systematic reviews show, when data from thousands of men are analyzed, subjectively perceived psychological stress is only weakly associated with testosterone levels, unlike in strictly controlled experimental models.
In the case of alcohol, hormone production is clearly dose-dependent. In cases of chronic alcohol abuse, ethanol and its metabolite acetaldehyde directly damage Leydig cells and suppress the production of the regulatory hormone that gives these cells the signal to synthesize testosterone. A marked decline in total and free testosterone is found specifically in men with chronic patterns of alcohol consumption.
Moderate consumption, however, is a different story: most studies have found no consistent clinically significant effect. Some short-term experiments have even shown a temporary spike in testosterone in response to small amounts of alcohol, but these changes quickly disappeared and had no lasting consequences.
As for medications, it is specific groups of potentially harmful drugs that disrupt hormonal balance. The main enemy of testosterone in this case is potent opioid painkillers. When taken over a long period, they literally “switch off” the mechanism in the brain that signals the body to produce the male hormone. There is even a separate term for this condition — opioid-induced androgen deficiency (a deficiency of male sex hormones). Statistically, this problem affects upwards of 80% of men who take high dosages of certain painkillers for an extended period. T
Diet and physical activity
Contrary to “superfood” advertising campaigns, there is no magic diet for men’s health — what matters to the body is overall balance and metabolic health, not specific foods. Both overeating and starvation are equally harmful to the hormonal system.
Too much food leads to obesity (which, as noted above, literally destroys testosterone). However, strict diets and a sharp calorie deficit signal to the body that it is in survival mode, causing it to conserve energy. In such cases, the first thing to be shut down is the reproductive function. Additionally, a deficiency of zinc, magnesium, or vitamin D can cause a slight drop in testosterone levels, but for men whose blood tests are normal, an extra dose of vitamins will do absolutely nothing.
There is no diet specifically designed to maintain “men’s health”
Large-scale meta-analyses confirm that physical activity does cause a substantial but short-lived spike in testosterone levels in men. Long-distance runners, however, have been found to show the opposite trend: excessive cardio exercise lowers baseline testosterone levels. This phenomenon is explained by relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) — with frequent endurance training, the body experiences a calorie deficit and deliberately suppresses the reproductive system. Thus, maintaining a stable hormonal balance requires moderation. Moderate strength training and adequate calorie intake stimulate testosterone production, while chronic excessive cardio training has the opposite effect. And the long-term effects of exercise programs in older people vary considerably depending on the type and intensity of exercise.
Environmental factors
In recent years, there have been increasingly frequent claims that microplastic pollution and household chemicals are to blame for the global decline in testosterone levels. The leading proponent of this idea is Shanna Swan, a leading environmental epidemiologist at the Icahn School of Medicine in New York. She has raised the alarm about the issue on major media platforms — from the podcasts of Joe Rogan and Andrew Huberman to Netflix documentaries. In her book Count Down, Swan argues that plastic and household chemicals are threatening humanity with a reproductive apocalypse.
Proving this hypothesis is more difficult than establishing the effects of obesity or diabetes. The problem is methodological: in today’s world, it is impossible to create a “clean” control group. Microplastics and phthalates affect people even before birth and remain with them throughout their lives. In a “cocktail” of hundreds of substances, it is difficult to identify a specific “culprit” and prove its direct effect. Nevertheless, it is worth looking at the factors currently under active investigation.
First on the list of prime suspects is bisphenol A (BPA) — a basic component of rigid, transparent plastics, epoxy resins, and the inner lining of food cans. As a structural analogue of estrogen, the substance can fool the body by binding to hormone receptors. Large-scale laboratory tests demonstrate that in animals, BPA suppresses testosterone synthesis in the testes and interferes with the activity of brain structures that initiate this process. Cell experiments have also shown that the substance disrupts the biosynthesis of cholesterol — the primary raw material for producing the male hormone.
However, when scientists test these findings in humans, they once again encounter contradictions. On the one hand, a large-scale meta-analysis of epidemiological studies in 2024 found an association in men between high concentrations of bisphenol and lower testosterone levels. On the other hand, the effects of BPA in real life appear to be quite modest. Another study, published in 2010, found that in adult men, higher urinary BPA levels were associated with only minimal fluctuations in sex hormones.
The next suspects are phthalates, which are used to make plastic soft and flexible. Their effects on fetal development are well documented. For example, Shanna Swan found that boys born to women with high concentrations of phthalates in their urine showed signs of reduced exposure to male sex hormones in the womb. This finding was later confirmed to varying degrees by large cohort studies in Sweden, Mexico and the United States, and Japan.
The link between phthalates and testosterone in adult men has also been documented, but the effect is usually minimal, inconsistent, and highly dependent on the specific chemical compound. Data from the U.S. National Center for Health Statistics show that these substances significantly lower hormone levels only in men over 60. In younger people, the body can metabolize and eliminate these toxins quickly.
For adult men, the problem is different: according to a meta-analysis published in March 2026, phthalates impair sperm quality and motility. In other words, plastic-induced “chemical castration” is not a threat to adult men, but fertility problems certainly are.
Chemicals significantly lower hormone levels only in men over 60
Next are the so-called forever chemicals (PFAS), which do not break down for decades, whether in the environment or in the body. Here, the findings are even more contradictory. Some studies have found a link between high concentrations of PFAS in the blood and low testosterone, while others have found no such association. Nevertheless, the link between “forever chemicals” and impaired sperm quality has been consistently confirmed.
A large systematic review by a group of researchers from Michigan notes that the decline in sperm motility and concentration associated with PFAS is much more consistently observed than their effect on testosterone levels.
Air pollution is also being considered as a factor in the global decline in testosterone. So far, this question has been addressed by only one large study, conducted by researchers in Beijing. From 2014 to 2019, they collected data on nearly 73,000 men aged 20 to 55 and compared their testosterone levels with concentrations of air pollutants both on the day of testing and during the preceding month.
They found that the dirtier the air immediately before the measurement, the lower the testosterone level. A 10-microgram-per-cubic-meter increase in the concentration of fine particulate matter was associated with a roughly 1.6% drop in testosterone, while for larger particles, the decline was 1.1%. The figures are small, but the effect proved consistent and statistically significant across the enormous sample.
Nevertheless, this study has significant limitations. First, the data do not show the effect that long-term exposure to a polluted environment may have on testosterone production. Second, it has not been established that particulate matter affects hormone levels directly rather than through some other factor. Third, pollution levels were assessed using data from urban monitoring stations rather than individual sensors — meaning the study does not account for who spent more time outdoors and who stayed indoors with an air purifier.
Finally, it is not entirely clear from the study data to what extent the participants’ lifestyle, stress, and sleep were taken into account — factors that may well accompany exposure to polluted air in a major city. In short, it is too early to speak of a sustained effect of air pollution on testosterone. In order to find a reliable answer, studies with individual exposure monitoring and long-term follow-up of the measured individuals are needed.
It is too early to speak of a sustained effect of air pollution on testosterone
The last factor under discussion is climate change. Here, science is still limited to hypotheses and assumptions. Scientists have demonstrated that extreme heat is a proven threat to male fertility. However, studies of men engaged in strenuous work in conditions of constant overheating (such as foundry workers) show that although heat stress damages sperm, it has virtually no effect on testosterone levels. A global report published by The Lancet in 2025 clearly distinguishes established reproductive risks from the hypothetical effects of climate on the endocrine system.
An aging population
Could it be that there is no real decline in testosterone at all, and that it is all due to statistical artifacts – for example, the population is aging, more older men with comorbidities are included in samples, and the average level is falling as a result? Scientists have repeatedly tested this hypothesis.
Virtually all major studies on the subject use statistics specifically adjusted for age: instead of comparing all men indiscriminately, they compare, say, 30-year-olds from a sample collected in the 1990s with 30-year-olds from a sample collected in the 2010s. Even with this methodology, the decline in testosterone persists.
The Massachusetts Male Aging Study in the United States – one of the first and best-known studies on the subject – shows that a man who was 60 in 1989 had, on average, higher testosterone levels than a man who reached that age in the 2000s.
A similar trend has been observed in a much more recent study by scientists at Tel Aviv University: after analyzing the results of tests performed on more than 100,000 men between 2006 and 2019, they found a sustained, statistically significant decline in testosterone that was independent of age. The trend persisted within each age group separately and could not be explained by the increase in obesity among the participants.
What a decline in testosterone levels means
From a biological perspective, the consequences of declining testosterone extend far beyond what is usually associated with “male strength.” They include loss of muscle mass, an increase in body fat (which, as noted above, only exacerbates the problem), an increased risk of osteoporosis, metabolic disorders, and an overall decline in quality of life. In some cases, fertility is also affected.
For the healthcare system, this translates into an additional burden on clinics. Demographic consequences, however, should be discussed with caution: there is simply no scientific evidence yet directly linking declining testosterone levels to falling birth rates at the population level. A man can have perfectly normal hormone levels and still experience reproductive problems for dozens of other reasons. Conversely, fertility is not necessarily affected in all men with low testosterone.
Can the spread of weight-loss drugs reverse this trend?
Importantly from a scientific standpoint, obesity has been shown to be the factor that has the strongest effect on testosterone levels. Could widespread weight loss driven by the growing use of drugs such as Ozempic reverse the downward trend in this hormone? GLP-1 receptor agonists — semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound) — slow gastric emptying and suppress appetite, causing patients to lose an average of 10–17% of their body weight.
Data from the past two years have so far supported this hypothesis. A retrospective study based on a sample of 234 men, presented at the Endocrine Society’s annual meeting (ENDO) in San Francisco in 2025, found that after starting treatment with these drugs, both total and free testosterone levels increased in men with obesity.
According to another study presented at the same event, over 18 months of treatment, the proportion of patients with normal testosterone levels in a group of 110 men with obesity or type 2 diabetes rose from 53% to 77% as they lost about 10% of their body weight. The researchers explain that weight loss increases levels of SHBG (sex hormone-binding globulin), which in turn raises total testosterone levels.
Weight loss increases total testosterone levels
However, there is no shortage of evidence pointing in the opposite direction. Animal experiments show that GLP-1 agonists are not always capable of restoring testosterone levels lowered by a high-fat diet. Nevertheless, the widespread use of GLP-1 therapy in the coming years could become the largest natural experiment in the history of endocrinology.
If the average testosterone level in the population begins to rise as obesity declines, this would provide one of the most compelling indirect confirmations of the metabolic hypothesis discussed above. If that does not happen, scientists will have to take a much closer look at other factors — the environment, modern lifestyles, and perhaps other potential causes that have yet to be identified.

Pyongyang routinely denounces military drills in the south as a provocation that heightens tensions.
The drills – named “Ulchi Freedom Shield” – are due to start on August 17 and will last until August 27. They will incorporate exercises to counter drones, GPS disruption, and cyberattacks as the US and its allies adapt to North Korea’s evolving capabilities.
“The US announced that the forthcoming exercises are quite different from the ones of the past five years and intended to master the ability of fighting a war on the basis of the new aspects of modern warfare,” the North Korean Foreign Ministry spokesperson said in the statement.
“It is our consistent principle of ensuring security to respond to a new level of a threat with a new level of a deterrent,” the statement, published by KCNA, added.
Lessons learned in Russia-Ukraine
North Korea sent an estimated 12,000-15,000 soldiers to fight for Russia in its war against Ukraine, and the country is now thought to be preparing the deployment of another 10,000.
Thousands died, but the deal provided North Korea with valuable battlefield experience, as well as payment in arms, energy and direct financial support, according to reports.
Colonel Ryan Donald, spokesperson for the US and South Korean Combined Forces Command, said this week that North Korea’s deployment to the European war had changed the threat his soldiers may face on the Korean Peninsula.
“They’ve taken those lessons they learned there and brought them back to North Korea,” he told reporters. “Our training accounts for that threat.”
Pyongyang’s Foreign Ministry statement said the US-South Korea drills are being staged “at a time when military and political situation is becoming more serious with each passing day in Europe, the Middle East and other parts of the world”.
North Korea also said on Friday that it would further strengthen its nuclear deterrence, accusing the US of lowering its threshold for nuclear weapons usage and pushing the world “to the brink of nuclear war”.
On Wednesday, North Korea fired a ballistic missile towards the sea off the Korean Peninsula’s east coast, just six days after firing another missile.
The Ulchi Freedom Shield drills will include 18,000 South Korean soldiers and counterparts from the 28,500-strong US contingent in the country.

Source: European Pravda, citing Latvian public broadcaster LSM
Details: The Latvian National Armed Forces said on the morning of 14 August that NATO fighter jets on patrol had successfully shot down a drone that had entered Latvian airspace as a result of Russian electronic warfare interference.
An air-raid warning previously issued in five areas of the country was lifted at 04:50.

Members of the public have been asked to call 112 (the unified emergency response centre in Latvia) if they notice anything suspicious.
