What I Saw In Sinaloa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:58:35 UTC
01:58:35 KST

What I Saw In Sinaloa
The U.S. is trying to destroy Mexican cartels. But so far, a turf war has only deepened.
Sign up for our newsletter about national security here.
Last Tuesday night, I was eating sushi with a Mexican police chief in downtown Culiacán, a city that had momentarily flickered back to life amid a bloody cartel turf war. At the table next to us was a birthday party. The police chief ordered a salmon roll. Through the window, I could see groups of families and friends walking on the sidewalk, past car dealerships and strip malls, after months of self-imposed lockdown.
Among them were three influencers who pulled up to a KFC down the street. They were dressed as food-delivery workers, carrying insulated bags on their backs, joking with one another and livestreaming everything with their phones. César Gastélum, the group’s front man, had become famous for such innocuous pranks. Even as thousands were murdered by the cartels, Gastélum, a stocky, bearded 24-year-old, posted videos of himself dancing in pajamas, dressing as a priest, sipping iced coffee. He had more than 700,000 followers on TikTok.
It was this kind of incongruity that had drawn me to Culiacán, the capital of Sinaloa. The city is the center of the fiercest and most consequential battle between armed groups in Mexico, and I wanted to untangle what was behind the surge of violence. From afar, it was difficult to tell whether someone like Gastélum was proof that the mundane and the horrific could coexist here, as they have for decades across Mexico, or whether he was a symbol of something else—the way drug cartels had quietly co-opted even the city’s least likely protagonists.
At about 8 o’clock, Gastélum and his friends were recording themselves waiting for their fried-chicken orders when two men on a motorcycle drove past. “Those guys scare me,” Gastélum said. He then seemed to regain his calm, joking about his skinny jeans in front of the camera when the motorcycle returned. It stopped momentarily in front of the three young men. The driver, wearing a black helmet with a face shield, raised a gun about two feet from Gastélum’s head and fired. The livestream captured the moment of the bullet’s impact and then went dark.
Someone on the city’s ambulance team texted me when the 911 call came in, and I ran across the street to the KFC. I got to the scene as police were arriving. Gastélum’s body lay at the drive-through’s exit, a ribbon of blood streaming toward the sidewalk. A cluster of soldiers gathered nearby, some of them scrolling through Gastélum’s TikTok feed. A small group of crime photographers were taking photos and uploading videos.
“As you can see, they have killed another influencer here in Culiacán,” José Ángel Beltrán of Luz Noticias said, narrating on Facebook Live.
Culiacán, for years the axis of Mexico’s drug wars, is now the focus of a U.S. effort to demolish drug cartels—something President Trump has said he’s willing to use military force to achieve. It is in many ways an understandable target: The Sinaloa cartel, which has administered the state for decades, is responsible for trafficking millions of kilos of fentanyl, meth, and cocaine into the United States. The Justice Department has indicted both the Sinaloa governor and the Culiacán mayor for cooperating with the cartel. Several of its leaders are serving life sentences in the U.S., and others have been targeted by Mexican security forces using intelligence from the United States.
And yet, so far, these actions have only deepened the civil war between two Sinaloa-cartel factions, one run by the children and supporters of Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán (the Chapitos), and the other run by allies of Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada García (the Mayos). In 2022, there were 476 homicides in Sinaloa. In 2025, it had 1,657. Government action against organized-crime groups in Mexico has almost always had such an effect—increasing violence without significantly altering the flow of drugs into the United States. But the current Sinaloa turf war—la narcopandemia, locals call it—has created new categories of victims, far from the foot soldiers and hit men targeted in previous spasms of violence. Now influencers and content creators are recruited by cartels to distribute their messages online. And university and vocational students have been kidnapped, presumably because their skills are needed by criminal groups. Each time a young person here is killed or vanishes, there are immediate questions about whom he or she might have been working for. When drug traffickers allegedly subsidize TikTok dances, a victim’s innocence can be almost impossible to discern.
As forensic police arrived at the KFC, Beltrán told me that another TikToker had been killed a few blocks away months earlier. A fitness influencer, El Tata, was murdered while leaving a shopping center. The body of a YouTuber, El Pinky, was found showing signs that he had been gagged and bound. About a dozen other influencers in Sinaloa have been killed, kidnapped, or attacked. Each time, the Mexican government investigated whether the influencers had somehow been linked to one group and targeted by the other. Last year, an unidentified plane dropped thousands of flyers over Culiacán that accused a number of influencers and musicians of having ties to the Chapitos (Gastélum was not on the list).
Standing in front of the crime scene as the forensic police hovered around Gastélum’s body with flashlights, I asked Beltrán why he thought a goofy livestreamer would be a target in a cartel turf war.
“Did you see that he was wearing a cowboy hat?” Beltrán asked me.
Cowboy hats have become a symbol of the Mayos faction of the cartel. The implication was that Gastélum, while performing juvenile pranks, had been making a subtle nod to one group’s power. Online commenters rushed to make the same point.
Beltrán filmed one last video of Gastélum’s body as it was taken away, and then he tapped me on the shoulder. Another victim had been found half a mile away: a man shot in the city’s botanical garden after a screening of a Lady Gaga documentary. I went with him to cover it. When we got there, it was dark, and the body was lit by a streetlight. Beltrán took his phone out again and started streaming.
“Hello again, everyone,” he said. “It’s another rough night in Culiacán.”
The next day, I drove 30 minutes from downtown Culiacán to a neighborhood called Costa Rica, on the outskirts of the city. I passed several motorcyclists who had their face covered by a ski mask. These punteros, as they’re called, have for years worked as low-level informants for the cartel. Even before the fracture of Sinaloa, the cartel was famous for its capacity to monitor every inch of Culiacán. In addition to deploying the punteros, it placed hundreds of cameras across the city and set up surveillance teams in residential neighborhoods.
The Mexican government has surged hundreds of soldiers and national guardsmen across the city, ostensibly to disrupt the criminal groups who have terrorized it. But the military presence is overwhelmingly performative. On the road to Costa Rica, I watched as punteros and soldiers nonchalantly drove past one another.
I pulled up to the squat house of Marta Pérez Guzman, whose son, David Antonio Ruelas Pérez, had been kidnapped by armed men along with his classmate José Isaías Ibarra Duarte. There were 2,154 disappearances in Sinaloa last year, but the kidnapping of Ruelas, 22, and Ibarra, 23, had received more attention than most. The men were students at an aviation school in Culiacán, and many here suspected that they had been abducted to work on cartel aircraft. There was another notable fact: Ibarra is a U.S. citizen, born in Los Angeles.
His mother, Graciela Duarte Valdez, had wondered whether that would be enough to nudge the U.S. government to act. After all, Trump had articulated in Truth Social posts and Fox News interviews his desire to intervene in Mexico. She had traveled to the closest U.S. consulate, in the neighboring state of Sonora, and made her case. Not only was her son still missing, but the Mexican attorney general’s office had obtained surveillance footage of the kidnapping and showed it to her. Through tears, Duarte described seeing footage of four men who wore ski masks and carried rifles getting out of a minivan and forcing her son and Ruelas into a second car. It all took only a few seconds.
She felt abandoned by the Mexican government’s investigators, who asked questions suggesting that the boys had been working for a cartel faction before the kidnapping. When she went to the U.S. consulate, officials took notes and thanked her for coming (when I asked the State Department about the case, a spokesperson told me in a statement that it was “aware of reports of the kidnapping of a U.S. citizen in Mexico” but did not elaborate). Duarte was despairing; she knew that just a small fraction of disappeared people were later found alive in Sinaloa. One day last year, she heard that Governor Rubén Rocha Moya was visiting her neighborhood. She ran to meet him.
“Please help,” she told the governor, as she held a missing-person poster with her son’s photo and name on it. Rocha told her he would try.
A few months later, Duarte was skimming her Facebook feed for information about missing people and recovered bodies when she saw a news story that said Rocha had been indicted by the United States for colluding with the cartel. The U.S. government had acted, but she could not bring herself to see the move as productive or helpful. Rocha temporarily resigned and fled Culiacán. The Mexican government announced that it would support him until the U.S. showed more evidence of his collusion.
“All I could think was that I had begged that man for help,” Duarte said. “But of course, he did nothing. He had been working for the cartel the whole time.”
About a third of Mexico is controlled by organized criminal groups, according to a U.S.-government analysis. Culiacán—even during its most peaceful stretches—has been a prime example. The cartel presence here has never been subtle. One man in his early 20s told me that his childhood friends had been recruited to work in fentanyl labs and would return smelling like chemicals for weeks. The children of cartel kingpins enrolled in the city’s top prep schools. In one cemetery, families of deceased cartel operatives erected graves the size of suburban homes. Each time the cartel’s fractures sent the city into spirals of violence—in 2010 and 2017—they ended the same way: not with the disintegration of organized crime but with one faction emerging as the victor.
The Trump administration believes that it can avoid repeating this pattern, partially by going after Mexican politicians who support the cartel—“all the government officials that are part of the ‘Culiacán clan,’” Sara Carter, the director of the White House’s Office of National Drug Control Policy, told a journalist earlier this year. The U.S. has also continued its decades-long strategy of targeting top cartel operatives, largely by funneling intelligence to elite Mexican-military units who have conducted a number of successful operations. That partnership is deeper than it has been in years. But I didn’t meet anyone in Culiacán who believes that the strategy will reduce violence here. So far, it hasn’t reduced drug flows, either. Even officials in the Mexican government who are in favor of attacking criminal groups privately dismiss the Trump administration’s absolutist goal of eliminating cartels, given the enormous demand for drugs in the United States.
“On Day one, President Trump designated major cartels—including Sinaloa—as Foreign Terrorist Organizations, unlocking powerful sanctions, asset seizures, and enhanced prosecutorial tools to crush their operations. We will not allow cartels to profit off of poisoning our children and grandchildren,” Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, told me in a statement.
As César Gastélum’s body was buried last week, some of the city’s influencers posted tributes to him, as if describing a fallen comrade. “We need to take care of ourselves,” one wrote to his 2.3 million followers. Even Mexico’s president weighed in, promising to find the assailants. Duarte had followed the news. Gastélum was just a year older than her son.
But she was following another story more closely. The government had detained a dozen young alleged cartel operatives in a rural area outside Culiacán. It published photos of the boys and men, their faces blurred. Many of their T-shirts were off, revealing skinny frames. Duarte zoomed in on one of them. It was hard to tell, but he looked at least a little bit like her son.

During July, the "Scythian Griffins" struck 1,293 enemy targets
Kyiv • UNN
In July, fighters from the "Scythian Griffins" regiment struck 1,293 targets, including an increase in the number of personnel and equipment hit. The commander plans to double the figures after the reorganization.
Based on the results of combat operations in July, the 423rd Separate UAS Regiment "Scythian Griffins" increased the total number of enemy targets hit by 15%. In particular, the number of enemy personnel hit (+57%), heavy motor vehicles (+139%), and UAVs of various types (+ 46%) increased significantly, the regiment’s media service reports, according to UNN.
Overall, during July, the regiment’s personnel hit: 338 enemy personnel, 589 shelters, 128 heavy motor vehicles, 2 tanks, 25 artillery systems, 73 fixed-wing and multirotor UAVs, 2 ground robotic systems, 62 warehouses and technical assets. The total number of hits for the month amounted to 1 293 verified enemy targets.
The military emphasizes that this increase in combat effectiveness occurred even before the final reorganization of the 423rd Separate Battalion into a regiment and became an example of how positive motivation affects the performance of every soldier and commander.
According to the commander of the "Scythian Griffins," Colonel V. Hersak, following its transformation into a separate regiment and the corresponding increase in combat capabilities, the number of targets hit should at least double within the next few months. "This is precisely the task I am setting for the newly appointed commanders of our battalions and their soldiers," said Regiment Commander V. Hersak.
As reported earlier, at the beginning of August, the 423rd Separate UAS Battalion "Scythian Griffins" was reorganized into the 423rd Separate UAS Regiment. V. Hersak was appointed commander of the regiment and received the military rank of colonel.

Defense argues Charlie Kirk murder suspect ineligible for death penalty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:56:47 UTC
01:56:47 KST

Defense argues Charlie Kirk murder suspect ineligible for death penalty
The defense team of Tyler Robinson, the man accused of killing conservative activist Charlie Kirk last September, has argued that the defendant should be spared the death penalty, as he only “hit the intended target.” The defense attorneys insist that the prosecution has been unable to prove the alleged shooter put other people’s lives at risk, thus committing aggravated murder.
The latter, which is a capital crime in the state of Utah, requires at least one “statutory aggravating factor” to qualify as such.
Kirk, a popular podcaster and co-founder of Turning Point USA, was shot in the neck and killed while speaking to about 3,000 attendees of an event at Utah Valley University in Orem on September 10, 2025.
Robinson was apprehended two days later. Investigators allege that he was the sniper who fired the fatal shot from a rooftop, about 130 meters (140 yards) from the packed venue.
In Tuesday court filings, Robinson’s defense attorneys argued that prosecutors had failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant “knowingly created a great risk of death to another other than Charlie Kirk.” Kathy Nester, Michael Burt, Richard Novak, and Staci Visser wrote that the “only evidence presented supports that the bullet traveled above, not through, the crowd,” and thus no one other than Kirk was in the line of fire.
Robinson’s defense team also pointed out that the alleged shooter did not specifically mention “any threat or intended harm to any other individual(s)” in communications with his romantic partner, Lance Twiggs, which was cited as evidence by the authorities.
The lawyers also sought to refute another potential aggravating factor, namely that Robinson targeted Kirk for political reasons. Citing the text messages between the defendant and his transgender lover, the defense team insisted that Robinson’s explanation that he had “had enough of [Kirk’s] hatred” refers to general “hatred” rather than a specific political viewpoint.
The prosecutors, in turn, contend that Robinson’s alleged motivation for the assassination stemmed from Kirk’s public opposition to same-sex marriage and gender transitioning.
According to family members and media reports, Robinson became radicalized and mentioned the conservative activist in conversations before the shooting. The unfired rounds recovered from the rifle allegedly used in the assassination reportedly bore inscriptions, including “Hey, fascist! Catch!”
Robinson’s defense team had petitioned Utah District Judge Tony Graf to bar prosecutors from seeking the death penalty back in June, accusing them of staging a “media tour” concerning a bullet fragment recovered from Kirk’s body. The defense attorneys alleged that this constituted a violation of restrictions on public comments on the case.
The hearing is expected to resume on September 1, with Robinson yet to enter a plea.

Iraq sends top security delegation to Riyadh after drone attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:56:13 UTC
01:56:13 KST

Breadcrumb
Iraq sends top security delegation to Riyadh after drone attacks
A high-level Iraqi security delegation is holding talks in the Saudi capital Riyadh in an effort to contain tensions between the two countries following drone attacks on Saudi energy facilities that Riyadh says were launched from Iraq, and subsequent US-Saudi airstrikes on Iraqi territory.
The Iraqi delegation is headed by Lt Gen Abdul Amir al-Shammari and includes Lt Gen Falah Shaghati, assistant director of the Intelligence Agency; Hamid al-Shatri, head of the Iraqi National Intelligence Service; Lt Gen Muhannad al-Asadi, commander of Air Defence; and Lt Gen Zaid Houshi, head of the Counter-Terrorism Service.
It is the first publicly announced visit by senior Iraqi security officials to Saudi Arabia since Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi received a renewed invitation to visit Riyadh.
An earlier visit was cancelled after US-Saudi strikes on Iraq on 29 July killed 20 people at facilities belonging to the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), an umbrella organisation that includes Iran-aligned armed factions.
An Iraqi security official told The New Arab that the delegation was holding talks with Saudi officials over the drone attacks that Riyadh says originated from Iraqi territory and targeted sites and facilities inside the kingdom, as well as the fallout from the subsequent airstrikes inside Iraq, which killed and wounded PMF members.
The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said Saudi officials had presented information and evidence they say showed that the attacks originated from Iraqi territory.
The evidence, the official added, appeared to indicate that the incidents "were not the first of their kind".
The Iraqi delegation, meanwhile, briefed Saudi officials on security and military measures taken by Baghdad to prevent further attacks from Iraqi territory and to pursue groups that might use Iraqi territory or airspace to launch attacks against neighbouring countries.
The talks will also address closer security and intelligence coordination between Baghdad and Riyadh, border controls and airspace monitoring, as well as the exchange of information on groups that possess or operate drones, the official said.
The two sides are also expected to discuss rapidly evolving regional security developments and their implications for Iraq, Saudi Arabia and the wider region.
Tensions after drone attacks and airstrikes
The delegation's visit follows an unprecedented security escalation between Baghdad and Riyadh.
The crisis began on 27 July, when the Saudi defence ministry announced that it had intercepted and destroyed several drones that it said had been launched from Iraqi territory and targeted oil facilities in the kingdom's Eastern Province and Riyadh region.
Tensions escalated further on 29 July when airstrikes targeted PMF positions inside Iraq, according to statements from Saudi and Iraqi authorities.
The Iraqi security official said the visit carried additional political significance because it could pave the way for a recalibration of security relations between Baghdad and Riyadh.
The talks will also cover preparations for Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi's expected visit to Saudi Arabia, including its security and military agenda, after an earlier trip was postponed following the latest escalation.
According to the official, the Iraqi delegation will seek to establish two parallel principles during the Riyadh talks.
The first is Baghdad's commitment to preventing Iraqi territory from being used to launch attacks against Saudi Arabia or other countries in the region. The second is Iraq's rejection of military strikes on its territory.
The meetings therefore represent "a test of the two countries' ability to contain the repercussions of the escalation and move from an exchange of accusations and strikes towards a higher level of direct security and intelligence coordination", the official said.
'Iraq does not want to be an arena for conflict'
Yasser Watout, a member of the Iraqi parliament's Security and Defence Committee, told The New Arab that the delegation's visit had come at an important and sensitive moment.
"We view it positively, as it opens the door to direct security dialogue to address the repercussions of the attacks that were said to have originated from Iraqi territory, as well as the strikes that targeted sites inside Iraq," Watout said.
He stressed that Iraq was committed to maintaining balanced relations with all neighbouring countries and would not allow its territory or airspace to be used as a launching point for attacks against another state.
"At the same time, protecting Iraqi sovereignty and preventing any recurrence of attacks on Iraqi territory are fundamental responsibilities of the state," he added.
Watout said the presence of senior officials from Iraq's intelligence services, air defence and counter-terrorism forces reflected the significance of the issues being discussed in Riyadh.
Those include intelligence sharing, airspace surveillance, border security, tracing the origins of drones and preventing armed groups from exploiting Iraqi territory to conduct cross-border attacks.
"The current phase requires moving beyond exchanging messages and accusations towards practical security coordination," Watout said.
Clear mechanisms should be established to deal with intelligence concerning potential threats or launches from Iraqi territory, he added, in a way that both protects Saudi security and preserves Iraqi sovereignty.
"Iraq does not want to become an arena for conflict or a platform for attacks against countries in the region, nor does it accept its territory becoming an arena for military retaliation by any party," Watout said.
"Direct security dialogue and coordination between the relevant institutions is therefore the best way to prevent these developments from recurring."
A date for Prime Minister Zaidi's visit to Riyadh has yet to be set, Iraqi government spokesman Haider al-Aboudi said on Monday.
Zaidi had been scheduled to travel to the Saudi capital on 30 July, but the visit was postponed amid the security developments and the latest regional escalation.

Hollywood stars Mark Ruffalo, Javier Bardem warn Gaza 'ceasefire' has not stopped killings
A coalition of prominent artists, including Mark Ruffalo and Javier Bardem, has urged the public to continue pressing for a permanent ceasefire in Gaza, warning that Palestinians remain exposed to daily violence, displacement and restrictions on humanitarian aid.
In a new statement issued on Wednesday, Artists4Ceasefire said there was "no ceasefire in Gaza", arguing that the announcement of a truce had not ended the devastating conditions faced by Palestinians in the enclave.
"Every day, Palestinians are continuing to experience horrific suffering," the group wrote. It said that more than 1,200 Palestinians in Gaza had been killed since the so-called ceasefire was announced in October last year, including 300 children in 300 days, while more than 4,000 people had been wounded.
The post also highlighted the fact that nearly 70% of Gaza’s territory remains under Israeli military control, despite the so-called peace plan put forward by US President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace, envisioning a full withdrawal of the Israeli army.

"As artists, we have the privilege of reaching people through our work and our platforms," the signatories said. "With that privilege comes a responsibility to keep demanding an end to this horrific suffering."
They called for a permanent ceasefire, unrestricted delivery of critical humanitarian aid and an end to what they described as the decades-long denial of Palestinian human rights.
"The only path to a lasting peace is when both Palestinians and Israelis live in freedom, justice, and equity," the statement said.
The group also urged followers to share the message, donate, contact elected representatives and continue speaking out over Israel’s conduct in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
"We need everyone working together to assert our shared humanity towards an end to this decades-long oppression, and to demand our collective liberation,” it added. “None of us are free until all of us are free."
Several of the statement’s signatories have previously used public platforms to call for a ceasefire and highlight Palestinian suffering.

More recently, he used the Oscars stage to say "No to war, and free Palestine", while other awards-season interventions have seen him call for sanctions and a boycott of Israeli film institutions he said were implicated in abuses against Palestinians.

‘Deal with it’: US presses Netanyahu to condemn settler violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:53:24 UTC
01:53:24 KST

The standoff involving extremist settlers in the West Bank village of Qusra has become an unusual point of friction between Jerusalem and Washington, with Israeli officials familiar with the matter saying the U.S. administration is pressing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to publicly condemn the violence.
Netanyahu has so far refrained from doing so. Defense Minister Israel Katz issued a condemnation instead, and officials say his remarks came only after American pressure reached senior levels of the Israeli government. Very senior White House figures are also involved behind the scenes, according to those familiar with the contacts. “The Americans want to hear a public condemnation from Bibi, and they haven’t gotten it so far,” one Israeli official said.
The crisis began after settlers surrounded homes belonging to Palestinian families in Qusra, blocked access to them and disrupted water and electricity supplies. One of the homes belongs to a family with U.S. citizenship, making the affair especially sensitive for Washington.
U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, one of the administration’s most outspoken pro-Israel figures, issued an unusually harsh condemnation Thursday, calling the acts “terror” and those responsible “Israeli terrorists.” He said the U.S. Embassy had intervened with Israeli authorities and demanded that the incident be addressed.
According to Israeli officials, Huckabee’s remarks were not an isolated reaction. Washington has been pressing Netanyahu directly to issue an unequivocal public condemnation, while the absence of such a statement has drawn attention both in Israel and among U.S. officials.
Katz, speaking at a ceremony marking the establishment of the settlement of Ganim, said: “Violent disturbances, I say unequivocally, we are against this.” He added that only the authorized Israeli bodies should exercise force and warned that such violence causes “very serious damage among our friends.”
Israeli officials believe Netanyahu is wary of personally confronting extremist settlers because of the political risk of a clash with the right and with coalition partners, and that this is why the message was instead delivered through Katz.
Washington, however, no longer views Qusra as a purely local incident. Israeli officials say the administration regards the involvement of an American citizen and Israel’s handling of the affair with particular severity. According to them, some in Washington see the response as ranging from negligence and gross mishandling to possible deliberate inaction.
The broader concern is that continued settler violence could ignite a large-scale uprising in the West Bank and complicate U.S. efforts to advance arrangements in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria.
An Israeli official familiar with the matter said the issue is especially damaging because it angers Israel’s closest allies. “They don’t accept that it can’t be enforced. Deal with it,” the official said, adding that the sensitivity increases significantly when U.S. citizens are affected.
‘Not just criticism from the American left’
Israeli officials say the damage extends beyond relations with the current administration. One senior Israeli official warned that violence by settlers can no longer be dismissed as a concern limited to the American left, pointing to declining support for Israel among younger Republicans and growing unease even in traditionally sympathetic constituencies.
According to Pew data cited by the officials, 57% of Republicans aged 18 to 49 held an unfavorable view of Israel in April 2026, up from 50% a year earlier. Among Republicans aged 18 to 29, 64% expressed an unfavorable view.
Other figures published in July showed a sharp generational divide: only 42% of Republicans aged 18 to 29 viewed Israel favorably, compared with 83% of Republicans aged 65 and older. Among the younger group, 40% held a favorable view of the Palestinians.
The concern also extends to evangelical Christians, long a central pillar of U.S. support for Israel. “The ethos is compassion for the weaker party,” one Israeli official said. “Israel is perceived as a country that allows this, doesn’t prosecute them and gives them free passage.”
Another senior Israeli official said weak enforcement in settler violence cases also undermines Israel’s longstanding argument that outside intervention is unnecessary because Israeli institutions investigate themselves. If enforcement is not effective or transparent, the official said, that claim becomes harder to defend in the U.S. and international arenas.
The criticism is not limited to whether investigations are opened, but also to how they are perceived from abroad. Officials familiar with the matter say there is often insufficient transparency about whether suspects are investigated, what conclusions are reached and what action follows.
Palestinian residents, meanwhile, have described cases in which soldiers are present but do not intervene against rioters, saying they are not acting as police and that complaints should be directed to law enforcement.
That argument is especially sensitive because in areas under Israeli security responsibility, Israel is expected to maintain order and protect the Palestinian population. Since Palestinian police cannot enforce the law against Israeli citizens, responsibility remains with Israeli authorities.
Oded Revivi, the former mayor of Efrat, defended Huckabee and rejected attempts to portray his criticism as hostile to the settlement movement. “Don’t try to label Ambassador Huckabee, one of the greatest friends of the settlement enterprise in the United States, as a leftist,” Revivi said. “If a true friend like Huckabee has to bang on the table, all of us need to stop and ask how we lost our way and fix it immediately.”
Danny Ayalon, a former Israeli ambassador to the United States, also warned that Huckabee’s public intervention signals a deeper erosion of support among groups that once backed Israel almost automatically.
For Washington, the central question is now whether Israel can demonstrate that it enforces the law equally. Israeli officials say the Americans are not satisfied with statements alone. They want arrests, investigations, indictments and steps ensuring that suspects in violent attacks are not simply allowed to remain free.
The Qusra affair was further aggravated by a dispute over the possibility of removing Palestinian families from their homes. Officials familiar with the matter said American pressure was one of the reasons that move did not go ahead.
The message from Washington, they said, was clear: the victims cannot be the ones forced to pay the price for the violence.
For now, Huckabee remains the most senior American figure to speak publicly about the affair. But officials in Jerusalem believe that if Israel does not change its handling of settler violence, the criticism could rise to a higher level.
One senior Israeli official summarized Washington’s message this way: “There is no violence without someone responsible. Deal with it.”

Passenger train derails and 11 people injured after carriages overturn in southern England
LONDON (AP) — A passenger train derailed Thursday in southern England, seriously injuring two people and causing minor injuries for nine others after three carriages overturned, the British Transport Police said.
The Southern Rail train from Victoria station in London to Eastbourne was carrying about 150 people when it went off the tracks outside the tourist town of Lewes.
Passenger Rob Bradley said the train began rocking as it picked up speed and the carriage he was riding in with his 6-year-old daughter jumped upward and the brakes immediately engaged.
“Everything got thrown forward. My laptop, my AirPods, our bags,” Bradley told the BBC. “The train kind of skidded for quite a while before it stopped and only then when we turned around did we see that the whole back of the train — literally where we were sat — was open and there was smoke and dust pouring into the carriage.”
He could then see the car behind had flipped on its side and slid down an embankment into a lower field.
Bradley said he and his daughter were uninjured but he could see other passengers from one of the flipped cars with blood on their heads and clothing. Another passenger told him they had been cut when a window shattered.
Aerial footage showed firefighters and paramedics treating passengers in a field next to the train, with several ambulances and three helicopters standing by.
All passengers were evacuated within about three hours, the transport police said.
The cause of the derailment is under investigation.

Trump White House says it’s losing $19B-$26B a year in revenue as countries dodge tariffs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:53:02 UTC
01:53:02 KST

Trump White House says it’s losing $19B-$26B a year in revenue as countries dodge tariffs
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump White House said in a new report on Thursday that countries are routing their exports through third countries to avoid U.S. tariffs, estimating that there are tax revenue losses of $19 billion to $26 billion annually.
The report specifically highlights that China responded to new tariffs in 2018 by sending their goods to other nations ranging from Mexico to Malaysia for packaging and limited assembly — a practice known as transshipping. That pattern made it look like U.S. imports from China had dropped, but enabled Beijing to continue growing its manufacturing sector in ways that could challenge U.S. factories and employment.
Peter Navarro, the White House trade adviser, told reporters on a conference call that China is laundering its exports through more than 40 countries, though he claimed that the issues raised in the report were really more about other nations enabling the avoidance of tariffs.
“For years, the great transshipment scam has let communist China launder its exports,” Navarro said.
The report comes ahead of a planned September visit by Chinese Leader Xi Jinping, who President Donald Trump described in flattering terms during his own visit to Beijing in May.
The Chinese government has described its relationship with the U.S. as one of “strategic stability,” yet its government policies that support exports of manufactured goods have destabilized the auto, metals and electronics sectors in America, Europe, Japan and elsewhere.
Navarro said that other nations such as India could also transship to avoid new tariffs and said that new trade frameworks pursued by the Trump administration are going to contain provisions that ensure trade partners that engage in the practice will be penalized.
The Trump administration has levied high tariffs on much of the world in hopes of protecting U.S. manufacturers, hitting allies and rivals alike with import taxes. At the same time, those tariffs have created new inflationary pressures at home.
The report includes a range of estimates for the scale of transshipments to avoid tariffs, citing government and private sector numbers to estimate roughly $34.2 billion to $303 billion of goods transshipped each year. It used a central figure of $75 billion worth of goods being transshipped to estimate how much in tax revenues have been lost.
To address the challenge, Navarro said that U.S. Customs and Border Protection has started to use artificial intelligence in a prototype program to stop transshipments. Navarro said that when an importer has been found to have falsified the origins of a good, its imports can be retroactively tariffed going back roughly a year.
The president’s tariffs during his second term have faced an array of legal challenges, with the Supreme Court overturning some of them in February. America continues to import more than it exports to the rest of the world, but the trade imbalance so far this year at $371 billion is running about $189 billion lower that it did during the same period last year.

Families mourn victims of Zimbabwe ferry disaster as death toll rises to 46
HARARE, Zimbabwe (AP) — Mourners gathered in a Zimbabwe fishing town Thursday to bid farewell to dozens of people who were killed when an overloaded ferry capsized on Lake Kariba this week, as police said the death toll rose to 46.
Dozens of mourners, including cabinet ministers, gathered at Kariba’s Nyamhunga Stadium, where coffins were laid out in the middle of the field under tents.
The ferry capsized on Zimbabwe ’s Lake Kariba on Tuesday. Police and the government agency responsible for the ferry have yet to give an official count of how many people were aboard or how many remain missing. Estimates have put the number of passengers as high as 153, while authorities say the aging ferry has a capacity of 90. The country’s disaster management agency on Wednesday said that 77 people had been rescued.
State broadcaster ZBC News reported that some families lost several members in the disaster. The ferry was traveling from Kariba town to rural communities and fishing camps, where residents rely heavily on fishing and on the vessel for transport because roads are damaged and public transport is scarce or virtually nonexistent.
Among those grieving was Collen Ndandalika, whom the broadcaster said lost his wife and three children.
“My wife and children all drowned. Two children have been recovered, but my wife and the other child are still missing. I still can’t believe this is a real world I am living in,” he said.
His wife sold goods bought in town to people in rural and fishing communities. She had asked their children to help with the business during the school holidays, he said.
“I have my brothers who are checking on the bodies to see if they can identify my wife and child. I am too traumatized to keep looking at dead bodies,” he said.
The disaster has also triggered criticism of the continued use of the aging ferry and what some say was a delayed rescue response to the sinking. Some survivors on Wednesday said they pleaded in vain with the captain of the overloaded ferry to turn back from strong waves shortly before it capsized.
President Emmerson Mnangagwa, in a condolence message, acknowledged that the tragedy had “exposed serious deficiencies in our maritime capabilities which we have to address immediately so that our places of recreation do not become death traps to the innocent.”
Mnangagwa declared a state of disaster and ordered government agencies to mobilize resources to assist victims and accelerate recovery efforts.
Kariba is the largest human-made lake in the world by volume and was created in the late 1950s and early 1960s by building a dam on the Zambezi River. The huge lake is now more than 200 kilometers (124 miles) long and up to 40 kilometers (25 miles) wide in places.

Poland says it thwarted Russian plot to kill an American citizen

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13

Russian plot to kill American citizen thwarted by Poland, prime minister says: "First situation of its kind"
A Russian plot to kill a Ukrainian-American citizen in Warsaw was thwarted by Poland before it could be carried out, the Polish prime minister said Thursday, marking the first time in decades that a Western leader has publicly accused Moscow of plotting to kill a U.S. citizen.
Western officials have previously warned that Russia has stepped up a campaign of targeted killings since President Vladimir Putin launched the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, saying they have disrupted several plots across Europe. But Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said this incident was unprecedented.
Tusk told journalists the suspect, who was allegedly recruited by Russia's secret services, had been arrested last Friday, Aug. 7.
"He was inconvenient from the point of view of the Putin regime, and at the last moment... we managed to prevent this execution," he added.
"This is the first situation of its kind in which someone, acting on Russian orders, decided to carry out an attack against an American citizen on the territory of another NATO country," he added.
It was the first time that "someone on the order of Russia" sought to attack an American citizen on the territory of another NATO country, Tusk said Thursday.
The American Ukrainian citizen "was uncomfortable for the Putin regime," Tusk said in a news conference. "We have to accept the assumption that the Putin regime will try to eliminate people who are inconvenient for various reasons."
The operation to disrupt the plot was carried out in cooperation with U.S. services, said Tomasz Siemoniak, Poland's minister overseeing intelligence services. He said the targeted victim was a U.S. citizen "of Ukrainian origin." Officials did not immediately provide further details.
The Russian Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Russia accused of trying to undermine Ukraine's allies
Russia has long been accused of targeting its enemies abroad, including by using rare poisons. But intelligence officials previously told The Associated Press that Russia's security services are now more brazen in their choice of targets, going after Russian activists and foreign supporters of Ukraine as well as military defectors.
Western officials see the campaign as connected to Russia's broader efforts to undermine European countries that support Ukraine. The AP has mapped about 200 acts of sabotage, arson and other disruption across Europe since the start of the war that officials have linked to Russia. Putin said in May that Russia is not waging a sabotage campaign against Europe.
British authorities accused Russia of being behind the killing of former FSB officer Alexander Litvinenko in London in 2006 with radioactive polonium and of attempting to kill former Russian military intelligence officer Sergei Skripal in Salisbury in 2018 with the nerve agent Novichok.
German authorities also said Russia organized the 2019 killing of Zelimkhan Khangoshvili, a former Chechen rebel commander who was shot in a Berlin park by Vadim Krasikov, a hitman who was later greeted by Putin after he was exchanged in a spy swap.
In June, a Russian artist who was critical of Putin was shot and killed at close range near his home in eastern Poland. Robert Kuzovkov, known by the pseudonym Semyon Skrepetsky was critical of Putin and Tusk said at the time that the killing had the hallmarks of a political assassination. He suggested it was possible Russia was behind it but Polish officials have not yet attributed it to Moscow.
Last year French officials disrupted a plot which they believe was aimed at killing Vladimir Osechkin, a Russian exile who lives under police protection and works to help military defectors flee Putin's war. Lithuanian officials also disrupted a plot last year to kill a Lithuanian supporter of Ukraine and another against a Russian activist. Officials in Germany have similarly broken up two plots: one to target the head of a German weapons company supplying Ukraine, the other against a Ukrainian military official.
Polish authorities arrested a man in 2024 in what they said was a plot to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. And that same year, a Russian helicopter pilot who defected was killed in Spain - with Russian operatives the prime suspects.
"This campaign is not by accident or chance," a senior European intelligence official previously told the AP. "There is political authorization."

Yemen at highest risk of major conflict since 2022 truce, UN warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13

Yemen at highest risk of major conflict since 2022 truce, UN warns
Aug 13 - Yemen faces its most serious threat of a return to large-scale war since a U.N.-brokered truce in 2022, U.N. envoy Hans Grundberg warned on Thursday, as the world body said more than half the country's population was experiencing acute food insecurity.
The warning follows an escalation in hostilities between Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi group and its internationally-recognised, Saudi-backed government that has raised fears of a broader return to war and a fuelling of wider regional tensions.
Grundberg told the Security Council that military activity had intensified along Yemen's frontlines. Recent Houthi attacks in the regions of Marib, Hadramawt, Mocha and elsewhere had caused military and civilian casualties, he said.
He said renewed Houthi attacks on commercial vessels in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden risked drawing Yemen further into wider regional confrontation, as regional trade and energy flows were already under pressure from the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, where control is contested in the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.
Grundberg called on the parties in Yemen's conflict to immediately de-escalate and work towards a robust ceasefire, saying attacks and threats against shipping as well as cross-border attacks must stop. He said a negotiated "off-ramp" remained possible and urged countries with influence over the parties to steer Yemen back towards negotiations.
The security deterioration has coincided with a worsening of Yemen's humanitarian crisis.
U.N. humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher told the council that more than half the population faced acute food insecurity, while 6 million people were at "Emergency" levels of food deprivation bordering on famine.
Both Grundberg and Fletcher called for the release of 73 U.N. personnel detained by the Houthis, along with workers from non-governmental organisations, civil society and diplomatic missions. Grundberg also said preparations to free more than 1,600 conflict-related detainees agreed in May were moving slowly and could be derailed by the wider escalation.
On July 20, the Houthis announced a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea in response to what they described as a Saudi siege of Yemen, an allegation Riyadh denies. A Saudi-led coalition responded with air strikes on what it said were Houthi military facilities in the port city of Hodeidah linked to threats against commercial shipping.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led military intervention the following year. Although the U.N.-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted major fighting, despite expiring six months later, efforts to turn it into a lasting political settlement have stalled as regional tensions have intensified. How a minor or major housing downturn could impact your city
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:48:56 UTC
01:48:56 KST

How four downturn scenarios could alter capital city property values
Double-digit declines in home values would make little dent in the gains accumulated across mid-sized housing markets during Australia's five-year housing boom, according to new analysis from property data firm Cotality.
The modelling illustrates how market pullbacks could impact capital city prices across four downturn scenarios: 5 per cent, 10 per cent, 15 per cent and 20 per cent.
Capital city breakdown
Years of subdued growth have left Melbourne with a relatively thin buffer if prices were to fall, with dwelling values peaking at $840,000 in November 2025.
"A decline beyond 10 per cent in Melbourne would return values to pre-pandemic levels," Cotality head of research Gerard Burg said.
Meanwhile, markets such as Perth, Brisbane and Adelaide have recorded exceptional growth over the past five years, giving them more significant buffers against declines.
"Even if Perth's housing market fell 20 per cent from its peak, the median dwelling value would still be around where it was in April 2025 after recording one of the strongest growth cycles of any capital city," Mr Burg said.
Modelling from ANZ also suggests property prices could plunge by 4.3 per cent this year and by 3.4 per cent in 2027 as the current market downturn intensifies.
This is driven by a 14.5 per cent peak-to-trough decline in Sydney values and a 12.8 per cent fall in Melbourne prices.
"Since our last forecast update in June, the housing market has softened a little more than we were expecting," economists Madeline Dunk and Adam Boyton said.
"Sydney and Melbourne prices have declined slightly more than our forecasts, and prices in Brisbane and Perth have started falling earlier than we expected.
"It is clear the combination of restrictive interest rates, recent tax policy changes and global uncertainty have dampened sentiment in the market."
A key sign of weakness in the market is auction clearance rates, which are sitting well below 50 per cent in major markets like Sydney and Melbourne. Clearance rates below 50 per cent have historically correlated with price falls.
Is a double-digit property downturn realistic?
PRD chief economist Diaswati Mardiasmo says it will take a global-financial-crisis-type situation for the market to fall by 20 per cent.
"A 20 per cent fall seems a little far-fetched to me. It would be a massive swing in the pendulum," Dr Mardiasmo told the ABC.
"I think a 5 per cent drop is more realistic at the moment, given inflation has been going down every month since March.
"What's happening right now in the market is temporary in nature because it's based on economic conditions like interest rates being high and the government's changes in property taxes."
Dr Mardiasmo believes if inflation continues on its downward trajectory to a level the RBA is comfortable with (about 3.4 to 3.5 per cent), the market will see a "change in the winds" by mid-to-late 2027.
ANZ economists also see prices recovering over 2028.
"Given the broader supply backdrop, and the capacity constraints in the construction sector, we think it is hard to see housing prices falling for an extended period," Ms Dunk and Mr Boyton said.
House prices not the 'main game', RBA says
RBA governor Michele Bullock says the board is monitoring the flow-on effects of the housing market downturn, but stresses it is not the bank's focus for future rate decisions.
"The main game here for us is excess capacity, [the] tight labour market, particularly in some areas like construction, the Middle East conflict, the AI boom. These are all the things that are front of mind in terms of risks to the inflation outlook," Ms Bullock said.
The RBA does, however, see house prices continuing "to decline gradually for a period", according to its latest set of staff economic forecasts.
Financial markets see a 60 per cent chance the RBA will deliver another 0.25 percentage point rate rise by the end of the year, which would take the cash rate to 4.6 per cent.

Japan Outraged by Putin’s Visit to Iturup Island, Which It Considers Own Territory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:48:16 UTC
01:48:16 KST

Japan reacted sharply to Vladimir Putin’s visit on August 13 to Iturup, which Tokyo considers its territory.
The Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs released a statement by Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi regarding the incident.
During his trip, Putin visited local facilities, including a fish-processing plant, a school, and a hospital, and spoke with the island’s residents.
The visit took place amid Russia’s increased military presence in the Kuril Islands. Moscow considers the archipelago a strategically important region, and there is a military airbase on Iturup.
The Japanese Prime Minister called the Russian president’s trip “absolutely unacceptable.” According to her, the visit contradicts Tokyo’s consistent position on the Northern Territories.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs stated that the Northern Territories are part of Japanese sovereignty. Officials there emphasized that Putin’s unilateral visit would have a negative impact on relations between the countries, which have already deteriorated due to Russian aggression against Ukraine.
Motegi reported that his ministry had summoned the Russian ambassador and lodged a protest with him. The Japanese side asked the diplomat to convey Tokyo’s position to the Russian government.
The Kuril Islands are an archipelago located between the Japanese island of Hokkaido and Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula. The territorial dispute between Russia and Japan concerns its four southern islands: Iturup, Kunashir, Shikotan, and the Habomai group of islands. Japan refers to them as the Northern Territories.
The border between the Russian Empire and Japan in the Kuril Islands was first clearly defined by the Treaty of Shimoda in 1855. In 1875, under the Treaty of Saint Petersburg, Russia ceded all of the Kuril Islands to Japan in exchange for recognition of Russian control over Sakhalin.
After the end of World War II, the Soviet Union established control over the entire Kuril Archipelago. Japan subsequently renounced its rights and claims to the Kuril Islands under the 1951 peace treaty; however, Moscow did not sign that document. Tokyo, meanwhile, maintains that the four southern islands are not among the territories to which Japan renounced its claims.
In 1956, the USSR and Japan restored diplomatic relations and ended the formal state of war, but they never concluded a peace treaty. The Soviet side agreed to transfer Shikotan and Habomai to Japan after the conclusion of a peace treaty, but Tokyo insisted on the return of all four islands.
In the decades that followed, Moscow and Tokyo attempted to resolve the territorial dispute but were unable to reach an agreement. Russia continues to administer the islands, while Japan considers them an occupied part of its own country.

European drought shrivels crops despite farmers’ best efforts to adapt

European drought shrivels crops despite farmers’ best efforts to adapt
The drought roasting much of Europe this summer is taking a heavy toll on crops across the continent, from potatoes in the Netherlands to corn in Bosnia. Triodos, a Dutch bank with a focus on sustainability, has warned that this could reduce gross domestic product across the EU by 1 percent for 2026 – or around €180 billion.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
A cloud of dust billows behind Maarten Janse’s tractor as he spreads a mixture of compost, straw and manure over a field to nourish the parched soil.
Janse's farm on the fertile land of the Netherlands' southwestern Zeeland Province is drying out despite his efforts to make it more drought resistant as accelerated human-caused global warming and a supersized El Nino batter fields across Europe.
The drought that is roasting much of Europe this summer is taking a heavy toll on crops across the continent, from potatoes in the Netherlands to corn in Bosnia and grapes in Italy. Even when farmers try to adapt, the extreme weather is hitting their crops and water supplies.
Read moreAnother heatwave hits Europe as drought and fires worsen
Triodos, a Dutch bank that has a focus on sustainability, published an analysis this week that estimated the heatwaves and drought could reduce gross domestic product across the European Union by 1 percent for 2026 or around €180 billion. Farmers are among the hardest hit, with their crops set to be badly affected by soaring temperatures and lack of water. In large parts of the Netherlands, farmers are no longer allowed to use water from streams and drainage channels to irrigate fields and orchards.
Another farmer in Zeeland, Hendrik Jan ten Cate, looks at a field full of withered potato plants that are almost all ready for harvest – a month early and with a significantly reduced crop. His potatoes are used to make French fries for companies including McDonald’s, but they’re likely going to be too small this year.
“People want long fries,” he says as he holds one of the potatoes. “That’s going to be tough this year.”
Ten Cate is one of the lucky farmers because he is allowed to irrigate his crops. But, even so, he estimates his harvest this year will be down by about one-third compared to average years.
“It's not just the drought that is the problem,” he says. “It is also the sun, the dry air and especially the hot days we have had this year. The potatoes just can't handle that combination very well.”
In Bosnia, where agriculture contributes roughly 5 percent of annual GDP and 10 percent of all employment, grain farmer Slavisa Lukic stood in one of his corn fields as stalks blew limply in the breeze. His crops have been hit by repeated heat waves and drought conditions. He said this year’s corn yield would be very poor, if he manages to harvest one at all.
Lukic remembers when he grew 6 to 7 tonnes per hectare on his farm. He expects this year’s corn yield will be around 1.5 to 2 tonnes per hectare.
Pointing to the drought-stricken land in northeastern Bosnia, Lukic said clover fields that once grew abundantly have all but disappeared. “Now they literally do not exist,” he said. “Nothing.”
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
The drought is even hitting one of the Czech Republic's most famous products: beer.
Plzensky Prazdroj, the country’s largest beer producer, expects to incur losses this year due to a stunted hops yield.
Jakub Zaoral, the brewer’s sustainability manager, said that changes in rainfall patterns – characterised by long periods of dryness with occasional heavy storms – mean that when rain does fall, it runs off the dry soil. That results in inconsistent yields and increasingly low groundwater levels.
“There’s no choice but to simply accept the fact that one year will be great and the next won’t be,” he said. “If it were to happen three times in a row, that could very well become an existential problem for hop growers.”
In Romania, some heat and drought-resistant crops like sunflowers have been less affected by the extreme conditions and yields have been plentiful. But the drought is still hitting home with record-low water levels on the Danube River disrupting grain transport, causing chronically congested terminals and an increasing pileup of crops with nowhere to go.
“In a short time, maximum 10 days, we will enter full blast in sunflower harvest, to be followed by corn,” Cezar Gheorghe, founder of grain consultancy firm Agricolumn, said. “Already farmers are in panic mode. They can’t find a place to store the corn and sunflower seeds.”
WatchRecord drought in France this summer
Cattle grazing plains in Hungary are turning to dust. No rain has fallen on Sandor Molnár's dairy farm since late May and he is having to buy expensive feed for his 130 cows.
“We’re trying to hang in there and hope for the best, hoping next year will be better,” he added. “To be honest, we’ve been saying that for a few years now, but maybe this time it will be.”
Elveden Estate, with more than 10,000 acres of farmland on the Suffolk-Norfolk border in eastern England, has built a reservoir that can hold enough water to fill about 200 Olympic-sized swimming pools.
Less than a year after opening, it's almost dry. Another reservoir is at about 20 percent capacity.
But the farm's water policy is paying off.
“The fact that we’ve invested significantly in reservoir storage and the infrastructure associated with pumping water has meant that we’ve been in a very strong position to continue to irrigate our crops through this growing season,” the farm's managing director, Andrew Blenkiron, said.
But every drop counts.
“We’re very concerned that we haven’t got enough water to see us through this season,” Blenkiron said. “We’ve got probably, if this weather stays as it is, six weeks of watering left to do.”
Janse uses no-till farming on his fields – not ploughing the soil, planting crops to cover the ground year-round and adding organic matter – to help cope with the whims of the weather as climate change triggers more extremes.
He has also diversified by running a popular campsite on his farm near the picturesque town of Veere. As he tends to his fields, guests walk by toward a lake where yachts and a river cruise ship sail past.
And as dry weather causes an increase in soil salinity in fields, Janse grows samphire, also known as sea asparagus, on a small patch of land. It's a crop that can thrive in salty conditions. But with no rainfall, even that is struggling this year.
“Samphire needs fresh water, and if there is only saltwater it doesn’t grow either,” he said.
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

Woman who fatally drugged two men while posing as sex worker jailed for 17 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:47:27 UTC
01:47:27 KST

A woman who posed as a sex worker and administered a deadly amount of sedative to two men has been jailed for 17 years, along with her accomplice.
Adina Mihai, 31, and her partner Madalin Dumitru, 30, who arranged for her to meet men at their homes, drugged their victims to steal from them.
She spiked the glasses of wine of four men with the sedative gamma-butyrolactone (GBL). Two, Malcolm King, 80, of Gloucestershire, and Gary Mouat, 36, of Oxfordshire, died.
Jailing Mihai and Dumitru, from Ilford, Essex, at Oxford crown court, Mrs Justice Brunner said: “Your intention was to incapacitate each victim making them deeply unconscious.
“The administration of the drug was haphazard and depended on the strength of each batch, the amount put into drinks, and the amount they drunk.
“If you had stopped for a moment to consider the risks, as you should have done, you would have realised that it carried a high risk of serious injury or death at the very moment you administered that drug. If you had done the most cursory research, you would know that GBL can be extremely toxic.”
The pair pleaded guilty to two charges of manslaughter and to administering poison to the two survivors, who cannot be identified.
Julian Evans KC, prosecuting, said: “While Dumitru waited nearby, Mihai would enter the victim’s home. There, she would persuade the victim to drink alcohol laced with GBL.
“Once the victim was unconscious, Mihai would look for property to steal. Then she would rejoin Dumitru, leaving the victim alone and unconscious.”
No sexual services were provided but the pair worked on the premise that victims would not report what had happened to the police out of embarrassment.
The court heard Mihai advertised online and the couple would take cash deposits before meeting the men. When their victims fell unconscious, she would steal watches, jewellery, aftershave and cash.
In a victim personal statement, Mouat’s son, aged eight, said the defendants had ruined his life.
He asked the couple: “Why did you have to kill my dad, you could have just taken the money, he was really kind, he would have given it to you.
“He was my dad and now he’s gone. I miss him every day and will never get to see him again. I will never be able to get another dad and that makes me feel so sad. You have ruined my life and all the plans we had to do things together. My family is destroyed now.”
King’s daughter, Caroline, said: “When my father was killed, the defendants did not only end his future. They stole mine as well.”
His younger sister, Jacky Seagroatt, said: “What haunts me every day is the way he died. I might have been able to come to terms with losing my brother if he had died naturally or as the result of a tragic accident. I cannot stop imagining what he went through or how frightened he may have been.”
Charles White, the senior crown prosecutor with the CPS, described the case as “unique”.
No other deaths, poisonings or thefts have been linked to the pair but police are keeping an open mind about the possibility of other victims.

Former Montreal anti-racism commissioner Bochra Manai is suing the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs (CIJA) for alleged defamation and a campaign to discredit her.
The Montreal Gazette and CBS Canada first reported on the lawsuit, which Manai filed with the Quebec Superior Court in Montreal.
The specific accusation against CIJA revolves around a visual montage in which CIJA allegedly compared her to Adolf Hitler. The montage is not searchable online currently; however, it is featured in the lawsuit.
Manai argues that the montage is just part of an almost three-year campaign orchestrated by CIJA with the aim of discrediting her and having her fired from the City of Montreal. She is seeking $125,000 in damages, split into $100,000 in moral damages for the alleged harm caused to her and a further $25,000 in punitive damages.
Manai's history at City of Montreal
Manai was appointed as city commissioner for the fight against racism and systemic discrimination in 2021.
After October 7, 2023, her relationship with CIJA deteriorated.
The precipitating moment seemed to be on October 28, 2023, when Manai decided to take part in a pro-Palestine, pro-ceasefire rally in Montreal, during which controversial Imam Adil Charkaoui gave a speech about "Allah, take care of these Zionist aggressors. Allah, take care of the enemies of the people of Gaza. Allah, count them all, then exterminate them. And don't spare any of them!"
Canadian police investigated the incident as a hate crime.
Manai: Attending the pro-Palestine rally in Montreal was her 'duty to humanity'
Manai defended her position in an op-ed in Le Devoir, saying her choice to attend the rally is her "duty to humanity." She did not publicly condemn the imam's remarks. She did, however, condemn Islamophobic and antisemitic acts committed in the weeks after October 7, saying "all are unacceptable, and the violence must be strongly condemned."
"Shooting Jewish schools and children is a crime that must be punished and has no place in a metropolis like Montreal. Targeting Muslim places of worship is just as important."
A few weeks later, in November 2023, CIJA called for Manai to resign.
“The choice of when she was silent and when she was vocal is very telling," said Eta Yudin, CIJA’s then vice-president, in the Montreal Gazette. "A step forward would be for her to resign or for the mayor to find someone to fill that role who would be aligned with the mayor’s own views on antisemitism and commitment to fighting antisemitism, Islamophobia and all forms of racism, and someone who has the moral clarity and leadership to gain the confidence of all minority groups and Montrealers.”
December 2023, CIJA called for the mayor to replace Manai
Then, in December 2023, CIJA and Federation CJA called on then-Mayor Valerie Plante to replace Manai, citing her attendance at several rallies while remaining silent about antisemitism. Manai's lawsuit cites a sentence in this CIJA publication - that she is “complicit by refusing to speak out against hate” - as "a serious accusation capable of significantly damaging her reputation."
CIJA again expressed concern in February 2025 when Plante promoted Manaï from Commissioner for the Fight against Racism and Systemic Discrimination to director of the Office of Commissioners of the City of Montreal.
“Such a promotion is simply scandalous,” CIJA said.
"She has been noted for her silence and inaction in the face of the antisemitism that has been rotting the city for more than 15 months.”
Manai alleges CIJA communications reinforced Muslim stereotypes
The accusations by CIJA of Manai's antisemitism are featured prominently in the lawsuit. According to the Gazette, Manaï alleges CIJA’s communications contributed to stereotypes associating Muslims with antisemitism and extremism, including by suggesting that she supported or tolerated extremist violence. The lawsuit argues this amounts to discrimination based on religion prohibited by Quebec’s Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms.
She also said the alleged campaign caused “harm to her reputation, dignity and integrity, humiliation, stress, anxiety and loss of enjoyment of life."
Regarding the alleged Hitler montage, the lawsuit says the comparison "equates the plaintiff with a figure who committed genocide against Jews and a leading figure of antisemitism, which constitutes an extreme attack on her honor and dignity."
Manai is still the director of the Office of Commissioners of the City of Montreal.
CIJA declined to comment when asked by the Post, citing that the investigation is ongoing.

Judge dismisses Trump administration lawsuit alleging Harvard failed to protect Jewish students
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:47:13 UTC
01:47:13 KST

A federal judge dismissed a lawsuit on Thursday by US President Donald Trump’s administration that alleged Harvard University failed to protect Jewish and Israeli students from harassment.
In his ruling, US District Judge Richard Stearns in Boston said the Trump administration’s lawsuit, filed in March, had not plausibly shown an ongoing violation of federal civil rights law on Harvard's campus.
Stearns said the government's allegations focused largely on incidents amid protests over Israel's war in Gaza during the 2023/24 school year, with only a handful of later incidents alleged in March 2025 that were "too isolated and episodic" to support a claim of ongoing civil rights violations.
The Louis D. Brandeis Center for Human Rights under Law Chairman and CEO, Kenneth L. Marcus, who served as the US Assistant Secretary of Education during Trump's first term, said the ruling set a negative precedent for future cases of discrimination.
“The rule applied in this decision would make it significantly more challenging for the Justice Department to win future civil rights cases, not just those involving anti-Semitism, by effectively raising the legal standard for enforcement.," he said.
“This is a significant and troubling departure from how civil rights enforcement has long worked and it should concern anyone who cares about accountability on antisemitism or any other form of discrimination.”
Judge says lawsuit didn't adequately allege failures
The judge said the lawsuit did not adequately allege failures by the university after the government told Harvard in June 2025 that it was not complying with Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. It bans discrimination based on race, color, and national origin in programs that receive federal funding.
The White House and Harvard did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Vast majority of antisemitic online content flagged by Jewish users stays online, EU Jews say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:47:02 UTC
01:47:02 KST

A new audit published by the World Jewish Congress (WJC) claims that the vast majority of antisemitic content reported by European Jewish community members remains publicly available online, pointing to what the organization characterizes as profound gaps in platform moderation and accountability.
The study, titled “Flagged and Failed: Platform Responses to Antisemitic Content Reported by Jewish Communities,” evaluates data collected between February 2025 and April 2026. The initiative was carried out under the WJC Hate Online: Preparedness and Empowerment (HO:PE) project, which was co-funded by the European Union under the CERV program.
According to the organization, this marked the first systematic, community-sourced dataset of online antisemitism gathered across the EU via a purpose-built reporting application.
The project used a dedicated reporting tool that enabled Jewish community members across Europe to document antisemitic URLs, categorize them using the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s working definition of antisemitism as an analytical framework, and indicate whether they had formally flagged the posts to host platforms.
Following the filtering of invalid entries, the published dataset comprised 754 distinct reports spanning six major social media platforms. To measure platform accountability, researchers conducted a liveness check throughout May 2026 to assess whether the reported content was still publicly accessible.
Furthermore, a specialized legal assessment was conducted for high-risk categories to evaluate potential thresholds for illegality under EU and member state laws, including the EU Framework Decision on Racism and Xenophobia.
Online hate spans a wide variety of tropes
The analysis presented by the organization demonstrates that online hate spans traditional tropes, Holocaust distortion, incitement to violence, and hostility related to Israel.
Facebook accounted for the highest volume of submissions at 34.4%, followed closely by Instagram and X/Twitter at 26% each, and TikTok at 9.7%. When examining how content remains online, the audit finds striking disparities in how platforms handle reported material.
Across all submissions evaluated in May 2026, the study contends that 81.3% of reported antisemitic posts, equaling 613 out of 754, remained live. A critical assertion of the study is that formally reporting content through a platform’s built-in mechanism made virtually no measurable difference in whether it was removed.
The overall removal rate hovered near 19% for content that was formally flagged, compared to roughly 18% for content left unflagged.
Platform-specific breakdowns highlight diverse enforcement realities: Facebook recorded the highest user-reporting rate in the dataset, with 76% of its 259 entries formally flagged by users, yet registered the lowest overall removal rate among major platforms at just 13.9%.
Instagram and X both showed removal rates of 12%-15%, with users reporting a relatively small percentage of encountered content directly to the platforms.
Standing apart as an outlier, TikTok removed 64.4% of all content in its dataset and 70.6% of content explicitly reported to it, making it the only major platform where the study recorded a majority of audited antisemitic posts being taken down.
The report’s category analysis illustrates that certain types of hate speech are vastly more resistant to moderation than others. Israel-related antisemitism proved to be the most persistent blind spot for moderators according to the data, with only 5.2% of such reports removed.
Content comparing Israeli policy to Nazism showed no removal across all reports
Most notably, the audit claims that content comparing Israeli policy to Nazism showed no removal across all 28 documented reports.
Conversely, explicit incitement to violence, such as calls to harm Jewish people or radical ideological incitement, carried the highest removal rate at nearly 35%, though dangerous material like terrorist propaganda and direct calls to murder still frequently lingered online. Overall, the legal assessment estimated that roughly 6% of all submissions crossed thresholds warranting individual criminal examination under European law.
The WJC concluded that self-regulatory reporting mechanisms are failing everyday users, leaving vulnerable communities exposed to persistent digital hate. In response, the report outlines direct recommendations for social media companies to audit their content moderation policies, demonstrate the operational efficacy of their reporting channels with transparent data, and address blind spots regarding conflict-related hate speech.
Regulatory bodies are also urged to use enforcement powers under instruments such as the Digital Services Act to scrutinize risk-mitigation practices. In contrast, national law enforcement agencies must establish clear referral pathways for illegal online incitement.

Ukrainian strikes on refineries cause 55% drop in Russia's seaborne oil product exports
Russia's seaborne oil product exports fell by 54.7% in July compared to the same month in 2025, to 3.93 million tonnes. Average daily shipments dropped by 33.3% compared to June.
Source: Reuters, with reference to industry sources and its own calculations
Details: Drones have attacked a number of major Russian oil refineries in recent months. The damage has forced facilities to undergo unscheduled repairs, resulting in reduced oil processing, fuel production and exports.
The largest decline was in shipments through the Arctic ports of Murmansk and Arkhangelsk – down 85.4% compared to June, to 44,000 tonnes.
Russia exported 1.25 million tonnes of oil products through Black Sea and Sea of Azov ports, 49% less than in June.
Exports through the Baltic ports of Primorsk, Vysotsk, St Petersburg and Ust-Luga fell by 16%, to 1.974 million tonnes. Shipments from Far Eastern ports also decreased by 16% to 664,000 tonnes.
Background:
- On 13 August, it was reported that the Orsk refinery had ceased operations after a Ukrainian drone attack. The drones damaged the facility's processing units.
- In July, Russia began redirecting fuel from Siberia to Moscow and increasing imports to contain shortages following the attacks on oil refineries.
