Cyprus ramping up pressure on Tel Aviv while eyeing Israel’s Merkava tanks for its army - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:46:48 UTC
01:46:48 KST

Cyprus is ramping up pressure on Israel to allow them to purchase Merkava tanks (Mk3 or Mk4), pan-Cypriot daily newspaper Phileleftheros reported on Monday.
The Merkava is the primary tank used by the IDF’s Armored Corps. While development for the tank began in 1970, it only entered service in 1979 and was extensively used during the First Lebanon War.
The Merkava Mark 4 Barak is the version of the tank that is currently in use.
According to Phileleftheros, opinions within the Israeli government are divided on the matter, with some in support of providing Cyprus with Merkava tanks and some against such a move, wanting the tanks to remain available to the IDF.
Phileleftheros noted that the Merkava’s suitability for Cyprus’s National Guard stems from two main reasons.
Israel-Cyprus talks reportedly stall because of Oct. 7
The first, being the similarity between Israel and Cyprus’s terrain; and the second being the proximity of the two countries, which would ease logistical support for the tanks.
Talks between Cyprus and Israel for the purchase of second-hand Merkava tanks had stalled with the outbreak of the Israel-Hamas War on October 7, 2023, reported Cypriot media, with Israeli reassurances that discussions would resume once the security situation had eased.
Several other contenders for Cyprus’s National Guard have been put forth, according to Cypriot media, including Greece’s Leopard 1A5 and France’s EBRC Jaguar.
The Leopard, however, has reportedly been rejected by Cyprus for not meeting the country’s national guard’s operational requirements.
Several contracts for smaller equipment, such as drones and other equipment that have shorter production times, have already progressed, according to Phileleftheros.
It added that contracts for larger equipment, such as armoured vehicles, are slated to begin in 2028.
Israel, Greece, Cyprus sign trilateral work plan
Currently, Cyprus’s National Guard is using Russian-built T-80 tanks, but Russia’s deteriorating relations with Western counties and sanctions placed upon it have made it difficult to reliably secure spare parts and ammunition.
In December 2025, Israel, Greece, and Cyprus signed a trilateral work plan for military cooperation for 2026.
Among other things, the plans include joint exercises and training, working groups in various fields, and strategic military dialogue on issues of joint interest.
The signing of the plans constitutes another step in deepening military cooperation among the countries and contributes to strengthening stability, security, and peace in the eastern Mediterranean region, the IDF told The Jerusalem Post at the time.
In 2024, Cypriot media had reported that the Mediterranean country had taken a delivery of Israel’s Barak MX anti-aircraft system.
Cypriot officials at the time declined to comment on the specifics of the report.
"The only thing I can say is we will and are doing everything necessary to bolster the deterrence force of Cyprus,” Cypriot President Nikos Christodoulides told reporters in 2024. “Not only because we are a country under occupation, but an EU member state in a region of particular geo-strategic importance.”
Yonah Jeremy Bob and Reuters contributed to this report.

They've survived 2 major earthquakes in Colombia: "A sense of powerlessness"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:46:45 UTC
01:46:45 KST

Colombia earthquake survivors are reliving a nightmare from 1999: "You feel a sense of powerlessness"
Jahir Rodríguez knew what was happening when he saw thick, dark clouds forming near his home in western Colombia on Monday morning. Parts of his dear Pereira were crumbling.
The urban planner and former professor also knows what happens next after a powerful earthquake devastates whole communities. He sprang into action after a deadly 1999 quake in Armenia, about 30 miles away from his current home, that killed around 1,200 people. He did so again three days ago when a 7.4 magnitude earthquake struck the same region, killing at least 281 people and trapping hundreds under debris across several states.
"You feel a sense of powerlessness," Rodríguez said as he recalled seeing glass shattering and water seeping through the cracked and fallen walls of shaken buildings.
"You will be here for years"
Rodríguez, who is 68 and retired, learned how to respond to earthquakes after the disaster in Colombia's coffee region at the turn of the century. He gained valuable insights from a delegation of Japanese responders who had faced a deadly quake in Osaka in 1995.
"It is a mistake to think that you will be here for days or months," Rodríguez said they told him. "You will be here for years."
Rodríguez, who also assisted after a major earthquake in Talca, Chile, in 2010, is referring to the encampments forming in parks across the city, a common sight after people lose their homes to natural disasters.
In Colombia, the new government, which took over just days before the quake, is helping set up the encampments, Rodríguez said. But that tactic may be shortsighted, he said, since people will remain displaced for years and need permanent living quarters now. He also says the primary concern right now is more dire.
"The first is to count people, the second is to organize them where they will be placed, and the third is the reconstruction plans," he said.
Getting people to leave their uninhabitable homes is hard, Rodríguez said. He spent the day after Monday's earthquake visiting with a friend and fellow urban planner whose apartment building toppled onto others. When he arrived, Rodríguez said, his friend would not move from the site out of fear that vandals would enter the building — something that was more prevalent after the 1999 quake.
"People are here in front of the sidewalk, watching their house," Rodríguez said with immense sadness.
He's seeing people making meals on the side of the road, and says it's hardest to think about what will come next for them.
"Days and days and days, nights and nights and nights, months and months and months in a shelter waiting to be helped," he said.
A blueprint for earthquake recovery
Everardo Murillo created a blueprint for long-term recovery efforts following the 1999 earthquake. Colombia's then-president, Andrés Pastrana, tasked him with creating the fund and organization to allocate money for people who lost their homes and businesses.
Since then, he's been consulting for other governments at the behest of organizations such as the World Bank, and he recently visited Venezuela after back-to-back earthquakes devastated parts of the country. In La Guaira, the hardest-hit city, he met with the governor and other local heads, businesspeople and members of the community to help with their recovery.
All those groups are vital to solve what Murillo calls the "social engineering" issue after disasters.
"People lose the route of their life. It's the hardest thing for a human being," he said. "How do I help that family who lost everything, whose home collapsed, who lost children, and also lost their belongings inside and is now on the street?"
Murillo said in the first phase of a disaster, responders must act fast. They need food, shelter and quick monetary help, along with temporary schooling for children. Then comes longer-term assistance like government handouts and loans.
He likes to hire those affected directly to work on recovery efforts.
"The first thing that emerges from within a disaster victim when something like that happens is a new kind of leadership," Murillo said. "Natural leaders emerge — people who step up."
Murillo said solidarity is something that can't be explained and helps responders learn from victims. He likes to pair up those who are feeling stuck and depressed about the catastrophe with those who are invigorated.
Lessons learned in a disaster's aftermath
Much of the response depends on how the governments react. Murillo, who also consulted in Haiti after its deadly 2010 earthquake, says Colombia benefits from established models and response systems.
He says that in Haiti, local leaders and victims didn't understand some things he took for granted — like the need for an ID card, documentation for their home or other basic information.
"There are a number of problems in the social realms that one only discovers by going there and seeing for oneself," Murillo said.
Murillo said Colombia got out of this disaster more easily than others. He compares the dozens of fallen buildings this week to the hundreds that toppled in Venezuela.
Many structures in the area where the earthquake struck this week were built to withstand the seismic rocking that destroyed entire neighborhoods in 1999.
But even those whose homes remain are going to be affected, Murillo said. Some people may have lost businesses and don't have the resources to bring them back, and communities may lack the infrastructure to recover.
That's part of the challenge for responders. There is a mix of people and problems to address all at once.
Jahir Rodríguez's sister, 65-year-old Liliana Rodríguez, lost her apartment in Monday's earthquake. Looking into her eyes, he said he sees hopelessness, pain and uncertainty, a look he knows well.
"They are just recovering from the earthquake," Rodríguez said. "They have not yet thought about tomorrow's story."
He's worried about what survivors will face next, like living in cramped shelters and navigating the financial logistics of finding a new home or job — all while grieving what they lost.

RSF-appointed governor resigns, defects to army as battles rage across Sudan
The Rapid Support Forces-appointed governor of Sudan's Kordofan region has resigned and left the group, becoming the latest in a string of defections hampering the paramilitary force as it continues to battle the Sudanese army
Hamad Mohammad Hamad Khalifa announced his resignation from the RSF in a statement televised by Saudi-owned Al Arabiya on Wednesday, citing "ongoing suffering" in areas controlled by the group.
"I, Hamad Mohammad Hamed Khalifa, announce my resignation as governor of the Kordofan region within the structures of the so-called Tasis government, which, regrettably, has become merely a political façade for the practices of the Rapid Support Forces," he said.
"Sudanese people today have no choice but to unite against all attempts to legitimise parallel forces or rogue militias that have squandered an entire generation's lifetime in the service of individual interests," he added.
Alongside being the governor of RSF-held Kordofan, which is split into North, South and West Kordofan, Khalifa was also a member of the presidential council for the RSF's rival government.
The RSF formed a rival government in April 2025, two years after fighting broke out in the capital, Khartoum, launching the country into a vicious civil war that is now in its fourth year.
Khalifa also called for the return of the Sudanese government to the remainder of RSF-held Kordofan and Darfur, which mostly came under the control of the RSF following the capture of El-Fasher.
The capture saw large-scale atrocities and human rights violations perpetrated by the RSF.
On the humanitarian conditions in RSF-held territory, Khalifa stated that there was a "complete inability to provide even the most basic humanitarian needs for the people of Kordofan and Darfur", by the rival government.
He added that the RSF was continuing "a policy of destroying cities and killing civilians without conscience or moral restraint".

Other RSF defectors include Al-Nour Ahmed Adam, also known as al-Gubba, an RSF commander who led five units in north Darfur that defected to the army in April.
In late July, the army took control of a major highway linking El-Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan, which had been under a partial siege, with Omdurman, opposite the capital Khartoum.
The army has continued pressing gains, in what conflict monitor ACLED has said marks the start of the war's third phase.
ACLED's Sudan researcher Ali Mahmoud Ali, and risk methodology lead Nohad Eltayeb said the army is  "seeking to build on its gains in Kordofan, and advance in the RSF strongholds, while the RSF attempts to relieve pressure on its western fronts through offensives in Blue Nile and drone strikes on Khartoum, and River Nile".
On Wednesday, the RSF launched drones targeting the capital Khartoum, as well as Omdurman, Atbara, and El Obeid, attacks which continued into Thursday.
Major RSF attacks were also reported in North Kordofan and the town of Kurmuk bordering Ethiopia, which had been recaptured by the army in July.
The army accused Ethiopia of aiding the RSF in the attack on Kurmuk. It denied the claims.
Ali and Eltayeb said that with the escalating fighting, both sides were likely to continue air and drone strikes, particularly in north Kordofan.
"Coupled with a steady trend of RSF fighters defecting to the SAF [Sudanese army], these trends point to a significant disruption of the RSF's supply lines and strike capacity," they said.
"It is therefore unlikely that the RSF can withstand offensives on three parallel fronts. The SAF advances, fragmentation of the RSF, and the shift to aerial warfare by both sides will continue to impact civilians nationwide," the two added.

In a letter to Hegseth, Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal noted that the aircraft carrier, with more than 5,000 US sailors and Marines, has been “continuously at sea for a record length of nearly seven months”. That surpasses any previous deployment of a US aircraft carrier without a port stop.

“Some deployments are longer than others, and I have more respect and gratitude for those sailors than anybody,” he added. “What they do in those high seas in those austere conditions with less port calls — it’s incredible.”
The navy did not immediately respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment. However, it told Stars and Stripes its “leadership is continuously conducting assessments to monitor and sustain the psychological readiness of every sailor”.

The talks also covered cooperation in unmanned and remote technologies, as well as energy security and Ukraine’s infrastructure reconstruction.
“Ukraine has unique experience and technological solutions in this field, which open up new opportunities for partnership,” Klymenko said, according to UNN-Ukraine.
The security meetings come as Ukraine increasingly prepares both its residents and infrastructure for winter, with Russia widely expected to target Ukraine’s power grid.
Recently, authorities have suggested that Russia may switch up its winter campaign of striking Ukraine’s power grid, instead targeting water supplies.
“Much attention during the meeting was devoted to energy security,” Klymenko said, adding that “Russia continues to strike our energy infrastructure, so Japan’s assistance is especially important.”
“We are also counting on receiving the necessary equipment as scheduled,” he continued.
On July 15, Ukraine and the EU officially signed a Drone Deal aimed at strengthening European security and boosting investment in Ukraine’s defense industry, reinforcing Ukraine’s growing role as a supplier of security for Europe.
Winter heating plans
Minister for Recovery, Infrastructure and Transport, Mykola Kalashnyk, met Nakagome on Tuesday, Aug. 11. to discuss critical infrastructure restoration and preparations for the upcoming heating season.
According to the ministry’s website, priorities include deploying modular boiler houses in Lviv, Kyiv, and Kherson regions with a combined capacity exceeding 400 megawatts (MW), along with building a reserve of water and wastewater equipment for winter operations.
“It is difficult to survive for more than three days without water and sewage,” said Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal on Aug. 4, adding that Russia has damaged or destroyed more than 80% of Ukraine’s electricity generation capacity since launching its full-scale invasion.
Nakagome arrived in Kyiv as Japan’s newly appointed ambassador to Ukraine in October 2024.
“Ukraine today may be East Asia tomorrow,” he said in his official statement, adding that Japan strongly supports Ukraine, and will continue to do so, aiming to “achieve a just and lasting peace as soon as possible.”
Ukraine-Japan cooperation continues as Russian President Vladimir Putin travels to Kuril Islands for the first time on Thursday, drawing fresh attention to the decades-old territorial dispute with Japan.
Years of cooperation between Japan and Ukraine
Cooperation between Ukraine and Japan currently runs through the fifth phase of the Emergency Recovery Programme – which has a budget of roughly $38.5 million and covers infrastructure, water systems, the maritime sector, healthcare, and agriculture.
In April, Ukraine received a $1.3 billion grant from Japan – the country’s second such disbursement funded by profits from frozen Russian assets under the G7’s Extraordinary Revenue Acceleration (ERA) initiative.
On May 30, Japan has added $14.7 million to NATO’s Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative to fund non-lethal equipment for Ukraine.
According to President Volodymyr Zelensky, PURL contributions have reached about $1.5 billion this year, with 28 countries participating so far.
Broader winter preparations
Estonia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced on Wednesday that it will provide €340,000 ($392,000) to help Ukraine prepare for the upcoming winter, with the funds directed particularly toward frontline areas.
On Monday, Aug. 10, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi chaired a meeting of the Energy Headquarters, reviewing forecasted electricity and gas balances alongside top diplomats.
Meanwhile, Ukraine continues to rely on foreign partners for the delivery of Patriot interceptors to defend its skies against Russian ballistic missiles, as the country faces critical shortages.
Separately on Wednesday, Kyiv authorities began compiling lists of residents who may need temporary relocation if Russian strikes cause prolonged heating outages this winter.

Luigi Mangione is expected to plead guilty Friday in his federal criminal case, where he is charged with stalking in connection with his alleged killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson on a midtown Manhattan street in 2024, The New York Times reported Thursday, citing sources.
Mangione is scheduled to appear in U.S. District Court in Manhattan on Friday for a pretrial conference with Judge Margaret Garnett, which was requested in a court filing on Tuesday by both prosecutors and defense lawyers.
He is separately charged in New York state court with murdering Thompson and other counts.
If Mangione does plead guilty in the federal case, his attorneys are expected to argue that he cannot be prosecuted for murder in the state case because of New York's double jeopardy law, The Times noted in its report Thursday.

Thompson, 50, was fatally shot outside the Hilton Hotel on Sixth Avenue in December 2024 while walking to an investors' event for his company's parent, UnitedHealth Group. Thompson's company is the largest health insurer in the United States.
Jury selection in the state murder case is scheduled to begin on Sept. 8.
Mangione's federal trial is currently scheduled to begin in January.
Garnett in January dismissed two federal criminal counts against Mangione, including one that accused him of the murder of Thompson through the use of a firearm during alleged stalking. Mangione had faced the possibility of receiving the death penalty if convicted on that count.
The two remaining counts in the case — interstate stalking resulting in death and stalking through use of interstate facilities resulting in death — each carry a possible maximum sentence of life in prison.

MINSK, 13 August (BelTA) - Belarusian Agriculture and Food Minister Yuri Gorlov held bilateral meetings with key international partners on the sidelines of a meeting of the EAEU Council on Agro-Industrial Policy in Almaty, Kazakhstan, the press service of the Belarusian Agriculture and Food Ministry told BelTA.
Yuri Gorlov met with Minister of Agriculture of Kazakhstan Aidarbek Saparov, Minister of Agriculture of the Russian Federation Oksana Lut, and Deputy Minister of Agriculture Jihad of Iran Akbar Fathi. The talks focused on expanding trade, cooperation projects, and food supplies.
In H1 2026, Belarusian food exports to Kazakhstan exceeded 128% year-on-year, confirming sustained growth in demand for Belarusian goods on the Kazakh market. The main export items are milk and dairy products, meat and meat products, and sugar. The sides noted that the well-developed retail network of Kazakhstan provides a solid foundation for further dynamic growth in Belarusian food supplies. They also discussed opportunities to deepen cooperation in agricultural raw material processing.
The meeting with Oksana Lut focused on bilateral cooperation, including the current state of mutual supplies of agricultural goods and food, as well as promising cooperation projects.
Iran, one of Asia’s largest producers and exporters of dairy products, is seen by Belarus as a promising market and potential cooperation partner. The sides discussed facilitating the certification of Belarusian poultry enterprises to allow their products onto the Iranian market. The Belarusian side expressed interest in expanding its export range and is ready to provide all necessary information to complete the certification procedures successfully.

Food Standards Agency should do more in the fight against ultra-processed foods | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:38:57 UTC
01:38:57 KST

Felicity Lawrence’s alarming piece on ultra-processed foods (Why are ultra-processed food firms panicking and suing? Because they know time is running out, 7 August) made no mention of the UK’s Food Standards Agency, whose primary statutory objective is to protect public health from risks arising from the consumption of food.
The FSA is an independent, non-ministerial government department. Its advice to ministers, and guidance to consumers, is informed by the most up-to-date scientific evidence, free of political or commercial considerations.
As Lawrence pointed out, food manufacturers see government action as a threat. And regulation is surely the most effective way to control profit-oriented companies, many of which pay little regard to the possible negative impact of their products until compelled to do so.
The FSA last published guidance to consumers on ultra-processed foods in February 2025. Given that “the science on harm caused by foods high in fat, salt and sugar is now settled”, it is perhaps time for it to consider updating this guidance and also whether to recommend government intervention.
Mike Pender
Cardiff

====================================================================================================

Ceuta showed just how easy it is to divide Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:38:56 UTC
01:38:56 KST

Within hours of the first pictures of tens of thousands of migrants swimming the short distance from Morocco to the Spanish north African enclave of Ceuta hitting social media on July 30, 22 EU leaders, US President Donald Trump and Israel had piled on to criticize Madrid.
The outbreak of hysteria and recrimination was a case study in 21st-century politics, driven by real-time images in a media echo chamber where populists set the agenda on migration, propagating fear, prejudice and demagogic proposals. Above all, the kneejerk reactions undermined trust between European allies and dealt a setback to EU efforts to jointly manage migration, counter people-smuggling and resist the weaponization of migrants by non-EU countries.
That Trump and US Vice President J.D. Vance should seize the opportunity to accuse socialist Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez of inviting the mass influx by allowing more than 1 million irregular migrants already working in Spain to apply for legal status is hardly surprising, given the US administration’s own relentless drive to detain and expel illegal immigrants.
On the other hand, European leaders who signed a letter to the European Commision, criticizing Spain and demanding an emergency meeting of interior ministers, should ask themselves how their behavior helps the EU implement a coherent response to migratory pressures. Many are open to charges of hypocrisy, since Germany and Italy have, between them, regularized hundreds of thousands of undocumented migrant workers at the request of employers who need their labor as the home workforce dwindles.
There was also a monstrous foreign policy double standard in the initial EU response.
When Poland and Lithuania faced a sudden influx of irregular migrants from Belarus in 2021, the EU rallied behind its eastern members and imposed sanctions on Minsk’s authoritarian regime, which stood accused of weaponizing displaced people from the Middle East. The previous year, the EU sent its Frontex border agency to help Greece repel a surge of migrants from Turkey at the countries’ shared border in Thrace, which had apparently been encouraged by Ankara to put pressure on the EU.
Yet this time, EU governments quickly fell into a divisive blame game, terrified by images that recalled the loss of control over borders in southeastern Europe in 2015, when more than 1 million mostly Syrian refugees entered the bloc.
Amid the internal finger-pointing, neither the EU leaders nor the European Commission dared question the role of Morocco, whose border guards apparently stood aside as more than 72,000 Moroccans, mostly young men, risked their lives swimming to Ceuta after seeing viral social media claims that “Spain is open.”
The incident occurred on Morocco’s annual Throne Day when King Mohammed VI, who does not recognize Spanish sovereignty over the territories of Ceuta and Melilla, just happened to be visiting the nearby northern city of Tetouan, once part of the Spanish protectorate. Some commentators have called the stampede to Ceuta a “Blue March,” in reference to the mass Green March that the king’s father, Hassan II, launched in 1975 in an attempt to claim the vast territory of Western Sahara, then a Spanish colony.
“In Morocco, nothing happens by chance,” said Anna Terron Cusi, a senior fellow at the Migration Policy Institute and a former Spanish secretary of state for immigration.
Even if the stampede to Ceuta started spontaneously with social media posts, she believed “this was a multi-actor, multi-factor event. It was more a geopolitical than a migration crisis.”
Intra-European party politics played a big role. It was not surprising that Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni should lead the assault on Sanchez. She heads the hard-right Brothers of Italy movement and faces a domestic challenge in elections next year from a new, even further-right party, led by a retired general.
Some Spanish and British anti-immigration politicians rushed to Ceuta to take selfies, one from Reform UK doing a standup interview on the beach to cash in on the purported alien “invasion.”
It was more bizarre that Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, who heads a center-left government, should co-initiate the letter with Meloni to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, and say that the EU should consider suspending Spain from the Schengen area of open-border travel.
A facade of European solidarity was restored after EU interior ministers held a hastily arranged videoconference. By that time, almost all the migrants had left Ceuta and returned to Morocco after realizing that they had no chance of reaching Europe. The “invasion” had deflated. In fact, irregular migrant arrivals in Spain fell sharply last year, while across the EU they are down for the second successive year, and far below the 2015 crisis peak — but the damage was done.
Italy and Spain are engaging in tit-for-tat passport and nationality controls on each other’s travelers, and Russian President Vladimir Putin, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and King Mohammed himself would have noted how easily Europe panics and turns on its own members at the first sight of migrants on its beaches.
Whether out of misinformation or malice, some EU ministers distorted the nature of the Spanish amnesty for undocumented migrants, labelling it a “pull factor” for mass migration. Italian Minister of Foreign Affairs Antonio Tajani claimed they were being granted Spanish, and therefore European, citizenship, rather than simply being given a chance to apply for temporary work visas.
Europe faces what in game theory is called the “prisoners’ dilemma,” and in social sciences a “collective action problem.” EU countries have a shared interest in preserving the Schengen zone of free movement, with open internal borders vital to the smooth operation of the economy, well-managed external borders to deter irregular migrants and combat people smugglers, and legal migration routes to permit an inflow of workers needed by businesses as the European population ages and shrinks.
Yet they keep undermining cooperation due to a seemingly irresistible short-term political interest in anti-migration grandstanding.
Paul Taylor is a senior visiting fellow at the European Policy Centre.

====================================================================================================

The Liberty Times Editorial: Increasingly risky travel to China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:38:55 UTC
01:38:55 KST

China’s State Council on July 31 announced the Regulations on Exit and Entry Administration. Set to take effect from Sept. 15, the regulation expands the People’s Republic of China’s powers to restrict people from leaving the country in the name of “safeguarding national sovereignty, security and development interests.”
International observers widely regard it as another step back to a closed China.
Given Beijing’s insistence that Taiwan is “a part of China,” experts warn Taiwanese traveling to China of increasing risk of indefinite detainment.
Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) Minister Chiu Chui-cheng (邱垂正) has likewise warned that China has repeatedly revised and expanded its national security laws, which are often vaguely worded and leave considerable room for arbitrary enforcement.
If the Chinese authorities do not want anyone to leave, then they simply cannot leave, Chiu said.
Since the beginning of this year, an average of 16 Taiwanese per month have reportedly gone missing in China, been detained for questioning or had their personal liberty restricted, the MAC said.
Despite the government’s repeated warnings that risks of traveling to China have sharply risen, some Taiwanese continue to think this does not apply to them. Combined with people and organizations in Taiwan eager to cooperate with Beijing, this gives the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) room to pursue its familiar two-pronged strategy of incentive and coercion in “united front” operations.
The details of the CCP’s new regulations reveal their arbitrariness.
Article 4 states that when a Chinese citizen contravenes export-control or technology import-export regulations in a manner that could endanger industrial or technological security, the relevant commerce authorities under the State Council may prohibit that person from leaving China.
When an exit ban concerns national security or the investigation of a criminal case, the authorities may withhold from the detained person information about the decision, Article 6 states.
Article 18 defines “immigration administration authorities” to include exit-entry administration bodies of public-security organs at or above the county level. In other words, local officials may decide whether to stop someone from leaving the country.
Although the new rules have not yet been officially implemented, there are affected people already voicing their complaints through various channels.
Their accounts suggest that this condition, approved by Chinese Premier Li Qiang (李強), essentially serves to give a firmer legal footing to China’s restrictive exit practices that have already generated controversy.
Chinese media defend the new rules as necessary to prevent the leak of sensitive technology, framing it as a response to the technological competition between China and the US. However, an even more compelling reason is that the CCP, increasingly uneasy about its political hold over the nation, is tightening its control.
Singapore Management University professor of law Henry Gao has warned that the regulation changes leaving the country from a right to a privilege granted by the state, and that anyone concerned with their situation should leave quickly while they still can.
Concerned about political stability at home, the CCP treats virtually anyone as a potential threat. Another example is the PRC’s Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress, which took effect on July 1.
President William Lai (賴清德) on Tuesday last week said that the law not only infringes upon Taiwanese sovereignty and facilitates the persecution of religious and minority groups, but also enables political scrutiny of people in other countries, achieving global censorship through transnational repression.
Lai has called upon the international community to collectively resist this malignant law.
Meanwhile, an Aug. 2 New York Times article entitled “How China Keeps Tabs on Foreigners” delved into how Chinese police use an online “Dynamic Control Platform for Overseas Personnel” to compile information on people from Taiwan and Hong Kong, as well as more than 300 foreign journalists.
Beyond basic personal information, the platform even integrates data from facial recognition systems, transportation records, medical information, hotel stays and consumer transactions, monitoring people’s movements and activities in extraordinary detail.
Taiwanese and Hong Kong residents are classified separately in the database, while people from the Five Eyes alliance — the US, UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand — are also specially marked. Foreign students, foreign spouses and those classified by Chinese authorities as “key persons” are placed under enhanced monitoring as well.
One New York Times reporter even found his own file in the system and concluded that it appeared to be a public security surveillance platform, rather than a hypothetical prototype.
This glimpse into China’s surveillance apparatus reveals that the CCP is using the latest technological tools to construct an increasingly dense and virtually seamless network of control.
Taiwan is on the front line of this authoritarian expansion. Beijing does not merely employ transnational repression as a means of intimidation; it also advances its “united front” strategy through business, education, tourism and other forms of cross-strait exchange.
The CCP extends its tactics of incentives and coercion simultaneously, exploiting the social networks that Taiwanese visitors to China maintain back home and turning interpersonal connections into potential pressure points.
Beijing has designated Minister of the Interior Liu Shyh-fang (劉世芳) a “diehard Taiwanese independence separatist.” Liu’s nephew, who worked for a Taiwanese-invested company in China, was dismissed from his position after Chinese authorities publicly targeted Liu and her family.
That is an example of how Beijing pressures Taiwanese businesses to make political statements. The more Taiwanese travel to China, the more personal information flows into China’s surveillance system. The aggregated data could then assist the CCP in political manipulation.
The MAC in a report submitted to the Legislative Yuan on July 29 said that from January 2024 to July 22 this year, 402 Taiwanese who traveled to China were reported missing, detained and questioned or had their personal liberty restricted.
The number has risen sharply from 55 cases in 2024 to 221 last year and 126 so far this year, and might just be the tip of the iceberg, with more undisclosed incidents, the MAC said.
Among those who were detained and questioned, 50 percent were current, former or retired government employees. How are Chinese authorities able to identify these people with such precision? What is routinely described as “cross-strait exchange” has already become an enormous testing ground for the CCP’s digital control capacity.
Beijing is also targeting Taiwan’s younger generation. China’s Taiwan Affairs Office (TAO) recently launched the “Taiwan Youth e-Home” (台青e家) platform, presenting it as a one-stop portal to find information on internships, employment, entrepreneurship, further education and exchange opportunities for young Taiwanese.
Officials have warned prospective users of the platform to exercise caution, as the Web site is also a direct way for Beijing to collect personal information on young Taiwanese. Registering on the platform effectively means handing over one’s personal details directly to TAO, along with the risk of a data breach.
There has also been a steep increase in cross-strait student exchanges, a Control Yuan investigation found. From 2022 to last year, the number of Taiwanese university and college students traveling to China for academic exchanges rose from 2,196 to 5,745.
Last year, 1,045 Taiwanese elementary-school students also traveled to China.
The personal information of those students, as well as their families could therefore be exposed.
Organizations within Taiwan have cooperated in carrying out China-related exchange programs, attracting students with unusually cheap participation costs, the investigation found.
The pattern resembles Beijing’s pre-elections practice of inviting Taiwanese neighborhood and village wardens to visit China on subsidized trips. Such activities serve not only to advance “united front” work, but also to expand Beijing’s collection of personal data, which would help it map interpersonal networks with greater precision and increase the vulnerabilities facing Taiwanese visitors to China.
The CCP is proceeding on three fronts: law, technology and “united front” operations. Through these channels, the Chinese government is deepening its level of control over Taiwanese society.
The cost of accepting small, immediate benefits can be exorbitantly high. For the sake of one’s personal safety — and that of one’s family and friends — it is worth revisiting a classic saying from the Confucian Analects, warning against entering a “risky state.”
Taiwanese should avoid travel to high-risk China.
Translated by Amy King

In the MSCI All Country Asia ex Japan Index, Taiwan’s weighting is set to climb to 30.03 percent from 29.75 percent.
Photo: CNA
The adjustments are to take effect after the market closes on Aug. 31, the global stock index compiler said in a statement.
Memory makers Nanya Technology Corp (南亞科技) and Winbond Electronics Corp (華邦電子), along with Phison Electronics Corp (群聯電子), Kinsus Interconnect Technology Corp (景碩科技), Nan Ya Printed Circuit Board Corp (南亞電路板) and Taiwan Union Technology Corp (台燿科技), are to be moved from the MSCI Taiwan Small Cap Index to the MSCI Taiwan Index in the latest adjustments.
The changes could raise the companies’ visibility among international investors and prompt portfolio adjustments by funds that track the benchmarks, the Taiwan Stock Exchange (TWSE) said.
Companies in the MSCI Taiwan Index, a regional component of the MSCI Global Standard Index, generally attract greater attention from global funds than those in its small-cap benchmarks, the exchange said.
Nanya Technology’s promotion is particularly notable after institutional investors had repeatedly identified the company as a candidate for inclusion in the global standard index.
Its elevation comes as Taiwan’s memory stocks gain momentum amid demand for artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure, rising orders for high-performance computing equipment and tight supplies of conventional memory chips.
Six Taiwan-listed companies — Taiwan Cement Corp (台灣水泥), Yang Ming Marine Transport Corp (陽明海運), Taiwan Business Bank Co (台灣企銀), International Games System Co (鈊象電子), eMemory Technology Inc (力旺電子) and Caliway Biopharmaceuticals Co (康霈生技) — are to be moved from the MSCI Taiwan Index to the MSCI Taiwan Small Cap Index.
The MSCI’s quarterly review comes as the TAIEX has rallied nearly 60 percent this year. The index closed up 1.11 percent at 46,021.48 yesterday.
This year’s gains have been driven largely by surging global spending on AI infrastructure, which has boosted demand for the products of Taiwan’s chipmakers, memory suppliers and other technology hardware makers.
The higher weightings also underscore the market’s growing importance in global equity benchmarks, the TWSE said.
Taiwan’s large technology companies account for a significant share of the nation’s market capitalization, meaning that changes in their valuations can have an outsized effect on the country’s index weight and on portfolios of international investors tracking MSCI benchmarks, the exchange said.

I am sorry that the parkrun spoils Janet Knowlson’s experience of her local park (Letters, 7 August). I wonder if she has ever spoken to a parkrunner or a volunteer? Many would tell of the camaraderie and their improved physical and mental health. Strangers become friends and even partners. We do not take over the park, as she alleges, rather we recognise that we share the space with other park users and are respectful of their rights and needs. Parkrun is for everyone and anyone, from children upwards, and not only runners. It is only competitive if you want it to be, and is equally welcoming to walkers. Parkrun is a huge success story, both in the UK and many other countries, and should be celebrated. It receives no public funding and each event relies on an army of volunteers, without whom it wouldn’t happen. Long may it continue.

A person in Norway’s Svalbard archipelago in the arctic has been fined 50,000 kroner (US$5,258) for using a foghorn to wake a sleeping polar bear, local officials said yesterday.
The incident took place earlier this month when a vessel was sailing in a fjord in northeastern Svalbard, about 1,000km from the North Pole.
“Its occupants are said to have spotted a polar bear sleeping on land,” the governor of the territory said in a statement.
Photo: AFP
“A person on board then used the ship’s foghorn, waking the animal, which moved to another location,” he added.
Neither the identity nor nationality of the person has been disclosed.
The governor’s office ordered the individual to pay the hefty fine, which the person agreed to do.
Under local regulations “it is forbidden to needlessly disturb, attract or pursue a polar bear,” which was declared a protected species in Svalbard in 1972.
About 260 polar bears were counted in the archipelago during the last scientific estimate, carried out in 2015.

Separately, the NDC passed the draft urban comprehensive flood control management program for next year to 2031.
The Ministry of the Interior proposed the program to address increased flooding in urban areas due to short-duration heavy rainfall, which often overwhelms drainage, the council said.
The project aims to complete disaster-risk maps for 25 urban areas over five years, establish flood-resilience assessment indicators for 311 urban areas, maintain 2,200 smart water-monitoring stations, and use artificial intelligence to improve flood simulations and pumping-station operations, it said.
Total funding for the project is NT$3.3 billion.

====================================================================================================

The flaw in Europe’s ‘one China’ policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:38:51 UTC
01:38:51 KST

Europe’s “one China” policy has always relied on deliberate ambiguity. It is a formula from the 1970s that means European governments recognize the People’s Republic of China while keeping unofficial ties with Taiwan.
However, the structure of the policy — recognizing “one China” without ever defining what that means — has slowly turned caution into inertia. Today, it forces Europe to confront a harder truth: Its commitment to democratic values collides with the limits of its own diplomatic tradition, one that protects stability, but often avoids clarity.
Europe’s unified response to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has often been cited as proof of its ability to act decisively when a democracy is under threat. Sanctions were coordinated within days. Military support flowed without hesitation. The moral framing was clear.
However, it is different for Taiwan. Any response to Chinese coercion is filtered through the constraints of the “one China” policy, which leaves the country’s status in a gray zone and transforms even minor engagements into diplomatic tests.
It is precisely against this backdrop that former Finnish prime minister Sanna Marin’s warning regarding a potential conflict in the Taiwan Strait acquires its full weight.
“I think this might be — I hope it won’t — but it might be much more complicated for different countries internationally to respond,” she said.
Marin identified a deeper structural problem in Taiwan-EU relations: Taipei does not fall within the same diplomatic architecture that enabled the EU to respond swiftly and effectively to the Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
In Ukraine’s case, the EU acted within a clear framework: A recognized state had been attacked, and supporting Kyiv aligned with Europe’s political principles and strategic interests.
However, it struggles regarding Taiwan, because the framework is ambiguous.
For Marin, acting decisively requires acknowledging that the issue at stake is not the defense of a single country in isolation.
“We need to understand that the matter of Ukraine, just like the matter of Taiwan, isn’t an issue of a single country. If we let countries like Russia attack an independent sovereign nation without serious and long-lasting consequences, it will set an example for others to use aggression to get what they want,” she said.
Her point is clear: The credibility of democratic defense depends on consistency, not geography, and it requires a willingness to confront coercion wherever it emerges — whether in Europe’s immediate neighborhood or across the Indo-Pacific region — with clarity, resolve and strategic coherence.
The “one China” policy has long constrained Europe’s room for maneuver, but the path toward a more coherent stance is visible.
By emphasizing what could unfold — noting that the challenges facing Taiwan do not necessarily take the form of “tanks, missiles or drones,” but instead emerge through “gray zone” actions that are far harder for the international community to confront — Marin called for a clear, unambiguous posture that leaves no room for interpretation.
Just as the premises that generate Europe’s long-standing ambiguity toward Taiwan are well understood, so, too, are the actions the EU — collectively and through its individual member states — must take to build an effective response to Chinese coercion.
As Marin said, democracies must stand firmly by their values and principles, and not appear weak in the face of aggression that violates international law.
Only then could inertia be transformed into a proactive approach, turning the ambition to defend democracy and freedom into concrete action.
Michele Maresca is an analyst at Il Caffe Geopolitico, an online international law journal, and the think tank Geopol21.

“As lifelong NBA fans, we are deeply honored for the opportunity to become stewards of the Los Angeles Lakers, one of the most iconic sports franchises in the world,” Kushner and Iger said in a statement to ESPN. “We have immense respect for the leadership and vision of Jerry and Jeanie Buss. Walter’s purchase, reported in June last year, ended the Buss family’s 46-year ownership.
The Lakers have won 17 NBA championships, second only to the Boston Celtics.
The club has been home to some of the league’s biggest superstars including Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, Shaquille O’Neal and Kobe Bryant.
LeBron James, the NBA all-time scoring leader, just left the squad for the Philadelphia 76ers after spending eight years and winning one title with the Lakers.
The team are moving forward with a lineup spearheaded by Slovenian superstar Luka Doncic.
The sale still requires approval from the NBA’s board of governors.
Jeanie Buss had continued to serve as the Lakers’ governor after the club was sold to Walter in a deal that further expanded the sports portfolio of his TWG Global holding company.
The company’s sports holdings include MLB’s Los Angeles Dodgers and a stake in English Premier League club Chelsea.

However, Walter is under federal investigation for possible tax fraud involving his insurance businesses.

“I am grateful to Jeanie Buss, the Buss family, the players and the staff for welcoming me into this chapter,” he said.

====================================================================================================

Total darkness, then sunset as eclipse wows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:38:50 UTC
01:38:50 KST

Spectators across Spain on Wednesday evening watched in wonder, some whipping off their protective glasses and rising to their feet in unison, as a rare total solar eclipse swept across the north of the country, plunging it into darkness.
Spain deployed a massive police contingent and set up special viewing spots across rural areas that offered the best views of the spectacle.
Viewers in Buitrago de Lozoya, a rural district north of Madrid, clapped and cheered as the sky dimmed and Baily’s beads — bright points of sunlight that shine around the edge of the moon during a total eclipse — glistened on the horizon just after 8:30pm, lasting barely a minute.
Photo: Reuters
“It’s impressive how the colors return little by little after totality — first the reds, then the blues — just like at dawn and sunset, totally deceiving your brain,” economist Diego Fernandez, 32, said.
Rafael Jimenez, 50, a resident of Madrid, said the event felt like science fiction.
“It was an absurd scene; we even got soaked when the garden sprinklers kicked in,” he said. “And then, just like that, we were watching the sunset again.”
Spain’s turn with the eclipse followed shortly after a less remarkable spectacle over much of overcast Iceland, although a break in the clouds in the far west of the Nordic country allowed tourists and locals a glimpse of the celestial phenomenon.
The eclipse was hidden behind clouds in central Reykjavik although the darkness of the totality was still evident.
“It was like a whole day just came at once and I felt goosebumps because it just made us think about ... the shortness of life, how time can be different and it depends on your perspective,” lawyer Eduarda Ortiz, 33, said in the Icelandic capital.
Millions of people gathered in Iceland and northern Spain to witness Western Europe’s first total solar eclipse in 27 years.
Brian May, former guitarist for the rock band Queen, was among them. He traveled to an observatory in Spain’s Teruel Province and chronicled the experience on his Instagram page.
“Here we go, the sun is disappearing. It’s amazing,” he said as the eclipse reached its climax and bystanders burst into cheers and applause after a countdown.
In Spain, authorities were expecting up to 6 million visitors in mostly rural areas under the eclipse’s path across the north of Spain and the Balearic Islands.
The Iberian Peninsula last witnessed a total solar eclipse in 1912, but another is due on Aug. 2 next year, and an annular eclipse is to follow in January 2028, completing the so-called “Iberian Eclipse Trio.”
The uncanny sensation when day briefly turns to twilight and some animals fall quiet, while the moon passes directly between Earth and the sun, has often been seen through history as an omen of cosmic struggle or a sign of divine power.
For Spain, the event has been a chance to showcase its less-traveled regions and draw tourists from its overcrowded beach resorts. Some seized the opportunity to get married, according to local press reports.
The eclipse took place in one of the country’s highest-risk periods for wildfires, with emergency crews fighting fires on Wednesday, including a large one in the southern Andalucia region.
Authorities rolled out a large-scale police operation and public safety campaign to make sure the crowds did not set off wildfires.
A small fire erupted near an eclipse viewing point in Peniscola, in the Valencia region, local authorities said.
The fire began in a vehicle and spread to 33 more before firefighters brought it under control, they said.
Emergency crews, including aircraft, were dispatched to the area.
The authorities dispatched 25,000 police officers to guarantee security around the eclipse observation sites and deployed nearly 100 planes and helicopters.
In Reykjavik, glasses that allow spectators to view the phenomenon without damaging their eyes have been sold out for days, as the country of about 400,000 people welcomed up to 80,000 visitors.
Totality reached Iceland’s westernmost coast at about 5:44pm, casting the far west of the island nation into total darkness for up to 2 minutes and 13 seconds.
The event drew casual observers and “eclipse chasers,” enthusiasts who crisscross the globe to be in the path of totality whenever and wherever an eclipse occurs.
In Spain, 43-year old Gema, who did not give her last name, said as she left the Buitrago de Lozoya viewing point: “Everybody tells you about it, but it is more beautiful than you imagine.”

16:38:50 UTC

Russian President Vladimir Putin yesterday visited Russia’s far-eastern Kuril Islands for the first time, prompting protests by Japan which also claims the territory.
Russian-Japanese relations have long been dogged by the contested islands, known in Japan as the Northern Territories and seized by the Soviet Union in 1945.
The Kremlin posted a video of Putin on one of the Kurils’ four main islands, with Russian media saying he visited a fish-processing plant and was given caviar.
Photo: Gavriil Grigorov, Sputnik via Reuters
It was the first visit by a Russian president since Dmitry Medvedev in 2010.
“The Northern Territories are an inherent part of Japan’s territory, both historically and under international law,” Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told reporters.
Putin’s visit “offends the sentiments of the Japanese people and is absolutely unacceptable,” she said, adding that it “made it more difficult to restore relations in the medium to long term.”
Putin traveled to the Kurils after visiting the nearby Russian island of Sakhalin on Wednesday, where Russia’s navy was conducting drills.
In Sakhalin, Putin, 73, held a meeting “on ensuring the security of Russia’s eastern borders,” RIA Novosti said.
Japanese Minister of Foreign Affairs Toshimitsu Motegi yesterdat summoned Russian Ambassador to Japan Nikolai Nozdrev to lodge a “strong protest” against Putin’s surprise move.
Motegi told the ambassador in the meeting that Putin’s visit would “have an extremely negative impact on Japan-Russia relations” already complicated by Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine, the ministry said in a statement.
Ties between Japan and Russia — which fought a war in 1904-1905 — have worsened since the full-scale conflict in Ukraine began in 2022.
Japan has joined other G7 countries in sanctioning Russia and giving money and nonlethal defense aid to Kyiv.
Putin on Wednesday called Japan’s sanctions “unprovoked.”
“Japan has identified Russia as a main source of threats. I would like to point out that we are not threatening Japan... On the contrary it has territorial claims against our country,” Putin said.
Russia and China have also moved closer, with their navies and air forces conducting joint exercises in areas around Japan, promoting frequent scrambles by Japanese jets.
North Korea, which this month termed Japan’s military buildup a “transformation into a war state,” has also sent troops and artillery shells to help Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Japan’s latest defense white paper issued this month again highlighted growing risks from all three countries.
The New York Times last month reported that Russia had turned Japan into a “den of spies” and a key source of dual-use technology needed for its war in Ukraine.
The Soviet Union took the strategically located volcanic archipelago north of Hokkaido in the final days of World War II and has maintained a military presence there ever since.
The contested isles are part of the volcanic Kuril archipelago, which runs in a broad arc from Russia’s Kamchatka peninsula down to Japan’s main northern island Hokkaido.
Their population of about 20,000 Russians lives in a harsh climate, but the islands have mineral deposits including gold and silver, and rich fishing grounds.
After the islands were occupied in 1945, Moscow deported their Japanese population of about 17,000 people.
The islands then acquired strategic importance, providing air and sea bases during the Cold War as the Soviet Union confronted the US and Japan.
“The Kurils have been fortified with Bastion coastal defense missile systems and SU-35 fighter aircraft. These provide Russia with instruments of control over sea lanes in the region, as well as leverage against Japan’s claim to the islands,” University of Tokyo Graduate School of Public Policy professor Yee Kuang-heng said.
“Putin’s visit may be a reminder of the cards he holds and also his displeasure with Japan’s continuing sanctions on Russia imposed after the invasion of Ukraine,” Heng said.

We know sleep, exercise and diet are vital for health. But why?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:38:44 UTC
01:38:44 KST

Sleep. Exercise. Eat well. It’s the oldest recommendation in medicine, repeated so often it’s become a cliche. We know the advice, even if we don’t always follow it. But have you ever stopped to wonder why these three seemingly different habits have such remarkably similar effects on our brains and bodies?
For generations we’ve treated them as separate prescriptions — sleep restores us, exercise strengthens us and food fuels us. Yet neuroscience is beginning to suggest something rather more elegant: they’re all essentially doing the same job.
What has changed is not the recommendations themselves, but our understanding of the biology beneath them. The more scientists study the brain, the clearer it becomes that cognition is astonishingly energy intensive. Although the brain makes up about 2 percent of body weight, it uses roughly a fifth of the body’s energy at rest. Every memory we retrieve, every decision we make and every creative insight carries a metabolic cost. Thought itself is an energy-hungry act.
Photo: AP
That raises an obvious question: where does all that energy come from? The answer lies deep in evolutionary history. More than 2 billion years ago, a primitive cell engulfed a bacterium. Instead of being digested, the bacterium remained, forming a long-term partnership with its host.
Over time, this arrangement became one of biology’s most important alliances. The bacterium became remarkably efficient at capturing the chemical energy stored in food and transforming it into ATP, the molecule that powers almost every biological process. The host offered protection, and together they made complex life possible.
That partnership is still running inside us today. Mitochondria — the descendants of that ancient bacterium — exist in almost every cell in the body. The exception is the mature red blood cell, which removes them to make space for hemoglobin and improve oxygen transport. Even here, biology reveals its logic: everything is shaped by trade-offs in energy efficiency.
For decades, mitochondria were introduced in biology textbooks as the cell’s “powerhouses” — important, dependable but rather dull. The stars of the show were undeniably neurons. Today, that picture is changing.
We’re discovering that neurons produce thought, ideas and emotions only because mitochondria continuously transform fuel into the energy they need. Intelligence depends not simply on the brain’s wiring, but on the uninterrupted flow of energy through that wiring. This is a subtle shift in perspective, but an important one.
Emerging evidence suggests that healthy mitochondrial function helps give rise to intelligence, including driving arithmetic and processing speed, working memory, healthier brain aging and greater resilience to stress. Mitochondria are no longer viewed as passive batteries but as active participants in the delicate balancing act that allows the brain to adapt, learn and flourish throughout life.
Suddenly, the oldest health advice begins to make much more sense. Exercise doesn’t simply boost muscle mass, it bulks up the hippocampus — a key region of the brain involved in learning and memory. It also encourages mitochondria to become more numerous and more efficient. We often imagine we’re training our bodies; we’re also strengthening the ancient energy system that allows our brains to work.
Sleep performs a different kind of maintenance. While we’re unconscious, the brain is astonishingly busy. Memories are consolidated and worn-out cellular components — including mitochondria — are repaired or replaced. So rather than thinking of sleep as simply rest, we can conceive of it, at least partly, as a mitochondrial maintenance shift, aimed at preparing the brain for another day of active learning, adapting and imagining.
Then there’s food. Mitochondria rely entirely on what we eat to perform their remarkable chemistry. The quality of that fuel matters. Diets rich in minimally processed foods provide the ingredients for efficient energy transformation, while diets that continually overwhelm the system appear to make that process less efficient over time.
Seen through this lens, sleep, exercise and diet stop looking like three separate pieces of lifestyle advice and become different ways of caring for the same biological inheritance. What fascinates me most is that this new understanding reaches far beyond physical health. Scientists are uncovering intriguing links between mitochondrial function and resilience, mood, personality traits and even our social lives.
For centuries we’ve tended to separate mind from body, as though thoughts somehow floated free of the flesh that produced them. The reality is that thoughts emerge from living tissue that must constantly capture, transform and use energy simply to exist.
The mitochondrial psychobiologist Martin Picard has argued that we’ve become accustomed to thinking of ourselves as molecular machines, when it may be more useful to think of ourselves as energetic processes. The brain is an organ whose every thought, memory and feeling depends on the continuous transformation of energy within billions of cells. Seen this way, sleep is no longer simply rest, and exercise is no longer simply fitness. Food is no longer simply fuel. They’re different ways of sustaining the ancient biological partnership that allows our bodies — and our minds — to flourish.
It’s remarkable to think that every idea you’ve ever had, every problem you’ve solved, every person you’ve loved and every hope you’ve held has depended upon an alliance forged more than 2 billion years ago. The tiny descendants of that ancient bacterium have been quietly working inside us ever since, making possible not just movement or metabolism but thought itself.
Perhaps that’s why the oldest health advice has survived every new scientific fashion. Long before we knew about ATP, oxidative phosphorylation or mitochondria, we recognized that people who slept well, moved regularly and ate nourishing food tended to flourish. We’re finally beginning to understand why.
It is forest fire season in Europe and North America, and the news is filled with harrowing images of disastrous fires filling the air with smoke. What about Taiwan? Taiwan has a unique forest fire profile. Unlike other nations, where the threat peaks in the dry summer months, that period is wet. Instead, major forest fires typically occur during October to April, when the country is drier. Moreover, “high temperatures are not the primary drivers of forest fires” as a study in Theoretical and Applied Climatology noted. Rather, the consensus is that dryness is the trigger of forest fires here, with

Wanting to assemble some fellow academics for a regular meal, he initiated a Saturday lunch, which quickly shifted to Saturday dinner. Then, sometime in 1974 or 1975, it became a weekly Wednesday night meal. Melyan never finished his PhD, but the weekly Wednesday dinner, now known as the Wednesday Night Old Farts (WNOF), has continued for more than half a century

Unknown Publisher

16:38:40 UTC
01:38:40 KST

Brazil’s data protection agency on Wednesday ordered Discord to suspend live streams, accusing the messaging platform of failing to protect children and adolescents after a teen girl was allegedly incited to commit suicide during a broadcast.
In a case described by one police officer as a “real-life horror show,” a 13-year-old girl in a small city in the center-west of Brazil was incited during a 45-minute live stream last month on Discord to self-harm and eventually kill herself.
Five teenagers have been arrested in connection to the death and a police operation saved “another girl who was about to commit suicide live on the Internet,” a police statement said.
Photo: AFP
“Live streams have been repeatedly used to facilitate violence, harassment, and the incitement of self-harm and suicide,” said the Brazilian Data Protection Authority, which gave Discord three days to comply with the suspension.
The agency cited “robust evidence that the company failed to adopt reasonable measures” to protect children and teenagers from such content.
Discord said in a statement it was “disappointed,” but was “carefully analyzing” the directive.
It rejected the agency’s “characterization” of the platform.
Discord said it had investigated and removed the invite-only group involved in the case and continued to co-operate with law enforcement.
Brazil has in the past few months sought to boost protections for children online, obliging platforms to link the accounts of users younger than 16 to their parents’ accounts, and verify user age.
Brazilian Ministry of Justice Coordinator-General for Combating Cybercrime Alessandro Barreto slammed a “terrible failure in moderation” by Discord.
“We witnessed truly outrageous acts being broadcast online,” he said.
He said the girl had been incited to kill an animal but “she couldn’t do it” and was then incited to kill herself, “all of it broadcast live.”
“We used to see adults grooming minors. Now, what do we see? Minors grooming other minors to commit barbaric acts. It’s called digital slavery. Girls are being enslaved online and coerced into committing truly barbaric acts,” he said.
One of those arrested, a 14-year-old boy, was “smiling as if he had just beaten a level in a game,” Barreto said. “The parents of most of the detained adolescents were completely taken by surprise.”

Taiwan targeted in AI-driven hacking campaign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:38:36 UTC
01:38:36 KST

Overseas hackers used artificial intelligence (AI) agents to target government agencies in a cyberattack last month, the Ministry of Digital Affairs (MODA) said yesterday, following a Financial Times report on the incident.
The Administration for Cyber Security said in a statement that its cybersecurity monitoring unit detected the attacks last month and that the National Institute for Cyber Security began issuing alerts on July 20.
An investigation was launched immediately, and the source, methods and scope of the attacks have been determined, while affected agencies have completed their responses, it said.
Photo: AP
The ministry did not disclose where the attacks originated.
According to the Financial Times report, published on Wednesday, researchers at Israeli AI start-up Dream were the first to detect the intrusion, which allegedly used open-source AI agents to build an autonomous hacking tool.
It also cited a source familiar with the matter as saying that Taiwan was the target.
The tool compromised at least 85 government user accounts and extracted more than 2,500 personnel records before the attackers expanded their operations to Taiwan’s nuclear safety agency and at least seven energy companies, the UK-based news outlet reported.
Dream did not attribute the attack to a specific group, but researchers said that internal communications linked to the operation were in simplified Chinese, suggesting the operators were likely connected to China.
Meanwhile, the agency said the attacks showed clear signs of originating overseas and involved a hybrid approach combining conventional hacking with AI agents such as OpenClaw.
AI agents can rapidly combine multiple attack techniques and use secondary systems, such as backup and testing systems, as stepping stones, making attacks faster, cheaper and more scalable, it said.
MODA said the government has established guidelines to address emerging AI-related cybersecurity threats and would continue to bolster its overall defenses and monitoring for potential attack paths.
Chinese cyberattacks on Taiwan’s key infrastructure from hospitals to banks rose 6 percent last year from the previous year to an average of 2.63 million attacks a day, the National Security Bureau said in January, adding that some of the hacks were synchronized with military drills in “hybrid threats.”
The threat of AI-assisted hacking campaigns has been growing for years, but ramped up dramatically over the past few months after top AI labs released models, such as Anthropic’s Mythos, which can rapidly conduct reconnaissance, identify vulnerabilities and take advantage of them.
Cris Thomas, a researcher and security advocate at the cybersecurity company Semgrep, said the hacking campaign was an illustration of just how quickly AI-assisted hackers could hit their mark.
However, Thomas cautioned against exaggerating the power of AI agents.
“There’s still a human in there somewhere. Somebody had to choose who to attack, had to establish an objective and give it a directive. It’s not totally 100 percent autonomous. There was a capable operator in charge that did that,” he added.

Freddie Freeman falls into dugout
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:38:33 UTC
01:38:33 KST

Freddie Freeman apparently avoided serious injury on Wednesday when the Los Angeles Dodgers’ first baseman took a frightening tumble down the stairs and into the visitors’ dugout while trying to catch a foul popup in the eighth inning.
Freeman was not sure whether he would play when the Dodgers begin an important four-game series with the MLB-leading Milwaukee Brewers, but he is grateful his freefall to the dugout floor was not worse.
“I didn’t hit my head, so that was the key part there,” Freeman said. “I am sore. Kneecaps are sore. Shoulder is sore. Hand sore. Wrist sore. I mean, I fell, [but] I’m in good spirits.”
Photo: Kiyoshi Mio / Imagn Images
Freeman stayed in the game and finished the top of the eighth, but Tommy Edman pinch hit for him in the bottom of the inning before Los Angeles closed out a 4-2 victory over the Kansas City Royals, their fourth in five games.
The right side of Freeman’s body took the punishment, but the 2024 World Series Most Valuable Player apparently did not break any bones. He was to wait to see how he felt in the morning before deciding whether to play when the back-to-back World Series champions welcome Milwaukee in a rematch of last year’s National League Championship Series. That game is to be played this morning Taiwan time.
Freeman said he simply miscalculated the location of the dugout railing while he tracked Isaac Collins’ foul pop.
“I went to lean, like I was going to lean against the rail to catch the ball — and obviously there was no rail,” Freeman said with a smile.
Freeman, who turns 37 in one month, said he was fortunate to fall all the way into the dugout, missing the top flight of stairs entirely. That is because when he landed, his head stuck out into the open space above the second flight of stairs that goes down into the visitors’ clubhouse instead of banging on the ground.
“Luckily, I was tall, so I missed everything else,” the 1.93m Freeman joked.
Photo: AP
The Royals rushed to Freeman’s side after the fall, urging him to stay on the ground.
Freeman got up anyway and the Dodgers’ training staff rushed across the field to check on him.
“I think that we really dodged a bullet,” Los Angeles manager Dave Roberts said. “Very scary visually. For right now, he’s in good spirits, which I think is a good sign. Just kind of total body soreness.”

KMT set to freeze drone development budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:38:28 UTC
01:38:28 KST

The Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) caucus is poised to freeze a NT$44.2 billion (US$1.37 billion) six-year budget for drone industry development, modifying an earlier proposal to scrap the funding entirely, as the legislature aims to pass this year’s long-stalled general budget today.
If the budget does not pass today, all caucuses have agreed that an extra session would be held on Monday next week to continue to review the bill.
The KMT caucus said the Executive Yuan’s drone program, which was only approved on Oct. 19 last year, posed a risk that a large sum would be allocated, and use of the funds determined later.
Photo: CNA
The caucus had previously demanded that the Executive Yuan pause the program and had proposed removing all budget items for the program under this year’s general budget, only agreeing to put funding back on the table for the next fiscal year after the legislature completes its review.
It has now been a record 350 days since the Executive Yuan approved this year’s budget on Aug. 21 last year, and sent it to the legislature for review eight days later.
While the KMT has been working to reduce the number of proposals to slash or freeze funding to expedite the budget’s passage, the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) reportedly wants to introduce more cuts.
The TPP has proposed to slash 2 percent of the entire budget, or NT$56.86 billion, including 60 percent of special budgets across all ministries.
The special budgets for 20 units are to be elimated, including the Control Yuan, the Judicial Yuan, the Executive Yuan and the National Development Council (NDC), it said.
Officials said that the budget being in limbo has not only affected the NT$75.2 billion for national defense, but has also affected funding for social welfare, major railway projects and high-tech supply chains.
National defense officials said that while jet and ship maintenance were still provided for per Article 54 of the Budget Act (預算法), new projects would not be able to proceed.
Officials said that the general budget being in limbo is preventing the government’s access to the first and second reserve funds, as well as the disaster reserve fund.
Access to the funds, which total NT$17 billion, could be vital, especially as Taiwan enters its typhoon season, when rapid response is critical, they said.
Subsidies for domestic travel and renovations of sports stadiums and facilities are also off limits due to the general budget being in limbo, they said.
People in the tech industry warned that the Executive Yuan’s 10 new major artificial intelligence construction projects are unable to launch ancillary measures as funding has been frozen, and that the delays could cause Taiwan to miss out on a critical phase for the development of the silicon photonics industry and co-packaged optics.
In addition, about 267 drone developers are having to pay out-of-pocket to transition to a non-China supply chain because funding for subsidies has been stalled, tech industry insiders said.
Entrepreneurs have also said that, with NDC funds being frozen, venture-capital companies are retracting investments, causing a wave of dissolving tech start-ups.

E Ink downgrades its revenue growth forecast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
16:38:27 UTC
01:38:27 KST

E Ink Holdings Inc (元太科技), the world’s biggest e-paper display supplier, yesterday revised downward its revenue growth forecast for this year to between 10 and 15 percent, from the 20 to 25 percent it previously estimated, as surging memory prices are hurting demand for its e-readers and e-notes.
The company had expected a transition from monochrome color e-paper displays to color displays used in e-readers and e-notes to continue this year.
However, rapidly increasing memory prices have caused customers to postpone new product launches, while demand for models from previous generations has also dwindled due to higher prices, E Ink said.
Photo: Chen Mei-ying, Taipei Times
That created “headwinds mainly for consumer products such as e-readers and e-notes,” E Ink chairman Johnson Lee (李正昊) told an earnings conference in Taipei. “We are seeing a double-digit revenue decline” in that segment.
Still, Lee has retained his forecast of “healthy growth” for the company’s Internet-of-Things business, mainly e-paper used in electronic shelf labels (ESL).
The IoT revenue would grow 20 to 25 percent annually this year, thanks to accelerating adoption of ESLs by large-scale US and European retailers, he said.
E Ink’s capital expenditure would remain at NT$8 billion (US$248.69 million) this year, as the company is building new production lines for large e-paper displays to optimize the unit cost of its digital signage products, he added.
Demand for 8-inch to 15-inch digital signage is robust, while demand for 32-inch digital signage fell short of company expectations due to affordability issues.
Digital signage e-paper displays are projected to grow at a high-single-digit percentage this year, it said.
This quarter, revenue would slide moderately from NT$10.22 billion in the second quarter due to sagging demand for e-paper displays used in e-readers and e-notes, Lee said.
“The third quarter used to be a peak season for E Ink. The pattern will be different this year,” he said. “The fourth quarter will be the peak season this year.”
E Ink’s net profit last quarter expanded 26 percent year-on-year to NT$3.73 billion from NT$2.97 billion. Earnings per share (EPS) rose to NT$3.23 from NT$2.58, while gross margin edged lower to 58.7 percent from 60 percent a year earlier.
In the first half of the year, net profit advanced 26 percent to NT$6.52 billion from NT$5.17 billion in the same period last year. EPS climbed to NT$5.65 from NT$4.5.
