Eritrea: Rising power along key global shipping arteries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:44:00 UTC
20:44:00 KST

Eritrea, a rising power along a global shipping artery
August 13, 2026
Across the Horn of Africa, geopolitical interests of various countries continue to cause tensions and conflict as part of the growing competition for political influence over the region.
In its own right, the small country of Eritrea appears to be gaining in importance within this context: The autocratic state run by long-standing ruler Isaias Afwerki controls strategically important coastal points on the Red Sea, especially with its ports of Assab and Massawa.
In July, a series of diplomatic consultations in Cairo involving regional powers like Egypt, Somalia, Eritrea, and a high-ranking US envoy highlighted Eritrea's growing role in helping to coordinate approaches to resolving serious security challenges in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea, and to facilitate trade.
Eritrea's unique location along this maritime route is notably becoming more and more strategic in light of international trade conflicts. The small nation's coastline near the Bab-al-Mandab Strait stretches for more than 1,000 kilometers (621.4 miles), bordering Sudan to the northwest and Djibouti to the southeast.
But Eritrea's main strategic importance relies on who is on the other side of the strait, which at its narrowest point measures less than 30 kilometers.
A small country at a strategically important location
"Yemen lies on the other side of the Red Sea, which makes Eritrea's location particularly interesting, as Yemen is in a state of crisis and maritime security in the region is at risk," Abdurahman Sayed, director of the Horn of Africa Centre for Regional Integration (CRI) in London, told DW.
"The only safe route in this area runs through Eritrea, where there are currently no security concerns."
The Houthi militia, propped up by Iran, have been attacking merchant ships in the Red Sea from the Yemeni coastline.
For the past ten years, Yemen has also been witnessing one of the world's worst humanitarian crises in its midst: Ongoing violence, economic collapse, droughts and floods have exacerbated the suffering in the country, according to a report published by the UN Refugee Agency last month.
Sayed meanwhile emphasizes that in Eritrea, the strong dictatorship entrenched for decades does not tolerate any type of dissent. In many international freedom indexes, the African nation often only comes second to North Korea.
Since the country was officially founded 32 years ago, there have been no elections in the one-party state under long-time ruler Afwerki.
A unique sense of stability — for now
But this is also exactly why there are no violent conflicts in the country. Compared to other players in the broader region like Ethiopia, Sudan, and Yemen, Eritrea appears to be an island of peace where it is easy to do business.
"For this reason, all countries — including regional powers such as Saudi Arabia and Egypt, which controls the Suez Canal — want to maintain stable relations with Eritrea," Sayed highlights.
At the same time, this could eventually prove to be the country's Achilles' heel: "The country is ruled by a single man, and there are no constitutional institutions. That makes the state very vulnerable should this strongman be removed from power," says Sayed.
There is no strong figure in the 80-year-old autocrat's inner circle seen as a clear successor. This has raised some concern that the security situation could collapse once the president might no longer be in power, according to Sayed.
Alternative to the Strait of Hormuz
Still, Eritrea continues to exert its influence as the Red Sea has emerged a crucial sea route for the world, and especially for the Gulf states — Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, according to Sayed.
The war with Iran has further reinforced the nation's position, as this crisis has once again shown the central geopolitical importance of maritime chokepoints such as Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb.
A viable alternative, should the Strait of Hormuz remain repeatedly blocked, would be for these Gulf nations and their partners to find routes via Saudi ports located further up on the Red Sea.
While the Saudis have pipelines running from some of the interior regions of the country from where oil is extracted and produced to the port of Yanbu-Al-Bahr on the Red Sea, this alternative route could easily be compromised when it comes to security, potentially driving up oil prices even higher than what they currently are.
"For this reason, Eritrea today is of great strategic importance. This has been the case for centuries and will continue to be the case," Sayed emphasizes.
Ethiopia demands direct Red Sea access
Meanwhile, Eritrea's neighbors, particularly landlocked Ethiopia, are fighting hard to maintain access to the Red Sea as a trade route, Sayed adds, in particular for oil exports from the Horn of Africa to the rest of the world, especially to Europe and the Americas.
For decades, Djibouti has dominated regional trade logistics as Ethiopia's most important seaport partner, while Eritrea has been sidelined economically.
But Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has for years been demanding sovereign access to the sea — more than three decades after the country's split with Eritrea: when Eritrea gained its independence in 1993, Ethiopia lost its direct access, and has since been relying on its neighbors for all its sea trade.
However, maintaining a sense of neutrality and balance is proving to be a walk on a tightrope: Earlier in 2026, the fragile relations with between Ethiopia and Eritrea's Asmara region had already threatened to escalate amid a dispute over Ethiopia's access to the maritime trade route.
"The key context for Eritrea's recent strategic maneuvers in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea is the escalating tensions with Ethiopia," says Michael Woldemariam, a researcher at the School of Public Policy at the University of Maryland and the Atlantic Council.
"Asmara is seeking to forge partnerships that can serve as a counterweight to Addis Ababa. Its recent diplomatic outreach to Egypt, Somalia, the United Arab Emirates' armed forces, Saudi Arabia, Ethiopian opposition groups, and even the US should be viewed against this backdrop," he tells DW.
Meanwhile, a new trade corridor on the Red Sea is also taking shape: In May 2026, Eritrea and Egypt signed an agreement to establish direct freight connections between Egyptian and Eritrean ports on the Red Sea to expand independent trade and supply chains in the region.
A grave record of human rights violations
Still, there are no long-term guarantees with Eritrea, since the country's short history is almost entirely marked by violence, resulting in many people seeking a better life elsewhere.
"The first people fled Eritrea for Sudan in 1967 to escape [former Ethiopian ruler] Haile Selassie's imperial army. In the 1980s, people fled in large numbers from the Ethiopian military dictatorship. Since 2001, people have once again been fleeing in large numbers from human rights violations, military service, war, and a lack of prospects," says Magnus Treiber, a migration researcher specializing in the Horn of Africa at the Institute of Ethnology at the University of Munich.
"The causes of flight have hardly changed. However, since the European Union now offers virtually no opportunities to seek asylum, Eritreans are now fleeing all over the world."
At least 700,000 people have left the country since its founding, which is about a fifth of its total population. The country's population growth, meanwhile, is under 2% — a low number compared to many countries in the region.
Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

Explosion at Rotterdam port site kills one, injures several
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
One person has been killed and several others injured in an explosion at a site in the Port of Rotterdam, police say.
The blast happened shortly after midday on Thursday at a company on the Moezelweg in Europoort, regional broadcaster Rijnmond reported. Police said they had no further information at this stage.
Multiple people were injured and taken to hospital. Six ambulances, a trauma helicopter and fire crews were sent to the scene.
Rijnmond reported that a hired maintenance crew had been working on pipelines at the site and that something may have gone wrong as those pipes were being disconnected.
Traces of an explosion were visible on a storage tank, the broadcaster said.
Earlier on Thursday, a power cut shut down systems at the Esso refinery on the Botlekweg, sending large flames and black smoke over the port as gas lines were emptied. The Rotterdam-Rijnmond safety authority said it had not established whether the incidents were connected.

Ukraine's cities show imbalance in winter preparations, high-rises most vulnerable – 'Winter. Cities Will Hold' project head
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
14:40:41 EEST
20:40:41 KST

The 2026-27 heating season will be the hardest for Ukraine since the start of the war, and preparations among major cities are uneven, Vitaliy Miroshnychenko, head of the "Winter. Cities Will Hold" project, said.
"Since the start of the full-scale invasion, this year's winter will be the hardest. The Energy Ministry has officially announced this winter as the hardest and harshest of the entire war period, one that will come with prolonged systemic outages. This is clear from several factors, because for a long time now there have been systemic destruction of energy infrastructure, systemic destruction of communications and everything that ensures the normal functioning of the energy sector. The second problem is the imbalance in preparation, which shows up in how ready different regions are to expand energy infrastructure," Miroshnychenko said during a discussion titled "Winter Is Near: Are the State and Society Ready?" at the Interfax-Ukraine press center on Thursday.
Kyiv, Ukraine's capital, is currently the best prepared, he said.
"It is more than 50% ready, but if we're talking about cities with a population of over a million, other large population centers, their readiness is estimated at no more than 20%. Why? Because we don't have state subvention funds, and local community funds are insufficient. Next is the resource gap. All funds of the Energy Support Fund have been contracted, and according to the European Commission and the Energy Ministry, additional hundreds of millions of euros are needed," the project head said.
Miroshnychenko stressed the vulnerability of major cities.
"There is no Plan B, and the main issue is high-rise buildings — water pumping for nine-story buildings and above, and heat and power supply. This mainly concerns high-rise development, which as a rule means cities with a population of over a million and regional centers," he said.
Ukrainian cities need to be ready for scenarios in which there may be no electricity for 24, 48 or 72 hours, which is why the NGO Civil-Military Movement developed the "Winter. City Will Hold" project, laying out algorithms for community actions in the event of blackouts and disruptions to heat and water supply, the project head said.
"The project's main goal is to raise the real readiness of Ukraine's largest cities through an independent audit, as well as a public winter resilience index, practical assistance and the deployment of rapid response teams. We serve as a national arbiter, with the Civil-Military Movement acting as an independent, objective arbiter of winter readiness and a real helper to Ukrainian communities. The key focus is concentrating resources on regional centers and, as I said, the capital, Kyiv. The only exception will be the city of Kherson because of the security situation, but in addition to that there will also be Kryvyi Rih, as one of the largest urban areas in Dnipropetrovsk region… Looking ahead, we will be forming so-called unity brigades — coordinated mobile technical teams responding to requests for assistance at critical infrastructure facilities, which will operate in various regions of Ukraine," Miroshnychenko said.
The project's task is to shift winter preparation "from formal reporting into the realm of real readiness," he said. The road map was developed based on the expertise of specialists in energy, heat and water supply, engineering life-support systems, civil protection, utilities, crisis management and information security.
The discussion also covered the actual readiness of shelters and Points of Invincibility, backup heat and water supply, the operation of critical facilities, a possible new wave of evacuations, and communities' capacity to accept internally displaced people.
Oleksiy Ivashyn, head of the Civil-Military Movement NGO, stressed that winter preparations should be based not on an optimistic scenario but on readiness for the worst-case development of events.
"We are not creating this project as a declaration, not just as a document for the sake of a document. We are bringing in specialists in energy, heat and water supply, engineering life-support systems, civil protection, utilities, information security and so on. Our task is to look comprehensively at community readiness — what happens with heat when there's no electricity, what happens with water, how life-support systems work, what to do in the event of a prolonged blackout, how to support the most vulnerable people who need it most. And overall, how local authorities, state services, volunteers, NGOs and utility companies should interact with each other," he said during the discussion.
Ivashyn described the project's first stage as developing a unified system and testing it in practice.
"The second stage of the project is providing direct assistance to local authorities, state services and residents themselves once the cold period begins," he said.
The "Winter. City Will Hold" project envisages comprehensive preparation of communities for the 2026/2027 heating season — from risk assessment to specific action algorithms in the event of shelling, prolonged blackouts, loss of heat and water supply, and other emergencies. The project's second stage will begin with the onset of cold weather and will focus directly on helping community residents.

Euronews Culture's Film of the Week: 'The End Of Oak Street' - Putting the Jurassic World franchise to shame
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:40:26 UTC
20:40:26 KST

A mysterious cosmic event uproots Oak Street from 80s suburbia to prehistoric times... It's the blockbuster surprise of the summer.
This year has seen her battle shared trauma through the exorcism of shimmering red fabric in Mother Mary. 2026 has also witnessed her navigate corporate threats to save a fashion magazine (The Devil Wears Prada 2) and fight off pesky suitors hungry for her husband's throne (The Odyssey).
Now, Anne Hathaway is striving to survive the suburban anxiety of 1980s America by taking a stotgun to a dinosaur's face in David Robert Mitchell's The End Of Oak Street.
Seriously, what can't this woman do? She's certainly making it clear that while Tom Holland and Zendaya may be the ideal poster couple for two of this summer's box office juggernauts (The Odyssey and Spider-Man: Brand New Day), 2026 is first and foremost a Hathayear.
She stars in Mitchell's return to the big screen after an eight-year absence, playing Denise Platt, the core of what is seemingly the perfect nuclear family - composed of Greg (Ewan McGregor) and their two children, Audrey (Maisy Stella) and Brian (Christian Convery). And let's not forget their delightful menace of a dog, Starbuck.
However, there's trouble lurking beneath the surface of their middle-class idyll. Denise and Greg aren't communicating properly and are on the verge of a divorce. He's doing stints as a pizza delivery man to cover up the loss of his job; she's growing tired of the provincial mum act and has been secretly writing a novel to process her unspoken desire to pack up and leave her family.
To make matters worse, Brian has broken the arm of a local bully and is secretly smoking (gasp!), while Audrey... Well, Audrey is worried about the potential divorce but is quoting Carl Sagan like a champ, so she's basically got her shit together when it comes to being a teenager.
Things do get significantly knottier when strange prehistoric plants begin sprouting in a neighbour's garden, and the radio mentions "usual ripples in space" and strange "solar flares". Before you know it, a flash in the night transports the entire community from 1982 to the prehistoric age, with jungle surrounding the outer boarders and paleontologically accurate dinosaurs starting to get very rowdy indeed.
"Mom? Is this the end of the world?"
Well child, it's more of an unexplained teleportation deal, but it sure does feel like Dinogeddon. Puts marital strife into perspective, don't it?
For his pivot from indie movies to big blockbuster thrills, the director of It Follows and Under The Silver Lake has delivered one of the best summer adventures of the year. It's certainly the best dinosaur movie since 1993.
Faint praise, granted, considering the absolute drivel the Jurassic World films have been, but when your survival dino thriller has enough heart to hold up to Jurassic Park, that's no small feat.
Mitchell wears his Spielberg / Amblin film influences on his sleeve, with unmistakable callbacks to E.T., The Goonies, and of course, Jurassic Park. These references are only cemented further with Michael Giacchino’s excellent score, which features all the hallmarks of a boisterous John Williams effort. However, more than a fetishistic 80s pastiche (we're looking at you, Stranger Things) or a derivative exercise in nostalgia baiting, Mitchell has instead fashioned a family adventure that is packed with tense set-pieces, suspenseful beats and crucially, heart. The director has clearly learned from Jaws how to gradually tease and smartly reveal his monsters before letting gnarly pandemonium unfurl, but at no point does he forget to develop character-driven moments.
By fleshing out the family's dynamics and never losing focus of their inner struggles, the fight for survival becomes grounded and even more suspenseful. We see it through some very deliberate framing and delicious split diopter shots (plaudits due to DP Mike Gioulakis), but also a character emphasis which leads to surprisingly heartfelt and at times shocking moments. And without wishing to unduly read too much into it, there's a potent metaphor in there somewhere for how displaced suburbia embodies existential dread.
Primarily though, The End Of Oak Street is a finely-tuned crowd-pleaser, a survival roller-coaster benefitting from brisk pacing, smooth editing, and decent genre-blending. It's a dinosaur adventure, with immaculately designed CGI beasties; a frequently funny blockbuster which understands the inherent absurdity of the Oak Street predicament, featuring Camarasaurus humping, a theropod discovering the joys of ice cream, and what Dr. Ian Malcolm would have referred to as "one big pile of shit"; and an action thrill ride that doesn't skimp on horror. Indeed, Mitchell orchestrates some ruthlessly effective kills and plenty of gasp-triggering sequences which shan't be spoiled here.
While that may sound like a bit of a discordant jumble, Mitchell's emphasis on characters makes these elements mesh and ring true.
For all it gets right, there are some issues along the way.
While Anne Hathaway carries the film with both strength and relatable pathos, a less fortunate McGregor is saddled with rickety dialogue and a line-delivery that sounds stilted. Granted, Greg is supposed to be the optimistic / dopey dad counterpart to Denise's more practically-minded mother, but some parts of his performance don't quite land.
Then there's the afterthought ending. Again, no spoilers here, but the screenplay seems to lose its nerve when certain plot conveniences are waved away with an all too abrupt happy ending. Despite fitting in well with the unabashed old-school Amblin adventure vibe, the final five minutes will rub some audience members up the wrong way.
The ride is thrilling enough during the runtime to not care whether The End Of Oak Street sticks to an ultimately familiar template, but a trick was missed for the finale. It makes you wish that some shadowy enigma was teased further regarding a certain spherical MacGuffin, or that the underlying Twilight Zone-ness of it all was leaned into a bit harder. Considering J.J. Abrams is lead producer, even a Cloverfield spin wouldn't have gone amiss.
Still, when a last-minute stumble is preceded by top-tier entertainment which manages to pack violent thrills with enough outlandish absurdity and heartfelt emotion, it's had to complain too much. And who's going to argue against yet another 2026 movie which Anne Hathaway has once again raptor around her little finger (without forgetting a vital assist from Starbuck)? Saur-tainly not us.
The End Of Oak Street hits cinemas on 14 August.

Colombia earthquake response tests new far-right government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:39:46 UTC
20:39:46 KST

Colombia earthquake response tests new far-right government
The disaster tests President Abelardo de la Espriella and his government as it scrambles to find survivors and provide aid.
Bogota, Colombia – A deadly magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck western Colombia barely 72 hours after far-right leader Abelardo de La Espriella was sworn in as the president.
The disaster killed more than 260 people, injured thousands and devastated cities and towns in the first major test of leadership for de la Espriella as his government scrambles to search for survivors and provide aid to the most affected communities.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Search efforts in Colombia enter ‘final phase’ as quake toll reaches 265
- list 2 of 4Photos: Hope fades in Colombia as teams dig for earthquake survivors
- list 3 of 4Colombia declares three days of mourning after deadly earthquake
- list 4 of 4Colombia scrambles to find survivors after deadly earthquake
The 48-year-old leader declared the disaster an “economic emergency” and announced three days of national mourning before touring the worst-affected areas.
Colombia has considerable experience responding to natural disasters. Firefighters were the first to reach the affected areas, followed by Civil Defence officials and other emergency services.
Meanwhile, humanitarian aid collected in the capital Bogota and other cities was flown to disaster areas, as temporary shelters were put up for people displaced by the tragedy.
Less than 24 hours after the earthquake, heavy machinery, cranes and excavators were operating in Cali, Pereira and other affected cities.
In smaller, more isolated towns, however, residents were still removing rubble by hand, with many communities without power or basic services.
On Tuesday, the government announced temporary relief for families in Risaralda, one of the hardest-hit areas, including subsidies on rent and a three-month suspension of utility payments for the affected residents.
But the response has been in part complicated by a failed transition from the outgoing leftist administration of Gustavo Petro.
The lack of a proper handover has left the National Disaster Risk Management Unit in a state of limbo, with an acting director from the previous government working with a new team.
There are several challenges before the government, forcing officials from two different governments to work together despite their differences and the deep polarisation following one of the closest elections in history.
The government said its disaster agency would not be the official source of updates. Rather, the executive and, in particular, the office of the president would be solely responsible for providing information, including the official death toll.
Hence, the updates have been slow, leaving people, including journalists, to piece together information from local authorities.
Some affected communities near the quake’s epicentre in Choco, one of Colombia’s poorest districts, live among dense rainforests. They lack proper roads and have long suffered due to state neglect and armed conflicts.
Communications in those areas remain difficult, making it hard to determine the full scale of the damage. Vital infrastructure has also been hit. Aviation authorities closed six airports due to the earthquake, while dozens of roads were affected by landslides.
In Cali, several floors of a prominent hospital collapsed, forcing about 600 patients to be moved into temporary tents. Many other medical facilities have also been damaged.
For a president who entered office promising “decisive leadership and an iron fist against crime”, the earthquake is an immediate and unexpected test. How he handles it and whether a deeply divided political class in Colombia can work together during the emergency will help define a presidency that has barely begun.

Evacuation was carried out around a railway station in Bavaria due to a suspected explosive device
Kyiv • UNN
In the town of Treuchtlingen, an object that may contain explosives was found on the railway tracks near the station. Buildings were evacuated, train traffic was suspended, and an investigation is underway.
Buildings near the railway station in the southern German state of Bavaria were evacuated as a precaution after police reported that an object found on the tracks might contain explosives, UNN writes, citing DW.
Details
According to the Middle Franconia police, emergency services evacuated the directly affected buildings, while federal police specialists continued examining the object.
A technician discovered the suspicious object on the railway tracks near the entrance to the station in the town of Treuchtlingen.
Specialists have already conducted an X-ray examination of the object, but police said that further examinations were necessary, as the possibility of an explosive hazard had not yet been ruled out.
Police reported that a robot was used to interact with the object for further examination.
Road and rail traffic remain closed while the investigation continues. Regional services have been affected, with trains stopping earlier at the relevant stations. Replacement buses and large-capacity taxis have been arranged.
Intercity trains were rerouted via the city of Ingolstadt. Police urged people to avoid the area and choose alternative routes.
As n-tv reports, police eventually stated that no explosives had been found on the object. However, they suspected that it had been deliberately placed there as a dummy device.

VITEBSK, 13 August (BelTA) – Chairman of the Vitebsk Oblast Executive Committee Aleksandr Rogozhnik met with a delegation of the Petrodvortsovy District Administration of St. Petersburg to discuss launching cultural projects and expanding industrial cooperation, BelTA has learned.
“Cultural institutions, together with their Vitebsk colleagues, are implementing various events. We are actively working in the fields of youth policy and healthcare. White House releases Trump's order to install steam catapults on new US aircraft carrier
The White House has released the full text of a memorandum from Donald Trump to Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, ordering a change in the construction of a new US Navy aircraft carrier, to replace the electromagnetic aircraft launch system with steam catapults.
The supposed superiority of steam catapults for launching fighter jets has been an obsession of the president’s since 2017 when, he says, he was convinced by a single conversation with a Navy officer that the electromagnetic system installed in modern aircraft carriers was too complex.
The presidential memorandum, titled, “Rebuilding the United States Navy and America’s Shipbuilding Industrial Base”, claims to address “a series of shipbuilding setbacks stemming from overly complex designs” for US Navy ships.
Section 2 of the memo includes the order to change the construction of the USS Doris Miller, a Ford-class aircraft carrier known as CVN-81, which is already two years behind schedule:
Sec. 2. Restoring Steam and Hydraulic Systems to Carriers. Within 60 days of the date of this memorandum, the Secretary of War, in consultation with the Secretary of the Navy, shall provide to the President, through the Director of the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) and the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs (APNSA), a plan on the required measures to replace the Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System and Advanced Weapons Elevators with steam and hydraulic systems for the construction of CVN-81, including timelines and resourcing requirements.

Pentagon complains of 'rampant misreporting' on morale of US sailors but uses screenshots from Iranian state media
The US military’s Central Command, or Centcom, posted what it called a “fact check” on social media on Thursday, accompanied by a graphic that labeled six recent reports about a mental health crisis onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, during a record-breaking deployment at sea tied to the war with Iran, as “false” or “misinformed”.
The graphic includes screenshots of six headlines, but fails to explain which news outlets published them. A review by the Guardian reveals that three of the headlines, which repeat the false claim that seven US sailors died in a brawl on the ship, were taken from Iranian media outlets based in Tehran.
The text of the Centcom post complains about “rampant misreporting” from “multiple media outlets” about morale on board the aircraft carrier deployed to the Middle East, but fails to explain that half of the outlets are linked to Iran’s government.
“One report alleged seven Sailors died in a brawl aboard the aircraft carrier and others have recently suggested a spike in suicidal ideations. These reports are FALSE”, the Centcom post reads.
But the Pentagon fact-checkers appear to be trying to discredit well-sourced, factual reporting from two specialist US news outlets, the Navy Times and Stars and Stripes, which first reported that multiple sailors have attempted to jump overboard, by lumping those reports together with propagandistic fiction from two Iranian state-owned outlets, Mehr News and Press TV, and a third, West Asia News Agency (WANA), which says it “strives to provide foreign audiences with news from Iran with a novel view and narrative.”
The Cenctom post ends by scolding the unnamed media outlets, calling their work “a disservice to our men and women in uniform and their loved ones”, reinforcing the false impression that the outlets spreading false information are American, not Iranian.

Trump orders US Navy to spend billions to install steam catapults in new aircraft carriers - reports
After nearly a decade of publicly complaining about the fact that US aircraft carriers use electromagnetic catapult systems to launch fighter jets, instead of the steam-powered catapults of old, Donald Trump has reportedly directed the US Navy to remove the modern launch systems from its aircraft carriers and install the old-fashioned steam catapults he prefers, according to the Wall Street Journal and Reuters.
The Journal reports that Trump signed a national security memorandum on Thursday directing the change he has had his heart set on since at least 2017, when he first described his brainwave to Time magazine.
“You know the catapult is quite important. So I said, ‘What is this?’ ‘Sir, this is our digital catapult system’”, Trump told the magazine in 2017, recounting a conversation he said he had with a US Navy officer. “It sounded bad to me. Digital. They have digital. What is digital? And it’s very complicated, you have to be Albert Einstein to figure it out. And I said–and now they want to buy more aircraft carriers – I said, ‘What system are you going to be’– ‘Sir, we’re staying with digital.’ I said, ‘No you’re not. You[’re] going to goddamned steam, the digital costs hundreds of millions of dollars more money and it’s no good’”.
A review of Trump’s public remarks shows that he has retold this story every year since 2017.
In 2018, Trump brought it up during a Thanksgiving day phone call with the commanding officer of the USS Ronald Reagan, an aircraft carrier docked in Hong Kong at the time. In 2019, he recounted his conversation with the “catapulter” to Republican donors at a fundraiser. In 2020, as the nation was grappling with a pandemic, the tale became a regular part of Trump’s campaign speeches. In 2021, he told the story at the CPAC convention. In 2022, he shared it in a campaign speech in Texas. He repeated it on the campaign trail in Iowa in 2023. At one of his final campaign events before the 2024 election, Trump told Tucker Carlson the same story.
After he returned to office in 2025, Trump brought up steam catapults during the swearing-in of Tulsi Gabbard as his director of national intelligence and then did so again in remarks to the crew of the USS George Washington, an aircraft carrier based in Japan.
“We built an aircraft carrier for $19 billion, which is crazy. The price is crazy,” Trump recalled last month at the Army War College in Pennsylvania. “It had all sorts of modern day things that were all- instead of using steam for the catapults, they used electric.”
“So when I went to the ship, because I came into office and the ship was way over budget, built in Newport News,” Trump said. “I said, ‘I want to meet the catapulter’, and a man came over, along with four of his assistants. And I said, ‘What’s better: electric catapult or steam?’ He’s been there for 25 years. He said, ‘Steam is better, sir. We can fix it with a hammer and a blowtorch. When the electric goes bad, I have to send to MIT to get geniuses over here.’ I said, ‘Steam is better?’ ‘Yes, sir it’s better’”.
According to the Journal senior Navy and industry leaders “have resisted the move due to the enormous expense of tearing out such a complex system that was integral to the design” of the latest aircraft carriers.

Donald Trump has welcomed the court of international trade’s ruling that supports his decision to end the de minimis tariff exemption. A policy which allows people and businesses to avoid paying duties on packages and shipments below $800 that are shipped the US.
The president called it a “BIG WIN”, branding the exemption one of “the most DESPICABLE loopholes in American Trade Policy”.
An Michigan-based auto parts manufacturer filed the suit, arguing that it should be refunded for the tariffs it paid when Trump ended the exemption – in light of the supreme court’s decision this year which struck down the president’s sweeping tariffs under International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA).
The trade court, however, ruled that IEEPA “authorizes the president’s recission of the de minimis exemption”.

Trump-led board reportedly votes again to close Kennedy Center for renovations
The board of the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts has once again voted to move forward with Donald Trump’s controversial plan to temporarily close the building for renovations, the New York Times (paywall) is reporting, citing two people with direct knowledge of the proceedings.
The decision will be subject to approval by a federal judge. In May, US district judge Christopher Cooperissued a temporary block on Trump’s demand to close the arts institution for two years of renovations, which was due to start in July after the board – mostly handpicked by the president – voted unanimously in favor. But Joyce Beatty, a Democratic US representative of Ohio who sits on the board, sued over the decision.
Cooper shut down the plan on the basis that “in ratifying President Trump’s closure announcement, the Board was derelict in discharging the full range of its responsibilities to the Center”.
“More specifically, the Board based its decision on an insufficient, one-sided presentation of information and neglected to consider the full range of its statutory obligations and potential adverse consequences of closure on programming and memorial functions,” Cooper went on.
He called the decision to halt operations during the renovation “ill-informed and seemingly preordained”.
According to the New York Times’s report, the board voted today “to close the Kennedy Center’s main building, while keeping a newer addition to the campus, known as the Reach, open for limited programming and to operate as an active memorial to John F. Kennedy.”
Ahead of the meeting, the board was presented with a 163-page plan for a $250m “renewal” project that includes structural repair work, new marble floors, $11.8m in “acoustical improvements” and a plan to temporarily move the famous 3,000-pound bronze bust of Kennedy to another building on campus.
Board members were provided with a comparison of two scenarios for renovations by an outside consultant. Both the consultant and the construction management firm, JLL, raised safety and cost concerns that they say would arise from keeping the building open during a phased renovation.
The proposal by JLL says the project would address chronic leaks, replace outdated equipment and redesign parts of the interior. Changes include new furniture, a new coffee shop, electronic ticketing kiosks and $7m in public restroom renovations. The target for reopening would be summer of 2028.
Judge Cooper said in his order that the board had a legal obligation to maintain the facility as a memorial to President Kennedy. Under the plan, memorial materials would be moved to a newer addition to the campus during the closure.
It was unclear immediately after the meeting, which was held virtually and was not public, whether the center intends to pursue the exact plan laid out in the report following the judge’s review.
The Kennedy Center has until next week to share its plan with Cooper, who will review his decision to consider whether the board carried out sufficient due diligence ahead of the vote.
We’ve reached out to the Kennedy Center for comment.
White House says it’s losing $19-$26bn a year in revenue as countries dodge tariffs
The White House has said in a new report that countries are routing their exports through third countries to avoid US tariffs, estimating that there are tax revenue losses of $19bn to $26bn annually, the Associated Press reports.
The report specifically highlights that China responded to new tariffs in 2018 by transshipping, sending their goods to other nations ranging from Mexico to Malaysia for packaging and limited assembly. That pattern made it look like US imports from China had dropped, but enabled Beijing to continue growing its manufacturing sector in ways that could challenge US factories and employment.
Peter Navarro, the White House trade adviser, told reporters on a conference call that China is laundering its exports through more than 40 countries, though he claimed that the issues raised in the report were really more about other nations enabling the avoidance of tariffs.
“For years, the great transshipment scam has let communist China launder its exports,” he said.
The report comes ahead of a planned visit next month by Chinese president Xi Jinping, whom Donald Trump described in flattering terms during his own visit to Beijing in May.
Navarro said that other nations such as India could also transship to avoid new tariffs and said that new trade frameworks pursued by the Trump administration are going to contain provisions that ensure trade partners that engage in the practice will be penalized.
The report includes a range of estimates for the scale of transshipments to avoid tariffs, citing government and private sector numbers to estimate roughly $34.2bn to $303bn of goods transshipped each year. It used a central figure of $75bn worth of goods being transshipped to estimate how much in tax revenues have been lost.
To address the challenge, Navarro said that US Customs and Border Protection has started to use artificial intelligence in a prototype program to stop transshipments. When an importer has been found to have falsified the origins of a good, its imports can be retroactively tariffed going back roughly a year, he said.

A federal judge has dismissed a lawsuit by the Trump administration that alleged HarvardUniversity failed to protect Jewish and Israeli students from harassment.
In his ruling today, US district judge Richard Stearns in Boston said the Trump administration’s lawsuit, filed in March, had not plausibly shown an ongoing violation of federal civil rights law on Harvard’s campus.
Stearns said the government’s allegations focused largely on incidents amid protests overIsrael’s war in Gaza during the 2023/24 school year, with only a handful of later incidents alleged in March 2025 that were “too isolated and episodic” to support a claim of ongoing civil rights violations.
The judge said the lawsuit did not adequately allege failures by the university after the government told Harvard in June 2025 that it was not complying with Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. It bans discrimination based on race, color and national origin in programs that receive federal funding.
The White House and Harvard did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.
Linked to Hegseth’s recent comments about the conditions on board the USS Abraham Lincoln, the Wall Street Journal is reporting that the USS George Washington will be sent to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln, as part of a previously scheduled rotation plan. The outlet cites unnamed officials familiar with the matter.
Pete Hegseth downplays conditions on USS Abraham Lincoln after reports of food shortages and a mental health crises on board
Defense secretary Pete Hegseth has said that concerns about conditions on board the USS Abraham Lincoln are “completely misrepresented”.
This comes after several reports about food shortages and an intensifying mental health crisis on the vessel, that has now been deployed for more than 200 days, after it was redirected to the Middle East to assist with the military operation in Iran.
“We make sure every ship, every crew, every captain has everything we can provide them at every single moment,” Hegseth told reporters in Panama, where he was attending a military demonstration. “Some deployments are longer than others, and I have more respect and gratitude for those sailors than anybody. What they do in those high seas in those austere conditions with less port calls – it’s incredible.”
Two leading specialist military papers, the Navy Times and Stars and Stripes, are reporting that there have been multiple attempts by sailors to jump overboard as poor conditions and mental stresses on the Lincoln reach the breaking point.
On Wednesday, Democrats on the Senate armed services committee wrote to Hegseth and the acting secretary of the US Navy, Hung Cao, for more information abut what action is being taken to improve conditions on board.
“There have been widespread reports of shortages of basic supplies, water contamination, plumbing issues, deteriorating mental health, deck safety concerns, and disruptions in the mail system, which have caused many care packages in route to the ship to be lost in transit for months,” Richard Blumenthal, a Democrat, wrote. The senator noted that the USS Abraham Lincoln has not made a port call in over 200 days – setting a record for consecutive days at sea.

More than 135 million people in Europe face temperatures over 35C
Europe is the fastest-warming continent in the world and in some places is ill-equipped to deal with hot weather.
More than 135 million people across Europe, mostly in France, Italy, Spain and the United Kingdom, face temperatures above 35 degrees Celsius (95 Fahrenheit) as the continent’s latest heatwave builds.
According to German weather service forecasts and 2025 population projections from the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre, nearly three in five Europeans, or about 340 million people, will feel temperatures surpassing 30C (86F) on Thursday. The figures line up with separate tracking from Austria’s Klimadashboard.

As Thursday unfolds, the UK and France are experiencing their fifth heat wave of the summer. Forecasters predict temperatures could reach 38C (100F) in central and southeast England, possibly marking the hottest day of the year.
France may see temperatures as high as 40C (104F).
The highest temperature in the UK so far this year was recorded on June 26, when the temperature hit 38C in eastern England.
Britain’s Met Office said earlier this week that only average conditions were needed for the rest of August to beat last year’s record for the hottest ever year.
More than one thousand wildfires have been recorded in England and Wales this year, according to data from the National Fire Chiefs Council.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will consider imposing a ban on disposable barbecues amid the risk of continuing wildfires.
“I do believe we need to get the message out loud and clear,” he said. “People should not be using those barbecues outside at this moment in time.”
‘Impossible and inhumane’ conditions
The UK’s Royal College of Nursing (RCN) said on Thursday that extreme heat is making parts of the National Health Service (NHS) an “impossible and inhumane” place to work and receive care.
Calls to the RCN helpline report staff collapsing on shift, experiencing heat-related seizures, and pregnant nursing staff working in temperatures above 30C, the RCN said. Many staff reported that they were working without access to air conditioning, fans or even adequate ventilation.
Both France and the UK are also facing widespread drought, like much of Europe, as shrivelled crops and drained rivers strain water supplies for households, farms and the environment.
This has forced governments to seek both short and long-term fixes to slow down the effects of what is widely seen as human-caused climate change.

Rethinking Humanitarianism | Will big donors “smell the coffee” or get left behind?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-13
11:38:15 UTC
20:38:15 KST

Share & more
Editor’s note: This episode was made in collaboration with Start Network as part of a series that explores what really drives change in the humanitarian system, and what it tells us about future efforts to transform the system for the better. Find previous episodes here.
Less than a year ago, Colum Wilson left his position at the helm of the humanitarian department in one the world’s largest donor governments.
After more than two decades of humanitarian work for the UK government, Wilson concludes that “the world's become a colder and crueller place where realpolitik tends to trump humanitarianism”.
“It was far easier to make a pure humanitarian argument to ministers then than it was now.”
In this second collaborative episode between Rethinking Humanitarianism and Start Network, Wilson joins hosts Tammam Aloudat and Christina Bennett to unpack how humanitarianism is being reshaped from the top down. They discuss the rise of populism and transactional humanitarian policy, the quiet “insurgency” of local responders getting on with change outside the formal system, the potentially disruptive power of middle-tier donors, alternative financing models, and new centres of humanitarian power.
In the end, Wilson predicts that the “battle for the heart of humanitarianism” will ultimately be “determined out in the rural areas of Somalia, and Bangladesh, rather than in Geneva, and London, and Washington.”
His advice for the traditional bilateral Western donor governments, like the one he once worked for? “What they have to do is smell the coffee and work with an agility that they’re going to find difficult,” otherwise, “they’re going to be left behind.”
On next week’s episode, Aloudat and Bennett explore how these seismic political shifts in donor governments are affecting states that traditionally received aid and, more importantly, the people they govern.
Guest
Colum Wilson, former Head of the Humanitarian Department for the UK's Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO); senior humanitarian policy advisor

Colum, I understand what you're saying. Colum Wilson
I don't have an answer. I mean, if this was easy, we probably wouldn't be sitting here having this conversation. We're not going to make a difference.’ What we need to do is to show that we can make a difference and that we have, we can bring back success stories. Tammam Aloudat
You, and I, and Christina will remember how, when it was mostly earthquakes and tsunamis and stuff, it was easier to – and Venezuela shows that – it's somewhat easier to get people empathetic with an act of God, if you want. But we've been facing two genocides over the past three years between Sudan and Gaza, and it's heavily political and tense within the politics of the UK and the European Union. That narrative you're talking about – creating stories of success and narrative difference that gets people on board – can it be the same as humanitarianism always [has] been? Just like ‘save lives’, as if we are in a bubble? From your position of having been inside the machine of government aid, what do you see the benefits and downsides to a political versus non-political humanitarian narrative?
Colum Wilson
I mean, the single thing, and it's maybe a simplistic answer, is human suffering. You know, we've got to be quite careful there because the way people are portrayed as victims of a crisis, victims of a man-made or natural disaster, is problematic, and we understand that. But the problem is, or the point is, that people will still respond to that. Now, in terms of political framing, one thing I would say is that our aspiring prime minister, waiting in the wings, has turned around and said, the way that the Gaza, the government responded to the Gaza crisis was initially wrong, is quite telling. Because I think for, on one level, if you like, there was a democratic disconnect between what the people were feeling in this country and what the government was doing. So I have hope.
Tammam Aloudat
That's a very good point. I think there has been a pressure that yielded that statement by Andy Burnham. Although in Arabic we have a saying: ‘A mountain went into labour and gave birth to a mouse’. His statement was, you know, ‘We may have not been fast enough in calling ceasefire three years ago’ is not exactly an atonement for, you know, what has happened. It's sort of ‘Maybe possibly we were wrong’, and there was a lot of commentary about you know this is not what this is not a massive change. He didn't call it genocide. He didn't call for a boycott. He didn't stop the sales of weapons. Is that enough?
Colum Wilson
Well…
Tammam Aloudat
Is that a real change in your mind, or is it just rephrasing the same sort of concern and prayers?
Colum Wilson
You know, I, I would imagine that quite a few people, colleagues, really, really big-hearted humanitarians at FCDO will be turning around and going, ‘Gosh, that's a major victory that Andy Burnham has said this, all right, this is an interesting new development’. And at the end of the day, one has to take a bit of a breath and recognise that it is just words – and by the way, three years too late. But you are basically… these are tiny little bits of brick, if you like, in the normative building, the normative environment. I mean, I started life with MSF and thought all this is rubbish, all this diplomacy stuff is absolute… there's another word I'd use for it, but not on air. What I have learnt over the years, though, is that you build the normative environment word by word, and, you know, that the kind of statements that ministers come out with around Gaza, okay, they will have been hard fought every single word about that. And as a P5 member – and we can have our questions about whether it's right or wrong that we're a P5 member, etc. etc. etc… – the bottom line is that people pay attention to the UK's position, and it changes the normative environment fractionally. So, if I can respectfully suggest, don't underestimate the power of words. But you know…
Tammam Aloudat
No, no, I’m not. My worry is at the, I mean, if I was a Palestinian or Sudanese, I'd contest that this is a major victory, given how slow and how late. But even in the tactical sense you've talked about, it is a change. Kier Starmer has not given anything near that. But who on earth knows? You know, you build this for 10 years, and then the next elections you have Nigel Farage and you're back to sub-zero. How much can we go incrementally, slowly building normative frameworks that an extreme right-wing politician [can] come and demolish with no regrets, as Trump did with USAID, and as potentially a, you know, a Reform UK might do with whatever is built until then?
Colum Wilson
I mean, you're talking about the nature of the times and why this moment in time represents a watershed, and I'll defer to here to Christina who's seen through many, many rounds of reform from the inside of the system. But you know, in my, my recollection of previous reforms, have been that they were against a backdrop where we were increasingly doing technical shifts to the perimeter, to the edges of the humanitarian system against a backdrop that was more or less stable. Now, two things have happened that has made the last two years absolutely tumultuous. The first thing is that the international geopolitical world order has shifted in ways that even the most pessimistic foresight products that FCDO was producing at the time had not anticipated. So the shifts are mega. And the second thing is, we've got– or that includes, I should say, a move to a realism, international relations realism that is really, really stressing our humanitarian frameworks. And the second is, of course, the recognition that our system is no longer fit for purpose, set against this shifting background, and therefore this now presents a moment of time, in time where we have an opportunity, like, this is a once in a generation opportunity. The time when I left FCDO, in fact, you know, you, you blink once and the whole world melts down, but this is basically the moment that we've been waiting for for all these years.
Christina Bennett
So if that's true, Colum, what you say is that we are at a major inflection point that's the one chance in a generation to make these fundamental shifts that we've all been talking about but have yet to make. You've talked about the fact that change is already happening on the ground. How then do you harness the power of governments to be able to enable that change? And do you think powerful donor governments will allow that reform to happen, or will they see a movement towards solidarity, a movement toward righting injustices as a threat to their ability to control?
Colum Wilson
Yes, I think is the answer. I do see a battle for the heart of humanitarianism ahead. In fact, it's already playing out. You know, the question of solidarity is quite interesting and now being tossed around as an alternative framework to govern and shape what we support and do. But I think that you're going to end up with a rump system that is essentially the same shape as the one we have at the moment, because it won't be able to shift quickly enough or in the right direction fast enough. But it will be small. I'll come and answer your question about what governments can do in this, but around that, you're going to get alternative models: regionalised, national models that centre sovereignty at regional or national level, that centres civil society. And by the way, this is not something that's going to happen in the future. It's happening now. At the best, you could end up with a confederated sort of global system that supports humanitarianism. At worst, you could end up with a fragmentation that so shakes the normative frameworks that they cease to be meaningful. Now, question about what, if you could call them ‘traditional bilateral Western donors’ can do in this melee: I think what they have to do is to smell the coffee and work with an agility that they're going to find very, very difficult. And I would say that there are some donors, and I'd call them middle-tier Western donors, that are already moving in this direction. But I don't think the principal big donors are going to be able to move fast enough in this direction, and they're going to become a little bit of an anomaly. They're going to be left behind. The new frameworks and ways of working will be being determined out in the rural areas of Somalia, and in the rural areas of, I don't know, Bangladesh, rather than in Geneva, and London, and Washington.
Tammam Aloudat
Is that a good or a bad thing?
Colum Wilson
Oh, it's interesting. I hadn't thought of attaching a judgement to it, but if you put me on the spot, I think it's a good thing. Because it's, basically we are shackled to Maslow's hierarchy, our entire humanitarian system. If you actually ask people what they want, they don't talk about the bottom tier of Maslow's hierarchy, and that fundamentally is what should be guiding us. So it's a question of agency. And if you use the servicing of people's agency as a principal driver, you are already building in all sorts of tensions with the existing centres of power.
Tammam Aloudat
Let me ask you, when you were an FCDO, how much does a government know, or consider, or factor in, or even care about what actually people, like… How much of it is a technical, or political, or agency calculation on behalf of the people that are affected?
Colum Wilson
Well, the first thing is you've got to be quite careful, and you'll forgive me for just correcting the assumption that FCDO is a single entity – it's got lots of people in it, and all those people have different perspectives. And what I can tell you is that there's a hardcore of humanitarians in there – I was fortunate, privileged enough to be one of them – that understand the way that things go. But the idea of leeching power away from the centre, from the donor control, is fundamentally going to be problematic. This is something, I'm not the first person to say this. You know you guys write about it the whole time, Christina lives the dream by transferring power out. We understand that. But fundamentally that is going to be problematic. So what you have is a lot of very, very good humanitarians who understand the technical ramifications, who understand the moral point of doing this, but are to some extent constrained by realpolitik of humanitarianism as an instrument of, if you like, power, global power.
Christina Bennett
We've talked about a lot of dynamics today. We've talked a lot about the history of the power of donor governments. If you were in control of the UK's humanitarian policy today, suspend disbelief, what would be the first thing you would do?
Colum Wilson
If you go into this imaginary world of views where it's decoupled from national interests, so that's the first thing to get out there, is you can set a policy frame that favours support for, if you like, all the stuff that's happening that would form ultimately a confederacy rather than a centralised system. So a way of supporting the growth, a thousand flowers blooming out there, and it comes down to a few important policy levers. One of them is cash. The cash revolution hasn't, hasn't been completed. We're only on 21 per cent or whatever it is now, and that's declining since last year. The second is moving away, wholescale, from the grant model. There's two reasons for that. One is it's no longer fit for purpose, there isn't enough money to hand out. And secondly, it is a major affront to people's dignity. So what we need to do is to start using the limited ODA that we've got to leverage other money, and insurance is a very good example of that. So I would be saying, well, you need to explain why you're responding, why you're not putting insurance frameworks in place beforehand. The third area is extensive use of the ecosystem of pooled funds, and that doesn't just mean CERF or country-based pooled funds. And I'm using the words really carefully: the ecosystem. So, feminist pooled funds, women's pooled funds, local civil, civil society pooled funds – that entire ecosystem. Obviously you’ve got to work out how the checks and balances work, etc., and that's not a small thing, you know. That's got to be reconciled with Daily Mail readers and whatnot back at home. But fundamentally, that represents a way of solving the wholesale-retail problem that is at the heart, one of the technical reasons why large scale support for localisation is quite difficult from big donors. So those, I've given you three policy levers. I would reframe the UK's humanitarian approach in those terms.
Christina Bennett
You’ve painted a picture of this federated ‘let a thousand flowers bloom’ ecosystem, and there are some who think that that is the future of aid. But what we also have alongside it: some very, very powerful interests re-centralising, pulling back from this idea that there is a, there is an ecosystem and going back to funding the oligopoly that has been the humanitarian enterprise for some time. If you were the UK government now, what would you do to influence those larger and smaller donor governments to move in the direction that you've explained to us?
Colum Wilson
Well, the first thing is, one of the issues that I have with FCDO – and I'm sure I don't think I'm going to upset anybody by saying this – is that FCDO, along with a lot of other top-tier bilateral donors, is risk-averse, bureaucratic, and highly path-dependent. So the first thing to do is to embrace an agility and willingness to look outside and understand what is going on across the rest of the constellation, the humanitarian ecosystem, as it's been framed out there, and understand that there are alternatives out there. The second thing I'd do – and this is something that gave me a lot of sleepless nights when I was in the previous role – was to mobilise donors around that agenda. Now that sounds easy enough, but as I said to you earlier, it was very difficult to get a coherent message out of donors because they're fractured by their own national interests. And you know, particularly with the rise of, sort of, populist governments across Europe, that's become even more intense. So you know, the German framing of humanitarianism in its recent strategy is quite interesting in that respect because it, it coasts very closely towards supporting national interest. So you've got all this problem going on. So then what you look for is new and emerging and middle-tier donors who have the agility, don't come with the geopolitical baggage necessarily, and whatnot. And I think that is the next centre of power that we need to invest in to try and mobilise towards shifting the system.
Tammam Aloudat
Just for our listeners' clarity, when you talk about the middle-tier donors, are we talking about Belgium, Luxembourg, Australia, or are we talking about new donors? What should we think about when you mention that?
Colum Wilson
It's a bit of both. There are some very innovative donors out there that are quite small. I mean, Swiss is one of them. Irish Aid, very very interesting what they're doing. Then there are what I'd call emerging donors. Again, it's a bit of a pejorative term, but you know countries where we used to go in and do old-style humanitarian support, like Bangladesh and Indonesia, they don't have the same frame. They don't have same framing of humanitarianism as we do. Whose humanitarianism is it anyway? But you know, can you imagine a coalition of those member states putting forward alternative models and supporting an alternative way of doing things. Yes, it represents a different centre of power, but it's either ignoring that or it's trying to support it in a constructive way. And I'd be in for the latter.
Christina Bennett
This episode has been about reform from above. Do you think that reform of the system, by the system, or from its, its patrons, the donor governments, is possible or desirable? And is ultimately the future of humanitarian action better off without them? Better off without those patrons that have been the major players in the system to date?
Colum Wilson
So you can't wish them out of existence. Let me answer your first, your second question first. You can't wish them out of existence. This is why I think where we're going to end up, if we scrolled forward and imagined ourselves sitting around this table in 20 years' time, what would we see? This is this idea of kind of rump system that I mentioned before, surrounded by a kind of a constellation, if you like, of alternative centres of power that, to a greater or lesser extent, are coherent, but not necessarily. So that's the future I think where it's going to end up for pragmatic reasons, because you can't undo the structures that we've got. The power is too entrenched. But to come to your first question, then, about whether a complete reset, if I can use that word, or a complete sort of white-sheet-of-paper reform is possible: the answer is no. And by the way, getting to that new configuration that I've described is going to be heavily, heavily contested, and it's going to be fought over the whole way. If you ask me whether the system can self-reform – and this is why the question about the World Humanitarian Summit 2026 I think is relevant – I don't think it can self-reform. I think it's too embedded. I think we had a political moment in 2016. Probably wasn't a powerful enough political moment, but you wouldn't be able to get that political moment again. And I think that reflects the fact that actually the system is too heavily embedded to be able to do fundamental self-reform. It won't, it won't wish itself out of existence.
Christina Bennett
So, as someone who's familiar with the system, what advice do you have for those working outside the system? Those movements that have emerged in countries like Sudan, like Myanmar, like other places that have something to give to the system, that are able to shift it from below, but that have to contend with powerful governments’ resistance to that locally-led change?
Colum Wilson
Well, I mean, again, I don't have a silver bullet answer here, and it's probably stating the bleeding obvious, but it's basically not waiting for the system to catch up. Trying to influence the existing system, the one that's so embedded where we can, but in the meantime, just getting on with it. And, you know, whether that's bringing weather forecasting in the last mile to people in Sudan, or whether it's bringing microinsurance to ground level in war zones, just get on with it, and then move it to scale. And that's going to require non-traditional alignments and partnerships. Again, it's a little bit of a hackneyed phrase, and you know the Global Partnerships Conference was nominally all about that. So you know, it's with the private sector, it's with philanthropies, and it's leveraging then into these places that sometimes are not necessarily comfortable to go into. So there isn't any big revelations there, Christina, but I think it is something to do with agility, and just not hanging around, and just walking the walk as well as talking the talk, because that's the only way it's going to shift.
Christina Bennett
Thanks for that, Colum. Thanks for being with us today and for taking all of our questions.
Colum Wilson
And thank you very much.

In the Lviv region, a 54-year-old man is suspected of systematically raping a 14-year-old girl who was his foster daughter. This was reported by the Office of the Prosecutor General, UNN writes.
In the Lviv region, a 54-year-old man is suspected of systematically sexually abusing a minor girl who, together with her two biological sisters, had been placed in his foster family for care. According to the investigation, the unlawful acts continued for about a year
In April 2023, three sisters aged 10, 11 and 17 were placed in a foster family in the Stryi district. After the eldest sister left to study, the two younger children remained under the care of their foster parents.
According to the investigation, in August 2025, taking advantage of the material and domestic dependence of the then-14-year-old foster child, the man began committing sexual acts against her.
Thereafter, for a year, the man systematically—at least three times a week—committed violent sexual acts against the girl and raped her.
According to the investigation, the man used psychological pressure, intimidation and physical violence, and, in order to suppress the girl's resistance, threatened to sexually abuse her younger sister.
In July 2026, the minor told an acquaintance who was abroad about what she had experienced. The acquaintance contacted law enforcement officers. After that, the man was detained.
Under the procedural guidance of the Stryi District Prosecutor's Office, he was notified of suspicion of committing lewd acts, sexual violence and rape of a person under sixteen years of age, committed by a person entrusted with duties concerning the victim's upbringing.
The suspect was remanded in custody without the right to bail.

Sexual assault survivors in Lithuania face long waits for help – and lost evidence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

20:37:01 KST

By Urtė Šlevaitė, LRT TV, LRT.lt.
People who have survived drug-facilitated sexual assault in Lithuania say they are being let down by a system with too few specialist services, no reliable way to preserve evidence, and long waits for care. The country’s social security ministry says changes are coming, but for now, campaigners say, survivors are often left to navigate the process largely on their own.
“A black screen, then nothing”
Ten years ago, comedian and human rights advocate Vita Žiba was sexually assaulted after being drugged. She says it took her a while afterwards to understand what had happened to her.
“First of all, you barely remember anything, because those drugs are usually designed specifically to suppress memory. I just remember having one drink, then another, and then – a black screen. The next thing I remember is being in some room, I don’t even know where, with some man’s hands all over me,” she said.
When Žiba shared her story on social media, she received an outpouring of support – within a week, roughly 800 women had come forward with their own experiences of sexual violence. But she also faced abuse online.
“A lot of older men wrote things like ‘you had it coming’, ‘it’s your own fault’, or ‘you should be grateful someone wanted you’,” she said.

Teens asked ChatGPT about arson punishment before setting fire to Givatayim Japanika restaurant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-14
11:41:47 UTC
20:41:47 KST

Two teens indicted for setting fire to a Japanika in Givatayim - Hanan Yaakov, 18, and Osher Bayach, 18, both from Rehovot - were revealed to have used ChatGPT to ask what the punishment for arson was before setting out to light the restaurant on fire.
According to the indictment, filed by attorney Tamar Teitelbaum of the Tel Aviv District Attorney's Office, Yaakov and Bayach conspired during the night between July 11 and 12 to set fire to the Japanika restaurant in Givatayim. At 1:10 a.m., according to the allegations, the plan was already underway.
At around 2:25 a.m., the two left Rehovot and traveled together to Bnei Brak. On Zeitlin Street, they obtained an electric scooter and three plastic bottles, each containing 1.5 liters of flammable liquid, for a total of approximately 4.5 liters. According to the indictment, they also obtained gloves, a face mask, and a means of ignition.
From there, the two continued on the scooter from Bnei Brak toward Givatayim. They wore black hoodies and carried the three bottles of flammable liquid in a bag hanging from the scooter's handlebars. At around 4:17 a.m., they arrived near the restaurant.
According to the indictment, at that point, the two pulled their hoods over their heads. Yaakov put on gloves and a face mask in an attempt to conceal his identity and make identification more difficult. Bayach remained near the restaurant and waited on the scooter, while Yaakov approached the restaurant alone, carrying the bag and the means of ignition.
Employee was inside Japanika when it was set on fire
The restaurant was lit at the time, and an employee was inside. Yaakov, according to the indictment, began emptying the three bottles of flammable liquid one after another. He poured the liquid over the doors and windows facing the street, along the entranceway, onto planters and vegetation, and across the area in front of the restaurant.
Immediately afterward, the indictment alleges, Yaakov ignited the flammable liquid. Within moments, a fire broke out and spread to the vegetation, a table, a shade structure, the doors, windows, and restaurant entrance. Yaakov ran back toward Bayach, got onto the scooter, and the two fled the scene together. No one was injured in the incident, but the restaurant sustained damage estimated at approximately NIS 13,500. The two are charged with aggravated arson.
However, the section detailing how investigators allegedly linked the two young men to the arson appears in the prosecution's request to keep them in custody until the end of legal proceedings. Prosecutors say they have a series of pieces of evidence beginning with the pair's departure from Rehovot and continuing through their escape from the scene of the fire.
According to the prosecution, security cameras documented Yaakov and Bayach leaving Rehovot, arriving in Bnei Brak, traveling toward the restaurant, the arson itself, and then their escape route back to Bnei Brak.
The evidence also includes testimony from the drivers who transported the two from Rehovot to Bnei Brak and back. One of the drivers also provided investigators with photographs, and his testimony indicated that during the trip, the two defendants connected their mobile phones to the vehicle's music system.
Yaakov's phone also provided investigators with a series of findings, according to the prosecution. A forensic extraction of the device uncovered communications between him and Bayach before the incident, taxi bookings made before and after the arson, and the phone's location at the time of the incident, which prosecutors say corresponded with security camera footage. Investigators also found searches and navigation requests for an address in Bnei Brak and for the Japanika restaurant.
According to the detention request, analysis of Yaakov's communications showed that he was the one who booked the drivers who transported the two and that his phone's location data corresponded with the route documented on camera. Prosecutors further allege that when he arrived in Bnei Brak, he activated an "operational" SIM card in his phone.
Suspected arsonists used ChatGPT to inquire about punishment
An additional detail found on Bayach's phone became a central part of the evidence presented by the prosecution. According to the detention request, before the arson, he corresponded with ChatGPT and asked questions concerning the burning of a business and the potential punishment.
Among other things, according to the prosecution, Bayach asked: "What is the punishment for burning down a store," "What does extended prison sentences mean," and "What does the severity of the case mean." He later also asked: "If the place was closed, there was no one around."
After the arson, according to findings from the extraction of his phone, Bayach followed reports about the incident. Prosecutors say he viewed articles published about the restaurant fire and documented them.
A moment from the interrogation room has also now taken on additional significance for the prosecution. Yaakov generally denied the allegations against him and exercised his right to remain silent. However, during a break in one of his interrogations, while Bayach had still not been arrested and before investigators had confronted Yaakov with the evidence, he asked an investigator: "If you know everything, why isn't there another person under arrest with me?"
Prosecutors present the statement as part of the overall body of evidence against the two. Bayach also exercised his right to remain silent during questioning.
The evidence also includes Fire and Rescue Services documents detailing the means used to extinguish the fire and the damage caused to the restaurant, as well as photographs of the scene taken by forensic investigators.
Bayach flees arrest, charged with impersonation
Almost a month after the arson, on August 5, police arrived in Rehovot to arrest Bayach. However, according to the second charge against him, the arrest turned into a foot chase. Police encountered Bayach near 49 Yaakov Tuchman Street, identified themselves as officers, and asked for his name. Prosecutors allege that Bayach falsely told them his name was "Yuval Bitau." When the officers tried to establish his identity, he began running and fled from them.
Bayach ran through Yaakov Tuchman and Struma streets and between buildings as officers chased him and called on him to stop. According to the indictment, he ignored their calls and continued fleeing until police caught up with him and arrested him at the entrance to a building at 155 Yaakov Tuchman Street. As a result of that incident, Bayach is charged, in addition to arson, with impersonating another person and obstructing a police officer in the performance of his duties.
The prosecution is now asking the court to keep Yaakov and Bayach behind bars until the conclusion of legal proceedings against them. The detention request describes the alleged act as a "serious and premeditated violent offense" carried out jointly and argues that arson poses a grave danger to the public, because "it begins with a match, and who knows where it will end."
Prosecutors particularly emphasized that the restaurant was not empty when it was set on fire. "The respondents came specifically in the dead of night to Givatayim, equipped with approximately 4.5 liters of flammable liquid and dressed in clothing intended to conceal their identities. They set fire to a lit restaurant, where an employee was present at the time."
